The Blog TimerWebFull, no signupNoneNo-install browser use

Browser vs App: Which Is Better?

The honest trade-off: a browser-based Pomodoro timer wins on speed-to-start, has no install or signup, and works on any device with a browser. A native app wins on background reliability, lock-screen integration, and rich statistics. For occasional or experimental use, the browser is better. For daily, multi-week practice, a native app justifies its install. We discuss this in detail at Google timer vs online timer.

Does The Blog Timer Compete?

Yes — for browser users. Our Pomodoro timer is free, ad-light, science-cited, has no signup, and uses timestamp-anchored timing that survives tab switches. We do not try to replace task-management apps, sync platforms, or gamification systems — for that, install a native app from the list above. We provide what the Google Search timer doesn't: persistence, accurate background timing, multiple intervals, and dedicated Pomodoro mode.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best free Pomodoro app?

Pomofocus.io and Forest are the most-used free options. For browser-only use, our Pomodoro timer needs no signup.

Which Pomodoro app has the best statistics?

Toggl Track and TickTick offer the most detailed analytics. Focus Keeper Pro has clean visualizations within the Apple ecosystem.

Is there a Pomodoro app for Mac?

Be Focused is native to Mac. Focus Keeper has a Mac app. Browser timers work universally.

What is the difference between Pomodoro and Flowtime?

Pomodoro uses fixed 25-minute intervals; Flowtime uses variable intervals based on actual focus. See our Pomodoro vs Flowtime comparison.

Does Apple Watch have a built-in Pomodoro?

No, but watchOS 10 supports multiple named timers, which approximates Pomodoro. Several third-party Watch apps add proper Pomodoro mode.

Are Pomodoro apps better than a kitchen timer?

Apps offer statistics and integrations; a physical kitchen timer removes the screen entirely. Many heavy Pomodoro users keep both.

guides.title: Best Meditation Timer Apps (Insight Timer, Calm, Headspace, Oak)
guides.excerpt: The best meditation timer apps in 2026 — Insight Timer, Calm, Headspace, Oak, Smiling Mind, Plum Village.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, Productivity Researcher · Updated 2026-05-27

The best meditation timer apps are Insight Timer (largest free library), Calm (premium guided), Headspace (structured courses), Oak (minimalist breath timer), and Smiling Mind (free, education-focused). Choose based on whether you want a simple timer with interval bells, guided sessions, or a full meditation curriculum. For a no-install browser bell, our online timers include meditation modes with interval chimes.

1. Insight Timer

Insight Timer is the largest meditation app by free content, with over 230,000 free guided meditations from teachers around the world. The timer feature itself is excellent: customizable interval bells, ambient sound options, and detailed session statistics. Free tier covers the timer and most guided content; the $5/month Member Plus tier adds courses and offline downloads. Best for self-directed meditators who want a vast free library.

2. Calm

Calm emphasizes production value over selection — fewer meditations but higher polish. Sleep Stories (audio bedtime stories) are a signature feature. Free tier offers a daily meditation; the $70/year Premium unlocks the full library. Best for users who want a comprehensive sleep + meditation app rather than a pure timer.

3. Headspace

Headspace structures meditation as a course curriculum, starting with basics and progressing to specialized topics (anxiety, sleep, focus). Andy Puddicombe's voice and the consistent course structure make it the easiest entry point for beginners. $70/year. Best for people new to meditation who want guided progression.

4. Oak

A minimalist free app focused on breath and meditation timers with a tiny library of guided practices. The breath timer (box breathing, 4-7-8) is particularly well-designed. No subscription. Best for users who want a simple, no-pressure timer without a content library.

5. Smiling Mind

Australian non-profit offering an entirely free meditation app, with programs designed for adults, students, athletes, and educators. Heavy emphasis on mindfulness curriculum for schools. No paid tier. Best for users who prefer non-profit/educational positioning.

6. Plum Village

The official app of Thich Nhat Hanh's meditation community, free, with bells and guided practices from the Plum Village tradition. The mindfulness bell timer is excellent — set random intervals for "moments of awareness" throughout the day. Best for users drawn to Buddhist/Zen traditions.

7. Waking Up

Sam Harris's app, emphasizing the philosophy and theory of meditation alongside guided practice. Substantial intellectual content (essays, conversations with neuroscientists) sets it apart. $100/year. Best for users who want depth beyond the app's timer.

Comparison Table

HeadspaceSample$70/yr~1,000 curatedBeginners, courses
OakFullFreeSmallMinimal timer
Smiling MindFullFree~500Schools, athletes
Plum VillageFullFree~300Buddhist tradition
Waking UpSample$100/yrSmaller, curatedPhilosophy

What Features Matter in a Meditation Timer?

  • Interval bells. Soft chimes at fixed or random intervals during a session, marking time and helping the mind return to focus.
  • Custom session length. Anywhere from 1 minute to 2+ hours.
  • Ambient sounds. Optional rain, wind, white noise during the session.
  • Opening/closing bells. Mark the start and end so the practitioner does not need to glance at a phone.
  • Statistics. Streak tracking, total minutes meditated, average session length — useful for habit formation.

Do You Need an App at All?

No. A kitchen timer with a soft bell works. A wristwatch alarm works. Our 10-minute timer works in any browser tab. The apps add curated content (guided sessions), social features (group meditations), and progress tracking, but if you have a personal practice you already know, a simple bell is enough. See our guides on meditation timers for beginners and binaural beats timers for practice-specific setups.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best free meditation timer app?

Insight Timer for variety, Oak for minimalism, Smiling Mind for structured free curriculum.

Which meditation app is best for sleep?

Calm leads on sleep content with its Sleep Stories. Headspace and Insight Timer also have strong sleep libraries.

How long should I meditate per session?

5-10 minutes for beginners; 20-45 minutes for experienced practitioners. See how long to meditate.

Do meditation apps work?

Research on mindfulness apps (Headspace and Calm have been studied) shows modest reductions in stress and improvements in well-being over several weeks of consistent use.

Can I just use a kitchen timer?

Yes — meditation does not require special equipment. A soft-sounding timer is enough.

What is binaural beats meditation?

A technique using slightly different frequencies in each ear to induce specific brainwave states. See our binaural beats timer guide.

guides.title: Best HIIT Timer Apps in 2026 (Tabata Pro, Seconds, Smart Watches)
guides.excerpt: The best HIIT and Tabata interval timer apps — Tabata Pro, Seconds, Garmin, Polar, smart watches.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, Productivity Researcher · Updated 2026-05-27

The best HIIT timer apps in 2026 are Tabata Pro (iOS, classic Tabata), Seconds Interval Timer (iOS/Android, highly customizable), Interval Timer by Deltaworks (Android-leading), Smart Watch built-in timers (Apple Watch, Garmin, Polar), and Workout Timer by Runtastic. The right choice depends on whether you do strict Tabata, mixed circuit work, or sport-specific intervals. For browser users, see our Tabata timer and HIIT interval timers guide.

What Should a HIIT Timer Do?

A HIIT timer needs to alternate clearly between work and rest intervals with audio cues loud enough to hear over music and breathing. It should support custom work/rest ratios (the classic Tabata is 20 seconds work / 10 seconds rest for 8 rounds; other formats vary widely), multiple sets with longer breaks between them, and ideally voice cues that count down the final 3 seconds of each interval. Visual prominence matters less than audio — your eyes are on the workout, not the phone.

1. Tabata Pro

The original iOS Tabata app. Simple, dedicated to the 20/10 protocol with options for custom intervals. Bright color changes (green for work, red for rest) make state obvious even from a sweaty glance. $2.99 one-time. Best for users who want a focused tool without subscription pressure.

2. Seconds Interval Timer

The power-user choice. Build complex multi-stage workouts: warm-up + 5 rounds of Tabata + cool-down, each stage with its own audio. Saves and shares timer programs. Available on iOS and Android. Free with paid pro features (~$5). Best for trainers and serious HIIT practitioners.

3. Interval Timer by Deltaworks

The leading Android free HIIT timer. Customizable intervals, voice prompts, multiple sets. No subscription. Best for Android users who want a polished free option.

4. Apple Watch Built-in Timer

watchOS 10 supports multiple named timers, which can be configured for HIIT but requires manual restart between intervals. For true HIIT on Apple Watch, the third-party app HIIT & Tabata Timer or Seconds is better. Best for wrist-only workouts where pulling out a phone is impractical.

5. Garmin / Polar / Wahoo

Dedicated fitness watches from Garmin, Polar, and Wahoo include interval workouts in their native fitness profiles. The Garmin Forerunner and Polar Vantage lines support custom workout creation with intervals down to the second. Best for runners and cyclists who want intervals tied to heart rate or pace data.

6. Workout Timer by Runtastic (Adidas Training)

The Adidas-owned Runtastic family includes a workout timer with preset HIIT and Tabata protocols. Integrates with the broader Adidas Training app for guided workouts.

Comparison Table

AppPlatformsCustom IntervalsVoice CuesPrice
Tabata ProiOSYesYes$2.99
Seconds Interval TimeriOS, AndroidHighlyYesFree / $5 Pro
Interval Timer (Deltaworks)AndroidYesYesFree
HIIT & Tabata TimeriOS, Apple WatchYesYes$3
Garmin ConnectGarmin watchesYesBeep/vibrateFree w/ device
Polar BeatPolar watchesYesYesFree w/ device
Adidas TrainingiOS, AndroidPreset focusYesFree / Premium
The Blog TimerWebYesAudioFree

What HIIT Protocols Do These Apps Support?

  • Tabata. 20 sec work / 10 sec rest, 8 rounds = 4 minutes total.
  • EMOM (Every Minute On the Minute). Begin a movement at the top of each minute; rest the remainder.
  • AMRAP (As Many Reps As Possible). A single long timer, work continuously.
  • 30/30 or 40/20. Longer work, shorter rest — beginner-friendlier than Tabata.
  • Pyramid intervals. Ladders like 30/30, 60/30, 90/30, 60/30, 30/30.

For details on each, see our guides on the AMRAP timer, EMOM timer, and Tabata variations.

Browser Timer for HIIT?

Yes, browser timers work for HIIT if loud-enough audio reaches you across the workout space. Our Tabata timer is purpose-built for the 20/10 protocol; we also publish guides on circuit training and boxing-style rounds. The trade-off: phone or laptop must stay awake and audible; native apps integrate with watches and headphones more cleanly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best free HIIT timer?

Seconds Interval Timer (free tier) on iOS and Android. Interval Timer by Deltaworks for Android-only.

Can my Apple Watch do HIIT timing?

Yes via third-party apps like HIIT & Tabata Timer. The native Workout app supports custom intervals in newer watchOS versions.

What is the standard Tabata interval?

20 seconds work, 10 seconds rest, 8 rounds = 4 minutes total. See our Tabata guide.

Do I need voice cues during HIIT?

Yes — visual cues are easy to miss when you are looking down or sweating. Voice cues that count down "3, 2, 1" before transitions are particularly valuable.

Can I create custom HIIT workouts in these apps?

Seconds and Smart Watch native apps support fully custom multi-stage workouts. Tabata Pro is more constrained.

Is HIIT effective for fat loss?

Research summarized in PubMed-indexed reviews shows HIIT is at least as effective as moderate continuous cardio for fat loss in less time, though individual response varies.

guides.title: Best Online Timers in 2026 (vClock, e.gg, Google, The Blog Timer)
guides.excerpt: Six online timers re-tested and compared: vClock, Online-Stopwatch, e.gg Timer, Big Timer, Google's widget, and The Blog Timer. Every link verified live.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, productivity researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-07-31.

The best online timers right now are vClock, Online-Stopwatch, e.gg Timer, Big Timer, the Google Search widget, and The Blog Timer. I re-opened every one of them for this update and ran the same checks: how fast it starts, what the alert sounds like, and what happens when the tab goes into the background. One tool from the previous version of this roundup, Timer.io, is now a parked domain, so it has been removed and replaced.

What makes a good online timer?

Five things, in order: instant start with no signup, timing that survives tab switching (timestamp-anchored rather than tick-counted), an alert that actually fires from a background tab, a display readable from across a room, and no hostile tracking. Most online timers fail at least one. The second criterion trips up more tools than any other, and it has a documented technical cause we cover below.

1. vClock

vClock bundles a countdown timer, alarm clock, stopwatch, and world clock into one clean site. The timer page has preset links from 1 minute up to 8 hours, a choice of alert sounds with a test button so you can hear the volume before committing, and a full-screen mode. You can bookmark a configured timer because the settings live in the URL. It is ad-supported, and like most timer sites its countdown is happiest in a foreground tab. Best for people who want one tab that does timer, alarm, and stopwatch duty.

2. Online-Stopwatch

Online-Stopwatch is one of the oldest timer sites on the web and it leans into personality: classroom countdowns, race-track timers, sensory timers without numbers, exam clocks, plus random name pickers and group generators for teachers. The advertising is heavy, with a paid "Go Ad Free" tier to remove it. That trade is worth it in a classroom, where the themed visuals genuinely hold kids' attention, and less worth it on your work laptop. Best for teachers and parents.

3. e.gg Timer

e.gg Timer has the best party trick in the category: the URL is the interface. Type e.ggtimer.com/10minutes into the address bar and the countdown is already running when the page appears; I tested e.ggtimer.com/5minutes while writing this update and it loaded straight into the count. That makes any duration bookmarkable. The rest of the tool is deliberately bare: minimal display, basic sound, nothing to configure. Best for keyboard-first minimalists.

4. Big Timer

Big Timer does one thing: an enormous full-screen countdown you can read from the back of a room. It replaces Timer.io in this roundup, which now sits on a parked domain. Big Timer is the tool I reach for when projecting a countdown in a workshop or timing conference talks, because the digits fill the screen and nobody has to squint. Best for presentations, workshops, and anywhere the timer is for an audience rather than for you.

5. Google Search timer

Typing "5 minute timer" into Google spawns a timer widget right in the results page. It is the fastest possible start and completely ad-free, but it lives and dies with that search tab: refresh and it is gone, and background-tab alerting is unreliable. We compare it against dedicated tools in depth at Google timer vs online timer.

6. The Blog Timer

Our own timers compete here, judged by the same five criteria. Every duration has a dedicated URL that loads directly into a ready countdown, like the 5-minute and 25-minute pages, with no signup and light advertising. The countdown is anchored to timestamps, so when a backgrounded tab comes back into view the remaining time is recomputed from the clock rather than from however many ticks the browser deigned to deliver. The full explanation lives in our timer accuracy guide.

Comparison table

ServiceSignupAdsSoundsDistinct strengthBest for
vClockNoYesMultiple, with test buttonTimer + alarm + stopwatchMulti-tool users
Online-StopwatchNoHeavy (paid removal)ThemedClassroom visualsTeachers
e.gg TimerNoLightBasicURL-as-interfaceMinimalists
Big TimerNoLightBasicRoom-scale digitsPresentations
Google SearchNoNoneSingleZero-friction startQuick one-offs
The Blog TimerNoLightMultipleTimestamp-anchored accuracyReliable countdowns

Why timers misbehave in background tabs

This is not superstition; browsers document it. Per MDN's setTimeout reference, Firefox clamps timers in inactive tabs to at most once per second, and Chrome goes further: after a page has been hidden for five minutes, its timers can be batched and checked only once per minute. A timer built on naive setInterval() counting therefore falls behind the moment you switch tabs. Implementations that anchor to real timestamps and recompute on tab focus stay correct no matter how hard the browser throttles. The gory details are in browser timer drift, and the mobile-specific failure modes in background timers on mobile.

Browser timer or native app?

The honest trade-off has not changed. A native phone timer wins on lock-screen alerts and OS integration. A browser timer wins on instant access from any machine, zero installation, and living in the same workspace as your work. If your day already happens in a laptop browser, a pinned timer tab is usually the more practical tool; if the alert must wake you from across the house, use the phone.

guides.title: Google Timer vs Online Timer (When to Use Each)
guides.excerpt: Compare Google's built-in timer to dedicated online timers — accuracy, features, when each is the better choice.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, Productivity Researcher · Updated 2026-05-27

Google's built-in timer works for quick one-off countdowns but lacks persistence and reliable background alerts. A dedicated online timer like The Blog Timer offers accurate timestamp-anchored timing, multiple concurrent timers, no tab-refresh data loss, and dedicated URLs per duration. For 30-second kitchen timers the Google widget is fine; for Pomodoro, HIIT, or any work that requires reliability, a dedicated timer is materially better.

How Does Google's Built-in Timer Work?

Typing a phrase like "5 minute timer" or "timer for 25 minutes" into Google.com triggers an interactive countdown widget that appears above the search results. Click Start and the timer counts down in the browser. When it reaches zero, the page plays an alert sound. The widget also supports stopwatch mode and accepts natural variations ("set a 1 hour timer," "10 minute countdown").

The widget runs entirely client-side once loaded — no continuous network calls — but it inherits all the limitations of browser-tab JavaScript: it can pause if the tab is backgrounded, and a tab refresh wipes the timer state entirely.

What Are Google's Timer Strengths?

  • Zero install, zero signup. Type the phrase, see the timer.
  • Universal. Works on any device with a browser.
  • Trustworthy brand. No third-party site to vet.
  • Voice integration. "Hey Google, set a timer" works on Assistant-enabled devices.

What Are Google's Timer Weaknesses?

  • Single timer. One countdown at a time per tab — multiple require multiple tabs.
  • Tab-refresh loses state. Accidentally close the tab and the timer is gone.
  • Background drift. Browser throttling in background tabs can cause audio alerts to fire late or be silenced.
  • Single sound. No customization.
  • No persistence. No history, no statistics, no relation to tasks.
  • No dedicated URLs. You cannot bookmark a "25-minute timer" page.

How Do Dedicated Online Timers Compare?

A dedicated timer like The Blog Timer addresses each of Google's weaknesses:

FeatureGoogle Search TimerThe Blog Timer
Setup time~3 seconds (type + click)~3 seconds (click bookmark)
Multiple timersMultiple tabs neededYes, in one tab
Background reliabilityOften driftsTimestamp-anchored, accurate
Custom soundsNoYes
Dedicated URLsNoYes (/5-minute-timer, etc.)
Pomodoro modeNoYes (link)
HIIT/TabataNoYes (link)
Mobile lock-screen alertNoWith service worker
Full-screen modeNoYes
CostFreeFree

When Is the Google Timer Better?

For three specific cases:

  1. One-off quick countdowns. "I need to remember to take cookies out in 8 minutes" — Google widget is faster than navigating to a dedicated timer site.
  2. You're already mid-search. The widget appears in the search results you're already looking at.
  3. You distrust third-party sites. Google is a known quantity.

When Is a Dedicated Timer Better?

For these cases:

  1. Pomodoro and productivity intervals. Auto-cycling work/break, session counting.
  2. HIIT and interval workouts. Multiple rounds, work/rest pairs.
  3. Recurring durations. Bookmark /25-minute-timer for daily use.
  4. Multiple concurrent timers. Pasta + bread + tea — Google needs three tabs; we run them in one.
  5. Reliable background alerts. When you switch to another tab to work, the timer must still fire.
  6. Reading the timer across a room. Large full-screen display.

What About Voice Timers (Hey Google, Alexa, Siri)?

If you have a voice-enabled device, that route is faster than either browser approach for a single quick timer. See our dedicated guides on Hey Google timers, Alexa timers, and iPhone (Siri). Voice timers also fire OS-level alerts that browser timers cannot match.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Google timer accurate?

Foreground accuracy is good; background-tab accuracy depends on browser throttling and can drift. See browser timer drift.

Does the Google timer work if my browser is closed?

No — closing the tab or browser kills the timer.

Can I run multiple Google timers?

Only by opening multiple tabs with separate searches.

Is The Blog Timer free?

Yes, free with minimal advertising and no signup.

What is the difference between Google's timer and a Nest Hub timer?

The Nest Hub timer is a hardware timer that runs locally on the device and alerts via speaker — much more reliable than the browser widget.

Which timer should I use for Pomodoro?

Use a dedicated Pomodoro timer like ours or a native app. Google's widget is single-cycle only.

guides.title: Best Free Pomodoro Timers (No Signup, No Paywall)
guides.excerpt: Hands-on comparison of 6 genuinely free Pomodoro timers: Pomofocus, Marinara, Focus Keeper, Forest, TickTick. Every link tested, every paywall mapped.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, productivity researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-07-31.

Six Pomodoro timers made this list, and every one runs a complete 25/5 cycle without asking for a card number: Pomofocus, Marinara Timer, Focus Keeper, Forest, TickTick, and our own browser timer. For this update I re-opened each one, clicked through the settings screens, and mapped exactly what sits behind each paywall. The short version: browser timers tend to stay free forever, while mobile apps have drifted toward subscriptions.

What counts as a free Pomodoro timer?

Three different things get sold under the word "free," and it pays to know which one you are looking at. Free forever means the timer costs nothing and the core features never expire. Free tier means the basic 25/5 cycle works but statistics, themes, or sync sit behind a subscription. Free with ads means full functionality paid for with your attention. Each review below says which definition applies, because the difference decides whether the app still works for you six months from now.

1. Pomofocus (best in a browser)

Pomofocus.io opens straight into a 25-minute session with no signup screen in the way. You can add tasks and estimate how many pomodoros each will take, which turns the timer into a light planning tool, and the app builds daily, weekly, and monthly focus reports from your sessions. Focus and break lengths, alarm sounds, and background sounds are all adjustable. There are free desktop builds for Mac, Windows, and Linux; Pomofocus itself warns that the Windows build is unsigned, so expect a SmartScreen prompt on first launch. The honest catch: syncing across devices requires an account, and the deeper report history is part of the premium tier. For a single browser on a single machine, the free version is the whole product.

2. Marinara Timer (best for teams, fully free)

Marinara Timer is a long-running free tool from the digital agency 352 Inc. It gives you three timers on one page: the classic Pomodoro sequence, a fully custom interval editor, and a plain kitchen timer. Its quiet superpower is that every timer gets its own shareable URL, so a remote team can literally watch the same countdown together during a group sprint. No signup, no payment tier at all. The trade-off is that the interface has not changed in years and there are no statistics or history of any kind. If you want a scoreboard, look elsewhere; if you want a timer that respects you, this is it.

3. Focus Keeper (best free iPhone and Apple Watch option)

Focus Keeper is a free download for iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch (watchOS 8 or later) with the standard 25-minute sessions, 5-minute short breaks, and a 20 to 30 minute long break after four rounds. The design is genuinely pleasant and the free tier covers the full cycle. One thing changed since our original review and it deserves saying plainly: the Pro unlock used to be a small one-time purchase, and it is now a subscription running from $3.99 a month up to a $199.99 lifetime option. Treat the free tier as the product, and it remains one of the best Pomodoro apps on iOS.

4. Forest (best if you need the game)

Forest plants a virtual tree when you start a focus session; leave the app and the tree dies. The free tier includes the core timer, the Deep Focus app-blocking mode, and group focus sessions, with browser extensions for Chrome and Firefox. Forest has also funded more than 2 million real trees through its partnership with the nonprofit Trees for the Future, which the paid version supports. Cons: the full catalog of tree species is paid, and if gamification does not motivate you, the whole premise is decoration. For people who feel a small sting when the tree withers, it works better than any statistics page.

5. TickTick (best free timer inside a to-do app)

TickTick ships a Pomodoro timer inside its free task manager, so sessions attach directly to the task you are working on. Basic focus records are included, and sync across devices comes with the free account. The cons flow from its nature: TickTick is a to-do app first, so the timer lives a few taps deep, and the richer focus statistics belong to Premium. Pick it when you want one app for both the list and the clock.

6. The Blog Timer (free, no signup, browser)

Our own Pomodoro timer belongs in the comparison, judged by the same rules. It is free with no account, and the countdown is anchored to timestamps rather than tick counting, so a backgrounded tab does not silently fall behind (the technical detail is in our timer accuracy guide). It keeps no statistics by design. If you want streaks, reports, or cross-device sync, one of the apps above will serve you better; if you want a 25-minute countdown that starts in two clicks, start here.

Free tier comparison

AppPlatformFree timerFree statsFree syncWatch out for
PomofocusBrowser, desktop appsYesRecent reportsAccount neededReport history is premium
Marinara TimerBrowserYesNoneShared URL insteadDated interface
Focus KeeperiPhone, iPad, WatchYesBasicProPro moved to subscription
ForestiOS, Android, extensionsYesYesAccountTree species are paid
TickTickAll platformsYesBasicYesTimer buried in a task app
The Blog TimerBrowserYesNoneNoneNo stats by design

What the paywalls actually hide

Across all five third-party tools, the same four features keep showing up behind the payment screen: long-term statistics history, cross-device sync, cosmetic themes, and integrations with calendars or task managers. What never sits behind a paywall is the timer itself. That matters, because the actual mechanism of the Pomodoro technique, described by its creator Francesco Cirillo at pomodorotechnique.com, needs nothing more than a countdown and the discipline to respect it. Everything else is bookkeeping.

Which one should you pick?

Quickest start with tasks: Pomofocus. Synchronized team sprints: Marinara Timer. iPhone and Apple Watch: Focus Keeper's free tier. Motivation through consequences: Forest. One app for list and clock: TickTick. A plain, accurate countdown with nothing to configure: our Pomodoro timer. If you are still deciding whether 25/5 is even the right rhythm for you, read our guides to the Pomodoro technique and Pomodoro versus Flowtime before you commit to any app.

guides.title: Pomodoro vs Flowtime (Which Productivity Method Wins?)
guides.excerpt: Pomodoro vs Flowtime — fixed 25-minute intervals versus variable focus-based intervals. When each works best.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, Productivity Researcher · Updated 2026-05-27

Pomodoro uses fixed 25-minute work intervals with 5-minute breaks; Flowtime uses variable work intervals based on how long focus actually lasts, with breaks proportional to work. Pomodoro fits structured tasks and people with low natural focus stamina; Flowtime fits creative or research work where interrupting flow at an arbitrary timer kills the work. Both are timeboxing methods — they differ in whether the box is fixed or elastic.

What Is the Pomodoro Technique?

Invented by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s. Work for 25 minutes, break for 5 minutes, repeat. After four pomodoros, take a 15-30 minute long break. The timer is rigid: when it rings, you stop — even if mid-thought. The technique externalizes self-discipline through the ticking timer. See our deep guide on the Pomodoro technique.

What Is Flowtime?

Created by software engineer Zoe Read-Bivens as a critique of strict Pomodoro for creative work. The protocol:

  1. Choose a task.
  2. Record the start time.
  3. Work until your focus naturally breaks (you check email, notice fatigue, hit a stopping point).
  4. Record the end time. Compute work duration.
  5. Take a break proportional to the work block — about 1/5 the work time (or use a sliding scale based on the duration).
  6. After the break, decide whether to continue the same task or pick up another.

The defining feature: no fixed work interval. Some Flowtime sessions are 12 minutes; others are 90. The timer measures, it doesn't impose.

How Do You Set Flowtime Break Lengths?

Read-Bivens published a recommended sliding scale:

Work BlockSuggested Break
Less than 25 min5 min
25-50 min8-10 min
50-90 min10-15 min
90+ min15-25 min

The principle: longer focus accumulates more fatigue and requires more recovery. The exact numbers are heuristics; the deeper goal is to respect what the work actually demands.

Pomodoro vs Flowtime: Side-by-Side

DimensionPomodoroFlowtime
Work intervalFixed 25 minVariable, until focus breaks
Break lengthFixed 5 min (15-30 every 4th)Proportional to work
Timer roleImpose structureMeasure structure
Interruption ruleVoid the pomodoroNote and continue
Best forFragmented tasks, ADHD, beginnersCreative work, research, writing
Worst forDeep creative flowLow natural focus stamina
EstimationCounts of pomodorosHours/minutes recorded
Anti-procrastinationStrong (25-min commit)Weaker (no upper bound)

Which Should You Choose?

Use Pomodoro when:

  • You struggle to start tasks (the small upfront commitment helps).
  • You have ADHD or short natural focus spans.
  • Your work fragments easily — email, shallow tasks, meetings.
  • You need to estimate task durations.
  • You are new to timeboxing.

Use Flowtime when:

  • Your work is creative — writing, design, music composition, research.
  • Interrupting at 25 minutes feels destructive.
  • You have strong focus stamina and need a system that respects it.
  • You want to measure focus duration as a data point (focus is the metric, not duration).

Can You Combine Them?

Yes. The most common hybrid: use Pomodoro to start (the 25-minute commitment defeats resistance) and switch to Flowtime once flow arrives (let the timer ring and continue working). Many writers and engineers use exactly this. Cirillo's original technique technically forbids continuing past the bell, but in practice the hybrid is widespread and works.

Tools for Each Method

  • Pomodoro: any of the apps in our best Pomodoro apps roundup; our Pomodoro timer; a kitchen timer.
  • Flowtime: a stopwatch or any time-tracker (Toggl Track, Clockify) used in the opposite direction — start when you begin, stop when focus breaks.

What Does the Research Say?

The empirical case for Pomodoro rests on attention-restoration and ultradian-rhythm research showing that performance on sustained tasks degrades after 20-30 minutes without a break. The empirical case for Flowtime rests on flow research by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, which shows that creative work has its own pacing and benefits from being uninterrupted. Both are partially correct — for different kinds of work.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Flowtime better than Pomodoro?

For creative work and people with strong focus stamina, often yes. For fragmented work, low natural focus, or beginners, Pomodoro is usually better.

How long is a Flowtime work block?

Variable. Typical blocks are 25-90 minutes depending on the work and the practitioner.

Can I do Flowtime in a Pomodoro app?

Yes — use the stopwatch mode rather than the countdown mode. Many Pomodoro apps include both.

What is the 52/17 rule?

A productivity finding from DeskTime data suggesting 52-minute work blocks with 17-minute breaks correlate with highest productivity. See 52/17 vs Pomodoro.

Does Flowtime work for studying?

Mixed — most students benefit from the structure of Pomodoro because study material doesn't generate flow the same way creative work does.

Who invented Flowtime?

Software engineer Zoe Read-Bivens, who published the method publicly in the late 2010s as a critique of strict Pomodoro.

For full citations and methodology, see our sources page.

guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, productivity researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-07-31.

The 52/17 rule runs 52 minutes of work against 17-minute breaks; Pomodoro runs 25 against 5. The short verdict: 52/17 wins for deep individual knowledge work done by people with real focus stamina, while Pomodoro wins for fragmented tasks, procrastination-prone starts, and anyone still building the focus habit. The rest of this page gives you the rules of each, the criteria that actually decide it, and a verdict table by scenario.

The rules of each method

The 52/17 rule

In 2014, time-tracking company DeskTime analyzed its most productive users and found the top 10% worked in cycles of roughly 52 minutes of work followed by 17 minutes of rest. Nobody prescribed that rhythm; it emerged from behavioral data, which is exactly why it caught on. Two details from the analysis matter in practice: the 52 minutes were spent with genuine intensity on one thing, and the 17-minute breaks were fully off-screen — walks and lunches, not email triage in another tab.

Pomodoro (25/5)

Francesco Cirillo developed the Pomodoro Technique in the late 1980s: 25 minutes of work, a 5-minute break, and a longer 15–30 minute break after every fourth cycle. It is more than an interval — the full system covers daily planning, interruption handling, and effort estimation. Our Pomodoro technique guide walks through the complete protocol.

52/17 vs 25/5: head-to-head

Dimension52/17 rulePomodoro 25/5
Work block52 minutes25 minutes
Break17 minutes5 minutes
Work-to-break ratio~3:15:1
OriginDeskTime behavioral data, 2014Cirillo, late 1980s
NatureDescriptive (observed pattern)Prescriptive (designed protocol)
Anti-procrastination powerWeaker (large commitment)Strong (small commitment)
Flow protectionGood — nearly an hour uninterruptedPoor — alarm can land mid-absorption
Break qualityReal recovery: a walk, a mealA stretch and a glass of water

The decision criteria that actually matter

1. Setup cost of your work. If loading context takes ten minutes — a codebase, a legal file, a half-written chapter — a 25-minute block spends 40% of its length just getting back in. That overhead argues for 52/17 or longer.

2. Your real focus stamina. Csikszentmihalyi's research on flow states describes absorption that builds over time; some people sustain it for an hour, others fade at 30 minutes. Match the interval to the stamina you have, not the stamina you want.

3. Procrastination pressure. Starting is a different problem from continuing. A 25-minute commitment gets you started on a dreaded task; a 52-minute commitment is easy to postpone all afternoon.

4. Whether you can actually take the break. A 17-minute break is a genuine walk outside. It is also conspicuous in some offices. If your environment only tolerates 5-minute pauses, Pomodoro fits reality better, whatever the data says.

5. Team rhythm. Pairs and study groups synchronize naturally on 25-minute cycles; 52/17 is an individual's rhythm.

One thing the methods do not disagree on: breaks themselves. Ariga and Lleras (2011) showed that sustained attention degrades over a long unbroken task and that brief breaks prevent the decline. Both methods institutionalize that finding; they differ only in spacing.

Verdict by scenario

ScenarioUse
Deep coding, long-form writing, analysis52/17
Starting a task you have been avoidingPomodoro
ADHD or short natural focus spanPomodoro
Studying several subjects in rotationPomodoro
Email, admin, and planning batchesPomodoro
Maker days with few meetings52/17
Office where long breaks are impracticalPomodoro, or 50/10 as a compromise
Focus span that varies wildly day to dayNeither — try the Flowtime technique

What DeskTime found when it re-ran the numbers

The 52/17 figure is not frozen. When DeskTime repeated the analysis, the most productive users' rhythm had already drifted to about 80 minutes of work per 17 of break by February 2020, and a 2021 re-run during widespread remote work found 112 minutes of work against 26-minute breaks. Read that as a caution: the exact 52 and 17 were a snapshot of one user base at one moment. The durable part of the finding is the shape — long, genuinely focused blocks paired with genuinely disconnected breaks at roughly a 3:1 to 4:1 ratio.

Limits of the evidence

The DeskTime result is a correlation in observational data, not a controlled experiment. Highly productive users may share traits — role, autonomy, motivation — that produce both the rhythm and the output. Pomodoro's evidence is the reverse: decades of practitioner validation with little peer-reviewed testing. No randomized trial has run these two head-to-head. Both reliably beat working with no time structure, and the best method remains the one you will actually sustain.

Run the two-week experiment

  • Week one, Pomodoro: run 25/5 with our Pomodoro timer and log output at the end of each day.
  • Week two, 52/17: pair the 52-minute timer with the 17-minute timer and keep the same log.
  • Judge by output, not by which week felt nicer. Focus methods are habits, and habits lie about their own effectiveness for the first few days.

Once you have picked 52/17, the 52/17 implementation guide covers the day-to-day mechanics: schedule templates, defending the blocks on a calendar, and adapting the ratio. If fixed intervals of any length keep interrupting you mid-thought, the elastic alternative is the Flowtime technique, and for the 90/20 variant grounded in body-clock research see the ultradian rhythm timer guide.

guides.title: Flowtime Technique: Steps, Break Table, and When to Use It
guides.excerpt: The Flowtime technique drops Pomodoro's fixed interval: work until focus naturally breaks, then rest proportionally. Exact steps, break table, and the flow research behind it.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, productivity researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-07-31.

The Flowtime technique replaces Pomodoro's fixed 25-minute box with a simple rule: pick one task, note the time, and work until your focus breaks on its own. Then take a break sized to how long you actually worked. No alarm cuts you off mid-thought. The clock records what happened instead of dictating it, which is why Flowtime fits deep, absorbing work that fixed intervals keep interrupting at the worst possible moment.

Where Flowtime comes from

The method traces to a 2016 Medium essay titled The Flowtime Technique, written by software engineer Zoë Read-Bivens under the byline Urgent Pigeon. Her complaint about Pomodoro was specific: the timer kept ringing while she was mid-thought, and racing it produced an anxiety she called "PomoStress." Her fix kept everything useful about Pomodoro — one task at a time, honest records, real breaks — and removed the one part that fought the work: the fixed interval.

The exact steps

  1. Pick one task. Flowtime keeps Pomodoro's single-task rule. Write the task at the top of a log sheet before you start.
  2. Record your start time. Open a stopwatch and let it run, or simply note the clock time in your log.
  3. Work until your focus naturally breaks. You catch yourself rereading the same sentence, reaching for your phone, or arriving at a clean stopping point. That is the signal to stop — not an alarm.
  4. Record the stop time. Stop minus start is your work length for the session.
  5. Take a proportional break, using the lookup table below. Time the break with a countdown so it actually ends.
  6. Log interruptions. Every time something pulls you off task, add a tally mark. Within a week the log becomes an accurate picture of your real focus span.

The break lookup table

Read-Bivens published rough break guidelines in the original essay, scaled to the work block that preceded them:

Work blockSuggested break
Under 25 minutes5 minutes
25–50 minutes8 minutes
50–90 minutes10 minutes
Over 90 minutes15 minutes or more

The numbers are deliberately loose. Longer focus builds more fatigue and needs more recovery; if you feel wrung out after a 70-minute session, take the 15 rather than the 10. Run the break on a countdown — a 10-minute timer covers the most common case, and a 15-minute timer handles the long sessions — because an untimed break is how a pause becomes an afternoon.

The flow-state research behind it

Flowtime's core bet is that the mental state psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi named "flow" is worth protecting at almost any cost. In Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990), he described full absorption in a task: time distorts, self-consciousness drops, and the work seems to propel itself. Decades of follow-up research, summarized in Nakamura and Csikszentmihalyi's The Concept of Flow, identifies the conditions that produce it: clear goals, immediate feedback, and a challenge matched to your skill. Nothing in those conditions mentions 25 minutes. Absorption arrives on its own schedule, and an arbitrary alarm is precisely the kind of external interruption that collapses it.

Breaks still matter, though, and Flowtime does not abolish them. In a 2011 study in Cognition, Ariga and Lleras showed that performance on a sustained-attention task declines steadily over time but that brief breaks preempt the slide, apparently by reactivating the task goal. Flowtime's answer is to keep the breaks and move them to the natural seams in your attention rather than dropping them on a fixed grid.

Flowtime vs Pomodoro vs 52/17

MethodWork blockBreakThe clock's job
Pomodoro25 min, fixed5 minDictates when you stop
52/1752 min, fixed17 minDictates when you stop
FlowtimeVariableProportionalRecords what you did

Pomodoro is the strongest anti-procrastination tool of the three; committing to 25 minutes is easy. The 52/17 rule keeps fixed intervals but stretches them to fit deeper work. Flowtime is the elastic option. For the head-to-head between the two fixed methods, see the 52/17 vs Pomodoro comparison; for running 52/17 through a real workday, the 52/17 implementation guide has schedule templates; and Pomodoro vs Flowtime covers that pairing in more depth.

How to run Flowtime with a stopwatch

The whole apparatus is a running clock and a log sheet with six columns: task, start, stop, work length, break length, interruptions. Start the stopwatch when you begin, glance at it when your focus breaks, write down the elapsed time, and start a break countdown. That is the entire loop.

Treat the first week as data collection rather than performance. Most people discover a surprisingly consistent natural session length — perhaps 40 minutes in the morning and 25 after lunch — and that number is worth more than any borrowed ratio. If you tend to drift without any external structure, run a silent 25-minute timer alongside the stopwatch and treat its alarm as a question ("still focused?") rather than an order to stop. Keep working if the answer is yes.

When Flowtime beats fixed intervals, and when it doesn't

Choose Flowtime when the work has a high setup cost — code, proofs, long-form writing, anything where reloading context eats ten minutes — and when your focus span varies too much for one interval to fit. It also suits people who find alarms genuinely jarring; some of us lose more to the interruption than we gain from the rest.

Skip it when you are procrastinating. An open-ended commitment is easy to never start, and Pomodoro's small fixed box is the better lever on those days. Fragmented admin work, study rotations across subjects, and team-synchronized cycles also favor fixed intervals. The honest summary: Flowtime is as much a measurement instrument as a work method. After two weeks of logs you will know your real focus span, and you can stay elastic or switch to fixed intervals sized to what the log actually shows.

guides.title: How to Use the 52/17 Method: Setup, Daily Schedule, and Adjustments
guides.excerpt: How to actually run the 52/17 method: the two-timer setup, a full-day schedule template, what to do in the 17-minute break, and when to adapt the ratio.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, productivity researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-07-31.

To run the 52/17 method, set a 52-minute timer, work one task until it rings, then set a 17-minute timer and leave your desk. Repeat three times before lunch and three after. That is the entire mechanism. This guide covers what the one-line version leaves out: the two-timer setup, a full-day schedule template, what to actually do with the 17 minutes, and how to adapt the ratio when 52/17 stops fitting. If you are still deciding between this method and Pomodoro, start with the 52/17 vs Pomodoro comparison — this page assumes you have picked 52/17 and want it to survive contact with a real workday.

The two-timer setup

Open the 52-minute timer in one tab and the 17-minute timer in another. Start the 52 when you begin working; when it rings, stop — even mid-sentence — and start the 17. The hard stop is the discipline. The rhythm itself comes from DeskTime's 2014 analysis of its most productive users, who worked in almost exactly this pattern without being told to, and the method only reproduces their results if you copy both halves: intense single-task work and a fully disconnected break.

Write down the one task the block is for before you start the timer. A 52-minute block with no named task degrades into 52 minutes of triage.

A full-day 52/17 schedule template

Six work blocks fit a standard 9-to-5 with an hour for lunch. That is 5 hours and 12 minutes of timed, single-task focus — more genuine deep work than most unstructured days contain.

TimeBlock
9:00 – 9:52Work block 1
9:52 – 10:09Break (17 min)
10:09 – 11:01Work block 2
11:01 – 11:18Break (17 min)
11:18 – 12:10Work block 3
12:10 – 1:10Lunch
1:10 – 2:02Work block 4
2:02 – 2:19Break (17 min)
2:19 – 3:11Work block 5
3:11 – 3:28Break (17 min)
3:28 – 4:20Work block 6
4:20 – 5:00Break, then plan tomorrow's blocks

On half days or heavy-meeting days, run the morning half only: three blocks between 9:00 and 12:10. Trying to wedge 52-minute blocks between back-to-back meetings produces orphaned 20-minute fragments; on those days, switch to Pomodoro 25/5 and return to 52/17 when the calendar clears.

What to do with the 17 minutes

The break is not the reward for the method; it is the method. DeskTime's data showed top performers spending breaks completely away from the screen. The research points the same direction: a 2022 meta-analysis in PLOS ONE found micro-breaks reliably raise vigor and cut fatigue, but recovering performance after cognitively demanding work tends to require breaks longer than 10 minutes. Seventeen minutes clears that bar — if you actually use it. Good options: a walk outside, stretching, preparing food, a household task, or sitting somewhere quiet doing nothing. Bad options: email, Slack, and feeds, which keep the same attention systems engaged and return you to block four no fresher than you left block three. Even the fact that a pause helps at all is well established — Ariga and Lleras showed brief breaks prevent the steady decline in sustained attention — but the break only counts if it is a real disengagement.

Defending the blocks on a calendar

Book your work blocks as private appointments so meeting invitations flow around them instead of through them. Set status to do-not-disturb while the 52-minute timer runs, and keep a scrap of paper for intrusions: when a thought or request lands mid-block, write it down and stay on task. If an interruption truly breaks a block — a call you must take — do not resume a 20-minute remainder as if nothing happened. Either restart a fresh 52 or salvage the rest of the hour with a single 25-minute Pomodoro and rejoin the schedule at the next block boundary.

Adapting the ratio

The 52 and 17 are defaults, not laws. DeskTime's own follow-ups make the point: by February 2020 its most productive users had drifted to roughly 80 minutes of work per 17-minute break, and the 2021 remote-work re-analysis found 112/26. Your numbers will drift too. Tune by signal:

SignalAdjustment
The alarm keeps landing mid-flow and you resent itLengthen the block: try 60/15, then 80/17
You fade well before the 52-minute markShorten: 45/15, or drop to Pomodoro 25/5 for a while
Breaks keep stretching past 17 minutesTime every break with the countdown, and put a start time on the next block
Focus span swings wildly between daysConsider the Flowtime technique, which sizes blocks to the day you are actually having

Change one number at a time and hold it for a week before judging. For more break-length options and what each duration is good for, see the break timers guide.

Common failure modes

Skipping the 17. The commonest failure. Momentum feels too good to interrupt, three skipped breaks later the afternoon is sludge, and the method gets blamed. The break is load-bearing; take it.

Screen-based breaks. Seventeen minutes of feeds is a posture change, not recovery.

Unnamed blocks. Starting the timer without deciding the task turns focused blocks into reactive ones.

Forcing bad days. Meeting-shredded calendars, sick days, and deadline sprints all break the grid. Fall back to shorter cycles or the elastic Flowtime approach, and restart 52/17 the next clean morning. A method you can leave and rejoin is one you will still be using in six months.

guides.title: How Long to Boil Corn on the Cob (Fresh, Frozen & Microwave)
guides.excerpt: Boil fresh corn on the cob 3-5 minutes and frozen ears 8-10 minutes. Modern sweet corn is tender-crisp in 30 seconds to 3 minutes; here are the exact times by ear size with a step-by-step method.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

The short answer: 3-5 minutes for fresh corn, 8-10 for frozen

Boil fresh corn on the cob for 3 to 5 minutes — modern super-sweet varieties turn tender-crisp in as little as 30 seconds to 3 minutes, with a full-size ear needing closer to a 5-minute timer for fully tender kernels. Frozen corn on the cob needs an 8-minute timer, and large frozen ears take up to a 10-minute timer. The most common mistake is boiling it too long and turning sweet kernels mushy.

Step-by-step: how to boil corn on the cob

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil before the ears go in. Use a pot wide enough to submerge the corn completely; crowding drops the water temperature and stretches the cook time. Iowa State University Extension notes that modern sweet corn needs only a fraction of the boiling time older varieties did.

  1. Shuck and silk the corn: peel off the husk and pull away as much silk as you can, then rinse under cold running water.
  2. Bring the water to a full boil first. Drop the ears into already-boiling water, not cold.
  3. Cover the pot and start the timer the moment the ears go in.
  4. Test a kernel at the low end of the range — corn is done when a kernel is bright, plump, and yields to a fingernail.
  5. Lift out with tongs and serve immediately with butter and salt.

Keep the water lightly salted or unsalted; heavy salting can toughen the pericarp (the kernel skin). Salt at the table instead.

Cooking times by type and ear size

Time depends almost entirely on ear size and starting temperature, not on a fixed rule. The National Center for Home Food Preservation (a USDA-affiliated program) publishes the most rigorous boil-through times — used for blanching ears before freezing, they double as reliable "fully cooked" benchmarks for boiling corn on the cob (NCHFP).

Corn on the cob (type & size)Boil timeResult / source
Fresh, tender-crisp (any size)30 sec – 3 minBright, snappy kernels — Iowa State Extension
Fresh, fully tender (mid-size ear)~5 min5-minute timer — soft, hot through
Small ear, ≤1¼ in (boiled through)7 minNCHFP
Medium ear, 1¼–1½ in9 minNCHFP
Large ear, >1½ in11 minNCHFP
Frozen corn on the cob (standard)~8 min8-minute timer
Large frozen earup to 10 min10-minute timer

Why such a wide range? Super-sweet and sugar-enhanced hybrids — the kinds in most supermarkets — hold more sugar and less starch, so they go tender far faster than older corn. Iowa State Extension is blunt that modern sweet corn "does not require the cooking time of yesteryear," and 30 seconds to 3 minutes is enough depending on how done you like it. Older, larger, or field-style ears sit at the high end of the range.

Frozen corn on the cob

Frozen ears go straight from the freezer into boiling water — no thawing needed. Because they start far colder than a fresh ear, plan on roughly double the time: set an 8-minute timer for standard frozen ears and up to 10 minutes for jumbo or large frozen cobs. Pull one ear out at 8 minutes and puncture a center kernel; if it's still cold inside, give it another two minutes. The USDA SNAP-Ed produce guide confirms corn is sold fresh, frozen, and canned year-round, so timing by starting state — not by season — is what matters.

Microwave and steaming methods

Microwaving is the fastest route and keeps more of the kernel intact. Iowa State Extension lists microwaving alongside boiling, steaming, and grilling as a valid quick method in the same short band for fresh ears. For one fresh ear, wrap it in a damp paper towel and microwave on high for about 2-3 minutes, turning once; add time in 30-second bursts for larger ears. Frozen ears take longer in the microwave, so start checking at 5 minutes. (For another microwave-friendly starchy side, see our guide to microwaving a potato.)

You can also skip the submerged boil entirely: steaming fresh corn in a basket above boiling water takes 3-5 minutes and leaves the kernels firmer than boiling — the same texture-first logic behind how long to steam broccoli.

Food safety, storage, and troubleshooting

Corn on the cob is a low-acid vegetable, but because you're boiling it to a tender texture, there is no internal-temperature doneness requirement like there is for poultry (165°F) or ground meat (160°F) per the USDA FSIS Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart. Doneness is judged by texture and color, not a thermometer. The real food-safety issue here is spoilage, not undercooking.

Storage: The USDA SNAP-Ed guide recommends refrigerating fresh corn in the husk for only 1-2 days. Corn sugars convert to starch rapidly at room temperature, which is why day-old corn tastes starchy and dull. For longer storage, the NCHFP method is to blanch ears (7-11 minutes by size), cool them immediately in ice water for the same number of minutes, drain, and freeze — skipping the blanch step is what causes off-flavors in home-frozen corn.

Washing: Rinse ears under cold running water and remove all silk before cooking; wash your hands for 20 seconds before handling fresh produce.

Common problems:

  • Mushy kernels — you overcooked it. Pull the next ear at 3 minutes and test.
  • Tough, starchy kernels — the corn was old (sugars turned to starch) or the water was heavily salted. Buy fresh, cook within a day, and salt at the table.
  • Cold center on frozen ears — the ear was too big for the time. Add two minutes and re-test a center kernel.

guides.title: How Long to Steam Broccoli (Stovetop & Microwave Times)
guides.excerpt: Steam fresh broccoli florets 4 to 6 minutes on the stovetop or 3 to 5 minutes in the microwave, with a time-by-cut table, food-safety storage rules, and a mushy-broccoli fix.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

How Long to Steam Broccoli (The Short Answer)

Steam fresh broccoli florets 4 to 6 minutes on the stovetop, or 3 to 5 minutes in the microwave. Set a 4-minute timer for small, crisp-tender florets and check; add another minute or two for softer texture or larger pieces. Start the clock only after the water reaches a full boil and the lid is on.

How to Steam Broccoli on the Stovetop

Cut one head of broccoli into evenly sized florets roughly 1 to 1.5 inches across — uniform size is the single biggest factor in even cooking. Pour about an inch of water into a pot, set a steamer basket above the water line so the broccoli never touches the water, cover, and bring to a boil. Add the florets, replace the lid, and steam 4 to 5 minutes for chopped florets, per Montana State University Extension. The University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture Cooperative Extension Service gives a slightly wider window of 4 to 6 minutes until "just tender." Test with a fork: it should pierce the stalk with light resistance. For very soft broccoli, push to the top of the range and set a 6-minute timer, then drain immediately.

How to Steam Broccoli in the Microwave

The microwave is the fastest route and preserves nutrients well because little water is used. Place chopped broccoli in a microwave-safe container with 2 to 3 tablespoons of water, cover with a vented lid or microwave-safe plate, and cook on high. Montana State University Extension recommends 3 to 4 minutes, until a fork slides through easily. Virginia Cooperative Extension (Virginia Tech) steams florets in a covered dish with a small amount of water for about 5 minutes on high for tender-crisp results. That spread reflects wattage differences — start at the low end, check, and add 30 seconds if needed. Let the covered container sit 1 minute before opening so the residual steam finishes the job gently.

Steaming Times by Cut and Method

Cut size moves the clock more than anything else. Use the table below as a starting point, then adjust by a minute in either direction.

Broccoli formStovetop steamMicrowave (high)Doneness cue
Small florets (~1 in)4 min3 minFork pierces with slight resistance
Medium florets (~1.5 in)5 min4 minBright green, crisp-tender
Large florets (~2+ in)6 min5 minFork slides through the stalk
Peeled stalks, sliced5–6 min4–5 minSlightly firm, no stringiness
Frozen florets (unthawed)5–7 min5–6 minHeated through, tender

The stovetop figures align with the Arkansas Cooperative Extension's 4–6 minute range; the microwave figures align with Montana Extension (3–4 min) and Virginia Cooperative Extension (about 5 min). Frozen broccoli is already blanched at the processing plant, so it needs only enough time to heat through — overcooking turns it limp almost instantly.

Variables That Change the Time

Several factors shift the numbers in the table up or down:

  • Floret size: Halving the diameter nearly halves the cook time. Cut uniform pieces, or smaller ones will overcook before the larger ones finish.
  • Starting temperature: Room-temperature broccoli steams faster than ice-cold florets pulled straight from the fridge.
  • Water volume and lid seal: A tight lid traps steam. Too little water (it boils dry) or a loose lid lengthens the time and can scorch the pot.
  • Altitude: Above roughly 3,000 feet, water boils below 212°F, so add about 1 minute of steaming per 1,000 feet of elevation.
  • Age of the broccoli: Older, woody stalks need a minute more; freshly picked, young heads soften in 4 minutes.

Food Safety: Storage and Reheating

Broccoli itself is a low-risk vegetable, but once cooked it becomes a perishable leftover governed by the same rules as any cooked food. The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) states that bacteria grow rapidly in the "Danger Zone" of 40°F to 140°F, and that perishable food must be refrigerated within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour if the room is above 90°F). Cooked broccoli keeps 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator, or 3 to 4 months frozen, per FSIS. Montana Extension notes that raw heads hold up to four days refrigerated in a loose bag. When reheating, FSIS advises bringing leftovers to 165°F measured with a food thermometer — for a bowl of broccoli, a quick covered burst in the microwave does this in 1 to 2 minutes.

Troubleshooting: Mushy, Gray, or Bitter Broccoli

Gray-green, limp florets mean overcooking — the chlorophyll broke down. Pull the basket the moment the color peaks at vivid green, and if you are serving it cold, plunge the florets into ice water ("shocking") to halt the carryover cooking that turns bright green to gray. Bitterness usually comes from overcooked stems or aging broccoli; peel the stalk's tough outer layer and trim any yellowing buds before cooking. Soggy texture means the florets sat in water — keep them above the water line in the basket, and don't add more than an inch of water. If you're moving on to other vegetables, see our guide to how long to roast vegetables and our guide to how long to boil corn on the cob.

guides.title: How Long to Microwave a Potato (Perfect Baked Potato Times)
guides.excerpt: A medium potato takes 5-7 minutes on HIGH in the microwave; two take 7-10, four take 13-18. Prick, flip halfway, rest 1-3 minutes. Times by size and wattage inside.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

How long to microwave a potato?

A single medium russet (about 7-9 oz) takes roughly 5-7 minutes on HIGH to cook through in the microwave. Plan on 7-10 minutes for two potatoes and 13-18 minutes for four. Prick the skin first, flip the potato at the halfway mark, then let it rest 1-3 minutes so the heat finishes spreading to the center. These ranges come from the USDA SNAP-Ed / Montana State University Extension recipe and the Mississippi State University Extension guide; your real time depends on size, count, and wattage.

Microwave potato times by size and quantity

Two cooperative-extension sources publish slightly different tables because they assume different wattages and potato sizes. Use the lower number for a high-wattage oven (1000W+) or a small potato, and the higher number for an older 700W oven or a large one. For one medium russet, most kitchens land around 5-7 minutes.

QuantityUSDA SNAP-Ed (Montana St. Extension)Mississippi State Extension
1 potato7-8 minutes4-5 minutes
2 potatoes10-12 minutes6-8 minutes
4 potatoes14-18 minutes13-15 minutes
6 potatoes—17-19 minutes

Mississippi State's lower single-potato figure assumes a smaller potato and/or a higher-wattage oven; the USDA/Montana figure is the safer starting point for a full-size russet. If you only have one, set a 7-minute timer and test with a knife.

The 4-step method that actually works

  1. Scrub and prick. Rinse the potato and scrub the skin, then dry it and pierce it 6-8 times with a fork. Piercing lets steam escape; an unpierced potato can burst. Both extension sources require this step.
  2. Place it right. Set the potato on a microwave-safe plate. For more than one, Mississippi State Extension advises arranging them in a circle, spaced apart "like the petals on a flower," and choosing potatoes of similar size so they finish at the same time.
  3. Cook on HIGH and flip halfway. Run the microwave at full power. At the midpoint, turn the potato over. The USDA SNAP-Ed recipe says "turn over halfway through cooking," and USDA FSIS lists turning food midway as a core step that eliminates the cold spots where bacteria survive.
  4. Rest 1-3 minutes, then test. USDA SNAP-Ed says to "let potato rest for 1-3 minutes." USDA FSIS explains why: during standing time, carryover heat keeps moving toward the center and the temperature can climb several more degrees. Test with the tip of a knife or a squeeze through a mitt — it should give easily.

What actually changes the time

Wattage is the biggest variable. USDA FSIS publishes a "Time-to-Boil" test: if a cup of cold water boils in under 2 minutes your oven is 1000W+ (use the low end of any range); if it takes about 3 minutes you're near 650-700W (use the high end). That single test explains why one reader's potato is done at 4 minutes and another's takes 8.

Size and count. A 5 oz potato cooks in roughly two-thirds the time of a 10 oz one. Doubling the potatoes does not double the time, but add 1-2 minutes per extra potato and keep them similar in size.

Variety. Russets (baking potatoes) are the standard for this method and the basis of the extension tables. Thin-skinned waxy potatoes (red, new) microwave a little faster because they are smaller and denser; sweet potatoes take about the same time as a russet of equal weight. For a conventional-oven alternative that gives you the crispy skin a microwave cannot, see our how long to bake a potato guide.

Food safety in the microwave

USDA FSIS is blunt that microwave ovens "can cook unevenly and leave 'cold spots' where harmful bacteria can survive," and the agency lists three fixes: stir or turn food midway, observe standing time, and verify doneness. For a plain baked potato with no meat or egg filling, the main risks are scalding steam and a dense, undercooked center rather than pathogens — but the same FSIS standing-time rule (the SNAP-Ed potato recipe specifies 1-3 minutes) is what finishes the cook.

A few potato-specific rules: never microwave a potato wrapped in foil, since metal arcs and can damage the oven (FSIS). Discard any potato with green patches or heavy sprouts before cooking — the green contains solanine, a glycoalkaloid that heat does not break down, so microwaving will not make a green potato safe. And because microwaves only penetrate about 1 to 1.5 inches (per FSIS), a very large potato can keep a hard, cool center; halve it or finish it in a conventional oven.

Troubleshooting common problems

Hard center, soft outside. The microwave only penetrates 1 to 1.5 inches (FSIS), so a thick potato finishes by conducted heat. If the center is still firm, add 1-2 minutes, rest longer, or halve the potato before cooking.

The potato exploded. You skipped the pricking step. Steam built up under the skin until it ruptured. Always fork it 6-8 times.

Gummy or wet texture. That is overcooking or moisture trapped against the skin. Do not wrap tightly in plastic that touches the skin, and stop as soon as a knife slides in easily.

One side done, the other hard. You forgot to flip at the halfway mark. Even with a turntable, FSIS recommends turning food top-to-bottom.

Getting crispy skin

A microwave cannot brown food — the oven air stays near room temperature, per FSIS — so you get a soft skin. For a crackling jacket, microwave until nearly tender, then transfer to a 450°F conventional oven or air fryer for about 5 minutes to crisp the skin. Setting a 5-minute timer for the crisp step keeps it from burning. The full oven method is in our how long to bake a potato guide.

guides.title: How Long to Poach an Egg (Perfect Runny Yolk Times)
guides.excerpt: Poach a large egg 3 to 5 minutes in barely simmering (about 180°F) water: 3 minutes for a runny yolk, 4 for jammy, 5 for thick. USDA cooks egg dishes to 160°F.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

Poach a Large Egg 3 to 5 Minutes for a Runny Yolk

How long to poach an egg? A large egg poached in 2 to 3 inches of barely simmering water is done in 3 to 5 minutes — 3 minutes gives a fully set white with a warm, runny yolk, 4 minutes produces a thick, jammy yolk, and 5 minutes firms the yolk up while keeping it soft (University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture; American Egg Board). The water should be quivering, around 180°F (82°C), not a rolling boil (Serious Eats Food Lab). For most cooks chasing the classic eggs-Benedict texture, set a 3-minute timer for runny or a 4-minute timer for jammy.

The Method Step by Step

Use fresh eggs — older eggs spread into wispy strands because their whites have thinned. The USDA specifically notes that Grade AA and Grade A eggs are best for poaching because their whites are firm and hold their shape.

  1. Fill a saucepan or deep skillet with 2 to 3 inches of water. Bring it to a boil, then lower the heat until the water is gently simmering — small bubbles on the bottom, barely breaking the surface.
  2. Break each egg into a small cup or ramekin first. Cracking straight into water often breaks the yolk or shells the pan with thin white.
  3. Hold the dish close to the water and slip the egg in. Repeat with remaining eggs, keeping them spaced.
  4. Start your timer immediately. Do not stir, and do not let the water return to a hard boil.
  5. Lift the egg out with a slotted spoon, drain on a paper towel, trim ragged edges if you like, and serve at once.

A splash of white vinegar (1 teaspoon per cup) is optional; it speeds the outer white setting and helps a loose egg hold together, but it is not required and adds no time.

Poaching Times by Doneness

Times below are for large eggs straight from the fridge dropped into ~180°F water. Add about 30 seconds for extra-large or jumbo eggs, and subtract 30 seconds for eggs at room temperature.

DonenessTimeWhiteYolk
Soft / runny3 minutesJust set, tenderWarm, fully liquid, flowing
Medium / jammy4 minutesFirmThick, spoonable, not runny
Firm soft5 minutesFirmThick and custardy, no longer liquid

Both the Arkansas Cooperative Extension and the American Egg Board describe the target as "whites completely set and yolks begin to thicken but are not hard," which lands at the 3-to-5-minute range. The Serious Eats Food Lab lands on roughly 3.5 to 4 minutes at 180°F for a fully set white with a soft yolk.

Variables That Move the Time

Water temperature is the biggest lever. A rolling boil (212°F) tears the white before it sets; bare-simmer water (~180°F) gives a clean, compact egg. If your burner runs hot, lift the pan off the heat for a few seconds after adding the egg, then return it.

Egg size and temperature matter. A cold jumbo egg needs closer to 5 minutes; a small room-temperature egg can be done in 2.5. For consistent results, pull the eggs out of the fridge 10 minutes ahead, or stick to large cold eggs and use the table above.

Freshness changes shape, not time. A fresh egg forms a tight ball; a 3-week-old egg fans out into threads. The cook time is the same, but a fresh egg looks far better on the plate.

Altitude. Water boils cooler above sea level, so poaching takes a touch longer at elevation — add about 30 seconds above 3,000 feet.

Food Safety: The Honest Trade-Off

Here is the part most poached-egg guides skip. A classic 3-minute poached egg has a runny yolk, and a runny yolk has not reached a safe temperature. The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service is explicit: "Always cook eggs until both the white and yolk are firm," and egg dishes should reach a safe minimum internal temperature of 160°F (71°C). Intact shell eggs may carry Salmonella Enteritidis, which can be in the yolk, the white, or on the shell — it is not just a surface problem you can wash off.

In practical terms that means:

  • Most healthy adults accept the small risk and eat soft, runny-yolked poached eggs. Use fresh, clean, refrigerated Grade A or AA eggs and cook them immediately.
  • High-risk groups — infants, young children, older adults, pregnant women, and anyone with a weakened immune system — should avoid runny yolks entirely. For them, cook to a firm yolk (toward 5 minutes or longer) or use pasteurized shell eggs, which the USDA says may be used safely without full cooking.
  • Storage: keep eggs at 40°F or below, never leave them out more than 2 hours, and use cooked egg dishes within 3 to 4 days (FSIS).

If you want a genuinely runny yolk and full safety, pasteurized-in-shell eggs are the only reliable route — home pasteurization of shell eggs is not practical without cooking the egg.

Troubleshooting Common Failures

Wispy, ragged whites. The egg is old, or the water is too hot. Buy fresh eggs and drop the temperature to a bare simmer. Straining off the thin outer white through a slotted spoon before poaching also tightens the shape.

Yolk breaks when you crack it in. Always crack into a ramekin first, then slide. Lower the dish to the surface before tipping.

White not set, yolk already hard. The water was too hot — the yolk raced past the white. Use 180°F water and pull at the time in the table for the texture you want.

Egg sticks to the bottom. Give it 10 seconds to set after slipping it in, then nudge gently with a slotted spoon. A nonstick or well-seasoned pan, or a deep pot with the egg dropped from close range, prevents sticking.

Cooking for a crowd. Poached eggs do not hold well — the Arkansas extension advises against making them ahead. The reliable restaurant trick: poach to the soft side, plunge into ice water, hold up to a few hours refrigerated, then re-warm in just-barely-simmering water for 30 to 60 seconds.

For the wider egg-cooking reference — soft-boiled, hard-boiled, and jammy timings — see our how long to boil eggs guide.
