guides.title: How Long to Cook a Burger (Stove, Grill & Oven Times)
guides.excerpt: Cook a 1-inch beef burger 6 to 10 minutes on the stove, 15 to 17 minutes in a 400F oven, or about 10 minutes on the grill to a USDA-safe 160F internal temperature.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

Cook a burger 6 to 10 minutes on the stove, 15 to 17 minutes in a 400°F oven, or about 10 minutes on the grill

For a standard 1-inch, 80/20 beef patty, that means roughly 3 to 5 minutes per side on the stovetop, 15 to 17 minutes unflipped in the oven at 400°F, or checking a grill burger at the 10- to 15-minute mark the USDA recommends. The only real finish line is internal temperature: ground beef is safe at 160°F (FSIS). Set an 8-minute timer for medium stovetop burgers, a 10-minute timer for well-done or a grill check, or a 12-minute timer as an oven midpoint.

Why 160°F matters more than minutes

Ground beef carries more risk than a whole steak because grinding spreads surface bacteria throughout the meat. The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service requires all raw ground beef, pork, lamb, and veal to reach a safe minimum internal temperature of 160°F, measured with a food thermometer (FSIS Ground Beef and Food Safety). Color is not a reliable signal: USDA research found roughly 1 in 4 hamburgers turns brown before it reaches a safe temperature (FSIS, Is It Done Yet?). Treat the minutes below as a planning tool and the thermometer as the verdict. If you're cooking poultry patties instead, see our grill chicken guide — ground poultry needs 165°F.

Cooking times by method and doneness

Times assume a 1-inch-thick patty formed from 80% lean ground beef. Thicker patties, colder meat, and leaner blends all add time.

MethodHeatTimeSafe finish
Stovetop skilletMedium-high~8 min (medium) to 10 min (well-done); 3–5 min per side160°F
Oven bake (no flip)400°F15–17 min (~140°F at 15 min = medium, still below safe)160°F
GrillMedium (~350–400°F)~4–5 min per side; check at 10–15 min160°F
Turkey / chicken burgerAnyAdd ~1–2 min per side vs. beef165°F

Stovetop doneness benchmarks run medium-rare at about 6 minutes total, medium at 7 to 8 minutes, medium-well at 9 minutes, and well-done at 10 minutes (The Kitchn). For an oven burger on a wire rack at 400°F, 15 minutes lands around 140°F (medium) and 17 minutes pushes it toward well-done (The Kitchn). On the grill, the USDA specifically advises checking each burger with a food thermometer after roughly 10 to 15 minutes of total cooking (FSIS, Is It Done Yet?).

How to cook a burger on the stove

  1. Use 80% lean ground beef; anything leaner than 90% tends to dry out and crumble (The Kitchn).
  2. Form 1-inch patties gently — overworking the meat makes it tough — and press a shallow dimple in the center so they stay flat instead of doming.
  3. Heat a skillet or griddle over medium-high until you see the first wisp of smoke, then add the patties.
  4. Cook 3 to 4 minutes, flip once, then cook another 3 to 5 minutes to your preferred doneness. Add cheese right after the flip and cover briefly to melt.
  5. Verify 160°F with a thermometer before serving (FSIS).

Set an 8-minute timer for medium patties and a 10-minute timer for well-done. Use a thin spatula and flip only once to keep the crust intact.

Grill and oven methods

On the grill: Preheat to medium (roughly 350–400°F). Grill burgers about 4 to 5 minutes per side, flipping once, and the USDA requires ground meats to reach 160°F on the grill just as they do indoors (FSIS, Food Safety Belongs on the Grill). A 10-minute timer is the right moment for that first temperature check. Building a full cookout? Our grill chicken timing pairs well on the same fire.

In the oven: Heat to 400°F and set patties on a wire rack over a foil-lined baking sheet so heat circulates underneath — no flipping needed. Bake 15 to 17 minutes; at 15 minutes a patty sits around 140°F (medium), which is still below the USDA safe minimum, so continue to 17 minutes or until a thermometer reads 160°F (The Kitchn; FSIS). Add cheese in the final minute and toast the buns on a separate rack for the last 5 to 6 minutes. A 12-minute timer marks the midpoint, when you should start watching closely.

Food safety, handling, and troubleshooting

Refrigerate ground beef at 40°F or below and cook or freeze it within 1 to 2 days. Keep raw and cooked items separate, and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours — 1 hour if the air temperature is above 90°F (FSIS). Safe minimum internal temperatures: whole beef, pork, veal, and lamb steaks and roasts 145°F with a 3-minute rest; all ground meats 160°F; all poultry 165°F (FSIS Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart). For a breakfast side, our bacon timing guide covers the safe-crisp window.

Quick fixes for common problems: dry, dense patties come from overworking the meat or using too-lean beef, so handle the beef gently and stick to 80/20; domed centers are prevented by the dimple trick; brown outside but undercooked inside means the heat is too high — drop to medium and trust the thermometer, since 1 in 4 burgers browns before it is actually safe (FSIS).

guides.title: How Long to Cook Quinoa (Stovetop & Rice Cooker Times)
guides.excerpt: Cook quinoa 15 minutes on the stovetop for white (20 for black) at a 1:2 quinoa-to-water ratio, then rest covered 10 minutes. A rice cooker finishes it on the white-rice cycle in 15-20 minutes. One cup dry yields about 3 cups cooked.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

How long to cook quinoa: the short answer

Cook quinoa on the stovetop for 15 minutes for white (pearl) quinoa, 18 minutes for red, and 20 minutes for black, using a 1:2 ratio of quinoa to liquid (1 cup dry quinoa to 2 cups water or broth) and finishing with a 10-minute covered rest off the heat. In a rice cooker, the white-rice cycle takes about 15-20 minutes. One cup of dry quinoa yields roughly 3 cups cooked.

The stovetop method, step by step

The reliable stovetop method is the same one Michigan State University Extension publishes: a 1:2 quinoa-to-liquid ratio, a quick boil, then a covered simmer until the liquid is absorbed and the grain is soft. Here is the precise sequence:

  1. Rinse 1 cup of quinoa in a fine-mesh strainer under cold water for 30-60 seconds. Quinoa's seed coat is coated in saponins, bitter compounds that taste soapy if you skip this step.
  2. Combine the rinsed, drained quinoa with 2 cups of water or broth and a pinch of salt in a saucepan.
  3. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat (about 3-4 minutes).
  4. Cover and reduce to a low simmer. Set a 15-minute timer for white quinoa (18 for red, 20 for black and tri-color blends).
  5. Rest covered for 10 minutes off the heat after the timer goes off. This is the step that turns out fluffy grain rather than a wet mess according to Foolproof Living's tested ratios.
  6. Fluff with a fork and serve.

Cooking times by quinoa type and method

Cooking time tracks the color of the seed: darker quinoa has a tougher outer layer and needs a few extra minutes. The liquid ratio and yield stay constant across all types. The per-color simmer times below match Foolproof Living's kitchen testing of white, red, black, and tri-color quinoa.

Quinoa typeLiquid per 1 cup drySimmer timeCovered restApprox. yield
White (pearl)2 cups15 min10 min~3 cups
Red2 cups18 min10 min~3 cups
Black2 cups20 min10 min~3 cups
Tri-color blend2 cups18-20 min10 min~3 cups
Rice cooker (any type)2 cups15-20 min (white-rice cycle)5 min natural~3 cups

Variables that change your result

Water ratio. The 1:2 ratio is the safe default and what MSU Extension uses. If you want firmer, separate grains for a salad, drop to about 1 3/4 cups liquid per 1 cup quinoa (the drier ratio that Foolproof Living tested head-to-head against 1:2 and found only minimally different); for soft, porridge-like quinoa, push toward 2 cups plus 2 tablespoons of liquid per 1 cup quinoa.

Rinsing. Most U.S. supermarket quinoa is pre-rinsed, but the package rarely says so plainly. Rinsing for under a minute removes residual saponin and any grit, and it is free insurance against bitterness.

The 10-minute rest. Skipping the rest leaves moisture still migrating through the seed. Covered and off the heat, the grain finishes steaming in its own residual heat and the last liquid absorbs without scorching.

Quinoa cooks much like other pantry grains. For comparison, see our guides on how long to cook rice and how long to cook oatmeal.

How to cook quinoa in a rice cooker

A rice cooker is the lowest-effort path because it handles the boil-simmer-switch-off automatically. Use the same 1:2 ratio (1 cup rinsed quinoa to 2 cups liquid), add salt, and run the white-rice cycle, which on most machines lasts about 15-20 minutes. Let it sit for 5 minutes after the cycle clicks off, then fluff. Red and black quinoa may need a couple of extra minutes on the same setting; if the machine shuts off and liquid remains, run a second short cycle.

Food safety and storage

Quinoa is a low-moisture dry grain, so the food-safety concerns arrive after cooking. The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service places cooked foods in the danger zone between 40 and 140 F, where bacteria multiply fastest per FSIS leftovers guidance. Follow three rules:

  • Refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour if the room is above 90 F).
  • Store cooked quinoa 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator at 40 F or below, or freeze for 3 to 4 months.
  • Reheat leftovers to 165 F, measured with a food thermometer. This is the same 165 F internal minimum FSIS sets for poultry, and it applies to reheated grain dishes and casseroles built on quinoa.

Troubleshooting: mushy, bitter, or crunchy quinoa

Mushy quinoa. Cause: too much liquid or too long on the heat. Fix: drain any pooled water, spread the quinoa on a sheet pan uncovered for 10 minutes so the surface dries, then fluff. Next time, measure the liquid precisely and do not lift the lid during the simmer.

Bitter quinoa. Cause: unrinsed saponin. Fix: rinse the raw grain longer (60-90 seconds) before cooking. If a cooked batch still tastes soapy, fold in a squeeze of lemon or a pinch of sugar to mask it, and rinse the next batch more thoroughly.

Crunchy or undercooked quinoa. Cause: not enough liquid, heat too low to maintain a simmer, or the lid was off. Fix: add 2-3 tablespoons of boiling water, cover, and cook another 3-5 minutes until the white germ spirals (the little "tail") release and the grain is tender.

guides.title: How Long to Bake Cookies (Time & Temperature Chart)
guides.excerpt: Most cookies bake at 350°F for 9 to 12 minutes. Use this time-and-temperature chart by type — chocolate chip, sugar, oatmeal, cut-out, shortbread, and bars — plus egg-and-flour safety temps.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

Most cookies bake at 350°F for 9 to 12 minutes

Bake standard drop cookies — chocolate chip, sugar, and oatmeal — at 350°F (175°C) for 9 to 12 minutes, until the edges are golden and the centers still look a touch underdone. Small or thin cookies finish at 9 minutes; large, chewy ones need 11 to 12. Cut-out sugar cookies bake at 375°F (190°C) for 8 to 10 minutes, and cookie bars in an 11×7 dish take 375°F for 15 to 18 minutes. Cookies keep cooking on the hot pan after it leaves the oven, so pull them early.

Cookie baking time and temperature chart

Times assume a fully preheated oven, dough portioned at 2 tablespoons, and a light-colored half-sheet pan lined with parchment. Start checking two minutes before the low end of every range.

Cookie typeOven tempBake timeDone when…
Chocolate chip (2-tbsp drop)350°F (175°C)10–12 min — set an 11-minute timerEdges golden, center pale and soft
Small / mini drop cookies350°F (175°C)8–10 minTops crackle, edges just set
Drop sugar cookies350°F (175°C)8–10 minEdges lightly golden
Oatmeal cookies350°F (175°C)10–12 min — try a 12-minute timerEdges set, tops no longer wet
Cut-out / rolled sugar cookies375°F (190°C)8–10 min — set a 9-minute timerEdges barely starting to color
Shortbread350°F (175°C)12–15 minBottoms golden, tops still pale
Cookie bars (11×7 dish)375°F (190°C)15–18 minToothpick comes out clean

Cookie bars baked in an 11×7 dish at 375°F for 15–18 minutes follow University of Illinois Extension, and cut-out (rolled) cookies at 375°F for 8–10 minutes match University of Wyoming Extension's "Baking It Up!". The 350°F (175°C) standard for chocolate chip, oatmeal, and drop sugar cookies is the published convention across home-baking references and university extension recipes.

Method: how to bake cookies, step by step

1. Preheat fully. Wait until the oven reaches temperature before the dough goes in — a cold start makes cookies spread flat. 2. Line the pan. Use parchment or a silicone mat; greasing the pan promotes spreading. 3. Space the dough. Leave at least 2 inches between portions so the cookies have room to spread. 4. Bake one sheet at a time on the middle rack for even heat; if you must bake two, swap and rotate them halfway through. 5. Pull early. Take the sheet out when the edges are set but the centers still look wet — they finish setting as they cool on the pan for 2 minutes, then move to a wire rack.

While the oven preheats you can launch any kitchen countdown — the same timer you'd use to bake a potato works for a sheet of cookies.

Variables that change the bake time

Several factors move a cookie out of the chart's range, and you should set the timer accordingly:

  • Dough temperature. Warm dough spreads fast and bakes thin in 8–9 minutes; chilled dough holds its shape and may need 11–12. The FDA recommends refrigerating cookie dough at 40°F or below, so dough straight from the fridge always bakes slower than room-temperature dough.
  • Cookie size. A 1-tbsp cookie finishes 2–3 minutes before a 3-tbsp one. Portion with a scoop so every cookie bakes the same.
  • Sheet color. Dark sheets overbrown the bottom; Colorado State University Extension notes that a dark pan can scorch cookies and recommends parchment or a lighter sheet.
  • Oven accuracy. Home ovens routinely run 25°F hot or cold. CSU Extension's food-safety specialists advise checking the dial against an oven thermometer before you trust it.
  • Altitude. Above 3,000 feet, CSU Extension recommends increasing the oven temperature by no more than 25°F and shortening the bake time to keep cookies from spreading.

Food safety: raw flour and eggs

Cookie dough is a raw food. Flour is a raw agricultural product that can carry Salmonella and pathogenic E. coli, and most homemade dough also contains raw eggs. The FDA states plainly that cooking is the only way to be sure foods made with flour and raw eggs are safe, that you should never eat raw dough or batter — and the agency explicitly warns against trying to heat-treat flour at home, since home methods may not kill all the bacteria.

Because most cookies contain eggs, the safe-cooking benchmark for egg dishes applies: USDA FSIS sets 160°F (71.1°C) as the safe minimum internal temperature for eggs and egg dishes. A thin cookie baked until its edges are golden and its surface is set reaches that temperature easily, which is why a fully baked cookie is safe to eat while the raw dough it came from is not. For styles that stay wet in the middle — gooey cookie bars or skillet cookies — the USDA's egg guidance says to verify 160°F in the center with a food thermometer.

Troubleshooting common cookie problems

Cookies spread into one puddle: the dough was too warm, the pan was greased, or the oven ran cool. Chill the dough 30 minutes, switch to parchment, and verify the temperature. Raw centers, burnt edges: the oven runs hot or the cookies are oversized — lower the temp 25°F and portion smaller. Hard, dry cookies: you baked past doneness; pull when centers still look slightly underdone. Pale, cakey cookies: too much flour — spoon flour into the cup and level it off rather than scooping. Uneven baking across the sheet: rotate the pan halfway through.

How to tell when cookies are done

Visual cues beat the clock. A drop cookie is done when the edges are firm and lightly golden and a 1-inch circle in the center still looks wet and puffy — it will set as it cools. Cut-out cookies are done when the edges just begin to color but the surface is still pale; shortbread when the bottoms are golden. For cookie bars and any thick or gooey style, confirm with a thermometer: 160°F in the center verifies both doneness and egg safety.

guides.title: How Long to Cook Oatmeal (Rolled, Steel-Cut & Microwave)
guides.excerpt: Rolled oatmeal takes ~5 minutes stovetop (2½–3 microwaved), quick oats 1 minute, steel-cut 15–30 minutes. Times and food-safety rules verified from Quaker, USDA FSIS, and university extensions.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

How long does oatmeal take to cook?

Cook rolled (old-fashioned) oatmeal about 5 minutes on the stovetop or 2½ to 3 minutes in the microwave; quick oats need about 1 minute on the stove; and steel-cut oats take 15 to 30 minutes of gentle simmering, depending on the cut. Instant oatmeal simply stands 2 minutes in hot liquid. These times come from Quaker's preparation guide and recipes from Oregon State University Extension.

Cooking times by oat type

The four shelf staples — instant, quick, rolled, and steel-cut — are the same grain milled to different sizes, so the main thing that changes is how long water takes to penetrate them. Use this table as a starting point; all ratios are liquid-to-oats by volume.

Oat typeLiquid : oatsStovetopMicrowave
Instant (precooked)~¾ cup : ½ cupStand 2 min in hot liquid60–75 sec (HIGH)
Quick (1-minute)1 cup : ½ cup~1 min1½–2 min (HIGH)
Rolled (old-fashioned)1 cup : ½ cup~5 min2½–3 min (HIGH)
Steel-cut (traditional)2¼–3 cups : 1 cup15–30 min simmer2½–3 min at 50% power (quick-cut only)

The figures above match Quaker's official directions for packaged oats, cross-checked against the University of Missouri Extension oats publication, which notes a standard ratio of roughly two cups of liquid to one cup of oats for rolled and quick varieties.

How to cook rolled oats on the stovetop

For one serving, bring 1 cup of water or milk to a rolling boil with a pinch of salt, then stir in ½ cup of rolled oats. Reduce the heat to medium and cook about 5 minutes (per Quaker's old-fashioned stovetop directions), stirring occasionally — set a 5-minute timer for standard texture. For a softer, creamier bowl, simmer up to 10 minutes instead (a 10-minute timer catches it before it turns to paste). The pinch of salt matters more than people think: Missouri Extension specifically notes it "brings out a nutty oat flavor" rather than making the cereal taste salty.

How to cook steel-cut oats

Steel-cut oats are whole groats chopped into gritty pieces, so they need real simmer time. Bring 3 cups of water to a boil, add 1 cup of oats, reduce to low, and simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring a few times; then let the pot stand 2 minutes off the heat before serving, per the Oregon State University Extension recipe. Quaker's own steel-cut instructions run a little longer — 25 to 30 minutes for the traditional cut — so set a 30-minute timer if you like them fully tender. Pre-soaking the groats overnight, or toasting them briefly in butter before adding liquid, shaves several minutes off and deepens the flavor.

Microwave oatmeal when you're short on time

The microwave is the fastest path for rolled and quick oats. Combine ½ cup of rolled oats with about 1 cup of liquid in a large microwave-safe bowl (use one bigger than you think you need — oatmeal climbs the walls as it foams) and heat on HIGH for 2½ to 3 minutes, stirring once halfway. Quick oats take 1½ to 2 minutes, per Quaker's microwave directions. Milk-based oatmeal foams more than water-based, so drop the power to 70% or pause to stir if it threatens to overflow.

Variables that change the cooking time

  • Liquid choice. Milk simmers near the same temperature as water but thickens the pot, so milk-based oatmeal can read "done" slightly earlier and creamier.
  • Altitude. Water boils at a lower temperature above 3,000 feet, so plan on extra simmer time — a little longer for rolled oats and several minutes more for steel-cut.
  • Cut and freshness. Older oats can be drier and need an extra splash of liquid; freshly milled steel-cut cook a minute or two faster.
  • Soaking. An overnight soak in water or milk can cut steel-cut morning cook time roughly in half.

If you also cook other breakfast grains, the ratios and reasoning carry over to our quinoa timing guide and rice timing guide.

Food safety and leftovers

Dry oats are a low-moisture shelf-stable good, so the safety risk is in how you handle the cooked pot, not the raw grain. Cool and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours of cooking — the window Missouri Extension states in its recipe notes. The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service supplies the underlying rule: bacteria multiply fastest in the "danger zone" between 40°F and 140°F, cooked leftovers keep 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator, and frozen oatmeal stays safe 3 to 4 months. Reheat leftover oatmeal until it steams throughout (165°F), and if you cook it with eggs or dairy, treat the bowl like any other perishable — never leave it on the counter.

Troubleshooting common oatmeal problems

  • Gummy or paste-like: too little liquid or heat that's too high. Cook at a simmer, not a boil, and start at the 1-cup-liquid-to-½-cup-oats ratio.
  • Bland: almost always missing salt. Add the pinch before the oats hit the water, not after.
  • Crunchy steel-cut: undercooked or under-liquid. Add ¼ cup of hot water and simmer another 3–5 minutes.
  • Boils over in the microwave: the bowl is too small or the power too high. Use a deeper bowl and drop to 70% power.

guides.title: How Long Is a Cat Pregnant? Gestation & Birth Timeline
guides.excerpt: A cat is pregnant for roughly 63–65 days (about nine weeks). Track week-by-week fetal development, pinking-up, labor stages, and care with our due-date countdown.
guides.content:
How Long Is a Cat Pregnant?

A cat is pregnant for about 63–65 days, or roughly nine weeks. VCA Animal Hospitals gives the normal feline gestation range as 60–67 days (averaging 63–65), and PetMD likewise places the average at 63–65 days, while peer-reviewed data from a review in Theriogenology puts the mean at 65.6 days across extremes of 52–74 days. The Merck Veterinary Manual notes that delivery typically occurs 64–66 days after breeding. For practical purposes, circle a due date about 65 days from mating and have your nesting box ready from day 60 onward. By comparison, how long dogs are pregnant runs a similar ~63 days.

Female cats (queens) are induced ovulators — eggs are released in response to mating — so breedings are usually spread over 2–3 days and the exact conception date is seldom known. That single fact accounts for most of the apparent variation in gestation length. To track how the whole timeline fits into a cat's life, see our cat lifespan guide.

Cat Pregnancy Timeline: Week-by-Week

Veterinarians split the pregnancy into three trimesters of about 20 days each. Here is what is happening inside the queen and what you can actually see at home.

WeekDaysFetal developmentOwner-visible signs & vet checks
10–7Fertilization; embryos migrate to the uterus.Essentially none. You may only know mating occurred.
28–14Embryos implant in the uterine horns; organs begin to form.Very subtle; possibly a slight rise in appetite.
315–21Embryos grow; a vet can palpate fetuses at ~2.5 weeks.“Pinking up” around day 16–20: nipples turn pink and become prominent — usually the first visible sign.
422–28Organogenesis well underway; kitten heartbeats detectable by ultrasound at 3–4 weeks.Slight weight gain, rounder belly; queen often calmer and more affectionate.
529–35Rapid fetal growth; skeletons begin to calcify.Belly visibly rounder; appetite increasing.
636–42Skeletons calcify; kittens visible on X-ray from about day 45 for an accurate head-count.Abdomen noticeably distended; breast tissue starting to swell.
743–49Kittens gain the bulk of their birth weight in this final trimester.Nipples/ breasts enlarged and darker; voracious appetite; grooming of belly and vulva.
850–56Fetal movement; X-ray count is now reliable.You may feel/see kittens kick; nesting behavior begins; milk may come in.
957–65Final maturation; kittens ready for birth.Queen seeks the nest, stops eating ~24 hours before labor, rectal temp drops below 100°F (37.8°C); labor begins.

The greenish-black discharge seen during delivery is the placenta (“afterbirth”) — one should be passed for every kitten, and queens normally eat them.

Factors That Affect Gestation Length

Most variation from the 63–65 day norm comes from biology and circumstances, not from anything going wrong:

  • Unknown ovulation date. Because queens are induced ovulators and mate repeatedly over 2–3 days, the day you saw mating is rarely the day of conception — so the “clock” can be off by a few days either way.
  • Litter size. Litter size may shift the timeline by a day or two, though the effect is small and the queen stays within the normal window.
  • Breed. Breed can nudge the average slightly — published breed means range from about 63 days (Siamese) to 65 days (Persian).
  • Queen’s age and health. First-time mothers and very young or older queens can fall outside the typical window; underlying illness or poor nutrition can shorten or prolong gestation.
  • Stress and environment. Cats can interrupt labor — pausing for 24–36 hours between kittens — if they do not feel safe, which makes the total delivery time look longer without being abnormal.

Caring for a Pregnant Cat

Nutrition by stage

A pregnant queen’s nutrient needs climb to about 1.5 times her pre-pregnancy level, and may exceed twice normal by the time of weaning. Switch her to a high-calorie diet labeled for kittens (growth) or pregnancy/lactation by the end of the first month and keep her on it through nursing. The Merck Veterinary Manual recommends about 25% more food in the last three weeks and 2–3 times her normal intake while nursing. Offer frequent small meals — late in pregnancy the kittens crowd the abdomen and she simply cannot eat much at once. Do not add calcium or vitamin supplements; excess calcium during pregnancy actually raises the risk of eclampsia (milk fever) afterward.

Veterinary care

Confirm the pregnancy and get a kitten count: abdominal palpation at ~2.5 weeks, ultrasound at 3–4 weeks, and an X-ray from about day 45 once skeletons calcify. Ideally, vaccinate before pregnancy — live vaccines must never be given to a pregnant cat, but a killed vaccine (such as most rabies shots) may be used if your vet deems it necessary. Bring a fecal sample so intestinal worms aren’t passed to the kittens, and ask about pregnancy-safe flea/tick products.

Setting up the nest

In the final week, give her a quiet, draft-free, observable spot — a cardboard box lined with old towels or sheets works well. She should be able to come and go, and you should be able to watch from a distance. Nesting-box temperature should stay 85–90°F (29–32°C) for the kittens’ first few days.

The three stages of labor

  • Stage 1 — cervix dilates, hidden uterine contractions begin. The queen is restless, paces, scratches at the nest, pants, and stops eating; her temperature drops below 100°F. This can last up to 36 hours in first-time mothers.
  • Stage 2 — visible straining. Each kitten is usually delivered in 5–30 minutes, with intervals averaging 10 minutes to an hour between kittens. Most queens deliver the whole litter within six hours.
  • Stage 3 — the placenta for each kitten is passed (greenish-black). Stages 2 and 3 alternate kitten by kitten, and it is normal for the mother to eat the membranes.

When to call the vet

Seek veterinary help immediately if you notice any of the following, which can signal dystocia (difficult birth):

  • Vaginal bleeding or discharge at any point during gestation — fresh blood is never normal before labor.
  • Visible, intense contractions for more than 20 minutes without producing a kitten.
  • A kitten visible in the birth canal that is not passed within 10 minutes.
  • Fresh blood from the vulva for more than 10 minutes.
  • The queen is lethargic, depressed, or running a fever above 103°F (39.4°C).
  • Greenish discharge with no kitten produced within 2–4 hours (it should follow a kitten quickly).

After the birth, watch for postpartum complications too: retained placenta, metritis (uterine infection), mastitis, and eclampsia — a dangerous calcium drop 3–5 weeks after delivery that causes tremors, stiffness, and seizures and needs immediate treatment.

A Typical Litter

Peer-reviewed data puts the average litter at about four kittens (mean 4.0), though individual litters can range well above or below that average. Your veterinarian can give you an exact number from an X-ray taken after about day 45. For context on how these kittens mature, see our guide to how long cats live and the dog lifespan comparison.

The Bottom Line

Cat pregnancy is short — plan on 63–65 days from mating, have a high-calorie kitten diet and a quiet nesting box ready by day 60, and know the dystocia warning signs above. Most queens deliver without help; your main jobs are good nutrition, a calm environment, and a clear sense of when to phone the vet.

guides.title: How Long Are Dogs Pregnant? Canine Gestation Timeline
guides.excerpt: Dogs are pregnant for about 63 days (range 57-72). Our vet-sourced guide walks week-by-week fetal development, pregnancy signs, whelping stages and litter size.
guides.content:
How Long Are Dogs Pregnant?

Dogs are pregnant for about 63 days — roughly two months — counted from ovulation or successful breeding. The accepted range runs from 57 to 72 days, with most bitches whelping (giving birth) between 57 and 65 days after mating. VCA Animal Hospitals, PetMD, and the Merck Veterinary Manual all cite ~63 days as the average, and that timeline is essentially the same across every breed and size; what changes from breed to breed is litter size, not how long dogs are pregnant.

The reason there is a span rather than one fixed number is that pregnancy is measured from ovulation, while most owners can only date it from an observed mating — and a bitch stays fertile for several days. Treat the due date as a several-day window, not a single calendar day. For the bigger picture of a dog's reproductive life, see our guide to how long dogs live and how canine gestation compares with cat gestation.

Week-by-Week Canine Gestation Timeline

A dog's nine-week pregnancy divides neatly into three trimesters of about three weeks each. The table below pairs fetal development (drawn from the Merck Veterinary Manual) with the signs you can actually see at home.

WeekFetal development (veterinary milestones)What the owner may notice
Week 1 (days 0–7)Fertilization in the oviduct; embryos migrate toward the uterus.Almost nothing. Behavior and appetite usually look normal.
Week 2 (days 8–14)Embryos continue to migrate; no implantation yet.No visible signs. A few females show mild “morning sickness” (occasional vomiting).
Week 3 (days 15–21)Implantation at ~day 18; small uterine swellings (deciduomata) form by ~day 21. Relaxin becomes detectable from ~day 22–27.Slight behavioral shifts (clinginess or irritability). Nipples may begin to enlarge slightly.
Week 4 (days 22–28)Embryos roughly double in diameter weekly; the fetal skeleton begins to calcify around day 28. Ultrasound is reliable after day 28.Appetite may dip or rise; the abdomen can look fuller. Your veterinarian can confirm pregnancy by ultrasound.
Week 5 (days 29–35)Rapid fetal growth; organs forming. Uterine swellings become less distinct on palpation after day 35–38.Visible weight gain; enlarged, pinker nipples; clear abdominal swelling.
Week 6 (days 36–42)Fetal skeletons become detectable on X-ray from ~day 42–45.Abdomen noticeably distended; appetite increases; the bitch rests more.
Week 7 (days 43–49)Skeleton is “quite prominent” by day 47–48; radiographs now give an accurate puppy count.Mammary glands swell; milk may appear; nesting behavior can begin.
Week 8 (days 50–56)Fetal dentition visible near term; late-gestation radiographs (>day 55) are best for estimating litter size.Puppies may be felt moving; the belly drops; restlessness and nesting intensify.
Week 9 (days 57–63+)Fetuses are fully developed and positioned for birth.Rectal temperature drops below 99°F (37.2°C) about 24 hours before labor; panting, digging, refusal of food.

Signs Your Dog Is Pregnant

Early pregnancy is hard to spot, which is why veterinarians — not home tests — confirm it. According to PetMD and VCA Animal Hospitals, the reliable owner-visible signs build gradually:

  • Enlarged, darker nipples (often the first clue, around weeks 3–4)
  • Weight gain of roughly 15–25% by the time of whelping
  • A swollen abdomen that becomes obvious by weeks 5–6
  • Appetite changes — either finicky eating or increased hunger
  • Nesting behavior (dragging blankets, digging) in the final week
  • Behavioral shifts: increased clinginess, irritability, or seclusion

A veterinarian can confirm pregnancy definitively with an abdominal ultrasound (reliable from about day 21–28), a relaxin blood test (from ~day 22–27), or an X-ray in the last two weeks to count puppies. Be aware that false pregnancy (pseudopregnancy) can mimic these signs — only a vet can tell them apart.

Factors That Affect Gestation Length

True gestation in the dog is about 63 days from ovulation. The wide quoted range (57–72 days from a recorded mating) mostly reflects the difficulty of pinpointing when conception actually occurred, rather than puppies developing faster or slower. Factors that move the apparent due date include:

  • Ovulation timing vs. mating date: Sperm can survive for days in the bitch's reproductive tract, and she is fertile for several days, so counting from a single observed mating introduces several days of uncertainty.
  • Litter size: Both very large and very small litters can shift the exact whelping day slightly.
  • Breed and size: The average stays ~63 days, but small breeds sometimes deliver a touch earlier and giant breeds a touch later.
  • Accuracy of breeding records: Two matings on different days widen the “expected” window; VCA notes that with two matings, birth typically falls 63–65 days later.
  • Maternal health and stress: Illness, poor nutrition, or stress can contribute to premature or delayed labor.

Caring for a Pregnant Dog

Good care during those nine weeks protects both the mother and her puppies. The cornerstones are nutrition, gentle exercise, and a planned whelping setup.

Nutrition. VCA and PetMD recommend feeding a high-quality diet labeled for “gestation and lactation” or “all life stages.” Food intake stays normal for the first two-thirds of pregnancy (about six weeks), then rises sharply. In the last three weeks, increase food by roughly 25–50% (up to 1.5 times normal) and switch to smaller, more frequent meals as the growing puppies crowd the abdomen. Diets rich in omega-3 DHA support puppy brain development and milk production. Avoid supplements unless your vet prescribes them, and never give any medication during pregnancy without veterinary approval — some common drugs are harmful to developing fetuses.

Exercise and routine. Let the bitch set her own activity level. Short, gentle walks are fine, but avoid strenuous exercise and rough play, especially late in pregnancy. Check for abnormal vaginal discharge and contact your vet with any concerns.

Preparing to whelp. In the last week, introduce a quiet whelping box lined with newspaper and clean blankets. Stock towels, a bulb syringe, and your vet's after-hours number. Check the rectal temperature twice daily in the final days — a drop below 99°F (37.2°C) signals labor within about 24 hours.

The Three Stages of Labor (Whelping)

The Merck Veterinary Manual and VCA describe whelping in three stages:

  • Stage I (12–24 hours): Uterine contractions begin and the cervix dilates, with no visible straining. The bitch becomes restless, reclusive, and may pant, tremble, refuse food, and vomit. Discharge is clear and watery.
  • Stage II (delivery): Visible abdominal straining delivers each puppy, normally 30–60 minutes apart. The whole litter is ideally delivered in about 7–9 hours. Discharge may be clear or blood-tinged (a green-black discharge before a puppy appears is abnormal — see dystocia below).
  • Stage III (placenta): The placenta follows each puppy (or several at once). It is normal for the mother to eat the placentas.

Puppies are usually born head-first (anterior), but hind-first (posterior) is also normal; only a true breech (tail or bottom first) may need help. Keep newborns warm — the whelping area should sit around 85–90°F (29–32°C) in the first days.

Litter Size by Breed

Average litter size is 4 to 6 puppies, but it varies widely with the mother's size, breed, age, and health. PetMD reports typical ranges as:

  • Small/toy breeds (e.g., Chihuahua, Pomeranian): typically 1–4 puppies (very small or toy dogs may have just 1–2)
  • Medium breeds (e.g., Beagle, Cocker Spaniel): around 3–6 puppies
  • Large breeds (e.g., Labrador, German Shepherd): 6–8 puppies, sometimes up to 10–12
  • Giant breeds (e.g., Mastiff, Great Dane): 8 or more; the record litter was 24 puppies, born in 2004 to a Neapolitan Mastiff named Tia (Guinness World Records).

First-time mothers tend to have smaller litters, and bitches bred very young or older also average fewer pups. The most accurate way to predict litter size is an X-ray at around 45 days of pregnancy.

When to Call the Vet (Dystocia)

Most dogs deliver without trouble, but know the warning signs of dystocia (difficult birth). Contact a veterinarian immediately if any of the following occur, per VCA and the Merck Veterinary Manual:

  • Stage I labor lasts more than 24 hours without progressing to delivery
  • Strong straining for more than 30 minutes with no puppy born
  • More than 2 hours pass between puppies when more are expected
  • A green/black or foul-smelling discharge appears but no puppy follows, or discharge continues heavily after delivery
  • The bitch is in obvious pain, exhausted, or a puppy appears stuck
  • Gestation stretches well beyond 65–70 days with no signs of labor

Brachycephalic breeds (Bulldogs, French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, Pugs) have a much higher rate of difficult deliveries and frequently need a planned C-section — discuss this with your vet well before the due date.

After whelping, monitor the mother's temperature, appetite, and discharge. Normal postpartum discharge (lochia) is dark red to black and odorless for the first few days; a foul-smelling or increasingly bloody discharge, fever, or lethargy warrants a vet visit. Weigh puppies daily — failure to gain roughly 10% of body weight per day after the first 24 hours is an early red flag.

Once the litter arrives, a new chapter begins. To put your dog's full life into perspective, see how long dogs live and how canine lifespans compare with cats and horses.

guides.title: How Long Do Cats Live? Average Cat Lifespan by Breed
guides.excerpt: Cats live an average of 13–17 years, while indoor cats often reach their late teens or 20s. See breed lifespans, life stages, and how to extend your cat's life.
guides.content:
How long do cats live?

The average cat lives 13 to 17 years, according to PetMD, with well-cared-for indoor cats frequently reaching their late teens or early 20s. The Merck Veterinary Manual notes plainly that some cats can live 20 years or more. At the extreme end, the oldest cat on record — a Texas tabby named Creme Puff — lived to 38 years and 3 days old, as documented by Guinness World Records.

That wide range exists because a cat's lifespan is shaped less by a single number and more by environment, genetics, and veterinary care. The biggest single lever is whether the cat lives indoors or outdoors, followed by breed, diet, and how early disease is caught. Below is everything that determines how long a cat lives — plus the breed and life-stage numbers owners actually search for. (If you are also planning for kittens, see our guide to how long cats are pregnant.)

Indoor vs. outdoor cat lifespan

Where a cat lives is the single largest predictor of how long it lives. PetMD reports that indoor cats commonly live 15–20 years, while cats allowed to roam outdoors unsupervised live, on average, just 2 to 5 years. The Merck Veterinary Manual is equally blunt: it is much safer for cats to stay indoors, because outdoor cats face traffic, predators, fights, toxins, and infectious disease.

The outdoor lifespan is cut short mainly by trauma (vehicles, predators), infectious disease spread by other cats (such as feline leukemia and FIV), and parasites. Supervised outdoor access — a leash and harness walk, or a secure enclosed patio — gives a cat enrichment without the mortality risk of free roaming.

Cat life stages and human-year equivalents

Cats do not age on a straight line. The American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) formula, cited by PetMD, holds that a cat reaches roughly 15 human years by age 1 and 24 human years by age 2, then adds about 4 human years for every calendar year after that. Cornell University's Riney Feline Health Center arrives at similar numbers, placing a 10-year-old cat near 53, a 12-year-old near 61, and a 15-year-old near 73 in human terms. (Exact estimates vary by a few years between experts; both are cited below.)

Vets group a cat's life into four stages, each with different health priorities:

Cat ageLife stageHuman-year equivalent
Birth – 1 yearKitten0 – 15
1 – 6 yearsYoung adult15 – 40
6 – 10 yearsMature adult40 – 56
10 – 14 yearsSenior56 – 72
15+ yearsSuper senior (geriatric)73+ (Cornell); ~76 (AVMA)

Kittens grow and socialize rapidly and need growth-formulated food and their core vaccines. Young adults are physically mature and prone to weight gain, so portion control matters. Mature adults begin slowing down, and Cornell recommends annual bloodwork to catch early kidney, liver, or thyroid changes. Cats 10 and older are seniors: Cornell and PetMD both advise exams and lab work every six months at this stage, since organ health can shift quickly and cats hide illness well.

Average lifespan by cat breed

Breed tilts the numbers, but less than many owners assume. Mixed-breed (crossbred) cats actually outlive purebreds on average — roughly 14 years versus 12.5 years for purebreds, per veterinarian Dr. Mary Gardner, cited by PetMD — thanks to hybrid vigor. Among popular breeds, larger cats tend to land at the shorter end and lithe Oriental breeds at the longer end.

BreedAverage lifespanNotes
Siamese15 – 20 yearsGenerally hardy; one of the longest-living popular breeds
Balinese18 – 22 yearsLonghaired Siamese variant; can reach the low 20s
Russian Blue15 – 20 yearsRobust natural breed
American Shorthair15 – 20 yearsEasy-going, low-maintenance
Burmese10 – 17 yearsSocial and long-lived with good care
Ragdoll13 – 18 yearsLarge cat; keep lean to protect joints
Maine Coon~13 yearsOne of the shortest averages; prone to HCM and hip dysplasia
Savannah12 – 20 yearsServal hybrid; broad range
Mixed breed / domestic shorthair~14 years (often 15–20)Hybrid vigor usually adds years over purebreds

These ranges come from PetMD's breed data. Note the Maine Coon — a perennially popular breed — sits at roughly 13 years, the short end of the spectrum, largely because its size predisposes it to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (a heart disease) and hip dysplasia. The Siamese, by contrast, commonly reaches 15–20. For comparison with other companion animals, cats outlive most dogs; see our guide to how long dogs live.

Factors that affect lifespan

Most of a cat's potential lifespan is determined by a handful of controllable factors rather than luck:

  • Indoor lifestyle. The gap between a 15–20 year indoor cat and a 2–5 year outdoor cat is the largest single factor in feline longevity.
  • Diet and weight. A complete, life-stage-appropriate diet protects organs and immunity. Obesity is directly linked to shorter lifespan, arthritis, and diabetes — PetMD notes overweight and obese cats do not live as long as lean ones.
  • Preventive veterinary care. Vaccines, parasite control, and routine bloodwork catch disease early. Cats hide symptoms, so annual (and biannual for seniors) exams matter more than they seem to.
  • Spaying or neutering. Fixed cats live longer, largely because spaying sharply reduces the risk of mammary and reproductive cancers and removes hormone-driven roaming and fighting.
  • Genetics and breed. Purebred status and breed-specific disease (HCM in Maine Coons, kidney issues in Persians, retinal disease in Balinese) set the upper and lower bounds.
  • Dental health. Periodontal disease is tied to kidney and heart disease; daily tooth brushing is one of the highest-return habits for extending a cat's life.
  • Enrichment and stress. Indoor cats need play, climbing space, and mental stimulation to stay active and at a healthy weight.

How to help your cat live longer

Translating those factors into a daily routine is straightforward. Cornell's Riney Feline Health Center and PetMD converge on the same core advice:

  • Feed measured meals of a complete diet matched to life stage (kitten, adult, senior), and keep your cat at a lean body condition — ask your vet to score body condition annually.
  • Keep the cat indoors, or offer supervised outdoor time only on a harness or in a secure enclosure.
  • Spay or neuter, ideally around 6 months, to cut cancer and roaming risk.
  • Stay current on vaccines and parasite prevention tailored to your cat's lifestyle — indoor cats still need core vaccines.
  • Brush teeth daily with pet-specific toothpaste and schedule professional dental cleanings as your vet recommends.
  • See the vet annually for cats under 10, and every 6 months for seniors, with baseline bloodwork to track kidney, thyroid, and liver values.
  • Adapt the environment as your cat ages: low-sided litter boxes, orthopedic beds, joint supplements, and easy access to food and water for arthritic seniors.

One reminder Cornell stresses: never assume a change in an older cat — weight loss, litter-box misses, night vocalizing, or reduced grooming — is simply old age. Those are often treatable signals of kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, arthritis, or dental pain. Early intervention is the difference between a cat that fades at 12 and one that thrives past 18.

The oldest cats on record

The verified record belongs to Creme Puff of Austin, Texas, who died in 2005 at 38 years and 3 days old, per Guinness World Records. A cat in the same home, Granpa Rexs Allen, lived to 34. These are outliers, not expectations — but they show the upper boundary of what's possible when genetics, indoor safety, and decades of consistent care line up. For smaller companion animals with much shorter lifespans, see our guides to how long rabbits live and how long hamsters live.

guides.title: How Long Does a Dog Live? Average Lifespan by Size
guides.excerpt: Dogs live 10-13 years on average. Small breeds reach 15+ years while giant breeds average 8-10. See lifespan by breed size, life stages, and longevity tips.
guides.content:
How Long Does a Dog Live?

A dog lives roughly 10 to 13 years on average, but the real answer depends almost entirely on size. Small breeds routinely reach 10 to 15 years (some top 18), medium breeds average 10 to 13 years, large breeds 8 to 12 years, and giant breeds just 8 to 10 years, according to breed-size data published by the American Kennel Club (AKC).1 That size gap is the single biggest predictor of a dog's lifespan — bigger dogs age at an accelerated pace, so a 7-year-old Great Dane is already a senior while a 7-year-old Chihuahua is only middle-aged.

If you are planning for a new puppy — or wondering how long dogs are pregnant before they arrive — see our related dog gestation guide. For other companion animals, our cat lifespan and rabbit lifespan guides break down those species.

Average Lifespan by Breed Size

The AKC groups dogs by size because, unlike most mammals — where bigger species live longer — the opposite is true inside the dog family. Scientists suspect large breeds grow so fast from puppy to adult that they accumulate age-related cell damage, and cancer, sooner.1

Breed sizeTypical weightAverage lifespanExample breeds
Small / toyUnder ~20 lb10–15 years (some to 18)Chihuahua, Pomeranian, Yorkshire Terrier, Pug
Medium~20–50 lb10–13 yearsFrench Bulldog, Cocker Spaniel, Border Collie
Large~50–90 lb8–12 yearsLabrador Retriever, Golden Retriever, German Shepherd, Boxer
GiantOver ~90 lb8–10 yearsGreat Dane, Bernese Mountain Dog, Mastiff, Irish Wolfhound

Across nearly 169,000 dogs in one large study, median lifespan was about 14.95 years for small dogs, 13.86 for medium, and 13.38 for large — body size mattered more than whether the dog was purebred.2

Average Lifespan of Popular Breeds

These are AKC-reported lifespan ranges for common breeds. Individual dogs often fall outside these bands depending on genetics, weight, and care.1

BreedSizeTypical lifespan
ChihuahuaSmall15–17 years
PomeranianSmall14–16 years
Yorkshire TerrierSmall12–15 years
Cocker SpanielMedium13–15 years
French BulldogMedium11–13 years
BoxerMedium/Large10–12 years
Labrador RetrieverLarge11–13 years
Golden RetrieverLarge10–12 years
German ShepherdLarge10–12 years
RottweilerLarge10–12 years
Great DaneGiant8–10 years
Bernese Mountain DogGiant7–10 years
Irish WolfhoundGiant8–10 years

Dog Life Stages and Human-Year Equivalents

The old “one dog year = seven human years” rule is inaccurate, the AVMA notes — dogs age far faster in their first two years, then the rate slows and varies by size.3 A common veterinary estimate is that a dog's first year equals about 15 human years, the second adds roughly 9 more, and each subsequent year adds about 4–5 human years depending on size.4

Life stageDog ageApprox. human equivalent
PuppyBirth – 6–12 monthsInfant – teenager
Adolescent / Junior1–2 years~15–24 human years
Adult2–6 years (giant) / 2–7+ years (small)~25–50 human years
SeniorLast ~25% of expected lifespan~50+ human years

The AVMA considers a dog “senior” at roughly the last quarter of its breed's expected lifespan, which lands earlier for big dogs:3

  • Small/toy breeds (<20 lb): senior around 8–11 years
  • Medium breeds (20–50 lb): senior around 8–10 years
  • Large breeds (50–90 lb): senior around 8–9 years
  • Giant breeds (>90 lb): senior around 6–7 years

Factors That Affect Lifespan

  • Body size and weight. Size is the dominant factor — giant breeds live roughly half as long as toy breeds. Keeping a dog lean matters too: research suggests obese dogs may live about 2 years less than dogs at a healthy weight, and roughly 34% of U.S. adult dogs are overweight or obese.1
  • Breed and genetics. Some breeds carry inherited disease risk (e.g., cancer in Golden Retrievers, heart issues in Dobermans). Responsible breeders screen for these, and breeds with larger gene pools tend to live slightly longer.2
  • Diet and nutrition. A complete, portion-controlled diet and avoidance of toxic foods reduce obesity-related disease and support longevity.
  • Neutering / spaying. Spay-neuter can reduce the risk of certain cancers (e.g., mammary, testicular) and pyometra, though the optimal timing varies by breed and size — discuss it with your vet.
  • Preventive veterinary care. Vaccines, parasite control, dental care, and regular checkups catch problems early. Early death in dogs under two is most often linked to trauma, congenital disease, or infection, per the AKC.1
  • Safety and lifestyle. Leashing, fencing, and supervising puppies prevent trauma (cars, fights) — a leading cause of preventable death.
  • Dental health. Periodontal disease is tied to systemic illness; routine cleaning is an underrated longevity lever.

How to Help Your Dog Live Longer

Practical, evidence-backed steps owners can take:1

  • Feed a balanced diet and measure portions to maintain a healthy body condition.
  • Keep your dog lean — you should feel ribs without excess fat cover.
  • Stay current on vaccines, heartworm, flea, and tick preventives.
  • Schedule annual (or twice-yearly for seniors) vet exams with bloodwork.
  • Know your breed's specific disease risks and their early symptoms.
  • Brush teeth and schedule professional dental cleanings.
  • Provide daily exercise and mental stimulation appropriate to age and breed.
  • Restrict access to toxins, roads, and aggressive animals.

Because giant breeds become seniors as early as 6, the AKC and AVMA both recommend stepping up to twice-yearly veterinary visits, senior blood panels, and joint/weight management as your dog enters its final life quarter.3

What Is the Oldest Dog on Record?

The longest reliably verified canine lifespan belongs to Bluey, an Australian Cattle Dog who died in 1939 at 29 years and 5 months.5 A more recent claim — Bobi, a Rafeiro do Alentejo reportedly 31 — made headlines in 2023, but Guinness World Records suspended and later stripped that title in 2024 after veterinarians and researchers questioned the evidence, leaving Bluey's record as the standing benchmark.5 Treat any “30-year-old dog” claim with skepticism; true exceptions to the size rules above are extraordinarily rare.

The Bottom Line

So, how long does a dog live? Expect 10–13 years as a rough all-breed average, plan for 15+ from a small breed, and 8–10 from a giant breed. The levers you control — lean weight, preventive vet care, dental health, and safety — reliably push your dog toward the top of its breed's range rather than the bottom.1

Sources: 1. AKC, “How Long Do Dogs Live?”; 2. AKC, “Why Do Small Dogs Live Longer Than Large Dogs?”; 3. AVMA, “Caring for Senior Cats and Dogs”; 4. UC Davis School of Veterinary Medicine, “Calculating Your Dog's Age”; 5. NPR (2024), on Bobi's title being stripped and Bluey's record.

guides.title: How Long Does a Horse Live? Average Equine Lifespan
guides.excerpt: A horse lives 25–30 years on average; ponies can reach 30–35. Learn equine life stages, horse-to-human age equivalents, care tips, and the oldest horse ever (62).
guides.content:
How long does a horse live?

A healthy domestic horse lives 25–30 years on average, and many well-cared-for animals now reach their mid-30s. Size shifts that number considerably: ponies routinely live 30–35 years and frequently into their 40s, while large draft breeds tend to sit on the shorter end of the range. In the wild, with no veterinary or dental care available, a Mustang or feral equine typically lives closer to 15 years.

These figures are averages, not ceilings. Improved nutrition, parasite control, dentistry, and sports medicine have pushed equine life expectancy steadily upward — roughly a quarter of today's horse population is over 15 years old. The oldest horse ever reliably recorded, an English barge horse named Old Billy, died in 1822 at the age of 62.

So when you ask how long a horse lives, the honest answer is: a quarter-century is normal, three decades is realistic with good care, and anything past 35 puts your horse in rare, exceptional company.

Horse life stages and human-year equivalents

Horses move through six broadly recognised life stages, and their care needs change at each one. Because there is no single, scientifically standardised "horse year" formula (unlike the rough rules used for dogs), the human-equivalent ages below are a practical approximation. A common rule of thumb counts about 6.5 human years per horse year up to age 4, then roughly 2.5 human years for each horse year after that. Treat it as a rough guide, not a precise clock — individual horses age at different rates.

Life stageHorse ageApprox. human equivalentWhat is happening
FoalBirth–12 months0–6Nurses the mare, then weaned at 4–7 months; very rapid early growth
Yearling1–2 years6–13Skeleton and coordination develop; growth plates still open
Young adult2–4 years13–26Most growth plates close by age 3; training under saddle often begins
Adult (prime)4–15 years26–54Physically mature; permanent teeth in by ~5 years; peak athletic years
Senior / geriatric15–25 years54–79Past physiological peak; only ~25% of horses remain past 15
Very old25–30+ years79–90+Rare territory — horses past 30 are classed as "very old" and make up only a small minority of the population

A note on telling a horse's age: veterinarians estimate a young horse's age from tooth eruption, because permanent dentition is typically complete by about 5 years. After that, the method becomes unreliable, as wear varies with diet, breed, and dental care. Per the Merck Veterinary Manual, equine teeth erupt continually to offset wear at roughly 2.5 mm per year until around age 17 — which is exactly why dentistry becomes so important in older horses.

Factors that affect lifespan

No single variable decides how long a horse lives, but the following factors consistently push the number up or down:

  • Size and build. As with dogs, smaller equines outlive larger ones. Ponies often reach their late 30s and sometimes their 40s, while heavy draft breeds generally average shorter lives than light riding horses. Breed itself has little independent effect once size is accounted for.
  • Diet and dental health. Forage quality and the ability to chew it are the backbone of longevity. Older horses lose grinding surface on their teeth and may need soaked "senior" feeds to maintain weight.
  • Veterinary and preventive care. Annual exams, vaccinations, faecal-based (targeted) deworming, and early detection of conditions such as PPID (Equine Cushing's) and arthritis add real years. Colic and lameness remain the leading reasons horses are lost.
  • Genetics and inherited disease. Some breeds carry manageable but serious risks — for example, severe combined immunodeficiency in Arabians or hyperkalemic periodic paralysis (HYPP) in Quarter Horses — that can shorten life if untested and unmanaged.
  • Use and workload. Racehorses peak at 2–5 years, while Olympic-level show jumpers peak around 10–14. Hard competitive use early in life can influence soundness — and therefore useful lifespan — later on.
  • Environment. Access to shelter, clean water, consistent turnout, and protection from temperature extremes matters most at the extremes of life: young foals and seniors both regulate body temperature poorly.
  • Wild vs. domestic. A wild horse that slows down from arthritis or can no longer chew effectively cannot keep up with the herd. That single disadvantage is why feral lifespans sit near 15 years versus 25–30+ for domesticated horses.

How to help your horse live longer

Longevity in horses is mostly the product of steady, unglamorous husbandry repeated for decades. The highest-impact habits are:

  • Feed for the life stage. Match forage, concentrate, and minerals to your horse's age and workload. Track body condition score, and shift to a senior ration when the teeth can no longer handle long-stem forage alone.
  • Stay on top of dentistry. Regular floating keeps the grinding surfaces even so the horse can actually chew. A horse that "quids" (drops half-chewed balls of hay) or loses weight should have its mouth examined promptly.
  • Maintain the hooves. Routine trimming or shoeing prevents thrush, abscesses, and the kind of compensatory lameness that accelerates arthritis.
  • Keep moving. Light, consistent exercise preserves muscle and joint mobility in older horses. Ask your vet what intensity suits your individual animal.
  • Schedule annual veterinary exams, including faecal egg counts so you deworm strategically rather than on a blind calendar, plus screening for endocrine disease in seniors.
  • Manage colic risk. Consistent feeding routines, always-available clean water (warm it in winter to encourage drinking), and good dentistry all reduce colic, since dental disease also predisposes horses to choke.

Even with excellent care, some risks — colic, accidental injury — can affect any horse at any age. As your horse enters its geriatric years, the goal shifts from performance toward comfort and quality of life.

The oldest horses on record

The longest-lived horse ever verified is Old Billy, foaled in 1760 in Woolston, Lancashire, England, and recorded by Guinness World Records as having died on 27 November 1822 at the age of 62. Billy worked much of his life towing barges for the Mersey and Irwell Navigation Company — a reminder that a hard-working life and a long one are not mutually exclusive.

Among Thoroughbreds, the longest-lived on record is Tango Duke (foaled 1935 in Australia), who died in 1978 at the age of 42. These outliers show the biological ceiling, not the expectation: reaching 35 is genuinely impressive, and reaching 40 puts a horse in rare company.

How horses compare with other companion animals

Horses are among the longest-lived common companion animals. A horse's 25–30 years vastly outlasts a typical dog or cat, and a pony's 35+ years is extraordinary for any mammal of that size. For perspective, compare these figures with how long dogs live and how long cats live — both species average well under two decades.

Equine development is also stretched out. A mare carries her foal for roughly 11 months (about 340 days, with a normal range of 320–365), so a newborn foal arrives far more mature than a puppy or kitten. That is a striking contrast when you look at how long dogs are pregnant — about nine weeks, less than a quarter of a horse's gestation. If you are weighing the commitment of smaller pets, a horse also outlasts how long rabbits live many times over.

The bottom line

A domestic horse is a 25–30-year commitment, frequently stretching into the mid-30s with good care and occasionally far beyond — Old Billy's 62 years has gone unbeaten for two centuries. Of the levers an owner actually controls, size is fixed at purchase, but dentistry, preventive medicine, sensible workload, and a steady routine are the day-to-day decisions that decide whether your horse lands near the bottom or the top of that range.

sources.title: Oldest Goldfish Ever (Tish, 43 years)

guides.content:
How Long Do Betta Fish Live? The Average Betta Lifespan, Explained

Betta fish (the Siamese fighting fish, Betta splendens) live an average of 3 to 5 years in captivity when they receive proper care, with most home-kept pets realistically landing in the 2 to 4 year band that reflects typical household conditions. That is meaningfully longer than the roughly 2 years the species lives under controlled laboratory conditions, where its lifespan has been measured at "around 2 y" (and likely shorter still in the wild, where predation and disease take a toll). With genuinely excellent lifelong husbandry, PetMD notes that some individuals have been reported reaching about 10 years — though such ages are rare, and any claim well beyond that is anecdotal and unverified (Guinness World Records does list an "oldest goldfish" — Tish, who lived 43 years — but lists no equivalent verified longevity record for bettas).

So the honest, short answer to how long do betta fish live is: expect 3–5 years with good care, plan for 2–4 in an average setup, and treat anything past 5 as a genuine achievement. How close your fish gets to the top of that range is determined almost entirely by tank size, water quality, temperature, and diet — the four levers we break down below.

Life stageTypical ageWhat's happeningHuman-age equivalent (approx.)
Egg0–3 daysFertilized eggs are tended by the male in a bubble nest; they hatch in roughly 24–72 hours at warm temperatures.Infancy
Fry (newly hatched)3 days – 2 weeksLives off its yolk sac, then begins free swimming and hunting microscopic prey; very fragile.Toddler
Juvenile2 weeks – 3 monthsRapid growth; color and fin type start to show. Peer-reviewed colony data shows bettas can mature and successfully mate as early as ~10 weeks after fertilization.Child → adolescent
Young adult (prime)3 months – 1.5 yearsFull color, peak activity and breeding condition; the stage most pet-store bettas are sold at.~20s into 30s
Mature adult1.5 – 3 yearsStill vigorous; this is where well-cared-for captives pull ahead of the ~2-year laboratory average.~40s into 50s
Senior3 – 5+ yearsColors may fade, fins thin, appetite and activity slow. Reaching 5 is considered old age; past 5 is exceptional.~60s+

Note: bettas do not have a formal, clinically standardized "years-to-human-years" conversion the way dogs are sometimes given one. The right-hand column is an illustrative comparison, not a veterinary standard; the stage age ranges are an approximate synthesis built around verified anchors (3–5 years captive, ~2 years in the lab, sexual maturity around 10 weeks).

Factors That Affect a Betta's Lifespan

The gap between a betta that dies at 8 months and one that lives past 4 years is almost always explained by husbandry, not genetics. The biggest levers:

  • Tank size. Bowls and unfiltered vases shorten life. A board-certified zoological-medicine veterinarian at the University of Illinois states bluntly that bettas "should not live in bowls" and need a 5-gallon tank minimum, with larger preferred; PetMD lists 2.5 gallons as an absolute floor but calls 5–10 gallons "ideal" because bigger volumes keep temperature and water chemistry stable.
  • Water quality. Ammonia and nitrite from waste and uneaten food are the single largest killer of captive bettas. A cycled, gently filtered tank plus regular partial water changes (about 15–25% weekly) is the baseline. Peer-reviewed husbandry guidance stresses that "good water quality is critical" because bettas are highly susceptible to illness when water degrades.
  • Temperature stability. Bettas are tropical fish. Both PetMD and the University of Illinois place the ideal range at 76–81°F (24–27°C); the published laboratory standard uses 28°C (~82°F). Stability matters more than the exact number — swings stress the immune system. Use a heater and a thermometer.
  • Diet. Bettas are carnivores that evolved to eat insects and larvae, not plants. High-protein betta pellets daily, with treats like bloodworms or brine shrimp in moderation, is the evidence-based feeding pattern. Overfeeding causes obesity and fouls the water; a practical rule is to feed only what the fish consumes in 3–5 minutes (roughly the size of its eye) once or twice a day.
  • Stress and tank mates. Males must be housed alone — two males will fight, often fatally. Constant sight of a rival (even in a neighboring tank) raises chronic stress. Compatible companions in a large enough tank include snails, ghost shrimp, African dwarf frogs, and small peaceful fish like corydoras or neon tetras.
  • Genetics and age at purchase. Most store-bought bettas are already several months old by the time they are sold, so a "new" fish may be closer to mid-life than you might assume. Heavy inbreeding for ornamental traits can also cap lifespan regardless of care.
  • Disease vigilance. Watch for clamped fins, white spots, lethargy, bloating, or hanging at the surface. Because fish decline fast, the first response to any change is to test the water and do a partial change — water issues are the root cause far more often than any exotic disease.

Practical Betta Care: The Setup That Reaches Year 4 and 5

Translating those factors into a routine, here is the care profile that the veterinary sources in this guide converge on:

Tank: 5 gallons minimum, cycled, with a lid (bettas jump). A low-flow or adjustable filter protects the labyrinth fish's delicate fins from suction. Add smooth hides and live or silk plants; avoid sharp plastic decorations that tear fins.

Water: 76–81°F with a heater matched to tank size (~3–5 watts per gallon). Test weekly for ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, and pH; keep pH stable (around 7 is fine, and bettas tolerate a wide 6.5–7.8). Always treat tap water with a dechlorinator — chlorine and chloramine suppress the immune system. Change 15–25% of the water weekly rather than doing rare "deep cleans" that crash the beneficial bacteria.

Food: A quality betta pellet as the staple, fed once or twice daily in tiny portions, with occasional freeze-dried or frozen bloodworms, brine shrimp, or daphnia. Remove uneaten food within minutes.

Companionship: A single male betta is a complete, happy pet on his own. If you want a community or a female sorority, size up to 10 gallons or more and add only peaceful, non-fin-nipping species — and be ready to separate individuals if personalities clash.

Health check-ins: A 30-second daily look (color, fins, appetite, activity) plus a weekly water test catches problems while they're still water-quality fixes rather than veterinary emergencies. If you want maximum lifespan, find an exotic/aquatic veterinarian before you need one in a crisis.

The Oldest Betta Fish: What's Actually Documented

Search "oldest betta" and you'll find hobbyist threads claiming 7, 9, even 15-year-old fish. The verifiable record is much harder to pin down: PetMD cites reports of bettas reaching roughly 10 years under excellent care, but there is no authenticated, independently verified longevity record for the species on par with documented record-holders in other pet categories. Treat any specific claim past about 5–7 years with healthy skepticism unless it is documented from hatching with photos and veterinary records — and treat any claim past 10 as folklore. The realistic ceiling a careful owner can aim for is the 5-to-7-year range, and hitting 3–5 years already puts a betta ahead of the species' ~2-year laboratory lifespan.

How a Betta's Lifespan Compares to Other Pets

At 3–5 years, a betta is a short commitment relative to most mammals — for context, a well-cared-for cat reaches the mid-to-high teens, and even small mammals routinely outlive fish (see how that stacks up in our guides on hamster lifespan and rabbit lifespan, or compare with a typical cat's lifespan). What a betta gives up in years it makes up for in low space and cost — but only if you give it the heated, filtered, adequately sized tank it actually needs rather than the bowl it's usually sold with.

Sources: PetMD (Perry, DVM, 2024; Zayas, DVM, 2026), WebMD (Flowers, DVM, 2025), University of Illinois College of Veterinary Medicine (Dr. Krista Keller, DACZM), Lichak et al., 2022 (peer-reviewed, PMC/NIH), and Guinness World Records (oldest goldfish record, for the Tish clarification). This guide is for general pet-owner education and is not a substitute for evaluation by an aquatic veterinarian.

guides.title: How Long Do Rabbits Live? Pet Rabbit Lifespan Guide
guides.excerpt: Pet rabbits live 8-12 years with good care, while wild rabbits average under 2. Learn how breed, diet, spay/neuter and indoor living shape rabbit lifespan.
guides.content:
Pet rabbits live 8 to 12 years — wild rabbits rarely reach 2

A healthy pet rabbit kept indoors with good diet and routine veterinary care typically lives 8 to 12 years. The Merck Veterinary Manual states that rabbits "fed a suitable diet and kept in a healthy environment can live as long as 10 to 12 years," and VCA Animal Hospitals note that rabbits can live up to 12 years, with validated reports of rabbits living to the ripe old age of 15. Wild rabbits, by contrast, have a life expectancy of less than two years. So the answer to "how long do rabbits live" depends almost entirely on whether the rabbit is a pampered indoor pet or a wild animal — and on the care decisions you make.

It is worth a reality check, though. A 2019 peer-reviewed UK study of 6,349 pet rabbits (O'Neill et al., published in Vet Record) found the average pet rabbit lives only about 4.3 years — far below the biological ceiling — because of preventable problems such as gut stasis, flystrike, and reproductive cancers. The gap between how long rabbits can live and how long they actually live is exactly what the care habits below are designed to close.

Rabbit gestation and life stages

Before a rabbit ever reaches adulthood, it has already come through one of the fastest pregnancies in the mammal world. Rabbits are pregnant for roughly 31 to 33 days, according to the Merck Veterinary Manual, with smaller litters (four kits or fewer) tending to carry a few days longer than large litters. For comparison, that is far shorter than how long dogs are pregnant (about 63 days) and considerably longer than the roughly 16- to 22-day pregnancy of hamsters.

Pregnancy stageTimingWhat is developingSigns an owner may notice
Early gestationDays 1–7Fertilized eggs travel to the uterus and implant; embryos begin formingUsually no visible signs; appetite and behavior often look normal
Mid gestationDays 8–21Organs develop, bones calcify, fur follicles form on the kitsSlight weight gain, increased thirst, rounding belly; a veterinarian may be able to feel fetuses in the abdomen around day 12 (Merck)
Late gestationDays 22–30Kits grow fur and shift into birth positionNoticeable belly, heavy nesting behavior, the doe begins pulling fur from her body to line the nest
Kindling (birth)Days 31–33Doe gives birth to 4–12 kits that are naked, blind and deafKits in a fur-lined nest; the doe usually feeds them only once or twice a day

Sources: Merck Veterinary Manual (Breeding and Reproduction of Rabbits); Mass Audubon notes wild cottontail gestation lasts less than 30 days with litters averaging five young.

Once born, rabbits move through clear life stages. There is no official veterinary standard for converting rabbit years to human years the way there is for dogs, so the human equivalents below are a rough, widely used guide and should be treated as approximate.

Life stageRabbit ageApprox. human equivalentNotes
Kit (baby)Birth – 6 months0 – 18 yearsWeaned around 4–6 weeks; small breeds reach sexual maturity by 3.5–4 months (Merck)
Junior / young6 – 12 months18 – 21 yearsMedium and large breeds finish maturing; ideal age for spay/neuter
Adult (prime)1 – 5 years21 – 45 yearsHealthiest, most active period; most preventable problems begin here with poor diet
Mature adult5 – 7 years45 – 60 yearsMetabolism slows; watch for weight gain, dental disease, arthritis
Senior7+ years60+ yearsIncreased risk of cancer, kidney disease and dental issues; biannual vet checks advised

Factors that affect lifespan

Why do some rabbits reach 12 while the average pet rabbit in the UK study made it only to 4.3? The variables below explain almost all of that gap.

  • Indoor vs. outdoor housing. This is the single biggest divider. WebMD's veterinary reviewers point out that outdoor rabbits face predators, weather stress, and mosquito-borne diseases such as myxomatosis, which is "invariably deadly" — one of several reasons rabbits are now recommended as indoor pets.
  • Spay or neuter status. VCA Animal Hospitals explain that spayed and neutered rabbits "tend to enjoy longer, healthier lives," because cancers of the ovaries, uterus, and mammary glands are a common cause of death in intact females. The RVC data backs this: females averaged just 3.7 years versus 5.2 years for males — a gap driven in part by reproductive cancers in unspayed does.
  • Breed and body size. WebMD notes that, as with dogs, "larger rabbit breeds live shorter lives than dwarf breeds, and purebred rabbits have shorter lives than mixed breeds." Giant breeds such as the Flemish Giant sit at the shorter end of the range — WebMD notes a large purebred may reach about 10 years — while small and dwarf breeds commonly reach the 8–12 year upper end.
  • Diet. The Merck Veterinary Manual ties longevity directly to a "suitable diet." Rabbits need constant access to grass hay (timothy or orchard), which grinds down their continuously growing teeth and keeps the gut moving — gut stasis was among the most common causes of death recorded in the RVC study.
  • Early illness detection. Rabbits evolved as prey animals and hide symptoms remarkably well, so by the time a rabbit looks sick it is often seriously ill. A rabbit-savvy veterinarian and annual (ideally biannual for seniors) exams catch problems like overgrown molars and respiratory infection early.
  • Exercise, enrichment and companionship. Rabbits are active and social. Several hours of supervised exercise daily, a rabbit-proofed space, and ideally a bonded companion all reduce stress-related and obesity-related disease.

How to help your rabbit live longer

Turning the 4.3-year average into a 10-plus-year lifespan comes down to a handful of repeatable habits, all of which are supported by the veterinary sources above.

Build the diet around hay. The largest share of a rabbit's daily intake should be grass hay (timothy, orchard or brome), supplemented with a daily assortment of leafy greens and only a small measured portion of high-fiber pellets. Avoid muesli-style mixes, which encourage selective eating and dental disease. Fresh grass and sugary items like carrots should be treats, not staples — WebMD warns they are too sugar-rich and can impair digestion.

Keep your rabbit indoors. Indoor housing removes the threat of predators and the mosquitoes that carry myxomatosis and Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease. If your rabbit spends time outside, use mosquito netting and never leave them unsupervised.

Spay or neuter by around 6 months. Beyond preventing reproduction — VCA notes a single female can produce up to 168 kits in a year — altering dramatically lowers reproductive-cancer risk in females and reduces territorial aggression and urine-spraying in both sexes.

Find a rabbit-savvy vet and schedule regular checkups. Rabbits are often classed as "exotic" patients, so confirm your vet has rabbit experience. Annual exams, and biannual exams once your rabbit passes age 6–7, catch dental disease, respiratory infections and masses while they are still treatable.

Rabbit-proof and exercise. Give your rabbit several hours out of the enclosure each day in a bunny-proofed room, and protect electrical cords and carpet edges, which VCA warns can cause electrocution or dangerous intestinal blockages. Provide chew toys to keep teeth worn and a large enclosure (at least 5 square feet for larger breeds, per the American Rabbit Breeders Association) as a base.

Prevent flystrike and monitor closely. Flystrike — when flies lay eggs on a soiled rear end and maggots eat into the skin — was the single most common recorded cause of death (10.9%) in the RVC study. Daily checks, a clean rear end, and soiled-bedding removal are life-saving routines in warm months.

The bottom line

So, how long do rabbits live? With indoor housing, a hay-based diet, spay or neuter surgery, and a rabbit-savvy vet, expect a pet rabbit to be with you for about 8 to 12 years, and sometimes longer — compared with how long cats live or the typical dog lifespan, rabbits sit in a similar decade-plus window despite their small size. Wild rabbits, facing predators and disease, live less than two years on average. The biology gives your bunny a long life; your care is what determines whether it gets to live it.
