guides.title: How Long Does an Oil Change Take? Shop, Dealer & DIY Times
guides.excerpt: An oil change takes 15-45 minutes - about 15-30 min at a quick-lube, 30-60 min at a dealer, and 30-45 min DIY. See what slows it down and how to plan ahead.
guides.content:
How Long Does an Oil Change Take? The Short Answer

An oil change takes about 15 to 45 minutes on average, depending on where you have it done. A drive-through quick-lube shop can get you back on the road in 15 minutes or less, a full-service repair shop or dealership usually runs 30 to 60 minutes once you factor in waiting time, and doing it yourself at home takes roughly 30 to 45 minutes once the car is set up. The actual labor is short; almost all of the variation comes from where you go, how busy the service bay is, and whether the technician bundles in a multi-point inspection.

If you are scheduling around a lunch break, plan for the upper end of that range. Kelley Blue Book's guidance is refreshingly blunt: even though dealership express lanes and quick-lube chains advertise getting you "in and out in 30 minutes or less," their real-world advice is to set aside a full hour for the service, including waiting time.

Average Oil Change Times at a Glance

Before getting into the variables, here is the baseline most drivers can expect for each type of service:

Where you get it doneTypical time (including wait)What you are paying for
Quick-lube / express shop15 - 30 minutesSpeed; oil and filter change plus a basic fluid top-off
Full-service repair shop30 - 45 minutesOil change plus a multi-point inspection
Dealership service lane30 - 60 minutesFactory-trained techs, OEM parts, often a longer queue
DIY in your garage30 - 45 minutes (up to 60)Savings and familiarity with your own vehicle

The 15-minute figure is a real one, not marketing fluff. Jiffy Lube explicitly markets its Signature Service oil change as completed "in 15 minutes or less," and AutoZone notes that if a quick-lube can see you immediately, the work itself can take as little as 15 minutes. The longer estimates almost always include time spent waiting behind other customers.

What Affects How Long an Oil Change Takes

The same car can spend 15 minutes or an hour in the bay depending on a handful of factors. Here is what actually moves the clock:

FactorEffect on how long it takes
Where you go (quick-lube vs. full-service vs. dealer)Largest swing of all - from ~15 min at a specialist quick-lube to 60+ min at a busy dealer
Wait time / shop backlogAdds 10 - 30 minutes or more; the work itself is fast, the queue is not
Vehicle accessibility (drain plug & filter location)Hard-to-reach plugs or a skid plate add 5 - 15 minutes; trucks and full-size SUVs take longer than compact cars
Oil typeSynthetic flows freely and drains fast; cold conventional oil drains slowly and can add a few minutes
Add-on servicesA new filter is normally included, but a full multi-point inspection can add up to 10 minutes, and a tire rotation adds more
DIY experience and toolsAn experienced home mechanic finishes in about 30 minutes; a first-timer can take an hour plus cleanup and used-oil disposal

Two of those factors deserve a closer look. The first is queue time - AutoZone pegs the in-shop range at 15 to 45 minutes and notes that the longer end almost always reflects customer backlog rather than slower work. Booking the first appointment of the day, or showing up mid-morning on a weekday, is the single biggest time-saver available to you.

The second is the multi-point inspection. Quick-lube shops specialize in speed and focus on draining the old oil, replacing the filter, and topping off fluids. Full-service shops and dealerships use the visit to also check brakes, tires, belts, and fluid levels, which is why a 15-minute job stretches toward 45 or 60. That extra time is not waste - it is where early problems get caught - but it does change how you should plan your day.

How Long Each Part of the Service Takes

If you have ever wondered why a 15-minute job can fill an hour, here is how the time breaks down inside a typical visit (these are typical estimates rather than figures from any single shop):

  • Pull-in, paperwork, and bay queue (5 - 20 min): Checking in and waiting for an open lift is usually the longest single chunk, especially at a dealership on a Saturday morning.
  • Lift the vehicle and drain the old oil (5 - 10 min): Synthetic oil drains quickly; cold conventional oil is thicker and slower, which is why some shops warm the engine first.
  • Replace the oil filter and refill (5 - 10 min): Most manufacturers recommend replacing the filter at every oil change, so this is normally bundled in rather than optional.
  • Lower, start, and verify the oil level (3 - 5 min): The technician runs the engine, checks for leaks, and confirms the dipstick reading.
  • Multi-point inspection and top-offs (0 - 15 min): Present at full-service shops and dealerships, absent or minimal at a quick-lube. This is also where a technician checks items like exterior lights, wiper blades, and battery water.

That last bullet is a good reason to pair your oil change with a quick mental checklist of your own. The same visit that tops off your washer fluid is an ideal moment to glance at the health of consumables - and since a quality car battery typically needs replacement every few years, having its voltage checked while the car is already in the bay costs you almost no extra time.

How to Make the Visit Faster (and Last Longer Between Changes)

You can shrink the time an oil change takes and stretch the interval before you need the next one. A few practical moves:

  • Book the first or second slot of the day. Backlog - not labor - is what turns 15 minutes into an hour. An early weekday appointment usually means you drive straight into an open bay.
  • Use the right oil for your engine. Modern vehicles on full-synthetic oil can typically go 7,500 to 10,000 miles between changes, and AAA cites intervals of 10,000 to 15,000 miles for synthetic oil. Conventional oil, by contrast, generally needs changing around every 5,000 miles, and synthetic blends fall in the middle at roughly 6,000 to 8,000 miles. Fewer visits means less total time spent waiting.
  • Follow the owner's manual, not the 3,000-mile sticker. The old "every 3 months or 3,000 miles" rule is outdated. AAA, Edmunds, and Kelley Blue Book all now recommend deferring to the manufacturer's schedule - often one year or 10,000 miles, whichever comes first - and trusting the car's oil-life monitoring system if it has one. Changing oil more often than recommended is harmless to the engine but hard on your wallet and your schedule.
  • Watch for "severe" driving conditions. Short trips of five miles or less, stop-and-go traffic, extreme heat or cold, dusty climates, and towing all degrade oil faster and call for a shorter interval. If any of those describe your commute, move to the more frequent schedule in your manual.
  • Bundle services when it makes sense. If you are already paying for the technician's time, adding a tire rotation (recommended every 5,000 to 8,000 miles) or a brake inspection is more efficient than booking a separate trip later.

DIY vs. Professional: Is It Worth Doing Yourself?

Changing your own oil is one of the few maintenance jobs still within reach of a home mechanic, and it can save you a meaningful amount - AAA estimates a DIY oil change averages about $40 versus a typical shop bill that can run $20 to $100 depending on the oil. The trade-off is time and effort. AutoZone notes that an experienced DIYer with the right tools can finish in about 30 minutes, but a first-timer should expect closer to an hour, plus cleanup and the trip to recycle the used oil. Quick-lube professionals change oil every day, which is why they can do in 15 minutes what might take you 45.

If your time is tight, the math often favors the shop. If you enjoy the work, want full control over the oil brand, or live far from a trusted mechanic, the garage is a perfectly good option - just budget the full hour and a safe way to get the old oil to a recycler.

The Bottom Line

So, how long does an oil change take? Plan for 15 to 45 minutes at a shop and 30 to 60 minutes at a dealership, with DIY landing around 30 to 45 minutes. The job itself is genuinely quick; the variables are the queue, the add-on inspection, and how accessible your particular vehicle is. Pick an off-peak slot, run the oil your manual specifies, and you will spend far less of your life waiting for the next one - especially on a modern engine that only needs service once a year or every 10,000 miles. And while the car is in the bay anyway, it is the perfect moment to check on your car battery's lifespan and the other consumables that keep you reliably on the road.

guides.title: How Long Does a Spray Tan Last? Days, Stages, and Tips
guides.excerpt: A spray tan lasts 7-10 days on average (lighter ~5, darker ~10). Learn the DHA science, fade stages, and dermatologist-backed tips to extend your glow.
guides.content:
How Long Does a Spray Tan Last? (Quick Answer)

A spray tan lasts 7 to 10 days on average, with most results falling in the 5- to 10-day range depending on the darkness of the solution and how you care for your skin. The active ingredient, dihydroxyacetone (DHA), only colors the top layer of your skin, and because that outer layer sheds and renews roughly every week, the color goes with it. Lighter shades fade in about 5 days, medium shades hold for 7-8 days, and darker shades can stretch to the full 10.

That timeline comes straight from dermatology sources. Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Dr. Jennifer Lucas explains that DHA reacts with proteins in the outermost skin cells to create a bronze pigment, but because "your skin is going to shed and exfoliate continually, replacing the outer cells weekly," a spray tan "only lasts about five to 10 days." Healthline similarly puts the average at up to 10 days, with shade-by-shade variation tied to DHA concentration.

This guide breaks down exactly what moves that number up or down, how the fade progresses day by day, and the aftercare that adds days to your glow. For the broader picture on UV tans, see our related how long does a tan last guide.

Factors That Change How Long Your Spray Tan Lasts

Three things set the ceiling on your tan's lifespan: how much DHA is in the solution, how you prepped your skin, and how you treat it afterward. The table below maps the biggest levers.

FactorEffect on DurationWhat's Happening
DHA concentration (shade depth)Lighter ~5 days; medium ~7-8 days; darker up to ~10 daysDarker solutions contain more DHA, so more pigment is deposited and it takes longer to shed away.
Exfoliation before the appointmentHelps color wear evenly and can extend the tanRemoving dead skin first gives DHA a fresh, even surface to bond with, so color wears off uniformly instead of patchy.
Skin moisture levelsWell-moisturized skin extends the tan; dry skin shortens itHydrated skin sheds more slowly. Dry, flaky skin accelerates cell turnover and strips color faster.
Chlorinated pools & hot tubsSignificantly shortens the tanChlorine is a chemical exfoliant that lifts color and dries skin, accelerating fade.
Hot showers & harsh soapsShortens the tanHeat opens pores and softens the skin barrier; stripping soaps speed cell loss.
Shaving & physical exfoliationRemoves a layer of color each timeEvery razor pass or scrub physically removes tanned cells.
Sweat & friction (tight clothes, workouts)Causes patchy, early fadeFriction rubs color off high-contact spots; sweat can lift the bronzer before DHA fully sets.

These variables all interact, which is why the same routine can produce different results on different people — your skin chemistry and habits are unique, and Healthline notes that how you care for your skin before and after the appointment plays a meaningful role alongside the DHA concentration itself.

How Long Each Stage Takes: The Fade Timeline

A spray tan moves through four fairly predictable stages as your skin cycles through its natural turnover. Here's what to expect from a typical medium-to-dark tan with reasonable aftercare:

  • Days 0-1 (Application & development): The bronzer you see immediately is just a color guide — the real tan is still developing underneath. DHA starts reacting with skin proteins within 2-4 hours and can continue developing for up to 24-72 hours, per Cleveland Clinic, so your final depth won't show until day two or three.
  • Days 2-4 (Peak color): Your tan reaches its darkest, most even point. Color looks richest and most uniform in this window — ideal for events.
  • Days 5-7 (Subtle fade): The first noticeable lightening begins, usually at friction points — underarms, inner elbows, hands, feet, and anywhere clothing rubs. On lighter shades, the tan is mostly gone by day 5.
  • Days 8-10+ (End of life): The tan fades to a softer warmth, then starts looking patchy as cell shedding becomes uneven. By day 10 most of the color is gone, and a full-body exfoliation can remove the remaining spots before your next appointment.

How to Make a Spray Tan Last Longer

None of these tips are magic, but together they can push a 5-day tan toward the 10-day ceiling. The American Academy of Dermatology's self-tanner guidance and Cleveland Clinic's spray-tan advice underpin most of these steps.

Before your appointment (prep is where most longevity is won)

  • Exfoliate for 1-3 days beforehand. A washcloth or gentle scrub removes dead cells so DHA bonds with fresh skin that will stay put longer. The AAD recommends spending extra time on thick-skinned areas — elbows, knees, ankles — where color grabs unevenly.
  • Skip oil-based products, lotions, and deodorant on the day. Oils create a film that blocks DHA from reacting with the skin, leading to a lighter, patchier tan.
  • Avoid waxing within 24 hours. Waxing temporarily opens pores and leaves the skin uneven, which shows up as spots.
  • Shave the night before, not the morning of. And ditch razors with moisturizing strips, which leave a barrier.

After your appointment (the 24-hour rule)

  • Wait at least 6 hours before showering. This gives DHA time to fully bond. Some "rapid" or "express" formulas allow a rinse in as little as 2-4 hours; ask your technician. With a standard solution, leaving it on for roughly 12 hours is the upper limit — Healthline notes that going longer can actually cause streaking.
  • Wear loose, dark clothing for the first 24 hours. Friction from tight waistbands, bras, or socks creates instant streaks and indentations while the bronzer is still active.
  • Avoid sweat, swimming, and exercise for the first day. Perspiration can run the color before it sets.

Throughout the tan's life (the extenders)

  • Take short, lukewarm showers. Hot water and long soaks soften skin and accelerate shedding. Use a gentle soap and avoid scrubbing.
  • Moisturize daily with a water-based, oil-free lotion. Hydrated skin turns over more slowly, which keeps color longer. Healthline advises avoiding oil-based products, which can create a barrier that keeps skin from holding onto the color, so choose a lotion that is free of heavy oils.
  • Swap vigorous exfoliation for very gentle smoothing every 2-3 days. You want to keep skin fresh without sanding off color.
  • Shave sparingly, with light pressure and a sharp razor. Each pass removes a layer of color, so shave only when needed.
  • Stay out of chlorinated pools, hot tubs, and salt water. Chlorine and salt are chemical exfoliants that strip DHA fast.
  • Top up with a gradual self-tanner. A light daily tanning lotion can refill fading color and add a few extra days.
  • Keep shampoo and conditioner off tanned skin. When you wash your hair, tilt forward so products — which often contain sulfates and silicones — run down your back instead of sitting on tanned skin. (Our how often should you wash your hair guide walks through a routine that's gentle on both.)

Safety Note: A Spray Tan Is Not Sun Protection

One critical caveat the AAD and Cleveland Clinic both stress: a spray tan does not protect you from the sun. "It is not a base tan," Dr. Lucas says — you still need a broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen, applied 15 minutes before going outdoors and reapplied at least every two hours. Peer-reviewed research also suggests DHA can temporarily increase UV-induced free radicals in fresh skin during the first 24 hours after application, so sunscreen and limited sun exposure are especially important while a brand-new tan develops.

The Bottom Line

Expect 7-10 days from a well-applied, well-maintained spray tan, with the range running from ~5 days for light shades to ~10 for darker ones. The biggest longevity levers are the DHA percentage in your solution, thorough pre-appointment exfoliation, and gentle, moisturizing aftercare — while chlorinated water, hot showers, and friction are the main things that shorten it. With the routine above, most people land at the upper end of that range. When this one fades, our how long does a tan last guide covers the UV version for comparison.

guides.title: How Long Does a Tan Last? Timeline, Tips & Self-Tan
guides.excerpt: A natural sun tan lasts about 7-10 days as your skin sheds its top layer. Here's how long each tan type lasts, what speeds fading, and how to extend it.
guides.content:
How Long Does a Tan Last? The Short Answer

A natural sun tan lasts about 7 to 10 days, after which your skin's outer layer naturally exfoliates and the color fades. That window is set by biology: the epidermis renews itself about every 30 days, continuously shedding the melanin-darkened cells a tan lives in. A spray tan or self-tan lasts a similar stretch — about 5 to 10 days — because it sits on the exact same surface cells.

No tan is permanent. Anyone who looks "always tan" either has naturally darker skin, uses self-tanner regularly, or gets repeated UV exposure. Below we break down exactly what controls the timeline, how each type of tan compares, and how to either stretch it out or fade it safely.

Quick comparison: how long each tan lasts

Type of tanTypical durationWhy
Sun tan (outdoors)7–10 daysMelanin darkens living skin cells, which shed on the ~30-day cycle
Tanning bed7–10 days (fades the same)UVA triggers melanin like the sun; no longer-lasting despite higher intensity
Spray tan / self-tanner5–10 daysDHA dyes only the dead surface layer, which flakes off weekly

What Changes How Long a Tan Lasts

The 7–10 day figure is an average. Where you land on that range — or whether you fall outside it — depends almost entirely on how fast your skin sheds.

FactorEffect on your tan
Moisture levelHydrated skin exfoliates more slowly, extending the tan. Dry skin flakes faster and fades sooner.
Exfoliation & scrubbingLoofahs, scrubs, and chemical exfoliants strip the tanned cells directly — the fastest way to lose color.
Shower temperatureHot water dehydrates skin and speeds fading; lukewarm or cool showers preserve it.
UV intensity & depthDeeper, slower tans built over several days tend to last slightly longer than a quick burn-and-peel.
Skin type / melaninPeople who naturally produce more melanin tan more quickly and may hold color longer.
Chlorine & salt waterBoth dry skin and accelerate exfoliation, shortening the tan.
How you got the tanUV tans (melanin) and DHA tans (surface dye) both fade on the cell cycle; DHA tans can start fading in as little as a day without care.

How Skin Tans — and Why It Always Fades

A tan begins when ultraviolet rays hit your skin. In response, pigment-producing cells called melanocytes ramp up production of melanin, the same pigment that colors your hair and eyes. That extra melanin darkens your skin tone — over the following 48 hours, according to the FDA. The color is, bluntly, a sign of damage: the FDA states plainly that "there is no such thing as a safe tan," because the melanin surge is your skin's attempt to shield itself from further UV harm.

Here's the catch that decides the lifespan. Melanin sits inside cells in the epidermis, your skin's top layer, and that layer never stops turning over. The Cleveland Clinic puts it simply: you make new skin cells constantly and "have new skin every 30 days," shedding roughly 40,000 old ones each day. As those melanin-rich cells flake off, the tan goes with them. A spray or self-tan fades by the same mechanism; its active ingredient, dihydroxyacetone (DHA), reacts with proteins in the dead surface cells, and when those cells shed, the color does too.

For a deeper dive on the sunless route — how DHA works, development time, and prep — see our guide to how long a spray tan lasts.

How to Make a Tan Last Longer

You can't stop skin turnover, but you can slow the shedding and stretch a tan toward the upper end of its range.

  • Exfoliate before, not after. Prepping smooth skin gives a tan (especially a spray tan) an even base — and removes loose cells that would otherwise flake off quickly.
  • Take lukewarm or cool showers. Hot water strips oil and moisture from skin, accelerating fade. Your shower routine matters beyond your tan — the same habits tie into how often you should wash your hair and care for the rest of your body.
  • Moisturize daily. Hydrated skin exfoliates more slowly. Use a fragrance-free lotion or a natural oil, and consider a tan-extender lotion, some of which stimulate melanin.
  • Skip harsh soaps, scrubs, and loofahs. Gentle, non-stripping cleansers preserve the surface layer.
  • Pat, don't rub, when drying off — rubbing is a form of exfoliation.
  • Avoid prolonged soaks in chlorinated pools, hot tubs, or salty ocean water, all of which dry skin and speed cell loss.
  • Drink water. Skin hydration starts from the inside; dehydration shows up as faster flaking.

Build the color gradually rather than burning. A tan acquired slowly over several low-UV sessions tends to sit deeper and last a bit longer than a single intense exposure that peels off within days.

How to Fade a Tan Safely

If you want the color gone faster — or it came out uneven — you can safely speed up the process without irritating your skin.

  • Exfoliate gently and regularly. A mild scrub or washcloth a few times a week lifts dead cells faster. Don't scrub hard enough to redden skin.
  • Take warm showers and use a soft loofah or exfoliating glove.
  • Try a gentle chemical exfoliant — lactic acid, glycolic acid, or salicylic acid — which loosens the bonds between dead cells.
  • Moisturize as you exfoliate. It sounds counterintuitive, but hydrated skin turns over more evenly and avoids the patchy look.
  • Be patient. Bleaching creams and harsh peels can damage skin and cause uneven tone. Most tans will fully clear within two to three weeks simply by letting the cycle run.

Sun-Safety Reality Check

It's worth saying directly: a tan is UV damage, not a health benefit. The FDA notes that the extra melanin in tanned skin provides only about SPF 2 to 4 — nowhere near real protection — and the American Academy of Dermatology recommends a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher, applied at about 1 ounce (a shot glass full) for the body and reapplied every two hours outdoors. The AAD's position is unambiguous: "There is no safe way to tan. Every time you tan, you damage your skin."

Tanning beds are no improvement. Their UVA output can be up to three times more intense than natural sunlight, and the World Health Organization classifies them as carcinogenic to humans. If you want color without the risk, sunless options — spray tans, self-tanner lotions, and tanning drops — are the safer route dermatologists recommend.

The Bottom Line

Expect a sun tan to last about 7 to 10 days and a spray or self-tan to last 5 to 10 days, both ultimately bounded by your skin's ~30-day renewal cycle. Moisturize, keep showers lukewarm, and exfoliate only before (not after) tanning to push toward the upper end. And whatever the color on your skin, it's no substitute for sunscreen — a tan gives you roughly SPF 2–4, while dermatologists want you at SPF 30 or higher.

guides.title: How Long Do Belly Button Piercings Take to Heal? Timeline
guides.excerpt: Belly button piercings take 6 to 12 months to heal on average, and can take up to 18 months. Here's the full timeline, factors, and infection signs to watch.
guides.content:
How Long Do Belly Button Piercings Take to Heal?

A belly button (navel) piercing takes 6 to 12 months to heal on average, with full healing stretching to up to a year — or even 18 months in some people. Cleveland Clinic notes that "a typical recovery period can be six months to a year, but that it may take as long as 18 months," and that some tenderness, redness, and crusting can linger for 12 to 18 months. Healthline puts the typical range at nine months to a year. The navel is one of the slowest-healing piercings on the body because your midsection bends, twists, and stretches constantly, and because waistbands and clothing rub the site all day.

In short: budget a full year, expect surprises (good and bad), and read on for what actually moves that timeline — and how to spot an infection before it becomes a problem.

What Changes the Healing Time

Healing isn't a fixed number — it shifts based on how you care for the piercing, what rubs against it, and your own body. Here are the biggest factors, and the effect each has on the clock.

FactorEffect on healing time
Aftercare routineCleaning twice daily with sterile saline (per the APP) keeps healing on track; over-cleaning, twisting the jewelry, or using alcohol and hydrogen peroxide can prolong healing by weeks or months.
Clothing frictionTight waistbands, belts, and rigid pants constantly irritate the site. The APP lists "friction and pressure from clothing" as a direct cause of prolonged healing and scar tissue.
Body movement & sleepBending, sit-ups, and stomach-sleeping jostle the jewelry. Cleveland Clinic attributes the long timeline to "all the bending, twisting and stretching your midsection does during the day."
Jewelry materialSurgical steel, titanium, niobium, or 14/18-karat gold are recommended. Nickel and low-grade alloys can trigger allergic reactions that mimic — or worsen into — infection.
Overall healthThe APP lists stress, nicotine, alcohol, and drug use as factors that prolong healing. Good sleep, nutrition, and not smoking shorten recovery.
Water exposurePools, hot tubs, lakes, and oceans introduce bacteria. The APP and Mayo Clinic both say to avoid submerging a healing piercing; Cleveland Clinic suggests waiting roughly 2–3 months before swimming.
Body type & anatomyA pronounced fold of skin at the top or bottom of the navel gives the jewelry more to anchor to. Very flat navels or deeper creases may heal more slowly or reject more easily.

How Long Each Stage Takes

Healing happens in phases, and knowing them helps you tell normal from worrying. Times overlap and vary from person to person, but here's the rough arc.

1. Initial reaction (days 1–14)

Expect some bleeding, localized swelling, tenderness, and bruising — all listed as normal by the APP. The site may feel warm and look angry. This is inflammation, not necessarily infection. Soreness and mild redness in the first few days are expected; Mayo Clinic advises contacting a healthcare professional if swelling, redness, or bleeding last longer than a few days.

2. Early healing (weeks 2–8)

The surface starts to settle, but you'll likely see "secretion of a whitish-yellow fluid that will form some crust on the jewelry," per the APP, along with itching and some discoloration. The tissue may tighten around the bar. This is the stage where people mistakenly think they're healed — but the channel inside is still open and fragile.

3. Deep healing (months 2–6)

Crusting tapers off for most people, the piercing looks settled, and the skin toughens. Still, the APP warns a piercing "may seem healed before the healing process is actually complete," because this kind of wound heals from the outside in. Resist the urge to swap jewelry or skip cleanings during this phase.

4. Full maturation (months 6–12, sometimes to 18)

The inner channel finishes closing and the skin fully toughens around the jewelry. Cleveland Clinic puts complete recovery at six months to a year, up to 18 months. Once healed, the jewelry may not move freely — don't force it.

How to Make It Heal Faster (and Last Longer)

You can't rush a navel piercing, but you can stop slowing it down. These habits keep you on the shorter end of the 6-to-12-month range and help the piercing last once it's healed.

  • Clean twice a day with sterile saline. The APP recommends a 0.9% sodium chloride wound wash — nothing else. Spray, let it sit, then dry with clean gauze or a paper towel. Don't over-clean; the APP warns it "can delay your healing and irritate your piercing."
  • Don't touch, twist, or rotate the jewelry. The APP and Cleveland Clinic both list handling as a top cause of irritation and infection. Hands off unless you're cleaning.
  • Dress around it. Wear loose, breathable, clean clothing — especially waistbands. For sports or tight clothes, the APP suggests a hard, vented eye patch (sold at pharmacies) secured with a bandage or elastic.
  • Skip the harsh stuff. Alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, iodine, antibacterial soaps, and ointments all damage cells and trap bacteria, per the APP. No swimming in pools, lakes, oceans, or hot tubs while healing.
  • Keep the jewelry in. Mayo Clinic: "always leave the jewelry in place during this time, even at night." The APP notes even healed piercings can shrink or close in minutes.
  • Choose the right jewelry. Surgical steel, titanium, niobium, or 14/18-karat gold reduce allergy and rejection risk. Avoid nickel alloys and brass.
  • Support your body. Don't smoke, manage stress, and sleep well. The APP lists nicotine, alcohol, and stress as factors that prolong healing.

If you're coordinating body care with the rest of your routine — say, scheduling around a fresh spray tan or a natural tan — give the piercing priority. A new navel piercing should not be exposed to tanning solution, sun, or chlorine, so heal first, bronze later. And because good general hygiene speeds every kind of recovery, our guide on how often you should wash your hair covers the broader shower-and-skincare rhythm that keeps healing skin clean.

Infection Signs: Normal vs. See a Professional

Some redness, swelling, crusting, and an off-white fluid are normal for weeks. Here's how Cleveland Clinic and the APP draw the line.

Probably normal (keep cleaning)

  • Mild swelling, tenderness, and bruising in the first 1–2 weeks.
  • Whitish-yellow crusting on the jewelry.
  • Itching and slight discoloration.
  • A tight feeling as the tissue heals around the bar.

Signs of infection (call your piercer or doctor)

Cleveland Clinic lists four classic warning signs:

  • Painful swelling or warmth — especially a hard, growing lump or abscess.
  • Increased or spreading redness or discoloration.
  • Pus-like discharge — yellow, green, gray, brown, white, or bloody, often smelly.
  • Feeling unwell — fever, chills, or (in rare, serious cases) signs of sepsis.

Don't remove the jewelry if you suspect infection — Cleveland Clinic and the APP both advise leaving it in to keep the channel open so the infection can drain; removing it can trap bacteria inside. If redness, swelling, or pus get worse after a few days of careful cleaning, see a healthcare professional. Allergic reactions (red, itchy, hive-like, dry skin that rarely oozes) can mimic infection — try an oral antihistamine or hydrocortisone, and consult a professional if it doesn't settle.

When to See a Piercer vs. a Doctor

  • See your piercer for: downsizing the bar after initial swelling, jewelry changes, checking placement, a bump or persistent crusting, and confirming whether what you're seeing is normal healing.
  • See a doctor for: spreading redness, severe or growing pain, pus, fever, chills, red streaks, or any infection that isn't improving with saline cleaning. Mayo Clinic also advises getting care promptly if swelling, redness, or bleeding last beyond the first few days.

The bottom line: a belly button piercing is a marathon, not a sprint. Plan for 6 to 12 months, up to 18, clean it twice a day with sterile saline, keep waistbands and fingers off it, and treat any spreading redness or pus as a reason to call a professional. Do that and your piercing will land on the shorter end of that timeline — and stay in for years once it's healed.

guides.title: How Often Should You Wash Your Hair? A Type-by-Type Guide
guides.excerpt: No single number works for everyone. Most people should wash their hair 1-7 times a week depending on hair type, scalp oil, age, and activity. Here is the breakdown.
guides.content:
How often should you wash your hair?

There is no universal number. How often you should wash your hair depends on how oily your scalp is, your hair type and texture, your age, and your lifestyle — so the honest answer is it depends, with most people landing somewhere between once a day and once every two weeks. For normal hair, the most common sweet spot is roughly 2 to 3 washes a week.

The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) puts it plainly: wash your hair based on how often it actually gets dirty or oily. If you have straight hair and an oily scalp you may want to shampoo daily; if your hair is dry, textured, curly, or thick, you can shampoo far less — at least once every 2 to 3 weeks. The Cleveland Clinic echoes this, noting that finer hair should be washed at least every other day, while coarse, tightly coiled hair can stretch to at least two weeks between washes.

A peer-reviewed study published in 2021 by Punyani and colleagues found that overall satisfaction with both hair and scalp condition peaked when washing about 5 to 6 times per week. Treat that result with caution, though: the roughly 1,500 adults in the study were all of Chinese ethnicity living in China, so it reflects that population rather than a global average, and your own hair type matters more than the group mean.

The table below translates the guidance into a practical, type-by-type schedule.

Hair / scalp typeRecommended wash frequencyWhy
Oily or straight, fine hairDaily to every other daySebum coats straight strands quickly, so they look greasy fast. The AAD notes daily shampooing may help; the Cleveland Clinic recommends finer hair at least every other day.
Normal hair (balanced scalp)2–3 times per weekMost people produce only enough oil to need a wash every couple of days, per Healthline.
Dry or wavy hairEvery 2–4 days (roughly 1–2 times per week)The Cleveland Clinic suggests semi-coarse hair can go 2–4 days between washes; natural oil takes longer to travel down the strand.
Curly or thick hairAbout once a weekCoarse, thick hair should be washed once a week, or whenever it feels like it needs it, per the Cleveland Clinic.
Coily, tightly curled, or textured hairOnce a week to every 2 weeksThe AAD, cited by Healthline, recommends tight curls and textured hair be washed no more than once a week or every other week to avoid breakage.

As the range shows, two people can both be “right” while washing on completely different schedules. The goal is to match your routine to your scalp's oil output and your hair's texture — not to hit a round number.

Factors that change how often you should wash

1. Sebum (scalp oil) production

Oil is the single biggest driver of what we call “dirty” hair. Your scalp's sebaceous glands produce sebum that keeps hair shiny and flexible, but too much of it leaves hair limp and clumpy. How much oil you make depends on genetics, sex, age, and environment — so two people with identical hair types can still need different wash schedules. Healthline notes that most people only produce enough oil to need a wash every couple of days, while a minority genuinely need to wash daily.

2. Hair type and texture

Straight, fine hair gets coated by sebum quickly and looks greasy fast, so it needs washing more often. Curly, coily, and thick hair is naturally drier because oil has to travel along a corkscrew-shaped strand to reach the ends — a slow journey that means less frequent washing is not only acceptable but healthier. The AAD specifically warns that over-washing textured hair, especially with harsh shampoos, can cause damage and breakage.

3. Age and hormones

Your oil glands are regulated by androgens, so oil output shifts across your life. The Cleveland Clinic explains that younger people typically have more active oil glands because hormone levels are higher, while sebum production slows with age. Women after menopause produce less oil, and older men see the same decline — so the schedule that worked in your twenties often needs loosening in your fifties. The AAD separately notes, in its guidance for children, that kids from 8 to 11 usually only need shampooing once or twice a week, while those 12 or entering puberty may need it every other day or daily.

4. Activity level and sweat

A sweaty workout spreads sebum through your hair and can leave it smelling less than fresh, so heavy exercisers often feel the need to wash more. But you don't automatically have to. The Cleveland Clinic's dermatologist advises sticking to your standard schedule — whether that's three times a week, once a week, or every other week — regardless of daily exercise. A simple rinse or a dry-shampoo touch-up between full washes is usually enough after the gym.

5. Chemical treatments, dirt, and styling products

Chemically processed hair (color, relaxers, perms) is more fragile and benefits from less frequent washing to limit damage. Heavy use of gels, hairsprays, creams, and serums can build up on the scalp and cause irritation, which may push you toward washing more often — or toward a clarifying shampoo once or twice a month to reset. Likewise, gardening, cleaning, or a day of outdoor exposure can trap dirt, dust, and pollen in your hair and warrant an extra wash.

Signs you're washing your hair too often

Over-washing is the more common mistake, especially among people who have kept the same daily-shampoo habit from their teens. Watch for these signals:

  • Dry, brittle hair and split ends — frequent shampooing strips the sebum that keeps strands flexible.
  • A tight, itchy, or flaky scalp — what looks like dandruff can actually be a dry scalp caused by over-washing, not a reason to wash more.
  • Frizz, especially in curly hair — textured hair shows moisture loss as frizz and dullness.
  • Hair that feels light or “squeaky” but won't hold a style — a sign the natural oils that give hair body have been removed.

If several of these sound familiar, both the Cleveland Clinic and Healthline suggest cutting out one wash per week, or extending the gap between washes by a day, and giving your scalp about a month to rebalance before judging the result.

Signs you're not washing often enough

Under-washing has its own warning signs, and they're mostly driven by oil, sweat, and product buildup rather than the hair itself:

  • A visibly oily or greasy scalp and roots that feel unclean to the touch — the most direct signal, per Healthline's dermatology guidance.
  • Itching, redness, or yellowish flakes — true dandruff and scalp inflammation can flare when oil and the yeast that naturally live on the scalp overgrow.
  • Hair that smells stale, especially after workouts or wearing a hat and helmet for long stretches.
  • Limp, heavy, or clumpy strands that won't volumize, caused by sebum weighing the hair down.

The AAD notes that seeing flakes is commonly a sign you're not shampooing frequently enough — or that you're using the wrong conditioner or scalp moisturizer for your hair type. Add one wash per week and watch whether the oiliness and flaking ease.

Finding your own frequency

Because the right schedule is personal, the fastest way to land on it is small, one-step experiments rather than a drastic overhaul. The Cleveland Clinic and Healthline both suggest adding or removing a single wash per week, then waiting about a month for your scalp's oil production to adjust before changing again. A few rules of thumb make the process easier:

  • Shampoo the scalp, not the lengths. The AAD recommends applying shampoo to the scalp and letting rinse-off clean the ends, which avoids drying out older, more fragile hair.
  • Condition every wash, focusing on the ends for fine or straight hair and the full length for dry or curly hair.
  • Use dry shampoo to stretch a schedule, not to replace washing entirely — it absorbs oil but doesn't actually clean the scalp.
  • Coordinate with the rest of your grooming routine. Hair-wash timing often has to work around other beauty schedules — for example, you'll want to plan showers around a fresh color, just as you'd time them around how long a spray tan lasts or how long a natural tan lasts, and avoid soaking new body art while checking how long belly button piercings take to heal.

The bottom line: there is no medically “correct” number of weekly washes, only the number that keeps your scalp comfortable and your hair looking and feeling healthy. Start with the table that matches your hair type, watch for the over- and under-washing signs above, and nudge by one wash at a time until you find your own balance.

guides.title: How Long Does Fermentation Take? Times by Food and Drink
guides.excerpt: Fermentation takes anywhere from 4 hours (yogurt) to 5-6 weeks (sauerkraut or lager). See the exact timelines for beer, bread, kombucha, kraut, and more.
guides.content:
How Long Does Fermentation Take?

Fermentation takes anywhere from 4 hours for a batch of yogurt to 5–6 weeks for slow-fermented sauerkraut or a properly conditioned lager beer. As a practical rule, most home ferments finish inside a window of about 12 hours to 4 weeks, with the exact duration set by three things: the microorganism (yeast versus bacteria), temperature, and how much sugar or salt is in the mix. There is no single universal “fermentation time” — so the honest answer is always “it depends on what you are fermenting.”

The quick-reference table below gives the typical range for each common ferment, followed by the science of why those numbers move up or down.

ProductDriving microbeTypical fermentation timeTemperature range
YogurtL. bulgaricus + S. thermophilus (bacteria)4–8 hours100–110°F (38–43°C)
Sourdough bread (bulk ferment)Wild yeast + lactic acid bacteria3–5 hours (room temp)68–78°F (20–26°C)
Ale beer (primary)Ale yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae)3–7 days55–75°F (13–24°C)
KombuchaSCOBY (yeast + bacteria)7–10 days72–85°F (22–29°C)
Lager beer (primary)Lager yeast (S. pastorianus)10–14 days, then 4–6 weeks conditioning46–56°F (8–13°C)
Sauerkraut / kimchiLactic acid bacteria3–4 weeks (5–6 weeks if cooler)70–75°F (21–24°C) ideal
Wine (primary)Wine yeast3–10 days (primary), then weeks–months aging60–70°F (16–21°C)

Times are typical home-ferment ranges compiled from university food-science extension sources, the Beer Judge Certification Program (BJCP) study guide, and peer-reviewed brewing/fermentation research; exact batches vary.

What Actually Changes the Duration

Every figure in the table above is a moving target. The same recipe can finish in half the time or take twice as long depending on a handful of variables. Here is what moves the needle most:

FactorEffect on fermentation time
Temperature (higher)Faster. Microbes reproduce more quickly, so yogurt at the warmer 110°F end of its range sets closer to 4 hours while the cooler 100°F end takes the full 8.
Temperature (lower)Slower, and below a floor it stalls. Sauerkraut below 60°F “may not ferment,” per the USDA.
Temperature (too high)Not just faster but worse: kraut above 75°F goes soft, and very hot fermentations produce off-flavors.
Sugar contentMore fermentable sugar = longer ferment, because the microbes have more substrate to convert. High-gravity beers and sweet wines take longer to finish.
Salt concentrationMore salt slows everything. In vegetable ferments that is intentional — salt suppresses spoilage organisms while letting lactic acid bacteria work.
Yeast vs. bacteriaYeast-driven ferments (beer, wine) usually finish primary faster than bacterial ferments (sauerkraut, kimchi), which need weeks to build enough acid.
Starter / pitch rateA larger, healthier starter finishes sooner. Under-pitched beer yeast stresses the culture and extends lag time.

The throughline is simple: fermentation is a biological process, and biology speeds up with warmth and slows down with cold. Every traditional ferment — from lagering beer in cold caves to keeping sauerkraut at 70°F — is really just a controlled choice along this temperature curve.

How Long Each Stage Takes

Beer: primary fermentation then conditioning

Ale yeast ferments warm and fast. Per the BJCP study guide, ale yeast works best at 55–75°F (13–24°C), and a peer-reviewed brewing protocol published through the NIH reports primary fermentation finishing in roughly 6 days for an ale versus 10 days for a lager. Maturation then adds about 3 days for an ale and around 12 days for a lager. Lager yeast (S. pastorianus) prefers colder temperatures of 46–56°F (8–13°C), and BJCP notes traditional lager styles may condition for four to six weeks — even months for strong lagers — because cold yeast works slowly and needs time to clean up byproducts.

Vegetable ferments: sauerkraut and kimchi

The USDA recommendation (via the National Center for Home Food Preservation) is to ferment sauerkraut at 70–75°F, where it is “fully fermented in about 3 to 4 weeks.” Drop the room to 60–65°F and the same batch takes 5 to 6 weeks. Below 60°F it may not ferment at all; above 75°F it turns soft and loses flavor. Kimchi follows a similar lactic-acid curve but is usually eaten younger — a few days at room temperature for fresh, tangy kimchi, or weeks in the fridge for a slower, sourer develop.

Sourdough: bulk fermentation in hours, not weeks

King Arthur Baking’s bakers let a typical sourdough bulk-ferment at room temperature for 3 to 5 hours. That window stretches or shrinks with dough temperature and kitchen warmth — a cold kitchen can push bulk fermentation past 8 hours, while a warm proofer can compress it. After bulk, shaped loaves usually cold-proof in the fridge overnight for flavor development.

Kombucha: 7 to 10 days to a safe pH

Michigan State University Extension reports that during kombucha fermentation the pH of the sweet tea drops from roughly 5 down to about 2.5 over the course of 7 to 10 days. That acidification is what makes the drink safe by suppressing pathogens. MSU’s guidance is blunt: if a pH of 2.5 has not been reached by day 10, the batch should be discarded rather than fermented longer — going too far produces an overly acidic, vinegar-like drink. (Kombucha is typically fermented at warm room temperature of about 72–85°F / 22–29°C, the optimal range identified in peer-reviewed kombucha research; MSU’s article focuses on safety and does not specify a temperature.)

Yogurt: the fastest common ferment

University of Missouri Extension specifies an incubation period of four to eight hours at 100–110°F. The warmer end of that range sets faster (closer to 4 hours); the cooler end takes the full 8. Refrigeration then halts fermentation by stopping lactic-acid development.

Wine: weeks to months

Primary alcoholic fermentation in wine — yeast converting grape sugar to alcohol — typically runs about 3 to 10 days, per home-winemaking guidance from Virginia Cooperative Extension (Virginia Tech), which recommends a dark room at about 70°F for red wines or 50–60°F for white wines. The longer timeline people associate with wine is really aging and malolactic (secondary) fermentation, which can run weeks to months as the wine clarifies and softens.

How to Tell When Fermentation Is Done (and Safe)

Time is a guide, not a switch. The most reliable signs that a ferment is finished come from the ferment itself:

  • Beer and wine: fermentation is done when the specific gravity (measured with a hydrometer) holds steady over two to three days, meaning the yeast has consumed the available sugar. Bubbles in the airlock slowing to a stop is a hint, not proof.
  • Kombucha: done when the pH reaches about 2.5, typically at 7–10 days. Use pH strips or a meter — taste alone is unreliable for safety.
  • Sauerkraut: fully fermented when bubbling ceases and the brine is clear with a tart flavor; at 70–75°F that is about 3–4 weeks.
  • Yogurt: done when it holds a clean set (gelled, not sloshing) and tastes pleasantly tart — usually 4–8 hours at temperature.

Safety red flags that mean discard, not wait: visible mold (fuzzy, raised, colored) on any ferment, a putrid or rotten smell (distinct from normal sour/tangy), soft or slimy texture in vegetables, or a kombucha batch that has not reached pH 2.5 by day 10. A normal ferment smells sour, yeasty, or tangy — never spoiled.

Practical Tips for Better Timing

  • Control temperature first. A $15 thermometer or a simple ferm chamber does more for consistency than any other variable. Hold ale beer at 65°F, yogurt at 110°F, sauerkraut at 72°F, and your timelines become predictable.
  • Pitch enough microbes. Under-pitched yeast or a tiny starter extends lag time and invites contamination. A healthy, generous starter shortens every ferment.
  • Weigh vegetables by salt, not by guess. Sauerkraut wants about 2–3% salt by weight of cabbage — too little and spoilage organisms win; too much and even good bacteria stall.
  • Measure, do not just watch the clock. For beer and wine use a hydrometer; for kombucha use pH strips. For sourdough, watch dough volume (look for a clear, noticeable rise rather than a fixed number on the calendar) rather than the calendar.
  • Plan the cold stage. Lagers, sourdough loaves, and aged wines all rely on a slow, cold phase for flavor. Do not rush it — that is where complexity is built.

For more timing breakdowns across cooking, brewing, and household tasks, browse the full guides library. Fermentation rewards patience and measurement in equal measure: pick the right temperature window for your product, confirm doneness with a measurement rather than a guess, and let the microbes do the work on their schedule — whether that is four hours for tomorrow’s yogurt or six weeks for a properly sour crock of kraut.

guides.title: How Long Does It Take to Get to the Moon? (Crewed & Probes)
guides.excerpt: A crewed Moon trip takes about 3 days on the fast Apollo-style path, while the fastest probe crossed lunar orbit in 8.5 hours. Here's what changes the time.
guides.content:
How Long Does It Take to Get to the Moon?

The short answer: a crewed trip to the Moon takes about 3 days flying the fast, direct path the Apollo astronauts used. Uncrewed probes span a much wider range — from 8 hours and 35 minutes for the fastest flyby to roughly 13–14 months for a fuel-sipping ion-engine spacecraft. As a NASA expert put it plainly, "to get to the Moon takes several days" — and those several days are still the benchmark for carrying humans there (NASA, 2025).

The Moon sits an average of 384,400 km (238,855 miles) from Earth, according to NASA. How quickly a spacecraft crosses that gap depends almost entirely on two things engineers trade against each other on every mission: the trajectory flown and the amount of fuel the launcher can deliver. Burn more fuel and you can fly nearly straight there in days; spend less and you accept a slower, looping path that can take weeks or months.

Mission Durations at a Glance

The table below collects the headline numbers from crewed and uncrewed lunar missions so you can see the spread in a single view.

Mission / methodTypeTime to reach the MoonPath
Apollo 8 (1968)Crewed — lunar orbit69 h 8 min (~3 days)Fast translunar injection
Apollo 11 (1969)Crewed — first landing4 days, 6 h, 45 min (launch to landing)Fast translunar injection
Artemis II (2026)Crewed — free-return flyby~5–6 days to lunar flyby (10-day mission total)Free-return trajectory
New Horizons (2006)Uncrewed probe — Pluto-bound8 h 35 min (crossed lunar orbit)High-speed escape trajectory
SMART-1 (2003–04)Uncrewed — ESA orbiter~13–14 monthsLow-thrust ion spiral
Typical uncrewed orbiter/landerUncrewed direct-ascent~3–5 daysTranslunar injection

Sources: Britannica (Apollo 8, Apollo 11, New Horizons figures); NASA (Artemis II timeline); ESA (SMART-1 cruise phase).

Factors That Change the Time

Three variables decide whether a lunar trip lasts hours, days, or months.

1. Trajectory: direct, free-return, or low-thrust

The single biggest factor is the shape of the path. A direct translunar trajectory — what Apollo used — fires the spacecraft on a near-straight shot that reaches lunar distance in about three days. A free-return trajectory is shaped so that the Moon's gravity slings the spacecraft back toward Earth automatically if anything fails; it is safer and more fuel-efficient but slightly slower. Fuel-efficient trajectories can take more time, potentially weeks or months, to reach the Moon, depending on how you do it (NASA, 2025).

At the far extreme, a low-thrust spiral uses a small ion engine to widen Earth orbit gradually over many loops until the Moon captures the craft — the route ESA's SMART-1 took for roughly 13–14 months.

2. Propulsion: chemical vs. ion

Chemical rockets (Saturn V, SLS, Falcon) produce huge thrust for a few minutes, flinging a spacecraft most of the way to the Moon in a single burn. They are fast but fuel-hungry. Ion (electric) propulsion accelerates gently but continuously; SMART-1's ion engine fired throughout a roughly 13-month spiral, trading speed for extraordinary fuel economy — it reached the Moon on a fraction of the propellant a chemical rocket needs. For cargo and future infrastructure flights, that trade-off is increasingly attractive.

3. The Moon's distance and launch alignment

The Moon does not orbit in a perfect circle. Its distance varies from about 362,600 km (225,309 miles) at perigee (closest) to about 405,400 km (251,903 miles) at apogee (farthest), averaging 384,400 km (238,855 miles) (NASA). Launching when the Moon is nearer saves a little time and fuel, but the effect is modest compared with trajectory choice. Launch windows also line up with where the Moon will be when the spacecraft arrives, since a direct flight aims at the Moon's future position, not its current one.

Apollo vs. Artemis: Why the Modern Trip Can Feel Slower

A common question is why a 1969 crewed mission reached the Moon in three days while today's Artemis program traces a longer path. The answer is mission design, not a step backward in technology. Apollo flew a brisk direct transfer to get astronauts to the surface and back as quickly as possible. Artemis II, by contrast, is an approximately 10-day journey around the Moon that launches, performs a lunar flyby, and splashes down — using a fuel-efficient free-return shape that carries the crew out to a maximum of about 252,760 miles from Earth, roughly 4,105 miles farther than Apollo 13's record (NASA, 2026). The flyby closest approach (about 4,070 miles from the surface) happens around day five or six of the mission.

In short, modern crewed missions often choose a slower, leaner path to save fuel, reduce risk, and test deep-space systems — not because the rockets are slower.

The Fastest and Slowest Lunar Trips on Record

Fastest: NASA's New Horizons probe, launched toward Pluto in 2006, crossed the Moon's orbital distance just 8 hours and 35 minutes after liftoff (Britannica). It did not stop — it was simply moving so fast that it blew past lunar distance en route to deep space, underscoring that a flyby is far quicker than slowing down to orbit or land.

Slowest (powered): ESA's SMART-1 took roughly 13–14 months to reach the Moon using an ion thruster, spiraling outward from Earth orbit in long, ever-widening loops (ESA). It proved that a small, cheap spacecraft could reach lunar orbit on a fraction of the fuel a chemical rocket needs.

How the Moon Trip Compares With Going to Mars

The Moon is, in space terms, right next door. Reaching Mars — about 50% farther from the Sun than Earth — takes seven to ten months on a direct route, NASA notes. NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter took about seven and a half months, and MAVEN about ten months. If you are weighing interplanetary travel times, our deeper write-up on how long it takes to get to Mars breaks down those mission profiles and the trajectory tricks used to make the longer trip efficient. For context, reaching Jupiter takes five to six years — but the Moon remains the only destination humans have reached in days rather than months.

The Bottom Line

  • Crewed, fast path: about 3 days (Apollo benchmark).
  • Crewed, fuel-efficient free-return: roughly 5–6 days to the lunar flyby, wrapped in a ~10-day mission (Artemis II).
  • Uncrewed direct probes: typically 3–5 days, depending on the target orbit.
  • Fastest flyby ever: 8 hours 35 minutes (New Horizons).
  • Slowest powered trip: ~13–14 months via ion engine (SMART-1).

The distance to the Moon is fixed at an average of 384,400 km — but the travel time is a design choice. Pick speed and you pay in fuel; pick economy and you pay in days, weeks, or even months. That trade-off is why "how long does it take" has no single answer, and why every lunar mission lists a different number on its flight plan.

guides.title: How Long Does It Take to Get to Mars? Trip Time Facts
guides.excerpt: A trip to Mars takes about 7-10 months (200-300 days) with today's rockets. Here is how trajectory, propulsion, and the 26-month launch window change that time.
guides.content:
How Long Does It Take to Get to Mars?

With the chemical rockets in use today, a one-way trip from Earth to Mars takes roughly seven to ten months, or about 200 to 300 days. NASA describes the interplanetary cruise phase of a typical mission as lasting "about 200 days," and notes that reaching Mars on a relatively direct route "generally takes somewhere between seven to ten months." There is no single fixed flight time, because Mars and Earth are always moving and the distance between them is constantly changing.

For comparison, reaching the Moon takes only a matter of days — the fastest crewed lunar transit, Apollo 8, made the trip from Earth orbit to lunar orbit in under three days. Mars, which orbits the Sun about 50% farther out than Earth does, is a fundamentally harder target, and every kilogram of mass you add stretches the schedule further.

Mars Travel Times by Mission

The table below shows how long real (and planned) Mars missions have taken. The spread — from roughly 200 days to around 10 months — captures almost every robotic mission flown in the modern era.

Mission / methodTravel timeNotes
Typical cruise (NASA baseline)~200 days (~6.5 months)NASA's average for the interplanetary cruise phase
Hohmann transfer (minimum-energy orbit)~259 days (~8.5 months)The most fuel-efficient path; only viable during launch windows
Perseverance rover (2020–21)~203 days (~7 months)Launched July 30, 2020; landed Feb 18, 2021
Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (2005)~7.5 monthsNASA orbiter still operating at Mars
MAVEN (2013)~10 monthsUsed a slower, lower-energy trajectory
Crewed round trip (planned)~3 yearsNASA estimates roughly three years away from Earth; crew must wait at Mars for the planets to realign for the return

Notice that faster is not always better. Perseverance and MRO moved quickly because they were aimed at a tight landing or orbit-insertion window, while MAVEN's 10-month cruise was a deliberate choice that traded speed for fuel economy. Every mission is a balance between how much mass you launch, how much fuel you can carry, and where the planets happen to be.

Factors That Change the Time

Three variables dominate the length of any Mars flight: the trajectory you fly, the propulsion you use, and the alignment of Earth and Mars. Payload mass is the fourth lever that ties them all together.

1. Trajectory — the path you cut through space

Spacecraft do not fly to Mars in a straight line. They travel along curved paths dictated by gravity and orbital mechanics, and the shape of that curve is the single biggest factor in travel time. The most fuel-efficient option is the Hohmann transfer orbit, an ellipse that has the Sun at one focus and touches Earth's orbit at departure and Mars' orbit at arrival. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory calculates that a textbook Hohmann transfer to Mars covers half of one orbit and takes about 259 days.

Flying a shorter, tighter arc can shave weeks off that time, but only by burning far more fuel. Because every extra kilogram of propellant means a heavier (and far more expensive) launch vehicle, mission designers usually accept the slower, cheaper path.

2. Propulsion — what pushes you there

Every Mars mission flown so far has relied on chemical rockets, which fire briefly at launch and then let the spacecraft coast for months. That coasting phase is why the trip takes 7 to 10 months: the craft is essentially thrown like a football, gliding toward a moving target. More advanced options — nuclear thermal propulsion, which NASA is actively developing, or ion engines that thrust gently for years — could eventually cut the transit in theory. None of these yet carry people, and they remain experimental for Mars-class payloads, so the 7-to-10-month floor stands for now.

3. Planetary alignment and the launch window

You cannot leave for Mars whenever you like. Because Earth and Mars orbit the Sun at different speeds, they line up for an efficient trip only about once every 26 months. During this window, Mars sits roughly 44 degrees ahead of Earth in its orbit — the geometry that lets a Hohmann transfer arrive exactly where Mars will be. Miss the window by a few weeks and the fuel cost climbs sharply, or the trip becomes impossible until the next opportunity rolls around. This is why Mars missions from around the world — NASA, ESA, China, the UAE — all tend to launch within the same few months of each other.

4. Mass — what you are carrying

A lightweight orbiter can be flung onto a faster track; a heavy lander carrying rovers, parachutes, and descent rockets needs a larger, slower trajectory and more fuel to brake at the end. Human missions, which must also carry life support, radiation shielding, and return fuel, are by far the heaviest payloads of all — one reason a crewed round trip is expected to last about three years.

How Far Away Is Mars?

The reason flight time varies so much is that the Earth–Mars distance is never constant. Mars is on average about 140 million miles (225 million km) from Earth, but that number swings dramatically as both planets circle the Sun:

  • Closest approach: roughly 34.7 million miles (55.8 million km). In August 2003 the two planets passed within about 55.76 million km of each other — the closest approach in nearly 60,000 years, tracked by both NASA and ESA.
  • Average separation: about 140 million miles (225 million km).
  • Farthest (solar conjunction): when Earth and Mars sit on opposite sides of the Sun, the gap can stretch to roughly 400 million km (about 250 million miles).

That constantly changing gap is the root cause of the 26-month launch window: only when the planets are arranged just right can a spacecraft make the crossing without carrying an impossible amount of fuel.

Could We Get There Faster?

With current technology, the 7-to-10-month floor is hard to break. Chemical rockets are near their practical limits, and carrying enough fuel for a much faster burn would require a launch vehicle far larger than anything operating today. The realistic near-term improvements are nuclear thermal engines, which could roughly halve the transit time for a crewed craft, and advanced ion propulsion for uncrewed cargo flights. For now, every rover, orbiter, and lander humanity has sent to Mars has spent the better part of a year getting there — and a crewed round trip, including the long wait for the planets to realign, would keep astronauts away from Earth for roughly three years.

The Bottom Line

So, how long does it take to get to Mars? Plan on seven to ten months — about 200 to 300 days — for any mission flying today, with about 259 days (roughly 8.5 months) being the textbook efficient Hohmann transfer. The exact figure bends with trajectory, propulsion, payload mass, and the once-every-26-months launch window. Crewed missions, once they begin, will stretch the journey into a multi-year expedition.

Curious how that compares with our nearest neighbor? See how long it takes to get to the Moon — a trip that, by contrast, is measured in days rather than months.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Japan: Month-by-Month Guide (2026)
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Japan is late March to mid-April for cherry blossoms, or November for autumn foliage. Month-by-month weather, crowds & costs.
guides.content:
When Is the Best Time to Visit Japan?

The single best time to visit Japan is late March to mid-April, when the cherry blossoms (sakura) sweep from south to north across the country and daytime temperatures in Tokyo and Kyoto sit in a comfortable 55-65 °F (13-18 °C) range. If you want to dodge the absolute peak crowds and prices that sakura season draws, the co-best window is November, when the autumn leaves (koyo) turn Kyoto and the mountains red and gold and the weather is crisp, dry, and clear.

Both shoulders are broadly endorsed by the Japan National Tourism Organization and seasoned operators: spring (March-May) and autumn (October-November) are the two windows when Japan is "at its most vibrant," with mild temperatures and lower rainfall than summer. Summer is hot, humid, and rainy; winter is cold but superb for skiing and snow monkeys. There is no truly bad month — only months that suit some trips better than others.

Japan Season-by-Season: Weather, Crowds, Cost & Daylight

Season / MonthsWeatherCrowds & CostBest ForDaylight (Tokyo)
Spring (Mar-May) Mild, dry; 55-70 °F (13-21 °C). Cherry blossoms bloom late Mar to early Apr in most cities; Sapporo around Apr 19. Highest crowds & prices around sakura (late Mar-early Apr) and Golden Week (Apr 29-May 5). Cherry blossoms, temple gardens, city strolling. ~12 hrs (Mar) → ~14 hrs (May)
Summer (Jun-Aug) Rainy season (tsuyu) early Jun to mid-Jul, then hot & humid; Tokyo can reach ~88 °F (31 °C). Hokkaido stays cooler and skips tsuyu. Moderate in Jun (quieter); domestic crowds spike for Obon (mid-Aug). Hiking the Japanese Alps & Hokkaido, Mt. Fuji climb (Jul), festivals (matsuri). ~14.5 hrs (Jun) → ~13.5 hrs (Aug)
Autumn (Sep-Nov) Sep still warm with typhoon risk; Oct-Nov cool, dry, clear. Foliage peaks Tokyo/Kyoto late Nov into early Dec. Shoulder pricing; November is busy (but less frantic than sakura peak). Autumn foliage (koyo), onsen, comfortable city sightseeing. ~12.5 hrs (Sep) → ~10 hrs (Nov)
Winter (Dec-Feb) Cold & dry on the Pacific coast (Tokyo ~40-50 °F / 5-10 °C); heavy snow on the Sea of Japan side & Hokkaido. Lowest crowds & cheapest outside New Year (Jan 1-3). February is peak ski season up north. Skiing (Niseko, Hakuba), snow monkeys, onsen, fewer tourists. ~9.5-10 hrs

Month-by-month highlights

  • January: Cold, dry, quiet, cheap after New Year — ideal for shrines, onsen, and snow country without crowds.
  • February: Peak ski season in northern Japan (Niseko, Hakuba); Sapporo Snow Festival (early Feb).
  • March: First cherry blossoms open in Tokyo around mid-to-late March (2026 forecast: Tokyo first bloom ~Mar 19); plum blossoms earlier in the month.
  • April: Full sakura bloom across most of Honshu; Golden Week (Apr 29-May 5) is a domestic travel crush — avoid if you can.
  • May: Pleasant, green, relatively uncrowded early in the month; one of the most underrated times to visit.
  • June: Rainy season (tsuyu) settles in across most of Japan; Hokkaido stays dry. Lower prices, fewer tourists.
  • July: Rainy season ends mid-month; Mt. Fuji climbing season opens; humidity and heat build.
  • August: Hot, humid, festival season (Obon mid-Aug); peak typhoon risk begins. Best in Hokkaido.
  • September: Warm with the highest typhoon likelihood; early koyo in Hokkaido's mountains.
  • October: Cool, clear, comfortable — excellent shoulder-season value; foliage begins descending.
  • November: Peak autumn foliage in Kyoto/Tokyo (late Nov); crisp, dry, beautiful — arguably the best month overall.
  • December: Cold and quiet; late foliage in Tokyo/Kyoto into early December; skiing opens.

The Cheapest Time and the Worst Time to Visit Japan

When is the cheapest time to visit Japan?

The cheapest time to visit Japan is late January through early March (excluding the New Year rush of Jan 1-3) and again in June, when the rainy season keeps international and domestic tourists away. Flights, hotels, and even some ryokan drop to their lowest rates in these windows, and major sights in Kyoto, Nara, and Kanazawa are genuinely quiet. February also overlaps with deep-snow skiing in Hokkaido, so if your goal is cities and culture rather than slopes, late January and June offer the best value.

For the budget-conscious who still want decent weather, early December and early May (just after Golden Week) are smart shoulder picks — cooler than summer, far cheaper than sakura peak, and well outside the typhoon window.

What is the worst time to visit Japan?

For most travelers, the worst window is mid-June to mid-July, when the rainy season (tsuyu) blankets Honshu. According to Japan-guide.com, drawing on Japan Meteorological Agency data, the rainy season runs roughly June 8 to July 20 in Tokyo and June 6 to July 19 in Kyoto/Osaka; only Hokkaido escapes it. It does not rain every day — the chance of rain on a given Tokyo day at peak tsuyu is about 45% — but skies are often overcast and humidity climbs.

The other times to think twice:

  • Golden Week (April 29-May 5): Domestic travel peaks; hotels sell out and prices double.
  • Obon (mid-August): Major domestic travel period; hot, humid, and crowded.
  • New Year (Dec 29-Jan 3): Many shrines, temples, restaurants, and museums close; transport is packed.
  • August-September typhoon season: Storms most often track near Japan in these months, with a real (if small) chance of disrupted trains and flights.

None of these make a trip impossible — Japan functions well year-round — but they raise the cost-and-hassle ceiling and lower the odds of clear skies.

Practical Planning Tips

  • Book sakura season 4-6 months ahead. Late March to early April is the single busiest window; hotels in Kyoto and Tokyo fill fast and prices peak. If you're flexible, chase the bloom north: it reaches Sapporo around April 19 and Kushiro (eastern Hokkaido) around May 5.
  • Hedge on cherry blossom timing. Bloom dates shift each year with the weather. The 2026 JNTO forecast had Tokyo opening around March 19 — earlier than the historical average of about March 24. Build a 3-4 day buffer into your trip and follow the live JNTO/japan-guide forecasts rather than locking dates months out.
  • Skip Golden Week. If your only option is late April to early May, know that April 29-May 5 is a cluster of Japanese public holidays and the busiest domestic travel stretch of the year. Shift a week in either direction.
  • Use the rainy season strategically. June is cheap and green, and some sights — moss gardens (Saiho-ji), hydrangeas at temples, hot springs — are arguably better in the rain. Pair a few mainland days with Hokkaido, which is largely unaffected by tsuyu.
  • For autumn foliage, aim for late November. The koyo front starts in Hokkaido in mid-September and reaches Tokyo and Kyoto around late November, with some trees holding color into December. November offers sakura-level beauty with lower prices and thinner crowds.
  • Layer up. Spring and autumn swing between warm afternoons and chilly evenings; pack light layers. Summer demands breathable fabrics and an umbrella; winter in the snow regions demands serious insulation.

If you're weighing Japan against other seasonal trips, the same shoulder-season logic applies to the best time to visit Iceland (aim for summer daylight or northern-lights winter) and the best time to visit Hawaii (shoulder months of April-May and September-October). For Japan specifically, the takeaway is simple: come for the cherry blossoms in late March to mid-April, or for the autumn leaves in November, and you'll catch the country at its most beautiful and most comfortable.
