guides.content:
The short answer: June to August for the midnight sun, November to March for the northern lights

The best time to visit Iceland depends almost entirely on what you came for. For the midnight sun, open highland roads, whale watching and hiking, aim for mid-June to late August, when the country gets 24/7 daylight and the warmest temperatures of the year. For the northern lights and ice caves, go between November and March, when the nights are long and dark enough for aurora viewing. If you want a balance — decent weather, fewer crowds and still a chance of aurora — the shoulder months of September and October (autumn colours) or late February to March are the savviest picks.

Iceland's weather is notoriously changeable in every season, so there is no single "perfect" window — as Lonely Planet puts it, the best season "depends entirely on what you want to experience." Use the breakdown below to match the month to your priority.

Iceland month-by-month: weather, daylight, crowds and cost

Average temperatures below are drawn from Lonely Planet's season reporting and the Icelandic Meteorological Office, which puts Iceland's long-run annual average at roughly 6°C on the south coast and 3°C on the north coast, with a substantially colder highland interior. The coldest months nationwide are December and January.

MonthAvg tempDaylightProsConsCrowds / cost
Jan−1 to 4°C~4–6 hrsPeak northern lights; ice caves; Christmas markets early onVery short days; storms, slippery roadsLow crowds / low–mid cost
Feb~0.4°C~7–9 hrsAurora still strong; snow sports; Winter Lights FestivalCold, unpredictable snowLow crowds / low cost
Mar~0.4°C~10–13 hrsEquinox = excellent aurora; longer days; skiingWeather still volatileLow–moderate / low cost
Apr3–6.8°C~14–16 hrsOff-peak pricing; whales and migrant birds return; roads clearingHighland roads still closed; some tours not runningFew crowds / low cost
May2–10°C~16–19 hrsLambs and puffins; waterfalls flowing; off-season dealsWeather unreliable; some nesting areas closedFew crowds / low cost
Jun~9°C~20–24 hrs (midnight sun)Midnight sun; peak hiking; Highlands begin openingNo darkness = no auroraHigh crowds / high cost
Jul~13°C (warmest)24 hrs daylightWarmest month; Highlands fully open; peak whale watchingBusiest month; book well aheadPremium crowds / peak cost
Aug~10.3°C~14–18 hrsStill warm; berries ripen; Culture Night & Marathon; first aurora late monthCrowded; popular sites busyHigh crowds / high cost
SepCooling~12–14 hrsAutumn colours; réttir sheep roundups; aurora returns; fewer touristsWeather turns stormy; roads get slipperyModerate / mid cost
OctCold, wet~9–11 hrsEquinox aurora; thin crowds; lower pricesShort days; rain and wind increaseLow–moderate / low cost
Nov~0–3°C~6–8 hrsStrong aurora; Iceland Airwaves festival; ice caves formingDark, cold; some sites closeLow crowds / low cost
Dec−1 to 4°C~4–5 hrsDarkest nights = best aurora odds; festive Christmas moodLimited daylight; storms can disrupt travelLow–moderate / mid cost (holidays peak)

Best time for the northern lights: late August to mid-April

Iceland sits directly beneath the auroral oval, which makes it one of the most reliable places on Earth to see the northern lights — but only when the sky is dark enough. Aurora season runs from late August / early September through mid-April, according to Guide to Iceland. The deepest darkness falls from November to January, while many travellers prefer the equinox months (March, April, September, October) for a better balance of dark nights and more stable weather.

Auroras most often peak between 10:30 p.m. and 1:00 a.m., with a wider window of about 9:00 p.m. to 2:00 a.m. Check the official aurora forecast from the Icelandic Met Office before heading out, and get away from city light pollution in Reykjavík for the clearest view.

Best time for the midnight sun, Highlands and driving: June to August

Summer is when Iceland truly opens up. From late June through July the sun barely sets, giving you near-endless daylight for sightseeing. The Highland F-roads open in July, unlocking the interior's volcanoes, glaciers and hot-spring rivers — but you'll need a 4WD vehicle rated for F-roads, and river crossings require experience. Visit Iceland, the official tourism site, covers seasonal driving rules in depth. Daylight peaks with the summer solstice around June 21, when the sun stays above the horizon on Grímsey Island in the north.

July is also the warmest month (averaging about 13°C / 55°F per Lonely Planet) and the height of whale-watching season. The trade-off is crowds: this is peak tourist season, so book accommodation and rental cars well ahead. Planning a broader trip? Our guides to the best time to visit Japan and the best time to visit Hawaii cover two other seasonal favourites.

The cheapest time to visit Iceland

The cheapest time to visit Iceland is the shoulder and off-season: April, May, September, October and into November. During these months, accommodation and rental-car rates drop significantly from their June–July peak, popular sites like the South Coast and Golden Circle thin out, and you can still enjoy reasonable daylight (especially April–May and September). Lonely Planet notes that April–May in particular offers "off-season discounts on accommodation and activities." You also keep a shot at the aurora from September onward. The main catch is that not all tours and Highland routes are open yet in spring, and autumn weather can turn stormy.

The worst time to visit Iceland

There is no outright unvisitable month, but the hardest time to travel is deep winter (late December to February) if your priority is sightseeing rather than the aurora. Daylight shrinks to as little as 4–5 hours, storms close roads regularly, and driving yourself becomes genuinely hazardous on ice and snow. The other weak window for a general holiday is late October to November, when autumn colour has faded, rain and wind peak, and many seasonal services have shut — though this same period is excellent for northern-lights hunters who don't mind the dark.

One honest caveat: Iceland's climate is warming. The Icelandic Met Office confirmed 2025 was the warmest year on record nationwide (national average 5.2°C, 1.1°C above the 1991–2020 mean), so historical "typical" conditions — especially snow cover in winter — are shifting. Treat any figure as a guide, not a guarantee.

Practical planning tips for any season

  • Always check conditions before you drive. Iceland's weather can change in minutes. Follow the official Safetravel.is advisories and the Road Administration (road.is) for closures, especially in winter and on Highland F-roads.
  • Layer up. Even in July, overnight temperatures can drop sharply and rain is possible year-round. Bring a waterproof outer layer, insulating mid-layer and sturdy waterproof boots no matter the season.
  • Book early for summer. Late June to early August is when Icelanders themselves travel, and international demand peaks. Reserve cars, accommodation and popular tours months ahead.
  • Go shoulder for value. May and September give you most of summer's accessibility at a fraction of the cost, with far fewer people at marquee sights.
  • Match your month to your goal. Decide your single must-do first — midnight sun, Highlands, puffins, whales, northern lights or ice caves — then work backward to the months above. Iceland rarely delivers everything at once, and it rewards travellers who pick a lane.

For a country this far north, the "best" time is really a question of priorities: chase light in summer, chase dark in winter, and split the difference in September or March for the best of both.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Hawaii: Month-by-Month Weather Guide
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Hawaii is mid-April to early June or September-October. Expect 78-85F warmth, calmer seas, smaller crowds, and lower prices in these shoulder months.
guides.content:
The Short Answer: Mid-April to Early June, and September-October

The best time to visit Hawaii is the shoulder window from mid-April to early June, and again from September through October. Daytime temperatures still sit in the low-to-mid 80s °F, the ocean is at its calmest (late spring) or its warmest (early fall), resort and airfare pricing steps down off the holiday peaks, and crowds thin out between school breaks. Go Hawaii, the state's official tourism authority, notes the islands really only have two seasons — summer (kau, May–October) and winter (hoʻoilo, November–April) — with average daytime sea-level temperatures of 85°F (29.4°C) in summer and 78°F (25.6°C) in winter. Because the weather is reliably balmy year-round, your timing decision is really about crowds, cost, surf, and what you want to see — not whether you'll be warm.

If you need a quick hierarchy:

  • Best overall value + weather: Late April to early June; September–October
  • Best for big-wave watching & whales: December–March
  • Best for guaranteed sun, calmest beaches & festivals: June–August (peak crowds and prices)
  • Cheapest: September–October, with a secondary window in February–early March

For comparison, the same shoulder-season logic that makes spring and fall the best time to visit Japan applies here: aim for the edges of the high season.

Hawaii's Weather, In Brief

Hawaii's climate is remarkably stable. Trade winds provide a near-constant cooling breeze, and the wettest months run November through March — though Go Hawaii stresses that winter rain is highly localized, so “if it is raining where you are, there is almost always a sunny spot to be found around the coast.” Nighttime temperatures run roughly 10°F lower than daytime. Near-shore water averages a comfortable 74°F (23.3°C) year-round, peaking at about 80°F (26.7°C) in summer.

One seasonal flip matters more than temperature: summer waters are typically gentle on all beaches, while winter sends Pacific storm swells into north shores, producing the legendary big waves that pull professional surfers to Oʻahu's North Shore. A few times each year the trade winds stop entirely and a humid south or west “kona” system moves in — the main source of sticky, stormy stretches.

Month-by-Month Guide: Best Time to Visit Hawaii

MonthWeatherCrowds & costBest for
Jan–Feb78°F days, coolest & rainiest months; big north-shore surfHigh post-holiday, then a budget dip in FebWhale watching (peak), big-wave spectating, fewer visitors late Feb
Mar–AprWarming, 78–80°F; spring break spike mid-Mar to early AprModerate; rises during spring breakWhale tail-end, calmer ocean, family travel
May–early JunDry, sunny, low-to-mid 80s; calm waterShoulder — lower prices, thinner crowdsBest overall balance; couples, snorkeling
Jun–Aug85°F, drier & hotter; south-shore surfPeak summer — highest demand outside holidaysFestivals, mango season, calmest beaches
Sep–OctHighs ~85–88°F; ocean warmest of year; occasional stormsLowest crowds & airfare of the yearBest value; warmest water, quietest beaches
Nov–DecCooling toward winter, rainier; surf returnsQuiet early Nov, then huge Dec holiday spikeWhale arrival (from Nov), Honolulu Marathon, holidays — book early

Lonely Planet corroborates the broad strokes: summer averages an 85°F daytime high and winter 78°F, and it names September and October as the cheapest, quietest months, with highs around 88°F and the warmest ocean of the year.

Cheapest Time and Worst Time to Visit Hawaii

Cheapest: September and October are the consistently cheapest months — Lonely Planet reports airfare from the U.S. mainland is usually at its lowest and hotel rooms are easiest to find. Late February through early March is a secondary budget window after the winter-holiday rush, when rain is more common but discounts return.

Worst (for cost and crowds): The last two weeks of December through early January are Hawaii's single busiest, priciest window, as travelers flee cold climates for the sun. Rooms become scarce and expensive; book months ahead or avoid entirely. The other stretch to think twice about is mid-June through mid-August, when schools are out and summer peak pricing applies — still beautiful, but you'll pay for it and share the beaches.

There's no truly “unvisitable” month — even the rainiest winter weeks usually deliver sun somewhere on the island the same day. “Worst” here means worst value, not worst weather.

Hurricane Season in Hawaii

Central Pacific hurricane season officially runs June 1 through November 30, according to NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center, though tropical cyclones can and do occur outside that window. Direct strikes on Hawaii are uncommon, but when systems do approach the islands it's most often in late summer and early fall — something to weigh if you're eyeing the otherwise-ideal September–October value window. It's a manageable risk, not a deal-breaker: keep an eye on forecasts, build a little flexibility into your itinerary, and consider travel insurance for an August–October trip.

By-Island Nuances

Hawaii's weather is highly localized — the windward (northeastern) sides of every island are greener and wetter, while the leeward (southwestern) resort coasts are drier and sunnier. A few specifics:

  • Maui — The premier whale-watching base from December through April, when thousands of humpbacks crowd the shallow channel between Maui, Molokaʻi, and Lānaʻi.
  • Oʻahu — Home to winter big-wave spectacle on the North Shore (Triple Crown of Surfing, Eddie Aikau) and Honolulu's year-round energy.
  • Island of Hawaiʻi (Big Island) — Kona coast stays drier and sunnier; Hilo is one of the wettest towns in the U.S. The same island holds sunny beaches and snow-capped Mauna Kea.
  • Kauaʻi — The lushest and wettest island; Nāpali Coast is stunning but its north shore gets the most winter rain.

Temperatures also drop about 3.5°F for every 1,000 feet of elevation — so Haleakalā on Maui and Mauna Kea on the Big Island can be 30°F colder than the coast. Pack layers if you've booked a sunrise summit.

Whale Season: A Winter Bonus

If seeing humpback whales ( koholā) is a priority, plan for November through April. NOAA's Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale National Marine Sanctuary reports that every winter thousands of whales travel to Hawaii's warm, shallow waters to mate, calve, and nurse — and they can be seen from shore and at sea across every island, with peak sightings January through March. An estimated 8,000–12,000 make the migration from Alaska each year.

Practical Planning Tips

  • Book 4–6 months ahead for Christmas/New Year and mid-June to mid-August. For shoulder months, 2–3 months is usually enough.
  • Target midweek flights (Tuesday–Wednesday) in shoulder season for the lowest fares.
  • Stay on the leeward coast (south/southwest) for the most sun if you're traveling in the rainier winter months.
  • Reserve must-do permits early — Hanauma Bay snorkel slots and Haleakalā sunrise reservations sell out, especially in peak summer and winter.
  • Respect the ocean: winter north-shore surf is for watching, not swimming. Heed warning flags and ask lifeguards about currents.
  • Check vog conditions if you have asthma and plan to visit Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park; volcanic fog can affect sensitive groups.

The same shoulder-season discipline that pays off here is what makes timing your trip to Iceland easier on the wallet, too — aim for the edges of high season and you'll almost always trade a little certainty for a lot of value.

Bottom line: For the best mix of warm weather, calm water, manageable crowds, and fair prices, book Hawaii for mid-April to early June or September to October. Come December–March for whales and big waves, June–August for peak sun and festivals — just expect to pay and share.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Ireland: Weather, Costs & Crowds (2026)
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Ireland is late May to September. May, June and September are the sweet spot: mild weather, long daylight, smaller crowds and lower prices.
guides.content:
The short answer: late May to September, with shoulder months the real prize

The best time to visit Ireland is late May through September, when the weather is mildest, daylight stretches well into the evening, and every pub, ferry, and visitor centre is open. Ireland itself describes its climate as "mild, temperate... with warm summers and mild winters," where "rain clouds will clear to reveal blue skies" and a freezing morning can warm into a glorious afternoon — the famous "four seasons in one day."

But the single smartest window for most travellers is the shoulder run of May, June and September. You get most of summer's long days and green scenery at noticeably lower prices and smaller crowds than the July–August peak, when Irish schools are out and accommodation, car hire and attractions fill up and cost most. If your priority is value above all, November to February is cheapest — at the cost of short days, scaled-back transport, and seasonal closures.

Ireland by season: what to expect month by month

Long-term averages from Met Éireann (Ireland's meteorological service) put monthly mean temperatures at roughly 5°C in January, rising to about 15°C in July, with an annual mean near 10°C (9.8°C over 1991–2020). Tourism Ireland reports August daytime temperatures typically ranging from 10°C to 19°C, and December averages of 7–9°C with snow "quite rare." Use the table below to match a season to your priorities.

Season / monthsWeatherCrowdsCostDaylightHighlights & best for
Spring
March–May		 Cool, unsettled; warming. March ~7–10°C, May ~11°C average. Low to moderate; St Patrick's week in March is busy. Low–moderate (spikes around 17 March). Lengthening fast; bright evenings by May. Bluebells in Wicklow, Burren in Bloom (May), Wild Atlantic Way drives. Best for: flowers, golf, road trips before peak pricing.
Early summer
May–June		 Mild and often dry; average highs approach 18°C by June. Moderate — busy but not yet peak. Moderate (lower than July–Aug). Longest days of the year. Bloomsday, Bord Bia Bloom, Dublin Pride. Best for: the weather/value sweet spot.
Peak summer
July–August		 Warmest and sunniest; August days 10–19°C, often higher. Highest — schools out, beaches and top sights busy. Highest; book early or risk sell-outs. Very long; late sunsets. Galway Arts Festival & Races, Rose of Tralee, islands & beaches. Best for: reliable warmth and the full events calendar.
Autumn shoulder
September–October		 Mild with dry spells; September mean ~13°C, cooling through October. Dropping sharply as schools return. Coming down from peak. Still long in September; shortening fast. Galway Oyster Festival, Cork Jazz, Bram Stoker Festival, fall colour. Best for: crowd-free sightseeing and value.
Winter
November–February		 Short, dark, wet and windy; December 7–9°C, January mean ~5°C. Snow rare. Lowest (except Christmas/New Year). Lowest off-peak rates. Shortest days of the year. Christmas markets, TradFest, cosy pubs, northern lights in Inishowen. Best for: budget and city breaks — not scenic road trips.

Sources: Met Éireann 1991–2020 30-year averages; Tourism Ireland ("Ireland's weather," August and December guides); Lonely Planet.

Cheapest time to visit Ireland

The cheapest time to visit Ireland is November to February, excluding the Christmas and New Year weeks. Hotels, restaurants and B&Bs drop to off-peak rates, and cities like Kilkenny, Limerick and Galway still offer good transport links to scenic spots — ideal for a low-cost city break built around cosy pubs, free museums (Dublin's National Gallery even shows its delicate J.M.W. Turner watercolours only in January, when light is weakest) and TradFest at the end of January.

The trade-offs are real: days are short, storms sweep in from the Atlantic, and rural roads can be icy, so independent road trips should stick to main routes. Many interpretive centres and remote hospitality go into winter hibernation, and transport services scale back. September and October are the smarter budget compromise — prices have fallen from their summer peak but attractions are still fully open and the weather is mild.

Whenever you go, locking in flights early is the biggest single money-saver; see our guide to the best time to book flights for the booking windows that matter.

Worst time to visit Ireland

There is no genuinely bad time, but two windows disappoint most travellers. Midwinter (late November to January) is the weakest match for a classic sightseeing holiday: the shortest daylight of the year, the highest storm risk, and the fewest open attractions and transport options. It suits city-breakers and budget travellers, not first-timers chasing the Cliffs of Moher or a Wild Atlantic Way drive.

The second "worst" scenario is booking July and August at the last minute. With Irish schools closed, accommodation, car hire and the most popular locales (Dublin, Kerry, the southern and western coasts) fill up fast, and leaving bookings late is "risky and not recommended." Peak summer is wonderful if you reserve months ahead — frustrating and expensive if you don't.

Practical planning tips

  • Pack layers, not a season. Ireland's "four seasons in one day" reputation is earned — bring a light weatherproof jacket and a jumper even in August, plus T-shirts for sunny spells.
  • Chase the shoulder edges. Late May, June and September deliver summer's long days at spring/autumn prices. June daylight is exceptional at this latitude (roughly 53°N) — for an even more extreme version of the long-day effect, see the best time to visit Alaska.
  • Book peak summer early. If July–August is your only window, reserve hotels, car hire and major attractions (Cliffs of Moher, Guinness Storehouse, island ferries) well ahead.
  • Expect rain, not downpours. "Soft" mist keeps the countryside green; persistent all-day rain is the exception. Build flex days into road-trip itineraries.
  • Combine with neighbours. Ireland pairs naturally with Iberia on a Europe loop — compare timing with our best time to visit Portugal to sequence the two.
  • Time a festival. St Patrick's Day (mid-March), Galway Arts Festival (July), Galway Oyster & Seafood Festival (September) and Cork Jazz (October) each re-define the best week to go.

The bottom line

For the classic Irish experience — green landscapes, dry-ish spells, long evenings and everything open — aim for late May to September. Choose May, June or September for the best balance of weather, crowds and cost; July and August if you want the warmest, busiest, most festival-packed version of the island; and November to February only if budget and quiet matter more than daylight and open roads.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Costa Rica: Month-by-Month Guide
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Costa Rica is mid-December to April (dry season) for sun, beaches, and wildlife. May-November is cheaper, greener, and less crowded.
guides.author: Suraj Giri
guides.content:
The best time to visit Costa Rica, in short

The single best time to visit Costa Rica is the dry season, from mid-December to late April, when skies are clear, trails are dry, and both coasts deliver dependable sunshine. According to the Costa Rica Tourism Board (Visit Costa Rica), this window — known locally as verano (summer) — is when rainfall is lowest and conditions are most consistent for beaches, volcano views, and wildlife watching.

The trade-off is that this is also high season, so prices and crowds peak between late December and March. If you want sunshine without the premium, late April (a transition month) and the July–August "little summer" are smart compromises. And if saving money is the priority, the green season (May to mid-December) drops rates sharply while keeping the mornings bright.

One important wrinkle: Costa Rica's two coasts run on different weather clocks. The Pacific side has a clean dry/wet split, while the Caribbean side stays rainier year-round and actually catches a dry spell in September–October — exactly when the Pacific is at its wettest. Where you go matters as much as when.

Costa Rica's seasons explained (and the Caribbean exception)

Costa Rica sits squarely in the tropics, so temperatures stay warm year-round — Lonely Planet places the average around 80°F (26°C). What changes month to month is rain, not heat. Per Visit Costa Rica's climate data, the country splits into two distinct weather regimes divided by its central mountain range:

  • Pacific coast — A well-defined dry season from December to March (April is a transition month); March is the driest and hottest month. The rainy season runs May to October (November is transitional), and rain falls mostly in the afternoon and early evening. There's a relative dip in rain during July and August called the veranillo, or "little summer."
  • Caribbean coast — No true dry season; even the drier months stay fairly wet. Two relatively dry windows exist: February–March and September–October. The rainiest month is December, influenced by cold fronts sweeping down from the Northern Hemisphere. Rain tends to fall at night and in the morning.

This is why September and October feel like two different trips depending on where you stand: soaking wet on the Pacific, comparatively dry on the Caribbean. It's a useful pattern to exploit if you're traveling on a budget.

Month-by-month: when to go

Here's how the year breaks down for weather, crowds, cost, daylight, and timing. Note that daylight barely shifts year-round — Costa Rica sits close to the equator, so you get roughly 12 hours of light whenever you visit.

MonthsWeatherCrowdsCostDaylightBest for
Mid-Dec – FebDry and sunny; Pacific at its clearestHigh (peak holiday season)Highest~12 hrsBeaches, volcanoes, hiking; northern humpback whales arrive late December
Mar – mid-AprDriest and hottest (March is the peak); April transitionsHigh (spring break, Holy Week)High~12 hrsSunshine, water sports, cloud-forest escapes from the heat
May – JunGreen season begins; sunny mornings, afternoon showersLowModerate–low~12 hrsAvoiding crowds, lush blooming landscapes, clearer volcano views
Jul – Aug"Little summer" (veranillo) — a relative rain dipModerate (summer travelers)Moderate~12 hrsWildlife spotting, cloud forests; southern humpbacks arrive in July
Sep – OctPacific: rainiest (up to 25 in/month); Caribbean: drierLowestLowest~12 hrsBudget travel on the Pacific, or head to the Caribbean coast
NovTransition; rains ease but weather is unpredictableLowLow~12 hrsShoulder-season deals, thin crowds before dry season returns

Cost column reflects relative seasonal positioning (high season vs. green season) rather than specific room rates, which vary widely by property and region.

For most first-time visitors chasing classic Costa Rica — Manuel Antonio, Arenal, Monteverde, the Nicoya beaches — the late-December-through-March window is the safest call. May, June, and November look a lot like the dry season with bursts of rain mixed in, and Lonely Planet flags May–June as the best window to skip the crowds while the landscape turns vivid green. September and October are the wild cards: best for budget travelers and surfers chasing big Pacific swells, but the least desirable weather-wise on the west coast.

The cheapest time to visit Costa Rica

The cheapest months to visit Costa Rica are September and October. This is the peak of the green season, when hotels cut rates, crowds thin out, and tour operators offer their deepest discounts. Visit Costa Rica notes that fall brings "reduced rates and light crowds," though it cautions that some hotels and attractions — particularly on the southern Pacific end — may close completely during this stretch, which is something to weigh when booking.

Lonely Planet agrees, calling September and October the best window for budget travelers and pointing out you'll find fewer crowds and more deals on both accommodation and travel. The catch is that it's also the height of the rainy season on the Pacific slope, with the possibility of flooding that can make point-to-point travel difficult.

If you want a smarter value play than gambling on peak rains, target the veranillo in July–August or the May–June shoulder: rates are still well below high season, but you'll get more usable beach hours. For airfare specifically, CheapAir's annual airfare study finds that Wednesday is the cheapest day to fly (about $102 less than Sunday on average), with Tuesday close behind, so building your trip around mid-week flights compounds the savings. See our deeper breakdown in the best time to book flights.

The worst time to visit Costa Rica

"Worst" is region-dependent, but if your priority is dry-weather activities on the Pacific coast, late September through October is the toughest window — it's the rainiest period of the year and the time when flooding can disrupt travel. It also overlaps squarely with the Atlantic hurricane season: NOAA's National Hurricane Center puts the peak of the season at September 10, with most activity occurring between mid-August and mid-October. While direct hurricane strikes on Costa Rica are uncommon, the increased storm activity feeds the heavy rains and surf that define this period.

Two other windows are "worst" only if they clash with your priorities. Christmas through New Year's and Holy Week (La Semana Santa) bring peak crowds and peak pricing — Lonely Planet specifically advises booking accommodation well in advance for these dates. And because the Caribbean coast runs on an opposite rhythm, its rainiest stretch is actually November through January (with December the wettest month), so the standard "avoid September" rule doesn't apply there. If you're weighing the Caribbean side of Costa Rica against other Caribbean destinations, our best time to visit Puerto Rico guide compares the timing.

Practical planning tips

  • Plan outdoors for the morning. In the green season, mornings are almost always sunny on both coasts, with clouds building around midday. Schedule hikes, beaches, and wildlife tours early; treat a dry afternoon as a bonus.
  • Pack for rain, not cold. Temperatures stay warm year-round, so skip heavy layers. Lonely Planet recommends a raincoat (plus a dry bag to protect your valuables), as rain can arrive without warning in the green season.
  • Book early for peak weeks. Christmas, New Year, Easter/Holy Week, and U.S. spring break sell out fast and command the highest rates. Reserve accommodation, popular tours, and in-demand restaurants well ahead.
  • Time wildlife to the season. Northern humpback whales arrive from the Pacific Northwest in late December; southern humpbacks migrate into Pacific waters in July. For surfers, August through November delivers the biggest waves on the Pacific coast.
  • Exploit the Caribbean flip. When the Pacific is drowning in September–October, the Caribbean (Puerto Viejo, Cahuita, Tortuguero) hits its drier stretch — a great budget-time escape.
  • Stack your flight savings. Combine green-season rates with mid-week travel (Tuesday/Wednesday departures) to cut both land and air costs. Our best time to book flights guide walks through the prime booking window in detail.

Costa Rica rewards flexibility more than most destinations: the difference between a soggy trip and a perfect one often comes down to which coast you pick in which month. For a broader Central America comparison, see our guide to the best time to visit Mexico. And if you're locking in dates, lean on the season table above — it tells you exactly what you're trading off whenever you choose to go.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Alaska: Month-by-Month Weather Guide
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Alaska is mid-June to August for long days, wildlife and cruises; September brings fall color and aurora. Full month-by-month guide.
guides.content:
The best time to visit Alaska is mid-June through August

The single best window to visit Alaska is mid-June through August, when the state serves up its longest days, warmest temperatures, peak wildlife activity, and the full roster of cruises, tours, and open lodgings. Travel Alaska, the state's official tourism organization, is blunt about it: June through August are "the most popular months to visit Alaska, with long daylight hours, the warmest temperatures, best wildlife viewing, and the most tours, activities, cruise options, and accommodations available." Lonely Planet agrees, calling summer "the best all-around season to visit Alaska."

That said, "best" depends on what you came for. September is the sweet spot for fall color and the first reliable northern lights. Late February and March are prime for dog sledding and winter festivals. And November through March is aurora season proper, when the long dark nights above Fairbanks light up green. Here is how to choose.

Alaska by season and month: what to expect

Alaska's climate swings hard by region, the Interior is far colder in winter and warmer in summer than the coast, so the figures below are general averages for the popular Southcentral/Anchorage and Interior corridors. Travel Alaska notes that by July, daytime temperatures in the Interior average around 70°F (and have been known to reach the 90s), while coastal areas and higher elevations rarely climb above 65°F. Daylight is the real headline: around the June solstice, Anchorage gets roughly 22 hours of functional daylight, per Visit Anchorage, and north of the Arctic Circle the sun does not set at all. By late December, that collapses to about 5 to 6 hours.

Month / seasonDaylight (approx.)Typical tempsWildlife & highlightsCrowds & cost
May (spring shoulder)~16–19 hrsHighs low 60s°F (~17°C); driest month statewideWhales and marine wildlife return to Alaska's waters; bears emergeLow crowds; lodging and flights roughly 20–40% below peak summer
June~19–22 hrsHighs mid-60s to 70°FMost trails snow-free; Denali Park Road opens to buses; midnight sun festivalsHigh season begins; book well ahead
July (peak)~18–20 hrsWarmest month — Interior ~70°F+, coastal ~65°FBear viewing peaks at Brooks Falls (Katmai) as salmon run; best all-round wildlifeBUSIEST month; peak cruise traffic; highest prices
August~14–16 hrsStarting to cool; tundra color appears late month in the northBears still active on berries and salmon; first aurora possible late monthHigh, but cruise traffic eases slightly
September (fall shoulder)~12–14 hrsCooling fast; often the wettest month on the coastPeak fall color (mid-to-late Sept south); aurora season opens; roads still clearThinning crowds; prices drop; great value
October~10–11 hrsAnchorage avg high ~42°F (5.5°C); snow returns to InteriorWildlife winding down; businesses close for winterVery quiet; many lodges/tours shut
November–March (winter)~5–9 hrs (shortest in Dec)Deep cold — Interior can hit -20°F, February often struggles above 0°F (-17.8°C); coast stays near/below 20°FNorthern lights (best Aug 21–Apr 21); Iditarod dog sled race in March; skiing, snowmobilingLowest prices; fewest visitors; limited services

Sources for the figures above: Travel Alaska (monthly temperatures, driest-month and wildlife-timing claims), Visit Anchorage (22 hours of functional daylight on the June solstice and roughly 5.5 hours on the shortest winter day), Lonely Planet (October Anchorage average of 42°F/5.5°C and the February -17.8°C reference), and the University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute (the August 21–April 21 aurora window).

The cheapest time to visit Alaska (and the worst time)

Cheapest: May, and September into October

If cost is the deciding factor, aim for the spring shoulder in May or the fall shoulder in September and October. Travel Alaska reports that shoulder-season travel "can cut your costs meaningfully without meaningfully cutting your experience," with May in particular offering flights and accommodations that "run 20 to 40 percent lower than peak summer rates." September is the more compelling deal for many travelers because aurora season opens in late August, fall color peaks, roads are still clear, and tour operators are sometimes willing to negotiate as the season winds down. November through March is the cheapest of all, but you trade away most classic sightseeing for cold and dark.

One booking note worth heeding: Travel Alaska recommends starting your search about six months out and booking no later than three months before a summer trip, last-minute Alaska fares are rarely cheap and the most popular lodges fill up regardless of season. (Pair this with our guide to the best time to book flights to time your airfare.)

Worst time: late October into November (for a classic trip)

"Worst" is relative in a state this varied, but for a first-time, sightseeing-and-wildlife trip the weakest window is late October through November. The cruise season has ended, many tour operators and lodges shut when the cruisers go home, bears are denning, and the weather is wet and dark before there is enough reliable snow for skiing or dog sledding. Lonely Planet cautions that by October "a distinct offseason atmosphere rolls in" and that cruise-focused businesses start closing for winter. If you are not specifically chasing the northern lights or winter sports, deep winter (November–February) is also tough: minimal daylight, sub-zero Interior cold, and limited access to the backcountry and kayaking that define an Alaska summer.

Three reasons to bend the rule

1. September for fall color and the first aurora

Travel Alaska describes brief but vivid fall: "the fall colors of the tundra and trees appear in late August further north and mid to late September further south, offering a stunning backdrop of red, yellow, and orange." Combine that with thinner crowds, lower prices, and the season's first dark skies, and September is arguably the smartest single month for photographers and value hunters.

2. November–March for the northern lights

The University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute is the authority here. Their forecast team explains that aurora viewing "may be best in locations with clear skies and around the spring (March) or fall (September) equinox," thanks to the Russell-McPherron effect, which roughly doubles your odds of a display compared with the solstices. Around Fairbanks (latitude 64.8°N) the aurora-viewing "season" runs roughly August 21 to April 21, and the best time of night is the three to four hours around midnight, typically 9 p.m. to 3 a.m. Their pragmatic tip: stay at least three clear nights and it is highly likely, though never certain, you will see the lights.

3. Late February and March for winter festivals and dog sledding

Travel Alaska singles out February and March for "dogsled races and winter festivals," and Lonely Planet calls March "possibly the best month for winter activities" thanks to longer days, slightly milder temperatures, and the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, the state's signature event.

Practical planning tips

  • Match the region to the season. The coast (Inside Passage, Anchorage, Kenai Peninsula) is balmier and wetter; the Interior (Fairbanks, Denali) is hotter in summer and far colder in winter. Pick one region and go deep, it is the single biggest money-saver, since hopscotching between regions means expensive bush flights.
  • Book early for summer. Peak accommodations "are typically $200 and up" per night, per Travel Alaska, and lodges near Denali fill months ahead. Use the six-months-out rule.
  • Lean on free and low-cost sights. Seven of Alaska's eight national parks charge no entrance fee, only Denali charges ($15, valid seven days). State park parking is roughly $5–$10 per vehicle, and public-use cabins run about $35–$65 a night.
  • Pack in layers. Travel Alaska's packing guidance is blunt: weather "can vary dramatically by region and season," so plan for sun, rain, and cold on the same day, even in July.
  • Time your flights smartly. Airfare is one of the largest line items on an Alaska trip. See our best time to book flights guide, then lock in early for summer or target shoulder season for the best fares.

Planning more seasonal trips? Our best time to visit Costa Rica and best time to visit Portugal guides break down those destinations the same way.

The bottom line

For most first-time visitors, mid-June through August is the best time to visit Alaska, it maximizes daylight, wildlife, and access, at the cost of peak crowds and prices. Shift to September for fall color, fewer people, and the first northern lights, or to February–March for dog sledding and winter festivals. Avoid late October and November unless you want quiet, cheap, and mostly closed. Whatever month you pick, book early, pack layers, and let your priority, wildlife, aurora, or value, drive the decision.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Puerto Rico: Month-by-Month Guide
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Puerto Rico is mid-December to April for dry, sunny warmth. See our month-by-month guide to weather, crowds, costs, and hurricane season.
guides.content:
The Best Time to Visit Puerto Rico at a Glance

The single best window to visit Puerto Rico is mid-December through April — the island's dry high season, when daytime highs hover in the low-to-mid 80s °F, humidity eases, and rain is infrequent. For the same sunny weather at a lower price, the late-April-to-June shoulder season is the smartest compromise; Lonely Planet calls April and May "optimal months for milder temperatures and emptier tourist spots."

It helps that Puerto Rico is genuinely a year-round destination. According to NOAA's official climate normals, San Juan's annual average temperature is 81.0 °F, with January — the coolest month — still reaching an average high of 83.2 °F, and August — the warmest — averaging a high near 89.1 °F. The one trade-off to plan around is the Atlantic hurricane season, which runs June 1 to November 30 and peaks around September 10. Manage that single variable and almost any month on the island works.

Puerto Rico's Weather, Season by Season

Surrounded by warm Atlantic and Caribbean water, Puerto Rico barely changes temperature month to month — what changes is the rain. NOAA's climate summary for the island defines a wet season from May through October, when tropical waves and afternoon thunderstorms do most of the watering, and a drier season from November through April, when passing cold fronts bring the occasional brief shower but far less sustained downpour. The north and El Yunque rainforest are lush and humid; the south coast around Ponce is noticeably drier, almost semi-arid; and the Cordillera Central mountains run several degrees cooler than the coast — useful to know if you're planning a road trip into the interior.

Daylight is generous year-round, too: expect roughly 11 hours of daylight in December and over 13 by midsummer, so short winter days are never really a constraint the way they can be at higher latitudes. Discover Puerto Rico, the island's official tourism body, pitches the destination accordingly — as a no-passport, year-round Caribbean escape served by dozens of daily nonstop flights into San Juan (SJU) and Aguadilla (BQN).

Month-by-Month Guide: When to Go

The table below breaks the year into six booking windows so you can weigh weather, crowds, cost, and timing at a glance.

Period Weather Crowds & Cost Best For Watch Out For
Dec–Feb (peak winter) Dry & sunny; highs near 83 °F, lows near 72 °F; lowest humidity of the year Highest crowds and prices; holiday dates sell out early Beaches, festivals, Rincón surf swells, and the Fiestas de la Calle San Sebastián in mid-January Premium flights and hotels; book months ahead
Mar–Apr (late peak) Still dry with calm seas; the best sunny-day odds land in February and March Busy through Easter, then thinning out Humpback whale watching off the northwest coast (tail of the season), hiking, and beach days Semana Santa (Holy Week) surges in both crowds and rates
May–Jun (shoulder) Warming up; sporadic showers that tend to pass quickly Notable price drops and fewer tourists Best value-for-weather; Noche de San Juan on June 23 Tropical storms become possible from the June 1 season start
Jul–Aug (summer heat) Hot and humid; highs routinely near 89 °F, and locals pack the beaches Moderate; islanders are on vacation Vieques and Culebra, local culture, and summer festivals Heat, humidity, and building hurricane risk by August
Sep–Oct (hurricane peak) Highs in the upper 80s °F; rain showers common; storm climatology peaks around Sep 10 Lowest visitor numbers and deepest discounts Budget travelers with flexible dates Highest storm risk; always carry travel insurance
November (transition) Hurricane season winds down; cooling breezes return Still cheap, slowly picking back up A quiet shoulder trip just before the December rush Late-season storms remain possible through Nov 30

Best Time for Beaches, Surfing, and Wildlife

Pick your months around what you most want to do:

  • Beaches: December to April gives you dry weather and calm seas for a classic beach day. Summer (July–August) offers the warmest water but the sand gets crowded with locals — arrive early to claim a spot.
  • Surfing Rincón: the northwest coast comes alive November through February, when Atlantic swells — occasionally approaching 20 feet — make Rincón one of the Caribbean's premier surf towns.
  • Whale watching: humpbacks pass the northwest coast (around Rincón, Aguadilla, and Isabela) roughly mid-January through March.
  • Bioluminescent bays: Mosquito Bay (Vieques) and Laguna Grande glow year-round, but they're most vivid on dark, moonless nights — plan around the new moon rather than the calendar month.
  • El Yunque rainforest: cooler and wetter than the coast year-round; it's best hiked in the drier winter months when trails are less slick.

The Cheapest Time to Visit Puerto Rico

If price is your priority, target August through October, when hurricane risk drives visitor numbers — and rates — sharply down. Lonely Planet notes that this window brings "a sharp drop in visitor numbers but also prices," and recommends stretching your budget by staying in paradores, the independent inns and guesthouses scattered through the smaller towns outside San Juan. September typically sees the fewest visitors of the year.

The catch is obvious: you're trading savings for storm risk. If you book this window, buy travel insurance, keep your dates flexible, and monitor the forecast once you arrive. For a better-weather compromise, late April to June delivers most of the high-season sunshine at a fraction of the cost — and pairing that shoulder window with our guide to the best time to book flights can shave even more off your airfare.

The Worst Time to Visit Puerto Rico

"Worst" depends on what you'd rather avoid. If it's storms, the riskiest stretch is mid-August to mid-October, the period NOAA identifies as when most Atlantic tropical-cyclone activity occurs, with the climatological peak falling on September 10. A direct hit is statistically uncommon in any given year, but the disruption potential — flight cancellations, power outages, closed attractions — is real enough that nervous travelers and anyone locked into non-refundable dates should steer clear.

If instead you're trying to avoid crowds and high prices, the worst time is the winter peak, especially the Christmas–New Year stretch and the week of the Fiestas de la Calle San Sebastián in mid-January, when flights and hotels hit their annual highs. The shoulder months (May–June and November) dodge both problems and are what we'd suggest to most first-timers — the same logic behind choosing shoulder seasons when weighing the best time to visit Mexico or the best time to visit Costa Rica.

Practical Planning Tips

  • Book the peak early. December through April is Puerto Rico's official high season; reserve flights and hotels months ahead, especially around Christmas, New Year's, and Easter (Semana Santa).
  • Use the passport-free advantage. Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, so Americans need no passport. Discover Puerto Rico highlights dozens of daily nonstop flights into SJU and BQN, which helps keep airfare competitive with other Caribbean islands.
  • Rent a car to escape the crowds. You can drive around the entire island in roughly five to six hours; a car unlocks the cooler Cordillera Central mountains and the quieter south coast near Ponce.
  • Match the month to the activity. Surf Rincón November–February; whale-watch mid-January–March; beach-lounge December–April; chase culture and festivals December–January; and save money August–October.
  • Hedge during hurricane season. If you travel June–November, buy travel insurance that covers weather disruptions, build flexibility into your itinerary, and follow local-authority guidance if a storm develops.

However you time it, Puerto Rico's near-constant warmth means there's no truly bad month — only trade-offs between price, crowds, and the small but real chance of a late-summer storm. Pick the trade-off that matters most to you and the island delivers the rest. For a different-flavored warm escape, see our guide to the best time to visit Portugal.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Portugal: A Month-by-Month Guide
guides.excerpt: Best time to visit Portugal: mid-May–June and Sept–Oct bring warm, sunny days, smaller crowds, and lower prices. Full month-by-month weather and planning guide.
guides.content:
The best time to visit Portugal is mid-May to June and September to October

Portugal's sweet spot is the shoulder seasons — mid-May through June and September through October — when daytime highs across the mainland sit in the comfortable 22–27°C (72–81°F) range, skies are reliably sunny, and the peak-summer crowds and prices have not yet arrived (or have just departed). Lonely Planet singles out these spring and fall windows as ideal for hiking, cycling and city sightseeing, noting that Portugal generally has good weather, claiming more than 300 sunny days a year. Rick Steves agrees, calling the mid-May–June and October window shoulder season, when the weather is nearly as good and the crowds subside.

Within that window, May is the single best all-round month: Lisbon averages a 22°C (72°F) high, wildflowers blanket the south, and it's prime time for the coastal Rota Vicentina and Via Algarviana trails. September to October is equally magic — the Douro Valley is deep in grape-harvest season, air temperatures are still warm enough for a swim, and the ocean off central Portugal is nearing its annual warmest (which peaks in October–November).

If your priority is beaches and warm water rather than sightseeing, the Algarve in July and August delivers — but expect packed sands and the highest prices of the year. For a deeper dive on when to lock in airfare, pair this with our guide to the best time to book flights.

Portugal season-by-season: pros, cons, and what to expect

Temperatures below are long-run averages for Lisbon (from Portugal's national weather service, IPMA) and give you a reliable mainland benchmark; the Algarve around Faro runs a touch warmer and drier, while Porto and the north are cooler and wetter. Use them to plan, then adjust up a few degrees for the south and down for the north.

Season (months)Avg high, LisbonCrowds & costProsCons
Spring (Mar–May) 19–22°C / 66–72°F (May) Low to moderate; prices rising but still well below summer Mild, sunny days; wildflowers in April; ideal hiking and city walking; Easter festivities and Liberation Day (Apr 25) March can be rainy and chilly, especially in the north; ocean too cool for swimming
Early summer (Jun) 26°C / 78°F Moderate; Festas de Lisboa and Porto's São João liven the cities Warm and sunny, festival-packed, long daylight hours; crowds have not peaked Accommodation in Lisbon/Porto books up around festival nights; getting hotter
Peak summer (Jul–Aug) 28°C / 82–83°F Highest — August is Portugal's busiest month; rates up ~30%+ Hottest, driest weather; warmest sea for swimming; full schedule of beach life and events Packed Algarve beaches, sky-high prices, advance booking essential; cities can be hot
Fall (Sep–Oct) 23–27°C / 72–80°F Moderate to low; crowds thin as schools go back Grape harvests in the Douro; warmest ocean of the year; great surf; mild sunny days Rain becomes more likely from October; some beach businesses start closing
Winter (Nov–Feb) 15–18°C / 59–64°F Lowest — rock-bottom prices and empty attractions Sunny, uncrowded Algarve cliff walks; mild southern days; ideal for budget and city trips Short days, more rain (rainy season runs Oct–Apr), colder wetter north; some sights keep shorter hours

A quick month-by-month temperature reference (Lisbon, daytime high)

Jan 15°C/59°F · Feb 16°C/61°F · Mar 19°C/66°F · Apr 20°C/68°F · May 22°C/72°F · Jun 26°C/78°F · Jul 28°C/82°F · Aug 28°C/83°F · Sep 27°C/80°F · Oct 23°C/72°F · Nov 18°C/64°F · Dec 15°C/60°F. Faro and the Algarve peak around 29°C/84°F in July–August and hold a warmer sea that reaches about 21°C/71°F in August and September.

Region nuance: Lisbon, Porto, the Algarve, the Azores and Madeira

Lisbon and the centre: The capital is mild year-round and at its most pleasant April–June and September–October. July–August is hot and crowded; November–March is quieter and cooler but still sunny between showers.

Porto and the north: Cooler and wetter than the south — this is the greenest part of the country. The shoulder seasons (May–June, September–October) are the smart pick, when it is not so rainy and there aren't crowds of tourists everywhere, as Lonely Planet puts it. Winter here is genuinely cold, grey and wet.

The Algarve (south): Portugal's beach engine. Summer is hot, dry and busy; the sea is at its warmest (around 21°C/71°F) in August and September. Winter is the surprise — daytime highs near 16–17°C/61–63°F and sunny cliff-top walks almost to yourself, though some resorts feel lifeless. For a contrasting Atlantic-outdoor trip, see our best time to visit Costa Rica.

The Azores: Best from May to October for sunshine, calmer seas and whale-watching — April–May is prime for migratory blue and fin whales. Weather is changeable year-round on these mid-Atlantic islands.

Madeira: A genuine year-round destination thanks to its subtropical climate. Spring is spectacular for the levada trails and exotic flowers in bloom, and avoids the summer crowds.

The cheapest time to visit Portugal

The cheapest time to visit Portugal is the low season from November to March. Lonely Planet notes that this is when prices drop and rock-bottom accommodation rates appear, while Rick Steves points out that sights run shorter hours and there are fewer activities. The Algarve stays sunny enough for enjoyable coastal walks, Lisbon and Porto hotels are at their cheapest, and you will often have major attractions almost to yourself. The trade-off: shorter daylight, cooler temperatures, and the rainy season (which runs roughly October to April), with the north getting the worst of the wet weather. For the best value-for-comfort balance, target the edges of shoulder season — late October, November, and March — where you keep much of the low-season pricing but get more agreeable weather. If you are comparing shoulder-season European escapes, our best time to visit Mexico guide covers a similar sweet-spot logic.

The worst time to visit Portugal

There is no genuinely bad time, but August is the most challenging month for most travellers. It is Portugal's busiest tourist month, when reserving in advance is essential and accommodation prices typically increase by 30% or more during the summer high season, according to Lonely Planet. The Algarve in particular is packed, inland areas can be uncomfortably hot, and you will share every viewpoint and restaurant with peak crowds. The other tricky windows are the wettest months in the north — November to February, when Porto and the Douro see cold, rainy days — and any major festival night in Lisbon or Porto in June, when rooms vanish and prices spike even though the atmosphere is electric. If you dislike crowds and heat, simply steer clear of July–August; if you hate rain, avoid the northern winter.

Practical planning tips

  • Match the region to the month. Cities and the north shine May–June and September–October; the Algarve is best June–September for beaches and November–March for quiet, sunny walks.
  • Book early for summer and festivals. August fills up months ahead, and Lisbon's Festas de Lisboa (peaking June 13) and Porto's Festa de São João (June 23–24) sell out city rooms. If a Fátima pilgrimage is on your list, plan for May 13 or October 13.
  • Time the ocean right. The sea off central Portugal is at its warmest in October and November thanks to shifting currents — surprisingly, often better for a late dip than midsummer.
  • Pack layers. Even in shoulder season, sunny 22°C afternoons give way to cool evenings, and the north can turn wet quickly. A light rain jacket is wise outside June–August.
  • Surf in the cool months. Waves are at their biggest from October to March, making autumn one of the best windows for surfers and wave-watchers on the Atlantic coast.
  • Layer in the wine country. September–October is harvest time in the Douro Valley — you can watch (and even join) grape treading, a uniquely timed experience.

The headline answer holds across almost every itinerary: for the best balance of weather, cost and crowds, plan your Portugal trip for mid-May to June or September to October. Everything else — beach-focused August breaks, budget winter escapes, Azores whale-watching in spring — is a deliberate trade-off from that ideal.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Mexico: Month-by-Month Weather Guide
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Mexico is December to April for dry, sunny weather. See month-by-month pros and cons, the cheapest months, and hurricane-season risk.
guides.author: Suraj Giri
guides.content:
The best time to visit Mexico is December to April

The single best window to visit Mexico is December through April, the core of the country's dry season, when skies are clear, humidity is low, and rain is rare across most of the country. Mexico's official tourism board divides the climate into just two seasons — dry (November to April) and rainy (May to October) — so the dry months are when beaches, ruins, and highland cities are all at their most pleasant. If you want one perfect stretch, aim for late November to mid-December or January through early March: dry, sunny, and before the spring-break and Easter price spikes hit the coast.

That said, Mexico is a 32-state nation with coastlines, deserts, and high-altitude cities, so the “best” month depends on where you're going. Cancún and the Riviera Maya follow a Caribbean pattern (with a real hurricane season), Mexico City sits at 2,240 m (about 7,350 ft) and stays mild, and the Pacific coast has its own surf and sargassum rhythms. The breakdown below covers all of it.

Seasons and month-by-month guide

High tourist season aligns with the dry season. The rainy season (roughly May/June to October) overlaps with Atlantic hurricane season, which NOAA defines as June 1 to November 30, peaking around September 10 with most storm activity from mid-August to mid-October. Use this table to weigh weather, crowds, and cost month by month.

PeriodWeatherCrowds & costBest for
Dec–Feb Dry and mild. Caribbean/Yucatán coast highs commonly around 28–30°C (82–86°F); inland Mexico City sees January highs of just 20–22°C (68–71°F). Pack a sweater for highland nights. Peak season. November–January are the most expensive months to fly; attractions and Tulum fill up around New Year. Beaches, Maya ruins, Mexico City exploring, and February whale watching off the Baja Peninsula.
Mar–Apr Still dry and warming. Ideal for hiking and outdoor sites before the heat arrives. Spring break swells Cancún, Puerto Vallarta, and Cabo. Semana Santa (Holy Week) can push fares to double the usual rate. Hiking in Oaxaca, the spring equinox at Chichén Itzá, and monarch butterflies (into March).
May–Jun The hottest, driest stretch before rains. May averages daily highs around 35°C (95°F) in Mérida, 30°C (86°F) in Guadalajara and Oaxaca City, and 26°C (79°F) in Mexico City. June rains begin. First low season — fewer crowds and the year's best hotel deals. Sunseekers, budget travelers, and Pacific surfing (swells build June–August).
Jul–Aug Hot, humid, and rainy with afternoon downpours (especially Mexico City). Cancún/Riviera Maya is oppressively hot and can be hit by sargassum seaweed. Domestic travelers push Caribbean beach prices up; still cheaper than winter peak. Whale sharks off Cancún (best July–August), big Pacific surf, and turtle releases near Puerto Vallarta.
Sep Rainiest month and peak hurricane risk on the Caribbean and Gulf coasts; poor visibility for Caribbean diving. Cheapest month on the coast; inland cities stay pleasant. Independence celebrations (Sept 15–16), Mariachi festival in Jalisco, and Mexico City culture.
Oct–Nov Rains ease, humidity drops, and the second dry window opens. October is prime for Copper Canyon trekking. Shoulder season — good value; book early for late November. Día de Muertos (early November), canyon country, and mild inland cities.

Cheapest time and worst time to visit Mexico

Cheapest time: Mexico has two low seasons — May to June and September to November — when accommodation and flight prices drop sharply. September is typically the cheapest month on the Caribbean coast, though you trade low prices for rain and hurricane risk. May and early June are the sweeter deal: hot but largely dry, with thin crowds before the rains set in. For the flight side of the equation, see our best time to book flights guide, and lock in fares one to three months ahead for domestic routes.

Worst time: For the Caribbean coast — Cancún, Tulum, and the Riviera Maya — the worst window is September through mid-October, when hurricane risk peaks (the climatological peak is September 10), rainfall is at its maximum, and dive visibility is poor. If you're set on the Caribbean in late summer, note that Puerto Rico and the wider Caribbean share this same September-peak hurricane pattern. For the Pacific beach resorts, the worst stretch for crowds (not weather) is spring break and Semana Santa, when fares can double and beaches are packed.

Regional nuances: Cancún, Mexico City, and the Pacific coast

Cancún and the Riviera Maya (Caribbean): Best December to April — dry, sunny, and outside peak hurricane season. Summer brings heat, humidity, afternoon storms, and sargassum seaweed on the beaches. The Pacific “Mexican Riviera” (Puerto Vallarta, Cabo) is never affected by sargassum, making it a smarter summer beach pick.

Mexico City (CDMX): A year-round destination thanks to its altitude. January is cool and dry (highs 20–22°C / 68–71°F). The rainy season runs June to August, when heavy but brief afternoon downpours are normal and actually clear the air pollution. October to November is many travelers' favorite window: mild weather, festivals, and the run-up to Día de Muertos.

Pacific coast: Puerto Escondido and the Mexican Pipeline see their biggest surf swells June to August. Los Cabos hits a sweet spot in the May–June shoulder season (warm days, cool nights, and warm seas) and again in October–November.

Practical planning tips

  • Match the region to the month. The Caribbean coast wants December–April; the Pacific coast shines in the May–June and October–November shoulders; inland cities are good almost any time but peak October–November.
  • Book around the big spikes. November–January (holidays) and Semana Santa (March/April) are the priciest windows; fares can double. Travel just before or after for similar weather at a fraction of the cost.
  • Plan for hurricane season if visiting June–October. A direct hit on any one spot is statistically rare — an average Atlantic season has 14 named storms and 7 hurricanes spread across the entire basin — but September carries the highest risk. Travel insurance and flexible bookings are worth it for Caribbean trips in fall.
  • Pack for altitude. Highland cities like San Cristóbal de las Casas, Mexico City, and even Guanajuato can be chilly at night in winter; bring layers even when the coast is hot.
  • Time wildlife and festivals. February is peak whale watching off Baja; July–August is best for Cancún's whale sharks; early November is Día de Muertos in Oaxaca. If you're weighing Mexico against another dry-season trip, our best time to visit Costa Rica guide follows a similar December–April dry-season logic.

Weather and climate patterns are averages and can vary year to year, especially during hurricane season. Check forecasts and any travel advisories close to your departure date.

guides.title: Best Time to Book Flights: When to Buy Cheap Tickets
guides.excerpt: Best time to book flights: 1-3 months ahead for domestic, 2-6 for international. Airline data reveals the cheapest days to fly, book, and the windows to avoid.
guides.content:
The Best Time to Book Flights: 1-3 Months Domestic, 2-6 Months International

The single best time to book a domestic flight is 1-3 months before departure, with most data pointing to a sweet spot around 28-45 days out. For international flights, book 2-6 months ahead. These windows reflect guidance from Expedia's 2026 Air Hacks Report (based on millions of Expedia booking data points), Google Flights' pricing study, and expert analysis from travel economists - and they consistently beat both booking too early and booking at the last minute.

The pattern is reliable because of how airlines price seats. Book more than roughly six months out and you usually overpay - carriers haven't started discounting inventory that far ahead, and Expedia found domestic tickets booked 180+ days out averaged about $130 more than those booked in the 15-30 day window, with international tickets running $190-$225 more. Wait until the final two weeks and you pay a different penalty: a last-minute premium for urgency, since business travelers (and people with no choice) will pay full fare.

Below is the booking window that matters most, broken out by trip type. The day you click buy matters far less than how many days out you are.

Trip typeBest booking windowWhat the data says
Domestic (U.S.)~15-60 days out; sweet spot ~28-45 daysExpedia's lowest fares fall 15-30 days out. Google found prices bottom out around day 39 (good range 23-51 days).
Mexico / Caribbean1-3 months outGoogle found lows around 50 days out (range 26-79 days). Short-haul behaves like domestic. Mind the September hurricane peak.
Europe2-6 months outGoogle found lows at 48+ days out; experts (TPG, Hopper) suggest 2-5 months for peak summer. Shoulder-season (May, Sept-Oct) is cheaper.
Asia / South Pacific5-7 months outPer Hopper (via The Points Guy), book 5-7 months ahead; longer routes and fewer carriers mean less last-minute inventory.
Thanksgiving~35 days out (range 24-59)Per Google, prices are lowest about 5 weeks before.
Christmas / holidays~51 days out (range 32-73)Per Google, aim to book by mid-to-late October.

Season-by-season: when to fly (and what to expect)

Booking window is half the equation; when you travel is the other half. The month you fly often swings the fare more than the day you book. This table pairs each season with the trade-offs that affect price, crowds, and weather.

Season / monthsCostCrowdsWeather & timing notes
Late Jan - Feb (post-holiday low)CheapestLowCold in the Northern Hemisphere, but prime dry season for the Caribbean and Central America.
Mar - Apr (spring break)RisingHighMild and pleasant; book 28-61 days out.
Jun - Aug (summer peak)Most expensivePeakLong daylight in northern latitudes; book by spring. Atlantic hurricane season begins June 1.
Sept - early Oct (shoulder)CheapLowGreat value, but peak hurricane window (mid-Aug to mid-Oct) can disrupt Caribbean, Mexico, and U.S. Southeast flights.
Late Oct - Dec (holidays)Most expensivePeakBook 32-73 days out for Christmas; fares jump inside 30 days.

Cheapest time and worst time

The cheapest time to fly

  • Cheapest days to fly: Tuesday and Wednesday. Google's data shows flying Monday-through-Wednesday is about 13% cheaper than weekend departures, and Expedia found Tuesday is roughly 14% cheaper than Sunday for domestic flights. For international routes, Expedia's 2026 data found Friday is the cheapest departure day - about 8% cheaper than Sunday.
  • Cheapest months to fly (travel): January (cheapest for domestic, per Expedia), August (cheapest overall - Expedia found August flights average about 29% cheaper than December), and September. NerdWallet similarly lists August, September, and January as the cheapest months to fly.
  • Cheapest month to book (buy the ticket): July, per Expedia's 2026 report - about 18% cheaper than booking in December.
  • Consider a connection: Google found taking a layover instead of a nonstop saves about 22% on average. If your schedule can absorb a stop, it's often the single biggest lever after timing.

The worst time to book or fly

  • Booking 6+ months out: you typically overpay. Domestic tickets bought 180+ days early averaged $130 more; international, $190-$225 more (Expedia).
  • Booking within 7-14 days: last-minute premium for urgency - fares with fewer than 21 days' notice are usually near peak.
  • Flying on a Sunday: the most expensive departure day for both domestic and international travel.
  • Flying in December, or peak summer (June-July): the highest-demand windows of the year.
  • Caribbean / Mexico / U.S. Southeast in mid-August to mid-October: peak Atlantic hurricane season. NOAA's National Hurricane Center notes the official season runs June 1 to November 30, with activity peaking around September 10 and most storms concentrated from mid-August to mid-October. You'll find lower fares, but a higher risk of disruption - worth weighing against the savings and buying travel insurance.

The "book Tuesday afternoon" myth, debunked

You've heard it: book on a Tuesday at 3 p.m. because that's when airlines release sales. The origin is real - decades ago carriers filed fares on Monday nights and competitors matched on Tuesday morning. But modern dynamic pricing has erased that edge. Google's study found booking on a Tuesday is only about 1.3% cheaper than booking on Sunday - statistically negligible. Expedia's 2026 report likewise found the cheapest day to book is now Friday (just 3% cheaper than Sunday). Hopper's economists say the same: there's no single "golden day" to click buy. How far in advance you book matters far more than which day of the week you do it.

Practical planning tips

  1. Set a price alert the day you know your dates. Google Flights, Hopper, and Kayak all track routes and email you when fares drop. Manual daily checking wastes time.
  2. Start watching domestic routes about 3 months out, and international routes about 5-6 months out. This is when competition and discounting kick in.
  3. Stay flexible by 2-3 days. Shifting a departure from Sunday to Tuesday or Wednesday is where the real midweek savings live - often $50-$100 per domestic ticket.
  4. Compare nonstop vs. connection. That ~22% layover saving (Google) can fund an extra day of the trip.
  5. For holidays, book by mid-October. Thanksgiving and Christmas fares are best 5-7 weeks out and climb sharply inside 30 days.
  6. Don't chase browser tricks. The "clear your cookies / use incognito" advice is largely myth - fares are set by demand and remaining inventory, not your search history.

Match your flight to the destination's best season

Booking the right window only helps if you're also flying at the right time of year. If you're headed to Portugal, aim for the May or September shoulder season when flights and weather both cooperate. For Costa Rica and Mexico, the December-through-April dry season aligns cheap post-holiday airfare with the best conditions. And for Alaska, the short June-August window is the one case where peak-season booking months ahead is unavoidable.

Flight prices are dynamic and route-specific; the figures above reflect industry averages from large-sample studies. Always confirm current fares with a price tracker before you buy.
