guides.title: How Long Do Spiders Live? Lifespan by Species & Type
guides.excerpt: Most spiders live just 1-2 years, but female tarantulas can reach 30. See how long spiders live by species and what factors extend—or cut short—a spider's lifespan.
guides.content:
How Long Do Spiders Live? (The Short Answer)

The average spider lives about one year, but across the world's more than 50,000 described species the real range runs from a few months to 30 years or more. As the Australian Museum puts it, "some spiders have life spans of less than a year, while others may live for up to twenty years," and the Animal Diversity Web notes that for most species "most spiders live for one year."

The spider you spot in the bathroom corner is almost always near the short end of that scale. Common house spiders, cobweb weavers, and jumping spiders typically persist for 1-2 years, while female tarantulas are the outliers — a Mexican red-knee tarantula female can live 25-30 years. Sex matters as much as species: in nearly every group, females outlive males, often by many years.

If you're comparing across animals, spiders sit far shorter than a house cat (see our cat lifespan guide) but far longer than the insects many of them eat — far longer, for instance, than mosquitoes or bees. Here's the breakdown by species.

Lifespan by Common Spider Species

Spider (species / type)Typical lifespanNotes
Common house spider (Parasteatoda tepidariorum)~1 year or more after maturityYear-round indoors; females deposit 12+ egg sacs. Penn State Extension
Black widow (Latrodectus mactans)~1 year; up to 3 wild, 4+ in captivity"Most spiders live for one year… some have lived 3 years in the wild." ADW
Zebra jumping spider (Salticus scenicus)1-2 years wild; 2-3 captivity"Females generally living longer than males." ADW
Longbodied cellar spider~2 years or more as adults"One year to mature… can live for two or more years as adults." Penn State Extension
Barn funnel weaverUp to ~7 yearsReported to live "as long as seven years, producing upward of nine egg sacs." Penn State Extension
Mexican red-knee tarantula (Brachypelma smithi)Females 25-30 yrs; males ~10Females mature at 6-7 yrs, males at 4-5. ADW

The pattern is clear: small web-building spiders that share your home sit near one year, ground-hunting and funnel-weaving species stretch to several years, and the large mygalomorphs (tarantulas and trapdoor spiders) can live decades. The same spider also tends to live longer in captivity than in the wild, where predators and winter take their toll.

Factors That Affect a Spider's Lifespan

A spider's biological potential is one thing; what it actually reaches in the wild is another. The Australian Museum is blunt that "spiders face many dangers that reduce their chances of reaching a ripe old age." The biggest variables:

  • Species and sex — the single largest factor. A female tarantula is built for decades; a male jumping spider may die months after his final molt. Females almost universally outlive males because they invest in egg production and often guard offspring, while males expend energy roaming for mates.
  • Predation — birds, reptiles, mammals, centipedes, scorpions, and other spiders all eat spiders. Hunting wasps are especially devastating: mud-dauber and pepsis (tarantula-hawk) wasps paralyse spiders and lay eggs on them so the larva can eat the host alive.
  • Parasites and disease — spiders suffer fungal infections, mite infestations, and parasitic worms. Mermithid nematodes, for example, live inside a spider and slowly consume non-vital tissue, eventually driving the host toward water so the worm can complete its life cycle.
  • Climate and winter — in temperate regions, the first hard frost kills most orb weavers and many annual species. Indoor spiders and burrowing species avoid this and so tend to live longer.
  • Food supply — slow seasons with few insects mean slow growth and fewer successful molts, which directly shortens life.
  • Shelter — spiders with a secure retreat (a burrow, crevice, or undisturbed web) survive molting and bad weather far better than exposed wanderers.
  • Captivity — protected from predators, frost, and parasites, with steady food, captive spiders routinely exceed wild lifespans. Widows reach 4+ years in captivity versus ~1 typical in the wild.

The Spider Life Cycle (Egg to Adult)

All spiders pass through the same three broad stages, and how long each lasts sets the lifespan for that species:

  1. Egg — females wrap eggs in a silk egg sac. A common house spider female may produce 12 or more sacs, each holding 140-380 eggs; a tarantula lays 200-400 in a single sac and carries it between her fangs. Eggs typically hatch in 1-3 months.
  2. Spiderling — after hatching, spiderlings disperse (often by "ballooning" on silk threads) and begin molting. Small spiders molt every few weeks early on; growth only happens at a molt, so the number of molts effectively defines how long the juvenile stage lasts.
  3. Adult — once mature, males stop molting in most species and focus on mating; females of long-lived species (especially tarantulas) keep molting for years. A female Mexican red-knee tarantula doesn't even reach sexual maturity until age 6-7, then may live another two decades.

This is why tarantulas live so long: they mature extremely slowly and the female keeps growing and molting long after maturity. A one-year house spider races through the same cycle in a fraction of the time. For a sense of how this stacks up against other animals, our elephant lifespan guide shows what decades-long maturation looks like in a mammal.

How to Help a Spider Live Longer

Whether you're tolerating a cellar spider in the basement or keeping a pet tarantula, the levers that extend a spider's life are the same ones nature withholds:

  • Keep the temperature stable — spiders are ectothermic, so a steady, species-appropriate temperature (around 24-27 °C / 75-80 °F for most tropical species) keeps metabolism and digestion working.
  • Provide correct humidity and a retreat — a deep, humid burrow lets tarantulas molt safely; a dry, undisturbed corner lets house spiders rebuild webs. The Australian Museum notes that burrows "buffer climatic extremes," which is exactly the benefit you want to replicate.
  • Offer clean water and regular, sized prey — a shallow water dish and 1-2 appropriately sized insects per week suit most pet spiders; avoid prey larger than the spider.
  • Minimise handling and stress — a fall from even a short height can rupture a tarantula's abdomen, and frequent disturbance discourages feeding.
  • Leave web-spiders alone indoors — if you don't want them, relocate rather than kill; a single house spider can remove hundreds of insects (mosquitoes included) over its year of life.
  • Quarantine new arrivals — mites and parasitic worms spread fast in captivity; isolate new spiders before introducing them.

With those basics, a captive spider will usually outlast its wild counterparts by a wide margin — often double or more. The same female widow that lives about a year outdoors can reach four or more years in a secure terrarium, and a well-cared-for tarantula may be with you for the better part of three decades.

guides.title: How Long Do Mosquitoes Live? Lifespan by Stage & Species
guides.excerpt: Adult mosquitoes live about 2 to 4 weeks — females longer than males, and some survive months over winter. Here's the lifespan by species and life stage.
guides.content:
How Long Do Mosquitoes Live?

Adult mosquitoes typically live about 2 to 4 weeks, with females usually outliving males, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The exact lifespan depends on the species, temperature, humidity, and other conditions. In practice, a female that finds plenty of blood meals and warm, humid shelter may survive a month or more, while males are generally shorter-lived. A few females that enter overwintering — a dormant state through the cold months — can stretch that timeline out to several months before laying eggs and dying in the spring.

In short: a few days for some males, a few weeks for most females, and up to several months for overwintering females of the right species. Below is how that breaks down by species and by life stage, the factors that change it, and how to manage mosquitoes around your home.

Mosquito Lifespan by Species and Type

There are more than 3,700 mosquito species worldwide, the CDC notes, and their adult lifespans differ. The figures below come from CDC lifecycle data and species accounts from the University of Michigan's Animal Diversity Web (ADW).

Species / typeTypical adult lifespan (female)Male lifespanEgg → adult development
Aedes aegypti & Ae. albopictus (yellow-fever & Asian tiger mosquitoes)~30–40 days in warm, humid conditions (up to ~117 days in lab settings)Shorter than females (ADW notes male longevity for Ae. albopictus is not well documented)~7–10 days; eggs survive drying for up to 8 months
Anopheles quadrimaculatus (common malaria mosquito)Averages ~21 days; maximum observed ~62 daysAverages ~7 days; maximum ~22 days~10–14 days (CDC); egg-to-adult ~14–27 days at ~23°C / 73°F (ADW)
Culex species (common house mosquitoes)~2–4 weeks; fertilized females overwinterA few days to ~2 weeks~7–14 days depending on temperature
General average (CDC)~2–4 weeks; females live longer than malesShorter than females~1–2 weeks in warm weather

A useful point of comparison: mosquitoes' adult lives are similar in scale to other familiar insects. Bees, for instance, also spend just a few weeks as adults (worker honey bees live roughly six weeks in summer), while longer-lived predators such as spiders can hunt mosquitoes across multiple seasons.

Factors That Affect Mosquito Lifespan

Why does one mosquito die in five days while another survives two months? The CDC and ADW point to a handful of overlapping factors:

  • Species. Lifespan is partly hardwired. Asian tiger mosquitoes (Aedes albopictus) commonly reach 30–40 days in temperate climates, ADW reports, while male Anopheles mosquitoes average about a week.
  • Sex. Females live longer than males. The CDC notes this directly, and in Anopheles quadrimaculatus the gap is stark — females average about 21 days versus roughly 7 for males (ADW). Males die soon after mating; females must survive long enough to take a blood meal and develop eggs.
  • Temperature. Mosquitoes are cold-blooded, so warmth speeds them up and shortens each stage, while cool weather slows development. Cold snaps below roughly 12°C (54°F) can send larvae to the bottom of a pool to wait it out (ADW). Extreme heat, conversely, can desiccate adults.
  • Humidity and moisture. Adult mosquitoes dry out quickly in arid air. High humidity measurably extends life — ADW reports the 30–40-day average for Ae. albopictus specifically in "temperate climate with relatively high humidity." Standing water is also essential for eggs, larvae, and pupae.
  • Food and host availability. Adults of both sexes feed on plant nectar for energy; females additionally need a blood meal to produce eggs. A female with reliable hosts and nectar can lay multiple batches of eggs — Anopheles females may produce 9–12 broods of 200–265 eggs each (ADW).
  • Predation and disease. Birds, bats, spiders, dragonflies, and fish cut adult (and larval) lives short. Fungi, protozoa, and nematodes also kill larvae.
  • Overwintering. In cold regions, fertilized females of some species (notably Culex and some Anopheles) shelter in barns, homes, caves, or storm drains and enter dormancy, surviving for months. ADW notes these females typically die right after laying their eggs the following spring.

The Four Life Stages of a Mosquito

Every mosquito passes through the same four stages — egg, larva, pupa, and adult — a transformation called complete metamorphosis. The first three stages live in or on water; only the adult flies. Penn State Extension and the CDC describe the timeline as follows:

  • Egg. Females lay eggs on or near water — some singly on the surface (Anopheles), others in floating rafts (Culex), and some glued just above the waterline of containers (Aedes). Eggs hatch in a few days to months. Aedes eggs are exceptionally tough: the CDC reports they can survive drying out for up to 8 months and even endure a southern U.S. winter, hatching only when water rises over them.
  • Larva ("wiggler"). Larvae live entirely in water, feeding on bacteria, algae, and organic bits. They molt four times. Penn State Extension notes larvae can become pupae in as few as 5 days when it's warm; ADW reports larval development can take as few as 4 days or extend to several weeks when food is scarce, depending on temperature and food.
  • Pupa ("tumbler"). The comma-shaped pupa still lives in water and swims but does not eat. Penn State Extension reports pupae develop into flying adults in about 2–3 days; ADW cites 2–6 days depending on species and temperature.
  • Adult. The adult emerges, rests briefly to harden its wings, then flies off. Only females bite (they need blood to make eggs); both sexes also feed on nectar. Adults typically live 2–4 weeks, per the CDC.

The full cycle from egg to adult commonly takes 1–2 weeks in warm weather — the CDC pegs Aedes at about 7–10 days and Anopheles at 10–14 days — but it can stretch to several weeks when it's cold or food is scarce. By contrast, mammalian life cycles unfold on a far longer clock: compare how long cats live (often 13–17 years) with the mosquito's month-long adult life.

How Long Mosquitoes Live Indoors

A female that slips into your house can survive the typical 2–4 weeks if she finds a blood meal and even a small amount of standing water — a plant saucer, a pet bowl, a clogged drain — in which to lay eggs. Aedes aegypti, in particular, the CDC notes, is well adapted to living near and even inside human homes. Stable indoor temperatures and humidity actually suit mosquitoes, so a single determined female can be a recurring nuisance. Males, which don't bite, are generally shorter-lived.

How to Help a Mosquito Live Longer — and Why You Usually Want the Opposite

If you were deliberately keeping mosquitoes (for research, as feeder insects, or classroom study), the same factors that lengthen their lives in nature apply: warm temperatures (around 25–28°C / 77–82°F), high humidity, a sugar source such as nectar or honey water for both sexes, and — for females — a blood meal so eggs can develop. Shallow, still, nutrient-rich water keeps eggs, larvae, and pupae healthy through the aquatic stages.

For almost everyone else, the goal is the opposite, because mosquitoes are the world's deadliest animals to humans: they spread malaria, dengue, Zika, West Nile virus, yellow fever, and more. Because every factor that lengthens a mosquito's life is something you can remove, the same science points to effective control:

  • Eliminate standing water — empty saucers, buckets, tires, gutters, and birdbaths weekly to break the egg–larva–pupa cycle. The CDC stresses that even small amounts of standing water are enough.
  • Lower humidity and seal entry points — screens, weather-stripping, and dehumidifiers make homes hostile to adults.
  • Use EPA-registered repellents (such as DEET, picaridin, or oil of lemon eucalyptus) on skin, and treat clothing/equipment with permethrin where appropriate.

If you live in an area with mosquito-borne disease and develop fever, rash, or severe symptoms after bites, contact a healthcare professional — this article is informational and not medical advice. For a sense of how much longer-lived warm-blooded animals are than the insects that pester them, see our guides on cat lifespan and how long bees live.

The Bottom Line

So, how long do mosquitoes live? Most adults live about 2 to 4 weeks, with females outlasting males, a short window shaped by species, warmth, humidity, food, and predators. The egg-to-adult journey typically takes 1–2 weeks in summer, but resilient eggs and overwintering females let mosquitoes return season after season. Understanding that lifecycle is also the key to keeping their numbers down around your home.

guides.title: How Long Do Bees Live? Lifespan by Caste and Season
guides.excerpt: Honey bees live 6 weeks (workers) to 5 years (queens). Learn how long bees live by caste and season, what affects their lifespan, and how to help them thrive.
guides.content:
How Long Do Bees Live? The Quick Answer

A honey bee's lifespan depends almost entirely on two things: its caste (worker, queen, or drone) and the season it was born in. Across a colony, bees live anywhere from a few weeks to several years. The figures most people want:

  • Worker bees: about 6 weeks during the active summer foraging season (on average about 15–38 days), but 4 to 6 months for workers born in fall that overwinter in the hive.
  • Queen bee: typically 2 to 3 years, with some queens reaching up to 5 years.
  • Drone bees (males): roughly 3 to 4.5 weeks (about 21–32 days), and most die immediately after mating.

So the short answer to "how long do bees live" is that an individual honey bee lives, on average, anywhere from about two weeks to five years depending on its role. The range is enormous because a queen and a worker share nearly identical genes yet can differ in lifespan by a factor of ten, a difference driven by diet, behavior, and the protective structure of the colony rather than DNA.

This guide focuses on the western honey bee (Apis mellifera), the species kept by beekeepers and responsible for most crop pollination. Other bees — bumblebees, solitary bees, carpenter bees — have different life histories, and even within honey bees the seasonal swing is large enough that "average" only means something once you specify the caste.

Lifespan by Caste and Season

Use this as your reference table. Numbers reflect the adult lifespan (after the bee emerges from its cell), drawn from entomology extension and peer-reviewed sources.

CasteAverage LifespanMaximum / Notes
Worker (summer)~6 weeks (on average 15–38 days)Spends the first ~2–3 weeks on hive duties, then forages until worn out
Worker (winter / "fat bee")4–6 months (150–200 days)Born in fall; lives through winter to rear the first spring brood, then dies
Queen2–3 yearsUp to 5 years; one study recorded a maximum of 8 years. Productive output usually drops after 2 years
Drone (male)~3–4.5 weeks (21–32 days)Dies immediately upon mating; survivors are expelled from the hive before winter

Notice the seasonal split in workers: a bee born in June may live only five or six weeks because foraging wears her wings and body out, while her sister born in September can live more than ten times longer simply by staying inside the hive through winter. The colony, not the individual, is what persists — a well-managed honey bee colony can survive for decades by continually replacing its members.

For comparison with other small creatures, the same question gets very different answers when you ask how long spiders live or how long mosquitoes live — most insects and arachnids measure their lives in weeks or months, making the multi-year queen honey bee a genuine outlier.

Factors That Affect Lifespan

Why does one bee live six weeks while another in the same hive lives six months — or six years? Research points to a mix of biological and environmental pressures:

  • Caste and job (the single biggest factor). Queens are fed royal jelly throughout development, which sets them on a completely different physiological track from workers. A queen lays up to 1,500–2,000 eggs a day at peak season while living for years; a worker does the hive's hardest physical labor and burns out in weeks. Even within workers, the transition from nurse bee (working inside) to forager (flying outside) sharply raises mortality, because foragers face predators, weather, and simple mechanical wear.
  • Season of birth. Summer workers are short-lived; fall-reared "winter bees" store extra fat and proteins (they are sometimes called "fat bees") and survive months inside the cluster. Day length, temperature, and the colony's brood-rearing cycle trigger this switch.
  • Nutrition and forage. A varied diet of nectar and pollen from many flower types is essential. The USDA Agricultural Research Service lists poor nutrition as one of the four pillars of honey bee decline, because a hungry bee has a weakened immune system and shorter life.
  • Parasites — especially Varroa mites. Varroa destructor is described by USDA researchers as "essentially a modern honey bee plague." The mites attach to bees and feed on their hemolymph (the bee equivalent of blood), and they also transmit viruses such as deformed wing virus. Beekeepers consistently rank Varroa as the number-one cause of colony losses.
  • Pathogens and viruses. Since the 1980s a wave of new pathogens — Nosema fungi, several bee viruses — has shortened both individual and colony lifespans.
  • Pesticide exposure. Sublethal doses of pesticides, including the neonicotinoid class, can impair navigation and immunity. USDA notes the data on field-realistic exposure is mixed, but combined with other stressors it raises mortality.
  • Queen age and genetics. Older queens lay fewer eggs and produce more drones, so most beekeepers re-queen a colony every one to two years to keep the workforce — and therefore average worker lifespan — strong.

Honey Bee Life Stages

Every honey bee — queen, worker, or drone — passes through the same four stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult. The total development time from egg to adult is what differs by caste, and it is striking that the queen, the longest-lived bee, develops the fastest.

The queen lays a single egg per cell. After three days as an egg, the larva hatches as a pearly-white, C-shaped grub that workers feed hundreds of times a day. Once the larva is full-grown, workers cap the cell with wax and the larva spins a cocoon and becomes a pupa, finally emerging as an adult.

CasteEggLarva (before capping)Capped / PupaTotal time egg → adult
Queen~3 days~6 days~7.5 days~16 days
Worker~3 days~5.5 days~12 days~21 days
Drone~3 days~6.5 days~14.5 days~24 days

After emergence, an adult worker spends her first two to three weeks as a "house bee" — cleaning cells, nursing larvae, building comb, and guarding the entrance — before graduating to foraging. A queen emerges, spends about a week maturing, then takes two or three mating flights, returns to the hive, and lays eggs for the rest of her life. A drone matures at about a week old, flies to drone congregation areas to mate, and dies at the moment of mating if successful.

The queen's longevity is a marvel of insect biology: she and a worker are genetically identical, yet she may live ten times longer. Researchers trace this to higher levels of a protective protein called vitellogenin, lower juvenile hormone, and strong resistance to oxidative stress — all set up by the royal-jelly diet she receives as a larva.

How to Help Bees Live Longer

Because a colony replaces its bees constantly, helping bees "live longer" mostly means supporting the colony and reducing the stressors that cut individual lives short. The USDA Agricultural Research Service and extension services recommend concrete steps for gardeners, homeowners, and beekeepers:

  • Plant pollinator-friendly forage. Grow a mix of flowers that bloom across the whole season so bees always have nectar and pollen. Good choices include red clover, foxglove, bee balm, and joe-pye weed. Diverse pollen is one of the best defenses against shortened lifespan.
  • Avoid spraying pesticides during the day. If you must use pesticides, apply them in the early morning or late evening when bees are back in the hive, never at midday when foragers are most active. Indiscriminate pesticide use is one of the easiest home-garden threats to remove.
  • Provide clean water. A shallow dish with pebbles or marbles gives bees a safe place to drink without drowning.
  • Leave some wild habitat. Untidy corners with bare soil, hollow stems, and late-blooming weeds feed both honey bees and the solitary bees that share the landscape.
  • If you keep bees, manage Varroa and re-queen. Monitor mite levels and treat with approved methods; supplementally feed syrup or pollen substitute during nectar dearths; and re-queen every one to two years so the colony always has a vigorous, high-laying queen.

None of these steps will make a single summer worker live for years — her biology is fixed — but together they keep the colony strong enough to produce long-lived winter bees and healthy queens, which is what ultimately determines whether the bees in your garden or apiary are still there next season.

A well-cared-for queen honey bee can outlive many small mammals relative to her size, though she will never approach a typical cat lifespan. The wonder of the hive is not how long any one bee lives, but how a few weeks of individual effort add up to a colony that can persist for decades.

Sources cited below include the University of Michigan's Animal Diversity Web, the Mid-Atlantic Apiculture Research and Extension Consortium (MAAREC) at the University of Delaware, a peer-reviewed review in the journal Age, the University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture Cooperative Extension Service, and the USDA Agricultural Research Service.

guides.title: How Long Does Resin Take to Cure? Full Timeline & Tips
guides.excerpt: Epoxy resin takes 24 hours to harden and about 72 hours to fully cure. See how temperature, pour thickness, and hardener speed change resin cure time.
guides.content:
How Long Does Resin Take to Cure?

Most clear art and tabletop epoxy resin takes about 24 hours to become hard to the touch and roughly 72 hours (3 days) to fully cure. ArtResin, one of the most widely used coating epoxies, states that after ~24 hours the piece reaches about 95% solidity and is hard to the touch, then continues to a full cure at the 72-hour mark (ArtResin, cure time). The headline range is therefore 24-72 hours, but the real answer depends almost entirely on three things: which resin/hardener you use, how thick you pour, and the temperature.

Broader range: a fast hardener can reach a tack-free state in about 2 hours and full cure in 2 days, while a slow or deep-pour system can take 5 days or more to fully cross-link (TotalBoat). So if you only remember one number, use 72 hours for full strength — and read the spec sheet for your specific product.

Factors That Change Resin Cure Time

Resin "drying" is not evaporation — it is a chemical reaction between resin and hardener. Anything that speeds up or slows down that reaction changes the timeline. Here is how the big variables move the needle, with manufacturer data:

Factor / resin typeEffect on cure timeSource figure
Art / coating epoxy (thin pour, ~1/8 in)Hard to touch ~24 h; fully cured ~72 hArtResin: 95% solid at 24 h, full cure at 72 h
Fast hardenerTack-free ~2 h; full cure ~2 daysTotalBoat Fast: 2 h tack-free, 2-day cure at 77 °F
Medium hardenerTack-free ~3 h; full cure ~3.5 daysTotalBoat Medium: 3 h tack-free, 3.5-day cure
Slow hardenerTack-free ~5 h; full cure ~5 daysTotalBoat Slow: 5 h tack-free, 5-day cure
Warmer temperatureSpeeds up the cure; heat also shortens working timeArtResin: warm bath cuts working time 10-15 min
Colder temperatureSlows cure; below the minimum temp it may never fully cureWest System min temps: 40-70 °F by hardener
Thicker pourGenerates more exothermic heat, cures faster at the core but risks yellowing/crackingTotalBoat max pour depth: 1/8 in (medium); slow up to 1/4 in (larger pours) or 3/8 in (small castings)
Deep-pour / casting resinFormulated for thickness; longer total cureSeveral days to full cure; always check the product's spec sheet

Stages of a Resin Cure — What to Expect

A resin pour moves through four distinct stages. Knowing them tells you when you can touch, demold, recoat, or load the piece.

1. Working time (pot life)

This is how long you have to mix, pour, and spread before the resin starts to stiffen. ArtResin gives you about 45 minutes of working time, and recommends applying it as soon as it has been mixed for 3 minutes (ArtResin, working time). For marine-grade systems the numbers are sharper: West System 206 Slow Hardener has a pot life of 20-25 minutes and a thin-film working time of 90-110 minutes at 72 °F (West System, 206). TotalBoat's hardeners gel in 10 minutes (Fast), 25 minutes (Medium), or 40 minutes (Slow) at 77 °F (TotalBoat).

2. Tack-free / gel stage

Next the surface becomes dry and no longer sticky. With a medium hardener this happens around 3 hours at 77 °F; a slow hardener reaches tack-free in about 5 hours (TotalBoat). West System 206 Slow reaches a solid state in 10-15 hours at 72 °F (West System, 206).

3. Demold / handle stage

For most coating epoxies this lands at the ~24-hour point: the piece is hard enough to handle, hang, or (for castings) pop out of a silicone mold. ArtResin is at about 95% solidity here (ArtResin, cure time). Demold time is not full cure — the piece is still gaining final hardness.

4. Full cure

Full chemical cross-linking — maximum hardness, scratch resistance, and the point at which you can sand, machine, package, or subject the piece to load — arrives around the 72-hour mark for a standard coating epoxy (ArtResin, cure time), anywhere from 2 days (fast) to 5 days (slow) for TotalBoat High Performance Epoxy (TotalBoat).

Practical Tips: Recoating, Demolding & Avoiding a Tacky Top

Demold time vs. full cure

Plan to demold at roughly the 24-hour mark (when the surface is hard), but wait the full 72 hours before sanding, drilling, or putting the piece into service. Demolding early risks fingerprints, warping, or pulling a soft underside.

The recoat window

If you need a second coat, you have two clean options. Apply the next layer while the first is still slightly tacky (typically within the first 24 hours) so the two layers chemically bond. If the first coat has fully cured (past ~72 hours), sand it lightly and wipe with solvent first so the new layer has mechanical grip.

Why your resin is still tacky after 24 hours

A sticky or flexible surface almost always traces back to one of four causes:

  • Off-ratio mixing — too much or too little hardener. TotalBoat's system is a strict 2 parts resin to 1 part hardener by volume (TotalBoat); measure precisely.
  • Incomplete mixing — scrape the sides and bottom of the cup and mix for the full recommended time (about 3 minutes for ArtResin).
  • Cold shop temperatures — below the hardener's minimum (e.g., 55 °F for TotalBoat, 60 °F for West System 206), cure slows drastically or stalls (West System, 105).
  • Too-thin pour or humidity — very thin films can struggle to generate enough exotherm to cure, and high humidity can interfere with the surface.

Speeding up (or slowing down) the cure

To cure faster: warm the resin and workspace slightly (a warm water bath before mixing helps), use a fast hardener, and keep pours within the recommended depth so heat can dissipate. ArtResin notes that warmth reduces working time by about 10-15 minutes (warmer conditions also speed the overall cure, though ArtResin does not quantify that reduction) (ArtResin, working time). To slow it down — useful in hot weather or for larger projects — switch to a slow or extra-slow hardener; West System's 209 Extra Slow gives 3-4 hours of working time (West System, 105).

Resin cure is one of several "how long do I wait?" craft processes. For comparison, cold-process soap takes 4-6 weeks to cure (a much longer water-evaporation cure), and spray paint dries in minutes to hours rather than days. If you are timing a multi-step build, our fermentation timeline guide walks through the same stage-by-stage thinking for living processes.

The Bottom Line

For the average art, tabletop, or coating project, expect 24 hours to hard and 72 hours to fully cure at normal room temperature (70-77 °F). Fast hardeners compress that to about 2 days; slow and deep-pour systems extend it toward 5 days. Always read the technical data sheet for your specific resin and hardener — the mix ratio, minimum temperature, and pour-depth limits on that sheet are what keep your piece from staying tacky forever.

guides.title: How Long Does Cold Process Soap Take to Cure? | Guide
guides.excerpt: Cold process soap takes 4-6 weeks to cure so water can evaporate and saponification finishes. Here's what changes during cure and how to speed it up safely.
guides.content:
How long does cold process soap take to cure?

Cold process soap takes 4 to 6 weeks to cure. That is the standard range Bramble Berry’s Soap Queen blog teaches — cold process soap takes about 4–6 weeks to cure, and while it can be used sooner, it lasts longer and performs better with the full cure. Unmold, cut, then let the bars rest four to six weeks in a well-ventilated area before use.

It helps to separate two ideas that get blurred:

  • Saponification — the chemical reaction between oils and lye — is essentially complete in 24–48 hours. After that the soap is technically safe to touch and technically safe to use, though it will be soft, harsh, and short on lather.
  • Curing is the multi-week drying and aging window that follows. Over 4–6 weeks the remaining 1–5% of slow saponification finishes, water evaporates, the crystalline structure firms up, and pH drifts down so the bar becomes mild, hard, and long-lasting.

So “done” depends on what you mean. Safe to handle: about 2 days. At its best: 4–6 weeks. Olive-heavy castile bars keep improving for 6 weeks to a year, according to Lovely Greens.

FactorEffect on cure time
Cold process (standard)4–6 weeks baseline
Hot processSaponification finishes in the pot; usable in ~1–2 weeks, optimal at 4 weeks
Melt-and-pour baseNo cure needed — ready as soon as it hardens (base is pre-saponified)
High-olive / 100% castile (>60% olive)6 weeks minimum (8–12 weeks optimal); 6–12 months for best results
High-coconut (>50%)Slightly shorter — 3–6 weeks
Salt bars~6–8 weeks — benefit from a longer cure for hardness
Shampoo bars~4 weeks (standard cure)
Water discount (less water in the recipe)Shortens cure; bar starts firmer
Thick bars / large loavesLonger — water takes more time to migrate out
High humidity, poor airflowSlows evaporation, can extend cure or cause “sweating”

What actually happens during the 4–6 weeks

Curing is not just “waiting.” Four measurable changes are taking place, and each one explains why a rushed bar disappoints:

  • Water evaporation. Fresh soap can lose 10–15% of its weight as water migrates to the surface and evaporates, according to the Petalmade curing guide. Less water means a harder bar that lasts longer in the shower.
  • Crystal formation. The saturated fatty-acid soaps organize into a solid crystalline structure. This is what turns a rubbery, sliceable loaf into a firm bar that resists pressure.
  • Saponification finishing. The bulk of the reaction finishes in a day or two, but the last traces of unreacted oils and lye keep combining for weeks. Lovely Greens notes that roughly 1–5% of the lye can need up to a month to fully react.
  • pH drift and mildness. Fresh soap sits around pH 10–12. As it cures, pH eases down toward 9–10, which is the difference between a bar that strips skin and one that feels gentle.

The lather transforms in parallel: an uncured bar often produces a thin, slimy foam, while a properly cured bar builds a stable, creamy lather. This is the same “wait for the chemistry to finish” principle behind how long resin takes to cure and how long fermentation takes — the ingredients are mixed long before the result is ready.

Stages: what to expect week by week

  • Day 1–2 (in the mold): Saponification runs and the loaf may “gel” (go translucent). The soap is still caustic to handle bare-handed.
  • Day 2–4: Bramble Berry’s Soap Queen kit tutorial recommends leaving the soap in the mold about 2–4 days before unmolding, then cutting it into bars.
  • Week 1–2: Fast water loss. Bars feel lighter and firmer but still slightly tacky; pH is still high.
  • Week 3–4: Hardening and pH drop become obvious. Lather improves and the bars stop feeling “wet.”
  • Week 4–6: Ready for most balanced recipes. Bars are hard, mild, and produce good lather.
  • Beyond 6 weeks: Castile and other olive-dominant soaps keep mellowing for months.

How to cure soap properly (and not slow it down)

  • Airflow, not containment. Stand bars on edge on racks or corrugated cardboard with space between them so air reaches every side. Never seal curing soap in plastic — it traps water and can cause DOS (dreaded orange spots / rancidity).
  • Cool, dry, indoors. Aim for room temperature with moderate humidity (ideally below 60%). A damp basement or a steamy bathroom extends the cure.
  • Turn the bars every few days so they dry evenly and don’t develop flat soft spots.
  • Avoid direct sun, which can fade colorants and overheat the surface.
  • Use a water discount (less water in the recipe) if you want a head start — the bar enters the cure already firmer.

Like watching how long spray paint takes to dry, the “dry to touch” moment arrives well before the coating (or, here, the bar) is truly finished. Patience is the active ingredient.

How to tell when cold process soap is fully cured

  • Touch test: The bar feels hard, dry, and slightly chalky — not gummy or tacky.
  • Weight test: Weigh a bar weekly; when the weight stops dropping, water loss is done.
  • Lather test: Wash with a corner. A cured bar builds creamy, stable lather quickly; an uncured bar feels slimy and dissolves fast.
  • Hand/oral “zap” test (traditional, use sparingly): A quick touch of wet soap to the tip of the tongue — a “zing” or zap signals active, unreacted lye and means more cure time. A pH meter or strip reading of roughly 9–10 is the more reliable modern version.
  • Err long for olive soap. If your recipe is high in olive oil, treat 6 weeks as a floor, not a target.

Faster alternatives: hot process and melt-and-pour

If 4–6 weeks is too long, two methods trade some control for speed. Hot process applies external heat so saponification finishes in the pot during the cook; Bramble Berry’s Soap Queen blog notes the soap can be cut within a day and is ready to use right away, and the Petalmade guide puts hot process at a 1–2 week minimum cure (4 weeks optimal). Melt-and-pour skips curing entirely — the base is already fully saponified, so it is ready to use as soon as it hardens in the mold.

Note that hot process still benefits from curing: the bars lose water and harden just like cold process, so “faster” means sooner-to-usable, not skip-the-cure.

Cure times above are drawn from soapmaking-industry sources (Bramble Berry / Soap Queen) and long-form soapmaking references. This guide is for hobbyist crafting, not medical or dermatological advice; if you have sensitive skin or a skin condition, patch-test any new soap and consult a dermatologist.

guides.title: How Long Does Spray Paint Take to Dry? Full Timeline
guides.excerpt: General-purpose spray paint dries to touch in about 20 minutes and is ready to handle in about 1 hour, is fully dry in 24 hours, and reaches maximum adhesion and chip resistance over about 5-7 days. See exact times by paint type, temperature and humidity.
guides.content:
How Long Does Spray Paint Take to Dry?

Most general-purpose spray paint is dry to the touch in about 20 minutes and ready to handle in about 1 hour, with a full dry time of about 24 hours and a complete cure (maximum adhesion and chip resistance) of about 5-7 days on plastic. Those headline numbers describe a fast-drying acrylic or lacquer aerosol sprayed at 70°F (21°C) and 50% relative humidity, which is the standard baseline that both Rust-Oleum and Krylon print on their technical data sheets.

But “dry” is not a single moment, it is a staircase, and the chemistry of the can matters enormously. A heavy-duty oil-based enamel like Rust-Oleum Stops Rust dries far more slowly: tack-free in 2-4 hours and handle-dry only after 5-9 hours. So the honest, short answer is about 20 minutes to touch for fast acrylics, up to several hours for enamels, 24 hours to be fully dry, and about a week to reach maximum adhesion and chip resistance.

Dry Times by Paint Type (Quick Reference)

Every figure below is taken from the manufacturer's own technical data sheet (TDS), measured at 70°F (21°C) and 50% relative humidity unless noted.

Paint type (example product)Dry to touchDry to handleRecoat windowFull dry
General-purpose acrylic (Rust-Oleum Painter's Touch 2X)20 minutes1 hourWithin 1 hour or after 48 hours24 hours
General-purpose acrylic (Krylon Fusion All-In-One)20-25 minutes1 hourPer label (about 1 minute between light coats)24 hr (7-day chip resistance on plastic)
Solvent-acrylic specialty (Rust-Oleum Metallic)1 hour4 hoursWithin 1 hour or after 24 hours24 hours
Oil-modified alkyd enamel (Rust-Oleum Stops Rust)2-4 hours (tack-free)5-9 hoursWithin 1 hour or after 48 hours24 hours

Sources: Rust-Oleum Painter's Touch 2X Ultra Cover TDS; Krylon FAQ and Fusion All-In-One product page; Rust-Oleum Specialty Metallic TDS (SPC-13); Rust-Oleum Stops Rust Enamel Sprays TDS (SRT-01).

What Slows Down or Speeds Up Drying

Temperature, humidity, film thickness, airflow, and resin chemistry all shift these numbers. Rust-Oleum and Krylon both publish the acceptable application window on their sheets.

FactorIdeal rangeEffect on dry time
Air temperature55-90°F (Rust-Oleum allows 50-90°F; Krylon 55-75°F)Cooler temps lengthen every stage; below 50°F curing becomes unreliable. Heat speeds solvent release but can cause a skin-over that traps solvent underneath.
Relative humidityBelow 60-65% RHHigh humidity slows evaporation, softens the film, and can cause cloudiness (“blushing”) in clear coats.
Film thickness1.0-2.0 mils dry film per coat (Stops Rust spec)Heavy coats trap solvent and can double or triple dry time, plus cause runs and sags.
Airflow / ventilationWell-ventilated, light breezeMoving air sweeps away solvent vapor and noticeably accelerates dry time.
Resin chemistry—Acrylics and lacquers flash off fastest; oil-modified alkyd enamels rely on oxidation and are the slowest.

The Four Stages of Spray Paint Drying

Understanding the stages prevents the two most common mistakes, touching too early and recoating at the wrong time.

  1. Dry to touch (20 min - 4 hr). A film has skinned over and will not transfer to a light fingertip. Fast acrylics hit this in about 20 minutes; metallics in about an hour; oil enamels in 2-4 hours. The piece is not durable yet.
  2. Dry to handle (1 - 9 hr). You can pick the object up without leaving prints or dents, but it will still scratch easily. Painter's Touch 2X and Krylon Fusion reach this in 1 hour; Stops Rust enamel needs 5-9 hours.
  3. Fully dry (24 hr). The paint film has hardened and the bulk of solvent has left. Rust-Oleum lists 24 hours to “fully dry” across its acrylic, metallic, and enamel lines. Light use is now safe.
  4. Full cure / maximum adhesion (about 5 - 7 days). This is the step people skip. Rust-Oleum's plastic-bonding paints and primers note that on plastic, maximum adhesion and durability is achieved in 5-7 days, and Krylon advertises its Fusion All-In-One as fully chip resistant after 7 days. Cure is a chemical process (solvent escape plus, for enamels, oxidation), not just drying. If you are planning to coat the painted piece in epoxy, wait the full cure before pouring resin so trapped solvent does not bubble the finish.

The Recoat Window: The Make-or-Break Hour

The recoat window is the single most important timing rule on the can, and it is counter-intuitive. For Rust-Oleum Painter's Touch 2X, you must apply the second coat either within 1 hour or after 48 hours, not in between. Stops Rust enamel uses a similar rule: within 1 hour or after 48 hours. The metallic specialty line is the exception: within 1 hour or after 24 hours.

Why the gap? The first coat is still releasing solvent. If you add a second coat while the first is half-cured (roughly 1-48 hours in), the new solvent re-activates the underlying film and the two layers wrinkle or lift. Wait the full window and the first coat is chemically stable enough to accept another. When in doubt, read the specific product label, because the recoat window is product-specific.

Practical Tips for Faster, Cleaner Drying

  • Hit the 70°F / 50% RH target. Spray in that sweet spot and the can's printed times will hold. If it is cooler or more humid, add time to every stage.
  • Several thin coats beat one thick one. Krylon recommends waiting about 1 minute between light coats. Thin films release solvent fast; thick films trap it and stay tacky for hours.
  • Keep air moving. A fan pulling fumes away (not blowing dust onto the piece) speeds evaporation and is also the manufacturer-recommended ventilation for safety.
  • Mind the recoat window. Decide up front whether you are doing back-to-back coats (within the first hour) or waiting two days, and commit to one path.
  • Build in a full cure week. For anything that will be handled, washed, or exposed to weather, treat day 7 as the real finish line for maximum hardness and adhesion, not day 1.

How This Compares to Other Craft Cures

Spray paint's week-long cure is fast compared with other finishes you may layer it with. Epoxy resin takes longer to cure in bulk pours, and handmade cold-process soap needs weeks to cure before it is mild and hard. If you are sequencing a multi-step project, plan each stage's full timeline rather than its surface-dry time.

The Bottom Line

For a typical craft project using a fast-drying acrylic spray, expect 20 minutes to touch, 1 hour to handle, 24 hours to be fully dry, and about a week to reach maximum adhesion and chip resistance. Switch to an oil-based enamel and every stage multiplies by several hours, but the 24-hour full-dry milestone stays the same. Always confirm against the specific can's label, because dry and recoat times are product-specific.

guides.title: How Long Do Tomatoes Take to Grow? Timeline by Type
guides.excerpt: Tomatoes take roughly 50-90 days from transplant to the first ripe fruit, about 100-140 days from seed. Determinate bush types ripen fastest; see the full stage timeline.
guides.content:
How long do tomatoes take to grow?

Tomatoes take roughly 50 to 90 days from transplanting to produce their first ripe fruit, which works out to about 100 to 140 days total if you start from seed. Clemson Cooperative Extension puts the range for a first harvest at 52 to 90 days after transplanting, depending on the cultivar. The University of Maryland Extension similarly lists 65 to 90 days from transplant to maturity. Add the 6 to 8 weeks you spend raising seedlings indoors, and a seed-to-plate crop normally runs three to four and a half months.

The single biggest source of confusion is that seed catalogs and extension guides count days to maturity from transplanting, not from the day you sow seed (Cornell is explicit about this). So a "60-day" tomato does not ripen 60 days after you plant the seed — it ripens 60 days after a young plant goes into the garden. Keep that distinction in mind and every timeline figure below falls into place.

How fast your tomatoes actually grow depends on the variety's growth habit, the cultivar's listed days-to-maturity, fruit size, temperature, sun, and how you train the plants.

FactorTypical effect on the timeline
Growth habitDeterminate (bush) types ripen a concentrated crop; Clemson notes most early-ripening cultivars are determinate, with the earliest fruiting in about 55-70 days from transplant. Indeterminate (vining) types range from about 57 to 90+ days and keep producing until frost.
Cultivar maturity classCornell classifies varieties as early (65 days or fewer), mid-season (65-80 days), or late-season (80+ days) from transplant.
Fruit sizeSmall cherry and grape tomatoes ripen fast (often 57-70 days); large beefsteaks are usually late (75-82 days).
TemperatureTomatoes grow best at 70-80°F days / 60-70°F nights. Below 55°F or above 90°F, pollination and fruit set drop and ripening stalls.
SunlightPlants need at least 8 hours of direct sun. Shade slows vegetative growth and pushes harvest later.
Starting methodBuying a transplant skips the 5-8 week indoor seedling phase, shaving more than a month off your calendar versus starting from seed.
Support and pruningStaking and pruning indeterminate varieties can hasten the first harvest by a week or more, Cornell notes, though it usually reduces total yield.

Stages: what to expect from seed to harvest

1. Germination: 5-12 days

Sown in warm mix, tomato seeds emerge quickly. Johnny's Selected Seeds reports tomatoes typically germinate in 5-7 days when the mix is held at 75-85°F (24-29°C). Cornell lists 6 to 12 days to emergence — about one week at 75°F — noting that seeds germinate best at 75-90°F and very slowly at cooler temperatures. Bottom heat and a seed-starting mix kept evenly moist give the fastest, most even stand.

2. Seedling stage: 5-8 weeks indoors

Cornell and Clemson both recommend sowing indoors 6 to 8 weeks before transplanting outside; Johnny's suggests about 5-6 weeks for growers who pot up promptly. Grow seedlings on at 60-70°F under supplemental light so they stay stocky rather than leggy. Clemson advises hardening off plants for a week before moving them out, and Cornell recommends waiting until nighttime temperatures are consistently above 45°F and all frost danger has passed.

3. Vegetative growth: ~3-4 weeks after transplant

Once in the garden, the plant puts on foliage and root mass. Tomatoes are warm-season annuals that want full sun and consistent moisture — about 1 inch of water per week, Cornell notes. Deep planting (setting the stem so only the top two or three sets of leaves show) encourages adventitious roots and a stronger start.

4. Flowering and fruit set: begins mid-summer

Yellow flowers appear at bloom time in mid- to late summer. Fruit set depends on warmth: Cornell warns that temperatures below 55°F or above 90°F cause poor pollination and blossom drop. Determinate varieties set most of their flowers within a short window; indeterminates keep flowering and fruiting on new growth until frost kills them.

5. Ripening: fruit colors up over weeks

Fruits ripen gradually from the blossom end toward the shoulders, and each cluster ripens from the base outward. A tomato that has "broken color" (started turning) will finish ripening indoors at 70°F, and Clemson points out that light is not required for ripening. Pick at first color change to avoid cracking and losses — you will not taste the difference versus vine-ripened fruit, according to the University of Maryland Extension.

Determinate vs. indeterminate: which is faster?

If speed is the priority, choose a determinate variety. These bush-type plants grow to a fixed size, set fruit over a concentrated window, and are usually the early-ripening cultivars. They are the fastest path to that first ripe tomato and the right pick for containers, short seasons, and a single big harvest for canning.

Indeterminate varieties take a little longer to start but keep vining and producing until frost, so they yield more over the whole season even if the first fruit is later. Clemson notes that most heirlooms (such as Cherokee Purple at 72 days, Brandywine at 78 days, and Rutgers at 82 days) are indeterminate, while some early hybrids (Sun Gold at 57 days, Early Girl at 60 days) are indeterminate but ripen fast. If your growing season is short or cool, plan on early-season varieties (65 days or fewer from transplant) to be sure of a harvest.

Practical tips for a faster, heavier harvest

  • Pick the right days-to-maturity. Read the catalog number carefully — it counts from transplant, not seed. For a short season, choose cultivars at 65 days or fewer from transplant.
  • Warm the soil early. Lay black plastic or landscape fabric two to three weeks before planting. UMD Extension recommends this, plus plastic plant enclosures, to push the first harvest earlier in cold springs.
  • Stake and prune indeterminates. Removing suckers and tying plants to stakes can bring on the first ripe fruit a week sooner and improve fruit quality.
  • Keep moisture even. Inconsistent watering causes blossom end rot and cracking. Mulch after the soil warms and supply about 1 inch of water weekly.
  • Feed, don't overfeed. Side-dress with a balanced fertilizer when the first fruits reach about an inch across. Excess nitrogen delays ripening and produces foliage at the expense of fruit.
  • Hurry the last of the crop. As fall approaches, topping plants and thinning leaves helps the plant finish ripening its remaining fruit before frost.

The bottom line

Plan on about 100-140 days from seed (or roughly 50-90 days from a transplant) to your first ripe tomato. A determinate cherry type in warm soil can hit the low end of that range; a late beefsteak started from seed in a cool climate can push the high end. The figures trace directly to university extension guidance and Johnny's trial data, so you can plan your planting date backward from when you want that first tomato. If you are mapping out the whole vegetable garden, our guides on how long potatoes take to grow, how long grass seeds take to grow, and how long it takes to grow an avocado from seed cover the rest of the calendar.

guides.title: How Long Does It Take to Grow an Avocado from Seed?
guides.excerpt: An avocado pit sprouts in 2-6 weeks, but fruit takes 5-13 years from seed (often never true-to-type). Grafted trees bear in 3-4 years. Here's the full timeline.
guides.content:
How long does it take to grow an avocado from seed? The honest answer

An avocado pit sprouts quickly — expect roots and a stem in 2–6 weeks — but a tree grown from that seed takes 5 to 13 years before it is mature enough to set fruit, and the fruit (if it ever arrives) will not match the avocado you ate. Those figures come from the University of California Riverside’s avocado extension experts and the California Avocado Commission. A grafted nursery tree, by contrast, typically bears its first fruit in just 3–4 years.

So there are really two timelines to keep in mind:

  • Sprouting the pit: 2–6 weeks
  • First fruit from a seed-grown tree: 5–13 years (UF/IFAS Extension averages it at about 7 years)

If you are growing a pit in a jar on the windowsill, treat it as a fun foliage houseplant — not a shortcut to homegrown guacamole.

What changes the timeline

FactorEffect on time to fruitNotes
Seed-grown (your pit)5–13 years to fruit, often never true-to-typeEvery seed is cross-pollinated, so the fruit will not match the parent (UC Riverside)
Grafted nursery treeFirst fruit in 3–4 yearsA cloned variety on proven rootstock (California Avocado Commission)
Outdoor, frost-free climateFaster and more reliableBest at 60–85°F; tolerates ~28–32°F once established
Indoor / windowsillAlmost never fruitsLow light and dry heat; grown for foliage only
Cross-pollination (A + B type)Better fruit set and retentionHaving a second variety helps, but is not strictly required
Soil and drainageFaster establishmentIdeal pH 6–6.5; mound the tree in heavy clay

Stages: what to expect, week by week and year by year

Weeks 1–2: Suspend and wait

Pierce the washed seed with three toothpicks and rest it broad-end-down in a glass of water, covering about an inch of the pit. Keep it warm and out of direct sunlight, topping up the water as needed. The California Avocado Commission says you should see roots and a stem start to sprout in about two to six weeks. The University of Nebraska Extension notes that the soil method — burying the pit pointed-end-up in moist potting mix — gives slightly faster results than the water glass.

Weeks 2–8: Root and shoot

A small root emerges from the flat end and a shoot from the pointed end. If six to eight weeks pass with no activity at all, the Commission recommends discarding the seed and starting over with a fresh one — some pits are simply duds.

Months 2–3: Pot it up

When the stem reaches 6–7 inches long, cut it back to about 3 inches to force branching. Once the roots are thick and the stem has leafed out again, plant it in rich humus potting soil in a roughly 10½-inch pot, leaving the seed half exposed. Water frequently with an occasional deep soak; keep the soil moist, never saturated.

Years 1–3: Vegetative growth

The seedling puts on leaves and height. When the stem hits 12 inches, cut it back to 6 inches to encourage bushy side shoots. Almost all of the plant’s energy is going into wood and roots at this stage — not fruit.

Years 5–13 (if ever): First bloom and fruit

A seed-grown tree finally flowers, but the result is a genetic unknown. UC Riverside is explicit: the seed is the product of cross-pollination, so planting a Hass pit does not produce a Hass tree — the fruit’s size, texture and taste are unpredictable. Expect heavy flower drop, too: an avocado tree can produce up to a million flowers yet set only about 100–200 fruit (roughly one in ten thousand).

Why a seed-grown avocado rarely matches its parent

Commercial avocados are grafted, not seed-grown, for a reason. UF/IFAS Extension explains that grafting guarantees fruit quality and pest resistance: a branch of a known variety is joined onto proven rootstock, so the resulting tree is effectively a clone of the parent. A seedling, by contrast, is a brand-new genetic combination. UF/IFAS warns that a seed-grown tree “will not have the same pest and disease resistance that the parent plant did,” and its fruit quality will vary. That is why every Hass avocado in a store comes from a grafted tree — all descended from the original Hass mother tree, which dates to 1926 and was still producing fruit decades later.

Practical tips — and when to give up on the pit

  • Want fruit? Buy a grafted tree. Both UC Riverside and the California Avocado Commission are blunt on this: a grafted nursery tree fruits in 3–4 years and gives you a predictable, named variety. A seed-grown tree is a decade-long gamble.
  • Plant outdoors in a frost-free spot. Avocados do best at 60–85°F with moderate humidity and tolerate only about 28–32°F once established. Give them full sun, protected from wind, planted in a non-lawn area.
  • Get the soil right. Aim for pH 6–6.5 with excellent drainage. In heavy clay, plant on a mound 1–2 feet high and 3–5 feet across so water does not pool around the crown.
  • Water deeply, then let it dry. Soak the soil, then allow the top to dry somewhat before watering again. Yellow leaves usually mean overwatering; brown, crispy leaf tips signal salt buildup — flush the pot slowly and let it drain.
  • Indoors means foliage only. UC Riverside notes that avocados grow best at 60–85°F and set fruit best at about 65–75°F, so hot, dry indoor air and low light work against the plant; keep it in bright but not scorching indirect light and mist the leaves occasionally. Do not expect fruit from a windowsill tree.

If your pit has sat dormant for 8+ weeks with no sign of a root, it is a dud — start a fresh one. And if you have nurtured a seedling for years hoping for Hass-quality fruit, the honest odds are against you: grafting is how the industry guarantees both quality and a 3–4 year harvest, and it is the practical route for any home grower who actually wants to pick avocados.

For other patience-testing garden timelines, see how long grass seed, tomatoes, and potatoes take to grow.

guides.title: How Long Do Potatoes Take to Grow? (Days by Type)
guides.author: Suraj Giri
guides.excerpt: Potatoes take 70-120+ days to grow: early types 70-90, mid-season 90-110, late/storage 110-130. Here is how variety, soil, and weather change the timeline.
guides.content:
How Long Do Potatoes Take to Grow?

Potatoes take roughly 70 to 120 days (about 2.5 to 4 months) to grow from planting seed pieces to a mature harvest, with most garden cultivars falling between 90 and 120 days. Iowa State University Extension and the University of Maryland Extension both put the typical days-to-maturity range for home-garden potatoes at 90 to 120 days after planting, and the University of Florida IFAS Extension narrows the practical harvest window to 80 to 115 days for most varieties. Where you land inside that span depends almost entirely on the variety you plant: early types finish fastest, late storage types take the longest.

If you only want small, tender "new" potatoes, you can dig them much sooner. The University of Maryland Extension notes that new potatoes can be harvested about 6 to 8 weeks (roughly 40 to 60 days) after planting, usually once the plants have flowered. Treat everything below as a planning guide, not a stopwatch. Real elapsed time swings with soil temperature, water, and weather.

The Short Answer by Potato Type

Seed catalogs sort potatoes into three maturity classes, and the class you choose is the single biggest factor in how long you will wait. Cornell University's vegetable growing guide frames it as early (around 65 days), mid-season (around 80 days), and late (more than 90 days) to first usable harvest. Combining that with the 90 to 120 day full-maturity windows from Iowa State and Maryland gives the practical ranges below.

Potato type / maturity classDays to harvestWhat you get and how it changes the wait
First early / early70 to 90 daysFastest crop; ideal for new potatoes. Small tubers, thin skins, eat soon. Examples: Red Norland, Yukon Gold, Superior.
Second early / mid-season90 to 110 daysThe sweet spot for most home gardens. Good yield, decent storage. Examples: Goldrush, Chieftain, Reba.
Maincrop / late (storage)110 to 130+ daysLargest yields and best keepers; thick skins for winter storage. Need the longest frost-free season. Examples: Kennebec, Elba, Katahdin.
"New" potatoes (any type)about 6 to 8 weeks (40 to 60 days)Immature tubers dug early while vines are still green; do not store well. Harvest after flowering.

Factors That Speed Up or Slow Down the Clock

FactorEffect on growing time
Soil temperatureSeed pieces will not sprout until soil reaches about 40 to 45°F; emergence takes 2 to 4 weeks (14 to 28 days). Above 80°F soil temperature, Maryland Extension warns that tuber development is inhibited, stalling the crop.
Air temperaturePotatoes bulking prefer cool summers (65 to 70°F). Heat slows bulking; frost kills vines and ends the season.
Water consistencyTubers need about 1 inch of water per week. Wet-dry swings during bulking (Iowa State) cause hollow heart, cracks, and knobs, but do not shorten the calendar.
Seed piece prepCutting and curing seed pieces, or "green sprouting" them indoors, can shave days off emergence and give an earlier start in cold springs.
Variety choiceChoosing an early vs. late variety moves harvest by 30 to 50 days, more than any other lever.

Stages of Potato Growth: What to Expect and When

The University of Florida IFAS Extension breaks potato development into five stages with approximate day ranges. Knowing them tells you what is happening underground long before you see it.

Stage 1: Sprout development (about 0 to 30 days)

After planting, eyes on the seed piece push sprouts up through the soil. Cornell notes sprouts typically emerge 14 to 28 days after planting, depending on soil temperature. The seed piece itself is the plant's energy source during this stage, so do not expect to see much above ground yet.

Stage 2: Vegetative growth (about 30 to 55 days)

Leaves, stems, and roots form and photosynthesis ramps up. The plant is building the factory that will later fill the tubers. This is when you "hill" soil around the stems to keep developing tubers covered and to prevent greening (green potatoes contain solanine, which is toxic).

Stage 3: Tuber initiation and set (about 55 to 70 days)

Tubers begin forming at the ends of underground stems (stolons) but have not enlarged yet. IFAS notes this usually happens before the plant flowers. This is also roughly when you can start stealing a few new potatoes.

Stage 4: Tuber bulking (about 60 to 120 days, depending on variety)

Tubers enlarge rapidly and accumulate starch. Iowa State highlights that tuber development typically begins in early to mid-June in temperate gardens, and that uniform moisture during this window drives your final yield. This stage overlaps the others and is where early versus late varieties diverge most.

Stage 5: Tuber maturation

Tubers reach full size and the plant tops yellow, senesce, and die back. Nutrients continue moving into the tubers and skins toughen, which is what allows storage. For storage potatoes, Iowa State and Maryland both recommend leaving tubers in the ground about 2 weeks after the vines die so skins set fully.

When and How to Harvest

Two harvest points exist for almost every potato planting:

  • New potatoes (about 6 to 8 weeks, roughly 40 to 60 days): Once plants flower, gently hand-dig around the hills and take a few small, thin-skinned tubers. Use them within about 10 days; they do not store.
  • Mature/storage potatoes (90 to 120+ days): Wait until vines have fully died back. To test maturity, Iowa State suggests digging one or two hills, if the skin rubs off easily the potatoes are immature and will not store, so wait several more days. Skins that hold firm signal readiness.

Harvest with a garden fork, digging wide to avoid spearing tubers. For storage, cure tubers for 10 to 14 days at 50 to 60°F with high humidity so cuts heal and skins thicken, then keep them dark at about 40°F. Never eat green tubers, discard them.

Practical Tips to Hit the Timeline

  • Plant early enough. Set seed pieces 2 to 4 weeks before your last frost once soil hits 40 to 45°F. Late planting pushes harvest into hotter weather that slows bulking.
  • Use certified seed potatoes, not grocery-store tubers, which may carry disease or sprout inhibitors that delay or stunt emergence.
  • Hill twice (around 6 to 8 inches tall, and again 2 to 3 weeks later) to protect tubers from light and to give stolons room to bulk.
  • Water steadily. Aim for 1 inch per week; mulch to even out soil moisture and prevent the cracks and hollow heart that wet-dry swings cause during bulking.
  • Pick the right variety for your season length. In short-season climates, lean on first-early types (70 to 90 days). In long, warm seasons, maincrop varieties (110 to 130 days) reward you with the best storage.

If you are planning a full vegetable calendar, the same cool-season logic applies elsewhere. You can compare timing with our guides on how long grass seeds take to grow, how long tomatoes take to grow, and how long it takes to grow an avocado from seed.

The bottom line: Plan for 70 to 120+ days from planting to mature potatoes, dig new potatoes around 6 to 8 weeks if you want them, and let the vines die back fully before harvesting for storage. The variety you pick moves that window more than anything else you can control.

guides.title: How Often Should You Wash Towels? The 3–4 Use Rule
guides.excerpt: Wash bath towels every 3–4 uses, kitchen towels daily, and washcloths after every use. Here's the science-backed breakdown on towel washing frequency.
guides.content:
How often should you wash towels? The short answer

Wash your bath towel after every 3 to 4 uses — which works out to about once or twice a week for someone who showers daily. That is the rule-of-thumb echoed by both environmental microbiologists and dermatologists, and it comes with one big condition: the towel has to dry completely between uses. If it stays damp, bunched up, or folded over, it should go in the laundry sooner.

Other towels run on a faster clock because they get touched more often and by more people. The quick version:

  • Bath towels: every 3–4 uses (about 1–2 times a week)
  • Hand towels: every 3–4 uses — the same baseline as bath towels (swap more often in busy or sick households)
  • Kitchen towels and dishcloths: daily
  • Washcloths and gym towels: after every single use

Here is why those numbers exist, when to bend them, and how to tell if your routine is off. (This is general household guidance, not medical advice — if someone in your home has a skin infection, a weakened immune system, or open wounds, follow your doctor's instructions.)

Towel washing frequency at a glance

Towel typeWash it every…Why
Bath towel3–4 uses (≈ 1–2×/week)Picks up dead skin, skin bacteria, and body fluids; dampness lets microbes multiply
Hand towel3–4 uses — same as bath towels (more in busy/sick homes)Touched by multiple hands; can spread germs between household members
Kitchen / dish towelDailyContacts food, raw-meat juices, and dirty surfaces — high cross-contamination risk
WashclothEach use (or ≥ 2×/week minimum)Loaded with dead skin and used close to the face
Gym / workout towelEach useSoaked with sweat and often left damp in a bag — ideal microbial breeding ground
Guest towelAfter the guest leavesUsed briefly but should be fresh for the next person

Why 3–4 uses? The damp-plus-bacteria problem

A towel looks clean right after you shower with it — after all, you were just washed. But it is actually doing second cleaning duty, scraping off whatever the water and soap left behind: dead skin cells, skin microbes, body oils, and (on body and hand towels alike) traces of fecal bacteria such as E. coli. Once that towel hangs damp and warm, it becomes an incubator.

Ryan Sinclair, PhD, MPH, a professor of environmental microbiology at Loma Linda University, puts it plainly: a used, damp towel is an ideal environment for bacteria to grow and multiply, and the longer it stays wet, the more they reproduce. Towels commonly pick up Staphylococcus aureus, fecal bacteria, and everyday skin flora.

Dermatologist Alok Vij, MD, of Cleveland Clinic lists the microbes a moist towel can sustain: fungi (the yeasts and molds behind athlete's foot, ringworm, and jock itch), bacteria including medication-resistant staph (MRSA) and E. coli, and viruses such as those that cause warts, norovirus, and pink eye. Add in allergens, microscopic fecal particles, and dead skin cells, and you have what he calls a genuine breeding ground for infection-causing organisms. The takeaway: the 3–4-use rule isn't about visible dirt — it's about keeping that microbial load in check before it can irritate your skin or spread to the next person.

Factors that change it

The 3–4-use baseline assumes a healthy person in a normal bathroom. Real life shifts the number up or down.

  • It never fully dries. If your bathroom is humid, the towel is folded or bunched, or it hangs without airflow, Sinclair recommends laundering it after just 2 uses. No drying = no pause in bacterial growth.
  • Someone is sick or has a skin condition. With an active infection — norovirus, the flu, MRSA/staph, ringworm, athlete's foot — or any open wound, cut, or surgical incision, a towel should be single-use and washed hot. The same goes for a compromised skin barrier from eczema or chronic skin conditions.
  • Someone is immunocompromised. A weaker immune system calls for more frequent changes to avoid loading the towel with opportunistic microbes.
  • It is humid or tropical. Dr. Vij suggests laundering bath towels 2–3 times a week (not the once-weekly minimum) in high-humidity environments because they dry slowly.
  • Shared use. Hand towels in a busy household get touched by every pair of hands. Cleveland Clinic notes that dirty towels can spread germs between household members, so in a large or busy household it makes sense to swap them more often than the every-3-to-4-use baseline.
  • Kitchen duty. Towels that wipe counters, hands, and dishes cross paths with raw food and foodborne pathogens. Michigan State University Extension advises changing cloth kitchen towels daily, and FoodSafety.gov calls for washing dishcloths often in the hot cycle of your washing machine.

How to make the 3–4-use rule actually work

The frequency only holds if your towel dries. A few habits buy you the full 3–4 uses:

  • Spread it fully open on the bar — never leave it folded, doubled over, or in a pile.
  • Hang it where air moves. A ventilated spot dries far faster than a cramped hook against a wall.
  • Run the bathroom fan while it dries to pull moisture out of the room.
  • Wash hot. Use the hottest water the towel's label allows, and dry thoroughly — heat and dryness are what knock back microbial growth.
  • Do not share with someone who is ill. Give sick household members their own towel and wash it solo after each use.

For the broader laundry routine, these intervals sit alongside the rest of your bedding schedule — see how often you should wash your sheets for the matching guidance, and pair your towel rotation with the lifespans in how long pillows last and how long a mattress lasts.

Signs you are over- or under-doing it

You are probably washing too rarely if…

  • It smells musty even when dry. That sour, damp odor is volatile organic compounds given off by multiplying bacteria and mold — Sinclair's telltale sign the towel is overdue, and a smell that can transfer onto your skin.
  • It feels stiff or scratchy instead of soft, a sign of built-up residue, skin cells, and soap scum.
  • You are getting breakouts, irritation, or recurring rashes where the towel touches — a possible sign the microbial load has climbed too high. (Check with a dermatologist if this persists.)
  • Someone at home keeps passing around the same minor infection (athlete's foot, pinkeye, a stomach bug).

You may be washing too often if…

  • Towels feel thin, rough, or frayed early in their life. Frequent hot washes and over-drying wear fibers out faster.
  • They lose absorbency — sometimes a sign of detergent buildup from more washes than needed.

For most healthy households, the sweet spot is simple: let bath towels dry fully, swap them at 3–4 uses, give hand towels the same 3–4-use treatment (more often when the house is busy or someone is ill), and retire kitchen towels to the wash at the end of each day. Do that and you stay well ahead of the bacteria without wearing your towels out prematurely.
