guides.title: The Best Time to Visit France (incl. Paris) by Month
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit France (incl. Paris) is April to June and September to October: mild weather, thinner crowds, and lower prices than peak summer.
guides.content:
The best time to visit France (incl. Paris) is mid-April to June and September to October

The single best window for most of France is the shoulder season: mid-April through June and September through October. Days are mild, the big summer crowds have not yet arrived (or have just left), and prices sit well below the July–August peak. In Paris, average daytime highs climb from about 16°C in April to roughly 23°C in June and back down to a comfortable 22°C in September, according to Météo-France normals for Paris-Orly (1991–2020).

Lonely Planet's local authors put it plainly: spring (especially April and May) and autumn (particularly September and October) are the ideal months to visit Paris because "crowds are thinner, but the weather is temperate and lovely." For the country as a whole, France's official tourism board notes the country spans four climate zones — oceanic in the west (including Paris), continental in the centre-east, Mediterranean in the south-east, and mountain in the Alps and Pyrenees — so the "best" month shifts depending on whether you are after café terraces, beaches, or ski slopes.

The short version: pick April–June or September–October for Paris and most of the country, May–September for the Côte d'Azur, and December to March for the Alps. Avoid mid-July to mid-August if you dislike heat and crowds, and know that August in Paris brings an odd trade-off — quieter streets and lower hotel rates, but a wave of restaurant and shop closures as Parisians head off on vacation.

France month-by-month: weather, crowds, cost and events

The table below uses Paris average daytime highs from Météo-France (Paris-Orly, 1991–2020 normals) as a benchmark. Expect the Riviera to run noticeably warmer — Nice averages about 13°C in January versus Paris's 7°C, and roughly 28°C in August — and the high Alps to be far colder and snowier in winter.

MonthWeather (Paris avg high)Crowds & costBest for / watch for
Jan~7°C — cold, grey, dampLowest prices; very quietMuseums, theatre, winter soldes (sales). Daylight is short.
Feb~9°C — chillyLow; Nice Carnival draws crowds southValentine's in Paris, Carnaval de Nice, Menton Lemon Festival.
Mar~13°C — variable, pack rain gearLow to moderateFirst blooms in parks; unpredictable weather.
Apr16°C — mildModerate; rises around EasterChestnut blossoms, café terraces, Paris Marathon.
May~20°C — pleasantModerate; many French public holidaysCannes Film Festival, French Open; expect closures on May 1.
Jun~23°C — warm, long daysModerate to busyFête de la Musique (Jun 21), lavender blooms in Provence.
Jul26°C — warm to hotHigh — peak domestic & international travelTour de France, Riviera beaches; book well ahead.
Aug26°C — hotVery high on the coast; Paris empties & some spots shutRiviera at its liveliest; Paris restaurant closures.
Sep22°C — mild, often blue-skiedModerate; la rentrée restarts cultural lifeWine harvests, Heritage Days, calm weather.
Oct16°C — crisp, autumn colourLow to moderate; rates easeVineyard colours, Montmartre grape festival, fewer crowds.
Nov~11°C — chilly, short daysLowBeaujolais Nouveau (third Thurs.), museums, Christmas lights late-month.
Dec~8°C — cold, festiveModerate around Christmas marketsStrasbourg & Alsace Christmas markets; ski season opens.

Cheapest time and worst time to visit France

The cheapest time is winter — November through February, excluding the Christmas and New Year weeks. Lonely Planet singles out December to January as the best window for budget travellers in Paris: sights are quieter and prices lower, and you can still enjoy ice-skating rinks, holiday lights, and the winter soldes. There is a second, counter-intuitive cheap pocket: August in Paris itself, when hotel rates often hit their lowest point because locals flee the heat — but you trade the savings for sweltering temperatures and a wave of shuttered bistros and boutiques. For the cheapest and pleasant experience, target late October, November, or early March.

There is no truly "worst" time — France is a year-round destination — but two windows disappoint the most travellers. The first is mid-July to mid-August on the Côte d'Azur and other coasts: everything is open and the weather is glorious, but the Riviera is packed, hot, and priced at its peak. The second is August in Paris, when many restaurants, small shops, and even some tour services shut for the month as Parisians take their vacances — Lonely Planet notes it "can be hard to get a good bistro meal." If your heart is set on classic Parisian café culture, August is the riskiest month. Winter in smaller towns and rural areas (and especially Corsica outside its narrow May, June and September window) can feel too quiet, with little open.

Region-by-region: timing the Riviera, the Alps, and rural France

Paris. Spring (April–May) and autumn (September–October) are the sweet spots. April brings blossoming chestnut trees and buzzing café terraces; September delivers what locals consider the city's bluest skies during la rentrée. Summer is warm and lively but crowded; winter is cheap and cultural but grey.

French Riviera (Côte d'Azur) and Provence. The prime beach season runs May to September. Nice's sea temperature reaches about 24°C in August, per Météo-France (Nice Côte d'Azur, 1991–2020), with daytime highs around 28°C. For warmth without the wall-to-wall crowds of July and August, May, June and September are ideal — and they are also the only reliably open months in highly seasonal spots like Corsica. The south shares its season with its neighbour; see our best time to visit Spain if you're stringing the Mediterranean together.

The Alps and Pyrenees. Ski season runs December to March (into April at altitude). The larger, higher resorts — such as Les Trois Vallées and Les Portes du Soleil — reliably open from early-to-mid December through mid-April, while lower resorts may only run mid-January to mid-March depending on snow. For cross-border ski planning, our best time to visit Switzerland covers the same mountain season. In summer (July–August), the high Alps become prime hiking country once the snow clears.

Rural France and wine regions. Many rural areas are highly seasonal — outside summer you may find almost nothing open. The grape harvest rolls through the Loire, Bordeaux, Champagne, Burgundy and the Rhône from late August to mid-September, making early autumn a rewarding time for wine country.

Practical planning tips

  • Book Paris well ahead. Accommodation fills early, especially from April to October and around public holidays; Lonely Planet advises reservations are essential at peak times and recommended year-round.
  • Watch the May holidays. May has more public holidays than any other month in France, and May 1 (Labour Day) brings widespread closures. It's a lovely, temperate month — just plan around the days off.
  • Layer up. Spring and autumn swing between warm afternoons and cool evenings; March weather is especially variable, so pack rain gear. Summer on the Riviera calls for sun protection; winter city breaks need a warm coat.
  • Embrace August mindfully. If you visit Paris in August, expect lower hotel rates but confirm restaurant reservations in advance, since many close. The flip side — lighter traffic — makes it a great month to cycle.
  • Pair it with a neighbour. France sits at the crossroads of Europe: combine it with the best time to visit Italy for a Riviera–Ligurian coast trip, or compare notes with the best time to visit London for an easy Eurostar city-hopping itinerary.

The bottom line: for the best balance of mild weather, manageable crowds, and value, plan your France trip for mid-April to June or September to October — and simply shift to May–September for the beaches or December–March for the slopes.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Greece: When to Go & Avoid Crowds
guides.excerpt: Best time to visit Greece: mid-May to June and September. Warm seas, open islands, thinner crowds, fair prices. Month-by-month guide to weather, costs and events.
guides.content:
The best time to visit Greece is mid-May to June, and September

Greece's single best travel window is the shoulder season on either side of peak summer: mid-May through June, and the whole of September. During these months the islands are fully open, the sea is warm enough to swim, daylight stretches late into the evening, crowds are thinner than in high summer, and prices sit well below the July-August peak. Greece has a classic Mediterranean climate - mild, wet winters and warm, dry summers with sunshine almost year-round - and the main warm, dry season runs roughly from May through September (shoulder months like April and October are milder and can still see some rain).

If you can pick only one month, choose September: the sea has warmed through all summer, school holidays are over, and airfares and hotel rates ease from their August heights. The island-hopping season unofficially opens with Orthodox Easter, which falls in April or May (12 April 2026; 2 May 2027), as hotels and ferries spin back up for the year.

The two shoulder windows have a slightly different character. Late May and June give you the longest daylight of the year - June peaks with sunshine in its second half - and the heady feeling of a country waking up for summer, though the sea has only just lost its winter chill, especially in the deeper Aegean. September delivers the inverse: marginally shorter days, but the warmest water of the year and a calmer, more relaxed pace as families head home. Sunshine is generous almost year-round, so even the edges of the season are reliably bright.

Greece month by month

MonthAthens daytime high (approx.)Sea and weatherCrowds and costHighlights
January~13°C / 55°FCold and wet; snow on northern mountainsLowest prices; many islands quietReduced site fees; Athens city culture
February~14°C / 57°FCold; brief sunny spellsLowest; carnival season beginsApokries (Greek Carnival)
March~16°C / 61°FCool, occasional showers; snow in mountainsLow; ancient sites uncrowdedReduced site fees; guided site tours
April~20°C / 68°FWarming, wildflowers; sea still coolLow to mediumOrthodox Easter (Apr/May); season opens
May~25°C / 77°FSunny, warm days; sea warmingMedium; first swimsIsland-hopping season starts
June~29°C / 84°FLong sunny days; first real swimsMedium-highLongest daylight; festivals begin
July~33°C / 91°FHot, dry; Meltemi wind; heatwaves possiblePeak prices and crowdsAthens Epidaurus Festival; beach life
August~33°C / 91°FHottest and driest (July-Aug average highs ~32-33°C)Peak; book 6 months aheadPanigiria; full island life
September~29°C / 84°FWarmest sea of the year; sunnyHigh but easing; good valueIdeal all-round month
October~23°C / 73°FCooling; mid-Oct seas pick up swellMedium; thinning outLast month most island hotels stay open
November~18°C / 64°FCooler and rainierLow; cheapest after peakReduced site fees resume (from 1 Nov)
December~15°C / 59°FCool and wet; mild on the south coastLow (except holidays)City breaks; Christmas

Temperatures are approximate daytime highs for Athens, drawn from WeatherSpark climatic data and Lonely Planet's reporting. Southern islands (Crete, Rhodes) run a few degrees warmer in spring and autumn, while the northern mainland and the deep Aegean stay cooler; January averages are noticeably milder in the southern islands - about 12°C in Heraklion (Crete) and Rhodes - versus roughly 5-6°C in Thessaloniki on the northern mainland.

Cheapest time to visit Greece

The cheapest time to visit Greece is the off-season, November to March. Airfares, ferry prices and hotel rates all fall steeply once the summer crowds leave, and between 1 November and 31 March the state reduces entrance fees at ancient sites and state-run museums - including the Acropolis and the National Archaeological Museum - making an Athens city break genuinely affordable. November still delivers average highs of around 18°C (64°F); by December the average high slips to about 14°C (57°F), and winter is the wettest part of the year.

The trade-off is real. On the smaller islands many hotels, restaurants and boat operators shut down for winter, and ferries that run daily in summer may drop to two or three sailings a week. Mainland cities - Athens, Thessaloniki, Kalamata - stay lively year-round, and November and December (outside the Christmas and New Year rush) offer some of the most tempting airfare and hotel deals of the year. If you want the cheapest swimmable beach trip instead, aim for late September or October: the sea is still warm, prices are falling, and most island hotels stay open through the end of October.

For budget travellers who still want islands rather than a city break, larger islands hold up better through the quiet months. Crete, Corfu, Kefalonia and Rhodes have enough year-round residents and built-up towns to keep restaurants and sights open, and Santorini in the off-season is famously peaceful - you can watch the famous Oia sunset without elbowing for a viewing spot. Just plan island-to-island moves around the reduced ferry timetable rather than improvising.

Worst time to visit Greece

There is no outright bad time, but two windows disappoint most travellers. The first is late July and August if you dislike heat and crowds: it is the hottest, driest period of the year (July and August are the hottest months, with average highs around 32-33°C / 90-91°F and daily peaks climbing higher) and the busiest, with peak airfares, packed beach clubs and congested ferries - book at least six months ahead if you must travel then. The saving grace is the Meltemi, a cooling north wind that blows through the Aegean mostly from June to September.

The second weak window is the depth of winter (January-February) for an island-hopping beach holiday: the sea is cold, many island businesses are shuttered, and ferry schedules are skeletal. For history and city culture, though, winter Athens is excellent - queues at the Acropolis vanish and the mainland stays well connected by bus, train and taxi.

Practical planning tips

  • Book early for July-August. Six months ahead is the benchmark for better airfares and hotel rates during peak season.
  • Mind the sea, not just the air. The deep cobalt Aegean takes longer to warm than the shallower Ionian off western Greece; by September the water everywhere has caught up. For the warmest off-season dips, head to the South Aegean - Rhodes, Karpathos, Folegandros and Santorini.
  • Pack in layers for shoulder season. March, April and October call for short sleeves plus a fleece and a water-resistant jacket; March can even bring snow to the mountains of Central Greece. Summer demands serious sun protection, because the Meltemi wind masks how strong the UV is.
  • Check ferry frequency in the off-season. Some inter-island flights route back through Athens in winter, and daily summer ferries can thin to two or three weekly sailings - plan island hops in advance or build in flexibility.
  • Target ancient sites in spring or autumn. March, April and October offer cool weather, thin crowds and lower prices for places like Delphi, Knossos and the Acropolis; stone and temples hold the summer heat, so midday in August is punishing.
  • Time a festival. Beyond Orthodox Easter, look for panigiria (local saints'-day village festivals with music, dancing and communal feasts), the Athens Epidaurus Festival (June-August) and Apokries, the Greek Carnival that leads into Lent.

Region nuance

Greece is not uniform. The southern islands - Crete and Rhodes - have a longer warm season and make ideal shoulder-season picks in May, September or October; even in January, Heraklion (Crete) and Rhodes average about 12°C, against roughly 5-6°C in Thessaloniki. The Cyclades (Naxos, Santorini, Paros) are windier and the sea is slower to warm. The Ionian (Corfu, Kefalonia) is greener and wetter but has shallower, warmer water earlier in the year. The northern mainland (Thessaloniki and the mountains of Epirus and Macedonia) gets genuinely cold, with snow - good for affordable skiing at Grevena and Metsovo, less so for beaches.

For a wider Mediterranean itinerary, Greece's calendar lines up closely with the best time to visit Italy and the best time to visit Spain; for a cooler-summer city contrast, see the best time to visit France.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Switzerland: A Month-by-Month Guide
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Switzerland is June to September for hiking and open alpine passes, December to March for skiing. Here is how to pick the right month.
guides.content:
The short answer: mid-June to mid-September

The single best window to visit Switzerland is mid-June through mid-September, when daytime temperatures sit in the 18–28°C (65–82°F) range, the high alpine passes and cable cars are running, and the country’s 65,000 km of waymarked hiking trails are largely snow-free. If your whole trip is built around downhill skiing, flip that: December to March is peak snow-sports season, with more than 5,000 km of groomed cross-country trails and the slopes at their snowiest. And if your priority is lower prices and thinner crowds, the late-April-to-May and September-to-October shoulders are the sweet spot, with the honest trade-off that some high routes and mountain hotels are still closed.

Switzerland essentially runs on two high seasons — summer for hiking and lake life, winter for skiing — so the “best” month depends almost entirely on what you came to do. Here is how to choose, month by month.

Switzerland month-by-month at a glance

MonthTypical daytime high*Crowds & costDaylightBest for / watch out for
January−2 to 7°C (28–45°F)High at ski resorts; quiet in citiesShortColdest, snow-sure skiing; New Year is busy and pricey.
February−2 to 7°C (28–45°F)Very high (school holidays)ShortPeak ski month; book lodgings months ahead.
MarchWarming, 8–15°C at lower elevationsHigh early, easing lateLengtheningSpring skiing; late snowstorms still possible.
April8–15°C (46–59°F)Low — cheap shoulderLongerBlooming lowlands; many high passes still closed.
May8–15°C (46–59°F)Low — cheap shoulderLongGreen valleys, waterfalls full; alpine trails snowed in.
June18–28°C (65–82°F)Moderate, risingVery longHigh passes open; a quieter alternative to August.
July18–28°C (65–82°F), hot spells >30°CVery high (peak)Very long, light past 21:00Best hiking and lake swimming; most crowded, priciest.
August18–28°C (65–82°F), hot spells >30°CVery high (peak)Very longPeak hiking; summer festivals; expect crowds everywhere.
SeptemberSummer warmth easing toward autumnModerate, fallingLongExcellent hiking, fewer crowds; top all-round month.
October8–15°C (46–59°F)Low — cheap shoulderShorterAutumn foliage and vineyards; high routes closing.
November8–15°C cooling to winterLowest (off-season)ShortCheapest, but foggy lowlands and “between-season” closures.
December−2 to 7°C (28–45°F)High at resorts over holidaysShortSki resorts re-open, Christmas markets; mid-month quiet.

*Temperature bands follow Switzerland Tourism’s seasonal ranges for typical daytime highs in lower-lying areas: 18–28°C in July–August, −2 to 7°C in January–February, and 8–15°C in spring and autumn. June and September are transition months that usually sit in the lower part of the summer band. Temperatures fall steadily with elevation — while Zurich (408 m) reaches July highs of around 24°C, Zermatt (1,608 m) tops out near 19°C.

What each season is really like

Summer (June–September) is when Switzerland earns its postcard reputation. The hiking network — 65,000 km of waymarked trails including the Via Alpina (Green Trail), which crosses the country from Sargans to Montreux — is snow-free, the lakes are warm enough to swim in, and days are very long (light well past 21:00). Temperatures climb into the 18–28°C band and can exceed 30°C in heatwaves. The catch: mid-July to mid-August is the busiest, most expensive period of the year, and that is also when you will queue for cable cars and share the panoramas. September is the connoisseur’s pick — still warm, still open, far fewer people.

Autumn (late September–November) brings golden larches in the Alps, grape harvests in the Valais and Ticino vineyards, and the cheapest accommodation outside deep winter. By October most high routes and mountain huts begin closing, and November settles into low cloud and fog in the lowlands — the classic Swiss “between seasons” lull when some hotels and restaurants simply shut for a few weeks.

Winter (December–March) is snow-sports heaven: world-class downhill slopes, more than 5,000 km of cross-country trails (including the Engadin Ski Marathon, which draws some 13,000 competitors), snowshoeing, tobogganing and storybook Christmas markets with mulled wine and fondue through Advent. Christmas/New Year and the February school-holiday weeks are the busiest and priciest; mid-January after the holidays is quieter and often the coldest, most snow-reliable time.

Spring (April–May) is the money-saver’s friend: the lowlands bloom, meadows turn green and waterfalls run full from snowmelt, prices drop, and crowds vanish. The honest caveat is that the highest hiking trails and many alpine passes stay snowed in until June, so a spring trip is best built around cities, lakes and lower-elevation walks rather than high-mountain ambitions.

Cheapest time and worst time

Cheapest time: the shoulders, April–May and October–November, are when flights, hotels and even some rail passes are markedly cheaper than in summer, and the fewest other travellers are around. November is the cheapest month of all — but it is also the greyest, with low cloud often parked over the plateau, and the most limited open infrastructure. If you want a balance of decent weather and lower cost, target mid-June or September.

Worst time: there is no month when Switzerland is genuinely unvisitable — the climate is moderate, “with no excessive heat, cold or humidity” — so “worst” is really about mismatch. Avoid mid-July to mid-August if you dislike crowds and high prices, and avoid the Christmas/New Year and February peaks if you do not ski, because ski resorts are packed and expensive while cities can feel quiet and damp. November is the trickiest month to love: cheap, yes, but foggy in the lowlands and dotted with “closed for the season” signs.

Practical planning tips

  • Book early for the peaks. For July–August hiking and the December–March ski weeks (especially February holidays), reserve trains, mountain huts and hotels months ahead — that is when demand is highest.
  • Ride the rails. Switzerland is built for train travel. The panoramic Glacier Express threads from Zermatt to St. Moritz over 291 bridges and through 91 tunnels in about eight hours, and the broader Grand Train Tour of Switzerland stitches the iconic routes together. A Swiss Travel Pass covers most trains, buses and boats across the network — check current seasonal validity before you commit.
  • Pack layers, always. Because temperatures swing hard with altitude, a July afternoon in Lugano can feel Mediterranean while a nearby peak is near freezing. Bring a compact umbrella or light raincoat even in summer — Switzerland Tourism recommends it year-round.
  • Mind the region. Ticino and the Lake Lugano area in the south have a milder, almost Italian climate and can be pleasant from April; the high Alps (Zermatt, Davos, St. Moritz) stay cold and snow-friendly far longer. Planning a wider European loop? Pair Switzerland with our guides to the best time to visit Italy or the best time to visit France.
  • Plan around daylight. Summer gives you light past 21:00 — ideal for long hikes and evening lake swims — while winter days are short, so start activities early and expect mountain transport to wind down by late afternoon.
  • Watch the lulls. Late October to mid-December and April to mid-June are “between seasons” at altitude, when some cable cars, huts and restaurants close for maintenance. City breaks (Zurich, Geneva, Basel, Bern) fill these gaps beautifully. If a city focus appeals, see our best time to visit London and best time to visit Amsterdam for comparable shoulder-season logic.

In short: come June–September for hiking and lakes, December–March for skiing, and April–May or October for fewer crowds and lower costs. Match the month to your main activity and you will rarely go wrong — the rest is just how many layers you carry.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit London / UK: Month-by-Month Guide
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit London / UK is May to September — warm, dry weather, 16-hour days and a packed festival calendar. Here's our month-by-month guide.
guides.author: Suraj Giri
guides.content:
The best time to visit London / UK is May to September

The single best window to visit London and the wider UK is May through September, when days are long, rainfall stays relatively low, and the festival calendar is at its fullest. Within that window, July is the warmest and sunniest month by Met Office average — averaging a high of 23.9°C with around 218 hours of sunshine — while June to August is the undisputed peak season for crowds, prices and open-air events.

If you want the city at its most exciting and don't mind paying for it, aim for summer. If you'd rather trade a few degrees of warmth for thinner crowds and lower rates, the shoulder months of March–April and September–October are the smart compromise. November to February is cold, dark and damp, but it's when London's museums, galleries, theatres and cosy pubs come into their own — and it's the cheapest time to go outside the Christmas holidays.

One honest caveat that applies year-round: British weather is famously unpredictable, and the official tourism board advises packing warm layers and a waterproof jacket no matter when you visit. Treat the figures below as averages, not guarantees.

London month-by-month: weather, crowds, cost and events

Climate figures below are Met Office 30-year averages (1991–2020) for the London (Heathrow) climate station — the UK Met Office's reference station for the capital.

MonthHigh / Low (°C)Rain & sunCrowds & costWhat it's best for
Jan8 / 359 mm; 61 h sunLow crowds, low cost (except NYE)Museums, galleries, sales — quietest month
Feb9 / 345 mm; 79 h sunLow crowds, cheapestChinese New Year; cold, can snow, short days
Mar12 / 439 mm; 124 h sunLow–moderate, risingDriest month of the year; clocks go forward
Apr15 / 642 mm; 177 h sunModerate, warming upLondon Marathon; spring blooms in parks
May18 / 946 mm; 207 h sunModerate — shoulder sweet spotChelsea Flower Show; two bank holidays
Jun22 / 1247 mm; 208 h sunHigh, climbing to peakLight until ~10 pm; longest days of the year
Jul24 / 1446 mm; 218 h sunPeakWimbledon, Pride; warmest, sunniest month
Aug23 / 1453 mm; 202 h sunPeak — school holidaysNotting Hill Carnival; Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo
Sep20 / 1250 mm; 157 h sunModerate, cooling offOpen House Festival; locals back at school
Oct16 / 965 mm; 115 h sunLow–moderateAutumn colour; London Film Festival
Nov12 / 567 mm; 71 h sunLowWettest month; Guy Fawkes, Jazz Festival
Dec9 / 357 mm; 55 h sunMixed — high at ChristmasChristmas markets, ice rinks; only ~8 h daylight

Source: Met Office, London (Heathrow) long-term averages 1991–2020. Read across the table and a pattern jumps out: rainfall is lowest in spring (March is the driest month at ~39 mm) and highest in late autumn (November tops the year at ~67 mm), while sunshine peaks in July and collapses to a gloomy ~55 hours by December.

The seasons in detail

Summer (June–August): peak season

This is when London is at its most exciting — beer gardens overflow, parks fill up, and the city runs a relentless programme of open-air events. June brings long, warm days (it stays light until around 10 pm); July rolls out Wimbledon, Pride and warm temperatures; August closes summer with Notting Hill Carnival on the last weekend of the month. The trade-off is well documented: expect packed Tube trains on hot days and to pay the highest hotel rates of the year. For the UK beyond London, VisitBritain confirms summer is prime time for the coast, festivals and outdoor pursuits — Wimbledon, the British Grand Prix at Silverstone and (in 2026) the Glasgow Commonwealth Games all land in these months.

Spring (March–May) & Autumn (September–October): shoulder seasons

These are the best-value windows for travellers who want decent weather without the summer scrum. Spring is a delightful time to visit, with flowers blooming and the clocks going forward in late March — and crucially, it's the driest part of the year by Met Office averages. May's Chelsea Flower Show and two bank holidays make it a particular favourite. Autumn swings between dreary wet-and-windy days and crisp, bright sunshine over spectacular autumn foliage; September is quieter as local children head back to school, and the Open House Festival opens normally-closed buildings to the public.

Winter (November–February): dark, cold, cultural

Winter brings cold, wet and grey days that don't seem to last very long at all — the sun makes a fleeting appearance before slipping away mid-afternoon. In December you get only about eight hours of daylight (roughly 8 am to 4 pm), and February can bring snow that tends to bring the city's transport to a grinding halt. But the major sights stay open, making this the ideal season to work through London's world-class museums and galleries, catch West End theatre, and hunker down in a traditional pub. Christmas markets, ice rinks at Somerset House and the Natural History Museum, and the London Jazz Festival add seasonal sparkle.

Cheapest time to visit London / UK

The cheapest time to visit is January and February, when flights, hotels and attractions hit their lowest prices after the Christmas rush. Demand collapses, the weather is at its least appealing, and short daylight hours keep casual tourists away — which is exactly why bargains appear. Early March and late October–November also offer shoulder-season value with noticeably better conditions than midwinter. The one winter exception to avoid on a budget is mid-December through New Year, when Christmas markets and festivities push rates back up to near-summer levels.

Worst time to visit London / UK

“Worst” depends on what you hate more — cold and dark, or crowds and cost. For most visitors the worst weather window is November to February: it's cold, wet (November is the wettest month), and by December you're down to roughly eight hours of daylight. If you're here for sightseeing rather than cosy pubs and theatre, these short, grey days can feel limiting. On the other hand, if you can't stand crowds, peak summer (July–August) is the worst time for you — packed Tube trains, long attraction queues and peak pricing. The pragmatic middle path for most travellers is to avoid both extremes and aim for May, June or September.

Practical planning tips

  • Book early for summer and Christmas. June–August and mid-December are the two demand spikes; lock hotels and major attractions (Tower of London, Warner Bros. Studio Tour, West End shows) several weeks ahead. For a summer Europe loop, you might pair the trip with our best time to visit France or the best time to visit Amsterdam, both an easy train ride away.
  • Pack for four seasons in a day. VisitBritain's official guidance is blunt: bring warm clothing and a waterproof jacket or raincoat whenever you come, plus an umbrella. Even in July, evenings can be cool, and rain is possible in any month.
  • Mind the daylight. In June you'll have around 16 hours of usable daylight; in December, only about eight. Plan indoor activities (museums, galleries, shopping, afternoon tea) for winter afternoons when it gets dark by 4 pm.
  • Layer up on transport. Summer Tubes can be sweltering and un-air-conditioned; winter ones are overheated. Dress in layers you can shed.
  • Region matters. London and the South-East are the warmest, driest corner of the UK — the Met Office figures above reflect that. Head north to Scotland, or west to Wales and Cornwall, and expect cooler temperatures, more rain and (in summer) even longer daylight. If your trip extends into the Alps, see our best time to visit Switzerland for mountain-season timing.

The bottom line: for the classic London experience — long, bright days, parks in full swing and a full events calendar — target May to September, with July the warmest and sunniest single month. For value and elbow room without misery, choose May, June or September. And whenever you book, bring that waterproof.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Amsterdam / Netherlands: Month-by-Month
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Amsterdam is mid-April to May for tulips, or September for mild, crowd-light days. Our month-by-month guide covers weather, costs, and events.
guides.content:
When Is the Best Time to Visit Amsterdam?

The single best window is mid-April through May, when the tulip fields are at peak bloom, canal-side terraces reopen, and the weather turns mild without yet hitting peak-season prices. Right behind it is September, the sweet spot for travellers who want lingering summer warmth, thinner crowds, and a lively festival calendar. If you care about one thing only — flowers — aim for mid-April to early May, when both Keukenhof and the open bulb fields are in full colour.

Honestly, Amsterdam rewards a visit in almost any month: it never gets brutally hot, it rarely freezes hard, and its museum and café culture was built for damp days. The real trade-off is between weather, crowds, and cost — and those three rarely peak at the same time. Here is how to choose.

Amsterdam Weather at a Glance

The Netherlands has a mild maritime climate — moderately warm summers, cool winters, and humidity year-round. By the long-run KNMI climate normals for De Bilt (the country's reference station), July is the warmest month with an average high of about 23°C (74°F), while February is the coldest with an average low near 1°C (33°F). The key thing to know: rain falls in every season. The KNMI climate record shows that even the driest month, April, averages about 12 days of rain and roughly 42 mm of precipitation, while July is the wettest month at around 85 mm, with the damp autumn months (October to December) close behind. Pack a raincoat and waterproof shoes no matter when you come — as the Dutch say, there is no bad weather, only unsuitable clothing.

Amsterdam Month-by-Month Guide

(70 / 51°F)		Warm; longest days of the year; Holland Festival beginsPeak season starts; queues at top sights grow

(44 / 36°F)		Light Festival; Christmas markets; ice rinks; canals lit with fairy lightsCold; short days (~55 sunshine hours); rain or slush over snow

The Cheapest Time to Visit Amsterdam

February is typically the cheapest month to visit Amsterdam — it falls in the quiet window just before tulip season kicks off, so hotels and flights drop to their lowest levels and the major museums are at their emptiest. January is close behind, and both months reward bargain hunters who do not mind cold, grey weather. October through March (skipping the festive spike around late December) is the broad budget corridor, with the official tourism board confirming autumn and winter as the “less busy” seasons. If you want low prices and tolerable weather, the value picks are March (before the bloom rush) and October, when you trade a little warmth for big savings and far shorter queues.

The Worst Time to Visit Amsterdam

There is no genuinely bad time, so this comes down to what you dislike most. If you hate cold, darkness, and grey skies, avoid November — it is the low point for sunshine and atmosphere, with few festivals to compensate, though it is cheap and uncrowded. If you hate queues and high prices, the worst window is July and August, when Amsterdam is at peak season: accommodation tops out, sight lines at the Anne Frank Huis and Van Gogh Museum get long, and the canals are at their busiest. The summer crowds are manageable with early booking, but travellers seeking a calmer, more affordable trip should steer around both shoulders of peak summer.

Practical Planning Tips

Book the big sights early

In peak season (June–September), reserve timed slots at the Anne Frank Huis and Van Gogh Museum at least six weeks ahead, and book popular restaurants about two weeks out. These sell out — planning ahead is non-negotiable in summer.

Time the tulips

Tulip season runs roughly mid-March to mid-May; Keukenhof, the famous spring garden in Lisse, opens for about eight weeks within that window (in 2026 it ran March 19 to May 10). For the open fields at their most colourful, target mid-April to early May. Blooms are weather-dependent, so check current field reports before you lock dates.

What to pack

Layers and a raincoat, always. Even in summer, Dutch weather is notoriously fickle and chilly spells happen — a light jacket and compact umbrella keep you prepared without marking you as a tourist. In winter, expect around 3°C (37°F) on average; bring a warm coat, scarf, and waterproof shoes rather than counting on snow, which rarely settles.

Region nuance

Coastal areas like Zeeland and the Wadden Islands get the best summer sun and more moderate temperatures than inland Amsterdam, while the bulb region (the Bollenstreek around Lisse) is the tulip epicentre. Sea temperatures range from about 5°C in winter to around 18°C in summer — warm enough for a North Sea dip only in high summer.

The Verdict

For most travellers, the answer is mid-April to May (for tulips and King's Day) or September (for mild, crowd-light days). Choose February for the lowest prices, July–August if you want the warmest weather and biggest festival energy and do not mind paying for it, and December if you want fairy-lit canals and ice rinks at a fraction of the summer cost. Wherever you go next, Amsterdam pairs neatly with our guides to the best time to visit London and best time to visit France for a wider European spring, or — if you are chasing sun after a grey Dutch winter — the best time to visit Spain and best time to visit Greece.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Thailand: Month-by-Month Guide
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Thailand is November to February, the cool, dry season with ideal beach weather. Here's a month-by-month guide to weather, costs & crowds.
guides.content:
The Best Time to Visit Thailand Is November to February

The single best window to visit Thailand is the cool, dry season from November to February, when the country emerges from the monsoon and settles into its most comfortable weather of the year. Daytime highs hover around 28 to 31°C (82 to 88°F), humidity drops, and rain becomes rare across most of the country. It is peak season for a reason, and that reason is near-perfect conditions for beaches, temples, and mountain trekking alike.

Thailand's official tourism body describes the climate as three distinct seasons: six months of rainfall during the wet season, three months of "dry and cooling breezes" in winter, and three months of intense summer heat, with average temperatures across the country ranging from 18 to 38°C. December and January are the coolest, driest months, while November and February form the comfortable shoulders on either side. If you are weighing Thailand against another tropical Asian destination that follows a similar dry-season logic, see our best time to visit Bali.

One important caveat: "cool" is relative. In Bangkok, daytime temperatures during this season still climb above 30°C (86°F), and an occasional cold snap that drops the mercury to around 20°C (68°F) is enough to send locals into puffer jackets. Up north, in the mountains around Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai, nights can fall to a genuinely chilly 13°C (55°F), and frost occasionally dusts the high peaks. Still, if you want to go sightseeing without being drenched in sweat, this is the only reliable window.

Season & Months Weather Crowds & Cost Best For / Watch Out
Cool & Dry
(Nov–Feb)		 Highs 28–31°C; low humidity; little rain. Bangkok cold snaps to ~20°C; northern mountains drop to ~13°C at night. Peak crowds and the year's highest hotel and flight prices. Book months ahead for Christmas, New Year, and Chinese New Year. Best for beaches, temples, trekking, and festivals (Loi Krathong in November, Chinese New Year in February).
Hot
(Mar–May)		 Dry and increasingly scorching. Averages ~30°C; the north regularly hits 36°C (97°F), and Bangkok has reached 40°C (104°F) in recent years. Low season outside the Songkran holiday; good deals on hotels, especially in Bangkok, which empties out as families head home. Best for Songkran (Apr 13–15) and peak tropical fruit. Avoid if you are heat-sensitive.
Early Monsoon
(Jun–Aug)		 28–33°C with rising humidity; short, heavy showers (often 20–30 minutes in the early evening) rather than all-day rain. Shoulder crowds. The Andaman coast (Phuket, Krabi) is quiet and cheap; the Gulf islands (Ko Samui, Ko Phangan, Ko Tao) hit their own peak. Best for the Gulf islands, green countryside, and waterfall swimming.
Late Monsoon
(Sep–Oct)		 The rainiest months; the only time rain can persist all day. Temperatures ease slightly. The lowest crowds and prices of the year; no need to book ahead. Best for budget travel and the northeast's thundering waterfalls. Watch for flooding in the north and northeast, which can occasionally reach Bangkok.

Note on daylight: Because Thailand sits close to the equator, day length stays remarkably consistent at roughly 11.5 to 13 hours year-round, so the seasonal lever is temperature and rainfall, not daylight.

Cheapest Time and Worst Time

The cheapest time to visit is the late monsoon, from September to October. This is the quietest, least expensive stretch of the year, with no need to book hotels in advance and deep discounts across both beach and inland destinations. May through July offers a middle ground: the Andaman coast in particular is "basically deserted" on weekdays, and even five-star resorts rent choice rooms for a fraction of their high-season rates. Rains during this early monsoon are typically brief, so the trade-off is manageable. For the absolute lowest prices, target September and October, when tourism thins to its annual minimum.

The worst time to visit depends on what you can tolerate. If you are sensitive to heat, avoid March through May, the hottest months, when temperatures in Bangkok have recently sat at 40°C (104°F) for prolonged stretches and the north routinely reaches 36°C (97°F). If you want to dodge heavy rain and any risk of flooding, avoid September and October, the wettest months, when the northeast's rivers swell and water can occasionally reach riverside areas of Bangkok. For most travelers, the real "worst" is not a season but a mismatch: showing up in April expecting comfortable sightseeing, or arriving on the Andaman coast in August expecting wall-to-wall sunshine. Plan around your priority, whether that is beaches, festivals, or a bargain.

One piece of reassuring climate context: Thailand's position largely spares it the strong typhoons that batter Vietnam and the Philippines, so the monsoon is mostly a matter of downpours rather than dangerous storms.

Practical Planning Tips

Book early for the cool season

From late November through February, demand is fierce. Reserve popular hotels, guesthouses, and domestic flights well in advance, especially around Christmas, New Year, and Chinese New Year (usually February). For the rest of the year, you can largely show up and still find good deals.

Mind the regional nuance

Thailand's three seasons do not arrive identically everywhere. The Andaman coast (Phuket, Krabi, the Phi Phi islands) follows the classic monsoon pattern: ideal November to April, wet and cheap from May to October. The Gulf of Thailand islands (Ko Samui, Ko Phangan, Ko Tao) sit under a different weather microclimate and enjoy their own peak during July and August, when the Andaman side is being rained on, making them the smart pick for a European-summer holiday. The north (Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai, Pai) is coolest and best for trekking from November to February, with November's waterfalls at their fullest right after the rains. Bangkok is a year-round city, but its most pleasant weather aligns with the November-to-February window. For a comparable island-hopping trip with its own shoulder-season logic, see our best time to visit Greece.

What to pack

Pack light, breathable layers for any season, plus a light jacket or sweater for the cool season if you are heading north, where mountain nights genuinely drop into the low teens (°C). During the monsoon months, carry an umbrella or a lightweight rain shell and plan outdoor sightseeing for the morning, when showers are less likely. Modest covering (shoulders and knees) is expected at temples year-round.

Time your trip around a festival

Thailand's calendar is reason enough to pick a specific month. Loi Krathong, on the night of November's full moon, marks the end of the rainy season with floating lanterns and banana-leaf boats on rivers and canals. Songkran, the Thai New Year from April 13 to 15, turns the streets into a nationwide, joyful water fight. Chinese New Year, usually in February, lights up Bangkok's Chinatown with lion dances and feasts. If escaping the northern winter is your goal, the November-to-February window is the mirror image of the cold-season planning we cover in our best time to visit London.

Hedge your expectations

Even in the "best" months, a stray shower is possible, and even in the monsoon, you will see plenty of sun. Build a little flexibility into your itinerary, check forecasts from the Thai Meteorological Department before you go, and you will find Thailand rewarding in virtually every season for a traveler who arrives prepared.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit Bali (Indonesia): Month-by-Month Guide
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit Bali (Indonesia) is May to July—dry, sunny and pleasant. Here's a month-by-month breakdown of weather, crowds, surf and prices.
guides.content:
The short answer: aim for May to July

The single best time to visit Bali (Indonesia) is the dry-season window of May to July, when humidity eases, rainfall turns scarce, skies stay clear, and the peak European and Australian school-holiday crowds are only just building (they land in force in July and August). The broader dry season runs from April to October, and almost any month in that stretch will hand you warm, sunny days — but May, June and July offer the best balance of reliable weather, comfortable temperatures and still-manageable crowds. Bali sits just 8 degrees south of the equator, so Indonesia's official tourism board describes the climate as tropical, with just two seasons, Dry and Rainy, and high humidity year-round. Temperatures hardly move from month to month, hovering between 28°C and 32°C (82–90°F) year-round, though it is noticeably cooler up in the central mountains.

In other words, Bali never really gets cold — it only gets wetter or drier. That makes it a genuinely year-round destination, and the “best” month depends less on thermometers than on what you want to do, how much you want to pay, and how many other tourists you are willing to share the island with. If you are mapping a wider Southeast Asia loop, it pairs neatly with our guide to the best time to visit Thailand, whose dry season broadly mirrors Bali's.

Bali's seasons at a glance

Bali has two dominant seasons driven by the monsoon:

  • Dry season (April–October): Southeast monsoon, low rainfall, lower humidity; the peak travel window (July–August) falls within it.
  • Wet season (November–March): Northwest monsoon, heavy (usually short) downpours, high humidity, the cheapest and quietest time to visit.

Because Bali is so close to the equator, daylight stays close to 12 hours all year (roughly 6am sunrise to 6pm sunset), so you never lose the long evenings that plague higher-latitude winters — a real advantage over European summer destinations like the Greek islands or Italy in the off season.

Month-by-month table

Monthly averages below are drawn from long-run Bali climate data; temperatures are monthly means and rainfall is total precipitation. Use them as a planning guide, not a forecast — tropical weather is variable and the monsoon can shift by a couple of weeks either way.

MonthAvg tempRainfallSeason & what to expect
January27.8°C350 mm (19 rain days)Wet peak. The wettest month. Hot, humid, frequent heavy showers, but they often pass quickly. Cheapest prices, fewest crowds. Decent east-coast surf.
February27.9°C280 mm (18 rain days)Wet. Still very rainy. Low season continues; great hotel deals. Chinese New Year (Jan/Feb) brings a short busy spell.
March27.9°C215 mm (20 rain days)Wet, transitioning. Rains begin to ease. Nyepi (Balinese New Year) usually falls in March — see the warning below.
April28.0°C90 mm (12 rain days)Dry season begins. A shoulder-month sweet spot: drier, greener scenery, fewer crowds. Easter can briefly spike demand.
May27.6°C75 mm (8 rain days)Ideal. One of the best months — dry, sunny, pleasant, and west-coast surf season swings into gear. Great value before summer peaks.
June27.0°C70 mm (7 rain days)Ideal. Excellent weather, lower humidity, prime hiking, rafting and west-coast surfing. Crowds building but not yet at maximum.
July26.5°C50 mm (4 rain days)Ideal but busy. Cool, dry, sunny. Peak surf on the west coast (Canggu, Seminyak). Highest crowds and prices as Australian/European holidays hit.
August26.4°C15 mm (3 rain days)Driest month. Statistically the least rain and most sunshine. Indonesia's Independence Day (Aug 17) brings parades. Peak crowds and prices.
September26.8°C40 mm (3 rain days)Shoulder gem. Still dry and sunny as crowds thin — arguably the best value-for-weather month of the year.
October27.7°C90 mm (6 rain days)Shoulder, turning wet. Showers return but sunshine persists. The Ubud Writers & Readers Festival draws a cultured crowd.
November28.3°C150 mm (10 rain days)Wet season returns. Rainfall climbs, humidity rises. Low-season pricing kicks in; a quieter, budget-friendly choice.
December28.0°C290 mm (16 rain days)Wet, with a festive spike. Warm but showery. Christmas/New Year brings a big, pricey influx of visitors escaping the northern winter.

Across the year Bali receives roughly 1,715 mm of rain over about 126 rainy days, with humidity sitting between 77% and 82% — highest in the wet months, most comfortable from June to September.

Cheapest time and worst time

The cheapest time to visit Bali is the wet-season low season — January to March, plus November. According to Lonely Planet, these months make up Bali's low season: the rain scares most crowds home, the island takes on a more relaxed vibe, and hotels and flights drop to their lowest rates. Downpours can be heavy, but Bali's tropical rain usually does not last all day, and the east coast still serves up decent surf at spots like Sanur. If you prioritize budget over guaranteed sunshine, this is your window.

The worst time to visit Bali depends on your tolerance. If you hate rain and humidity, January and February are the toughest months — the wettest, muggiest and least predictable, with 280–350 mm of rain each and 18–19 rainy days. If your priority is avoiding crowds and high prices instead, the peak of July, August and the Christmas/New Year period in December is when the island is most packed and most expensive, with flights, hotels and headline spots like Kuta at their most congested.

There is one date-specific caveat that outranks the weather: Nyepi, the Balinese Day of Silence. Falling in March (its exact date follows the lunar saka calendar and changes each year), Nyepi is a sacred day on which the entire island shuts down — no flights, no transport, no beaches, no lights, and everyone stays indoors. Both Indonesia's official tourism authority and travel experts note that Ngurah Rai International Airport closes for 24 hours. The night before is spectacular, with loud parades of ogoh-ogoh demon puppets, but if your itinerary lands on Nyepi itself, plan to stay put at your hotel and embrace the stillness — or simply check the date and route around it.

Practical planning tips

Book early for the peak window. If you are targeting July, August or the festive fortnight around New Year, lock in flights and accommodation months ahead — this is when demand from Europe, Australia and North America converges on the island, and the best-value villas in Seminyak, Canggu and Ubud go early.

Chase the shoulder months for the best deal. April–June and September–October give you most of the dry season's sunshine at a fraction of the peak-season cost, with noticeably thinner crowds. September in particular is a connoisseur's pick: dry, sunny, and quietening down.

Pack for heat, humidity and the occasional downpour. Lightweight, breathable clothing is essential year-round; add a light rain jacket or compact umbrella if you are visiting between November and March. The sun is strong — reef-safe sunscreen, a hat and a refillable water bottle matter in every season. If you plan to visit the central mountains (Mount Batur, Mount Agung, the Kintamani area), pack a warm layer: Mount Agung rises above 3,000 metres (3,031 m) and temperatures up high are considerably cooler and wetter than on the coast.

Match your surf to the coast. Bali's wave quality flips with the monsoon. The west and south coasts — Canggu, Seminyak, Uluwatu — fire during the dry season (roughly May–September), with the best, most consistent swell from June to August. In the wet season, winds swing and the east coast comes into its own, with spots such as Sanur offering rideable waves when the west coast is onshore. Water temperatures stay warm (around 27–29°C) all year, so no wetsuit is needed.

Mind the region nuance. Bali's south (Kuta, Seminyak, Nusa Dua, Uluwatu) and the east coast (Sanur, Candidasa) stay drier for longer than the mountainous centre and north. The area around the central volcanoes receives considerably more rainfall than the coast, so a sunny day in Seminyak can still mean a soggy afternoon in Munduk or Bedugul. For the nearby Nusa Islands (Nusa Penida, Nusa Lembongan), calm dry-season seas make crossings and diving far more pleasant than during the rougher wet months.

Don't fear the wet season entirely. Bali is close enough to the equator that fully formed tropical cyclones rarely reach the island, so the wet season is more about heavy rain than dangerous storms. Showers tend to be intense but short, often arriving in the late afternoon or overnight and leaving sunny mornings behind. With the right expectations — and far lower prices — the wet months can be a genuinely rewarding time to explore temples, rice terraces and waterfalls with fewer people around.

The bottom line

For the classic Bali experience — blue skies, dry trails, prime surf and comfortable evenings — May, June and July are the sweet spot, with September as the smart value pick and April and October as agreeable shoulder months. Come in the wet season (November–March) if you want the lowest prices and fewest crowds and don't mind some rain. Whenever you go, temperatures stay in the high-20s to low-30s Celsius, the days run close to 12 hours of daylight, and the island's beaches, temples and rice terraces are waiting.

guides.title: Best Time to Visit New York City: Month-by-Month Guide
guides.author: Suraj Giri
guides.excerpt: The best time to visit New York City is mid-April to early June and September to October—mild, scenic, and event-packed. Here's how to pick the right month.

sources.author: NYC Tourism + Conventions
sources.title: Weather and Climate

sources.author: Lonely Planet (Healy, B.)
sources.title: The best time to visit New York City in 2026

sources.author: NOAA / National Weather Service New York (OKX)
sources.title: Normals and Extremes, Central Park, NY (1991–2020 normals)

sources.title: Average Monthly & Annual Temperatures at Central Park

sources.title: Tropical Cyclone Climatology — Atlantic Hurricane Season

guides.content:
The best time to visit New York City is mid-April to early June, and again from September to mid-October

The single best window to visit New York City is mid-April through early June, with a near-equally-great second window in September and October. During these months you get mild, mostly dry weather, long daylight hours, and the full lineup of outdoor dining, park life, and cultural events—without the wilting humidity of high summer or the hotel-price spikes of the December holidays. Lonely Planet singles out late April to early June and late September to mid-October as the best stretches for weather, and calls May “perhaps the best month for New York City weather.”

That said, New York is genuinely a year-round city—there is no month when the museums, Broadway, restaurants, and energy shut down. The trade-offs are real, though: summer is hot and expensive, winter is cold and festive, and early spring can swing between T-shirt and parka in the same week. Below is how the twelve months actually stack up, using 1991–2020 climate normals recorded at Central Park by the National Weather Service, then a breakdown of the cheapest and worst times to go.

New York City month-by-month: weather, crowds, cost, and events

Temperatures below are the 30-year average daily high / low in °F for Central Park (NOAA/NWS, 1991–2020 normals). Precipitation is the monthly average in inches.

MonthAvg high / low (°F)Why go (pros)Trade-offs (cons)
Jan39° / 28°Cheapest hotels after the 1st; New York Fashion Week; Lunar New Year in Chinatown; ice skating at Rockefeller Center & Bryant ParkCold and dark (sunset ~5pm); occasional snowstorms; Christmas/New Year rates still high early in the month
Feb42° / 30°Lowest crowds and prices of the year; Fashion Week; cozy bars and bistros at their bestColdest-feeling month; below-freezing days; risk of blizzards (~10″ of snow falls on average)
Mar50° / 36°St. Patrick’s Day Parade; spring starts stirring; still-affordable; ~4.3″ rain keeps numbers downUnpredictable—can be balmy or wintry in the same week; trees still bare
Apr62° / 46°Cherry blossoms in Central Park, Brooklyn Botanic Garden & Roosevelt Island; outdoor dining reopens; mild and uncrowdedSome rainy, cool days; Broadway still in pre-Tony warm-up
May71° / 55°The peak-value month—warm, low humidity, Fleet Week, new Broadway shows ahead of the Tonys; long daylightHotel prices begin climbing toward summer; a rainy day possible (~4″ monthly)
Jun80° / 64°Pride March; Puerto Rican Day Parade; outdoor movies and SummerStage; warm eveningsHumidity and hotel rates both rising; the first sticky, muggy days arrive late in the month
Jul85° / 70°Macy’s Fourth of July Fireworks; free Shakespeare in the Park; beach weather at Coney IslandHottest month and most humid; highest hotel prices of the year; thickest tourist crowds
Aug83° / 69°US Open tennis begins late month; locals escape to beaches, leaving some neighborhoods quieterPeak heat-island humidity between the skyscrapers; storms possible; expensive
Sep76° / 62°Start of the best second window—warm but cooling; West Indian American Day Parade; Feast of San Gennaro; Broadway reopens en masse after Labor DayPeak Atlantic hurricane activity—NYC can feel storm remnants; first few days still humid
Oct65° / 51°Fall foliage peaks in city parks; Comic Con; Open House New York; Village Halloween Parade; crisp and scenic—Lonely Planet calls October one of the most pleasant monthsHotel rates stay near summer levels; a tropical-remnant rainy day still possible early month
Nov54° / 42°NYC Marathon; Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade; holiday windows start going up; prices dip slightlyDaylight shrinking fast (sunset ~4:30pm by month’s end); noticeably colder; grey days
Dec44° / 34°Holiday magic—Rockefeller Center tree lighting, Bryant Park market, Fifth Avenue window displays; rare early snow (~5″ on average)Cold and crowded; hotel prices “skyrocket to summertime levels” for the holidays; short days

The cheapest time to visit New York City

The cheapest time to visit New York City is January through early March, excluding holiday weekends and major events. Once the Christmas and New Year rush clears, hotel rates drop to their lowest point of the year—Lonely Planet notes that prices “skyrocket over Christmas, but you’re likely to find a bargain from early January,” and that winter’s “long, cold months of January and February” are exactly when deals appear. The official NYC tourism board confirms winter is “cold and sometimes snowy with less daylight,” which is precisely why fewer tourists compete for rooms.

Two caveats: avoid the Martin Luther King Jr. and Presidents’ Day long weekends, and avoid the week of New York Fashion Week, when industry visitors fill midtown. Early March is similarly affordable and slightly less brutal weather-wise. A secondary value pocket exists in late April and early November, when spring and fall demand haven’t fully peaked but the weather is far kinder than in deep winter.

The worst time to visit New York City

There’s no month when New York is unvisitable, but the least rewarding stretch for most travelers is late July through mid-August. Highs average around 85°F (29°C) in July, but the urban heat island traps humidity between the buildings, making it feel far hotter; July also averages the most precipitation of any month (~4.6″) and the highest hotel rates and tourist crowds of the year. If you’re sensitive to heat or traveling on a budget, this is the window to skip.

The other honest caveat is tropical weather in September and early October. The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs June 1 through November 30, according to NOAA, and NYC’s official tourism board notes the city is “occasionally hit by Atlantic storms (primarily August to early November), but direct hits from major hurricanes like Superstorm Sandy in 2012 are rare.” Translation: a direct strike is unlikely, but a rainy, windy day or two from a storm’s remnants is a real possibility in early fall—worth checking the forecast, not a reason to cancel.

What to pack and how to plan your trip

Pack in layers, always. NYC weather “can vary from day to day, and even hour to hour,” per the city’s tourism board. In spring and fall, a light jacket or fleece over short sleeves is the universal uniform; add a compact umbrella (April, July, and August each average over 4″ of rain). Summer demands breathable fabrics, sunscreen, and a refillable water bottle—subway platforms can hit 100°F (38°C) even when street-level air is merely warm. Winter requires a real coat, gloves, a hat, and waterproof boots; average annual snowfall at Central Park is about 29.8″, with January (8.8″) and February (10.1″) the snowiest months.

Book ahead for peak windows. Hotel inventory tightens dramatically around the holidays (mid-December), the NYC Marathon (first Sunday of November), Pride (late June), and the US Open (late August). For these, reserve 3–4 months out. For the cheaper January–February window, you can often book 4–6 weeks ahead and still find good rates. Broadway tickets, museum timed-entry passes, and popular restaurant reservations should be locked in early no matter the season.

Mind the region. Manhattan’s midtown core runs hotter than the boroughs thanks to concrete and glass, while waterfront areas in Brooklyn and Queens (Coney Island, Rockaway) catch cooling breezes in summer and bite colder in winter. Central Park is often a few degrees cooler than surrounding streets in summer and a few degrees colder on calm winter nights. If you’re pairing NYC with a European city break, our guide to the best time to visit London shares the same shoulder-season logic, and Italy’s timing windows line up almost perfectly with New York’s for a transatlantic spring or fall trip.

The bottom line

For the best balance of weather, scenery, events, and value, aim for mid-April to early June (peak in May) or September to October (peak in October for fall color). Chase deals in January and February, embrace the festive chaos of December if holiday magic is the goal, and only brave July and August if free outdoor concerts, beach days, and steamy sidewalk energy are exactly what you came for.

guides.title: How Long Do Snakes Live? Lifespan by Species & Care Tips
guides.excerpt: Pet snakes live 10-30+ years by species: corn snakes ~15-20, ball pythons 20-30, boas 25-35. Learn what affects snake lifespan and how to help yours live longer.
guides.content:
How Long Do Snakes Live? The Quick Answer

Most pet snakes live 10 to 30+ years, with popular beginner species averaging roughly 15–25 years in good captivity. Small, fast-maturing colubrids such as garter snakes sit at the lower end (around a decade), while boas and pythons routinely reach 25–35 years and occasionally more. That makes a snake a genuinely long commitment—longer than a rabbit or a hamster, and on a similar scale of years to a well-cared-for house cat, scaled up well beyond the life of a betta fish.

Every figure below traces back to a published source—chiefly the University of Michigan's Animal Diversity Web (ADW) for species longevity records and VCA Animal Hospitals for husbandry. Treat each number as a range rather than a promise: an individual snake's actual lifespan depends on species, genetics, and above all the quality of care it receives.

Snake Lifespan by Species

SpeciesTypical captive lifespanDocumented recordNotes
Corn snake (Pantherophis guttatus)~15–20 years32.3 yearsHardy, forgiving beginner snake
Ball python (Python regius)~20–30 years~50 yearsLong-lived; the most popular pet python
Common kingsnake (Lampropeltis getula)~15–20 years33.3 yearsDocile, robust colubrid
Boa constrictor (Boa constrictor)25–35 years40 yearsLarge snake; captives outlive wild ones by 10–15 years
Garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis)~6–10 years20 yearsSmall and short-lived by snake standards

Longevity records from the Animal Diversity Web (ADW), University of Michigan Museum of Zoology. The pattern is clear: boas and pythons generally outlive colubrids, and captives of nearly every species outlive their wild counterparts—sometimes by a very wide margin.

Wild vs. Captivity: Why Pet Snakes Live Longer

In the wild, most snakes face heavy mortality early in life. Garter snakes, for instance, average only about 2 years in the wild, with most individuals dying in their first year; boas average roughly 20 years in the wild versus 25–35 in captivity. The reasons are familiar—predation, disease, starvation, drought, and winter-kill are all but absent in a well-run terrarium. ADW notes that wild longevity data for corn snakes is sparse precisely because predation and disease make wild lifespans so much shorter than captive ones. Captivity removes those pressures, which is why the single biggest determinant of your snake's lifespan is the environment you build for it.

Factors That Affect a Snake's Lifespan

Husbandry: temperature, humidity, and enclosure

Snakes are ectothermic—they depend on their surroundings to regulate body temperature, digestion, and immune function. VCA Animal Hospitals recommend a heat gradient in every enclosure: a cooler end around 70–75°F (21–24°C), a warm basking end of 90–95°F (32–38°C), and an overnight drop to roughly 65–70°F (18–21°C), monitored with thermometers at both ends. Without that gradient a snake cannot digest properly, mount an immune response, or behave normally. Humidity matters just as much: most species do well at 40–70% humidity, which keeps them hydrated and allows them to shed in one clean piece. Poor or fragmented sheds (dysecdysis) are an early warning sign that temperature or humidity is off.

Diet and feeding

Captive snakes do best on whole dead prey—typically mice or rats sized to the snake's girth. VCA specifically warns against live rodents: even a small bite from a mouse can cause a severe, potentially life-threatening infection. Whole prey is nutritionally complete, so vitamin supplements are rarely required. Feeding frequency runs roughly twice a week for growing juveniles and weekly to biweekly for mature adults. Persistent refusal of food (anorexia) can signal stress, wrong temperatures, shedding, or serious illness—including kidney failure, intestinal parasites, or viral infection—any of which can shorten life if ignored.

Genetics and species

Some of the lifespan gap is simply built in. A ball python's biology lets it routinely reach 20–30 years; a garter snake's does not. Within a species, heavily line-bred color morphs can carry weaker immune systems or congenital defects, so choosing a healthy, ethically bred animal matters as much as choosing the right species.

Enclosure safety and cleanliness

Waste should be removed every 24–72 hours and the cage fully washed weekly. VCA lists newspaper, paper towels, and artificial turf as safe substrates and warns that cedar shavings are toxic to reptiles; sand, gravel, corncob, and wood shavings carry impaction risk if swallowed. So-called "hot rocks" or "sizzle rocks" are both ineffective and dangerous as heat sources and should be avoided.

Common health problems that shorten life

The conditions most likely to cut a captive snake's life short are preventable: respiratory infections (often from cool, dry, or drafty conditions), external parasites such as snake mites, intestinal worms, and—especially in boids—inclusion body disease, a fatal viral illness that quarantine is designed to keep out of a collection. Egg-binding (dystocia) in breeding females is another life-threatening emergency. The common thread is that nearly all of these are caught early by an observant keeper working with a reptile veterinarian.

Snake Life Stages

A snake's life moves through several broad stages, and the care emphasis shifts at each:

  • Egg. Most pet species are oviparous (egg-laying), though boas and garter snakes give live birth. Incubation runs from several weeks to a few months depending on species and temperature.
  • Hatchling or neonate. The most fragile stage. The first shed and first meals are critical milestones, and husbandry errors here are often fatal.
  • Juvenile. A period of rapid growth and frequent feeding, when most of the animal's adult size is put on.
  • Adult. Sexual maturity arrives anywhere from 1–5 years depending on species (garter snakes mature at roughly 3–4 years; large pythons later). Feeding slows and stability becomes the priority.
  • Senior. Older snakes may eat less, shed less cleanly, and become less active. Lower perches, gentler handling, and closer health monitoring all help.

How to Help Your Snake Live Longer

Most of longevity is simply consistent, species-appropriate husbandry sustained over years. The checklist that moves the needle most:

  • Build a proper heat gradient with thermometers at both ends—70–75°F cool, 90–95°F warm—and a modest overnight drop.
  • Hold humidity in the species' range (often 40–70%) using a large water bowl that also supports healthy shedding.
  • Feed whole, frozen-thawed prey of the right size on an age-appropriate schedule; never leave live rodents unattended with the snake.
  • Use safe substrate (paper, towels, reptile carpet) and keep the enclosure clean—daily waste removal, weekly wash.
  • Provide hides and secure climbing branches so the snake can thermoregulate and feel secure; chronic stress suppresses immunity.
  • Quarantine every new arrival to avoid introducing mites or infectious disease into an established collection.
  • Find a reptile veterinarian before you need one. Persistent anorexia, wheezing, bubbles from the nose, swellings, or stuck sheds are all reasons to book an exam promptly.

Done well, this care routinely lands snakes in the upper end of their species' range—and sometimes well beyond it. The documented captive records—a 32-year corn snake, a roughly 50-year ball python, a 40-year boa—were all animals living in controlled, consistent environments. There is no secret to a long-lived snake; there is only steady, correct care sustained for decades.

Health note: This is general husbandry information, not veterinary advice; for any health concern, consult a licensed veterinarian who treats reptiles. Signs of a sick snake—open-mouth breathing, wheezing or nasal bubbles, prolonged anorexia, abnormal feces, swelling, or repeated poor sheds—warrant prompt evaluation. Seek emergency care immediately if a snake is gasping/open-mouth breathing continuously, weak or flaccid, twisted/abnormal posture, severely bloated, or non-responsive.
