guides.title: How Long Does a Cold Last? Timeline, Stages & Recovery
guides.excerpt: A common cold lasts 7 to 10 days, with the first symptoms appearing around days 1 to 3 and symptoms often peaking around days 4 to 7. Learn the cold stages, how long it stays contagious, and when to see a doctor.
guides.content:
How Long Does a Cold Last?

A common cold lasts 7 to 10 days in most adults and older children, with the first symptoms usually appearing within 1 to 3 days of catching the virus and symptoms often peaking around days 4 to 7 before gradually easing. The Cleveland Clinic and MedlinePlus (NIH) place typical recovery at about a week to 10 days, while the Merck Manual notes that symptoms usually resolve within 10 days. A nagging cough can linger into the second week, and in some cases a post-cold cough hangs on for several weeks after the rest of the illness has cleared.

Most colds are caused by viruses — rhinoviruses are the most common culprit — and more than 200 different viruses can trigger one. Because colds are viral, they follow a predictable course that medication can ease but not shorten. Below is a day-by-day look at what to expect, when you are most likely to pass the cold on, and which symptoms mean it is time to call a doctor.

The Timeline: Cold Stages, Day by Day

The Cleveland Clinic describes the common cold in three stages — early, active, and late — and notes that the first symptoms typically appear within one to three days of picking up the virus. Here is how a typical cold unfolds:

StageTimingWhat happensTypical symptoms
Incubation 12 hrs – 3 days after exposure The virus enters your nose, eyes, or mouth; no symptoms yet, but you may already be contagious. None
Stage 1 — Early Days 1–3 First symptoms appear; this is when you are most contagious. Tickle or sore throat, sneezing, runny or stuffy nose, mild cough, hoarseness
Stage 2 — Active / Peak Days 4–7 Symptoms are at their worst; the Cleveland Clinic says symptoms typically peak during this stage. Body aches, headache, fatigue, watery eyes, low-grade fever (more common in children)
Stage 3 — Late Days 8–10 Symptoms wind down; most people feel largely recovered. Fading congestion; a lingering cough is common
Post-cold cough Up to 2 weeks (sometimes longer) A dry, nagging cough can outlast the cold itself. Cough only; otherwise feeling well

A few details are worth knowing. The Merck Manual notes that symptoms usually “disappear within 10 days,” although the cough “often lasts” into a second week, and the Cleveland Clinic adds that a nagging cough can sometimes persist for weeks after a respiratory infection. One common worry — nasal mucus that turns thick and yellow or green — is normal and, on its own, does not mean you have a bacterial infection.

When It Is Contagious

Yes, the common cold is contagious, and you can spread it before you even know you are sick. The Cleveland Clinic reports that you can be contagious for up to two weeks, including a day or two before symptoms appear, but you are “most contagious when your symptoms are at their worst — usually the first three days you feel sick.” MedlinePlus similarly notes that people are “most contagious for the first 2 to 3 days” and that a cold is most often not contagious after the first week. The Merck Manual adds that a cold is “most contagious during the first 1 or 2 days after symptoms develop.”

Cold viruses spread mainly through respiratory droplets released when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks, and by touching contaminated surfaces and then touching your eyes, nose, or mouth. Practical steps to limit spread:

  • Wash hands often with soap and water for at least 20 seconds.
  • Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or the bend of your elbow.
  • Stay home from work or school, especially during the first few days.
  • Avoid sharing cups, utensils, and towels.

When a cough or sore throat leaves you unsure whether it is a simple cold or something else, it helps to compare: a cold is usually milder and slower-moving than the flu or strep throat, both of which tend to bring higher fever and more abrupt, intense symptoms.

When to See a Doctor or Seek Emergency Care

Most colds resolve on their own, but certain signs mean you should contact a healthcare provider — and a few warrant urgent or emergency care. The red flags below are drawn from the CDC, the Cleveland Clinic, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), and MedlinePlus.

See a doctor for an adult if you have:

  • Symptoms that last more than 10 days without improvement, or that get worse.
  • A high fever, or a fever that lasts longer than four days (CDC).
  • A fever that returns after a fever-free period.
  • Shortness of breath or wheezing.
  • Chest pain, ear pain, or an asthma flare-up.

Get medical care right away for a child or baby if they have:

  • Any fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in an infant younger than 3 months (12 weeks) (AAP — call your pediatrician immediately).
  • A fever lasting more than 24 hours in a child under 2, or more than 3 days in a child 2 or older (AAP).
  • Trouble breathing, fast or labored breathing, nostrils flaring with each breath, wheezing, or ribs showing with each breath.
  • Blue lips, or signs of dehydration such as not eating or drinking.
  • Ear pain, excessive crankiness or sleepiness, or a cough lasting more than three weeks.

Seek emergency or urgent care for anyone with:

The CDC lists these as reasons to seek care regardless of age:

  • Trouble breathing or fast breathing.
  • Dehydration.
  • A fever lasting longer than four days.
  • Symptoms that last more than 10 days without improving.
  • Symptoms (such as fever or cough) that improve and then return or worsen.
  • Chronic medical conditions, such as asthma, COPD, or heart disease, that get worse.

These warning signs can signal a complication. The Cleveland Clinic notes that colds can lead to ear infections, sinus infections, asthma flare-ups, bronchitis, or pneumonia. If your cold seems to settle in your chest or sinuses rather than clearing, read more about how long bronchitis lasts and how long a sinus infection lasts.

Treatment Context: What Helps (and What Doesn't)

There is no cure for the common cold, and no medication can shorten its 7-to-10-day course. The CDC is blunt: “Antibiotics don't work against viruses and won't help you feel better,” and taking them when you do not need them can cause side effects — from rash to severe allergic reactions, antimicrobial-resistant infections, and C. diff infection — without benefiting you. Thick or colored mucus alone is not a reason to take antibiotics. Antibiotics have a role only when a bacterial complication (such as an ear infection or bacterial pneumonia) develops on top of the cold.

What actually helps is symptom relief while your immune system clears the virus. The CDC describes these supportive measures:

  • Rest and plenty of fluids.
  • A clean humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer, and saline nasal spray or drops.
  • Steam from a bowl of hot water or a shower.
  • Over-the-counter pain relievers and fever reducers (such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for adults.
  • Throat lozenges or cough drops to soothe a sore throat.

Age limits matter a great deal. The CDC cautions that OTC cough and cold medicines are not recommended for children younger than 6 and can cause serious, sometimes life-threatening side effects — though young children can still take acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever at the correct dose. Lozenges should not be given to children under 4, and honey — which can ease a cough — is safe only for children at least 1 year old, because of the risk of infant botulism in babies under 12 months. The Merck Manual adds that aspirin should not be given to children or teens recovering from a viral illness, due to the risk of Reye syndrome.

Supplements like zinc, vitamin C, and echinacea are popular but not reliably effective. The Merck Manual notes that zinc may slightly shorten the duration of cold symptoms, and the Cleveland Clinic notes zinc may shorten the illness and reduce symptoms — but most experts do not recommend these supplements as treatment. Zinc nasal spray has been linked to permanent loss of smell, so it should be avoided.

One important exception: if your cold-like symptoms are actually COVID-19 or the flu, antiviral medications can help — but only if started early. The CDC recommends getting tested if you suspect either, especially if you are at higher risk of severe illness: COVID-19 treatment works best started within 5 to 7 days of symptoms, and flu treatment within 2 days.

The Bottom Line

A cold lasts about a week — plan for 7 to 10 days, expect to feel worst around days 4 to 7, and know that a cough may linger a little longer. Rest, fluids, and time do most of the work, and antibiotics will not help a viral illness. Watch for the red flags above, and contact a healthcare provider if your symptoms cross those lines.

This article is health information, not medical advice. It summarizes publicly available guidance from the CDC, the Cleveland Clinic, the Merck Manual, MedlinePlus (NIH), and the American Academy of Pediatrics. If you or your child are seriously ill — trouble breathing, a high or persistent fever, or symptoms that are getting worse — contact a healthcare provider or seek emergency care.

guides.title: How Long Does Strep Throat Last? Timeline & Treatment
guides.excerpt: Strep throat symptoms typically ease within about a week (5 to 7 days) even without antibiotics. Antibiotics ease symptoms within 24 to 48 hours and help prevent rheumatic fever — see a doctor for care.
guides.content:
How long does strep throat last?

Strep throat — a sore throat caused by group A Streptococcus (GAS) bacteria — typically lasts about a week (5 to 7 days) when left untreated, with the overall course sometimes extending toward 7 to 10 days. With the correct antibiotic, most people feel noticeably better within 1 to 2 days and are no longer contagious after roughly 24 hours of treatment.

Here is the part that matters most: antibiotics do two things that simply waiting cannot. They make you non-contagious quickly, and they prevent serious complications such as rheumatic fever and kidney inflammation. But they work only against bacterial strep — the majority of sore throats are viral, which is exactly why a throat swab should come before any prescription. The durations below are drawn from the CDC, Cleveland Clinic, the American Academy of Pediatrics, Nemours KidsHealth, the UK NHS, and the peer-reviewed StatPearls overview of group A strep pharyngitis.

Strep throat day-by-day timeline

StageWhat typically happensContagious?
Exposure (Day 0) Bacteria enter the throat. No symptoms yet. The incubation period lasts 2 to 5 days. Yes — you can spread it before symptoms appear.
Days 1–2 Symptoms come on suddenly: severe sore throat, pain when swallowing, fever, red and swollen tonsils, sometimes white patches or streaks of pus, tender swollen glands in the neck, and tiny red spots (petechiae) on the roof of the mouth. Headache and stomachache are common in children. Yes.
Days 2–3, untreated Symptoms peak. Fever and throat pain are usually at their worst, then gradually begin to ease. Yes.
Days 2–3, with antibiotics After the first dose, fever usually drops within about 12 to 24 hours and throat pain begins to ease by the second or third day. Antibiotics shorten overall symptom duration by roughly 16 to 24 hours. No — after 24 hours on antibiotics, once fever is gone.
Days 5–7 (up to 10), untreated Symptoms typically self-resolve within about a week (5 to 7 days), though the overall course can sometimes extend toward 7 to 10 days. Yes — you can remain contagious for up to 2 to 3 weeks without treatment.
Recovery Most people recover fully. Without antibiotics the body still has to clear the bacteria, and the risk of complications lingers for two to three weeks. —

Two practical clues help tell strep apart from a viral sore throat: a cough and runny nose are far more typical of a viral illness, while strep tends to strike quickly rather than build over several days. Strep is also most common in school-age children (ages 5 to 15) and spreads quickly through classrooms and households, though adults get it too; it is uncommon in children under 3. If those viral symptoms dominate instead, the illness is more likely to follow the curve of a common cold or the flu than a bacterial throat infection.

Clinicians often weigh a short set of signs — fever, swollen and tender neck glands, white patches or pus on the tonsils, and the absence of a cough — to estimate how likely strep is before swabbing. The more of these features that are present, especially in a child or teenager with a sudden sore throat, the more reasonable it is to get a test rather than wait it out. None of them alone is diagnostic, which is exactly why the swab, not the symptom pattern, decides whether antibiotics are appropriate.

When it is contagious

Strep throat is contagious from the moment the bacteria take hold — before any symptoms appear — and it stays contagious until the bacteria are cleared. The incubation window is 2 to 5 days after exposure, and an infected person can spread the bacteria for a few days before they feel ill. Some people carry group A strep in their throat without ever developing symptoms, yet they can still pass it to others.

How long you remain contagious depends almost entirely on whether you take antibiotics:

  • On antibiotics: you are generally no longer contagious after 24 hours of treatment, provided your symptoms are improving and your fever is gone. Some clinicians use a 12-to-48-hour window.
  • Without antibiotics: you can continue to spread strep for up to 2 to 3 weeks, even as you start to feel better.

The bacteria travel in respiratory droplets — coughs, sneezes, and shared saliva — and on contaminated hands, cups, and utensils. The main preventions are straightforward: wash hands often (for at least 20 seconds), avoid sharing food, drinks, toothbrushes, or utensils, and cover coughs and sneezes. Children can usually return to school, and adults to work, 24 hours after starting antibiotics and being fever-free.

When to see a doctor or seek emergency care

This is the section to act on if anything feels serious. Strep throat is usually manageable, but it can occasionally signal a more dangerous infection or a complication that needs urgent treatment. (The red-flag lists below are adapted from the NHS and the American Academy of Pediatrics.)

Get emergency care immediately (call your local emergency number — 911 in the US, 999 in the UK) if you or your child shows:

  • Difficulty breathing, pauses in breathing, or struggling to catch breath
  • Blue, grey, or pale skin, lips, or tongue
  • Inability to swallow saliva, with drooling (a possible sign of epiglottitis or a peritonsillar abscess)
  • Extreme drowsiness, floppiness, or inability to wake or stay awake
  • Severe dehydration — no urination, dry mouth, or no tears when crying
  • A stiff neck with fever, or a seizure

See a doctor the same day (urgent care or your clinician) for:

  • A sudden, severe sore throat with fever and swollen neck glands, especially with no cough
  • A sore throat lasting more than a few days, or a child who looks distinctly unwell
  • A rough, sandpaper-like rash spreading across the body (a sign of scarlet fever, which can accompany strep)
  • Fever that returns or worsens after you had started to improve
  • Painful or swollen joints, chest pain, shortness of breath, or dark, tea-colored urine — possible signs of rheumatic fever or kidney inflammation following strep

Follow up with your clinician if symptoms have not improved within 48 hours of starting antibiotics, or if new symptoms appear (earache, sinus pain, persistent fever, nausea, or vomiting). As a general rule, any sore throat that is severe, getting worse, or simply not resolving deserves professional evaluation rather than self-treatment — the same instinct that applies to lingering sinus infections or bronchitis.

Treatment context: why antibiotics matter (but only for bacterial strep)

Antibiotics help only against bacterial strep throat — they do nothing for the viral sore throats that cause most cases. That is why a clinician confirms the diagnosis with a throat swab before prescribing:

  • Rapid strep test (rapid antigen detection test): results in about 5 to 20 minutes. It is highly specific, though its sensitivity ranges from roughly 70% to 90%.
  • Throat culture: the laboratory gold standard, with results in 1 to 2 days. A negative rapid test in a child is usually backed up with a culture to be certain.

When strep is confirmed, the standard treatment is a 10-day course of an appropriate antibiotic — penicillin or amoxicillin are first-line, with alternatives such as cephalosporins, azithromycin, or clindamycin for people with a penicillin allergy. The aims are threefold:

  1. Shorten the illness — symptoms begin improving within a day or two, and overall duration is modestly reduced.
  2. Stop transmission — you become non-contagious about 24 hours after starting treatment.
  3. Prevent complications — this is the most important reason. Untreated strep can lead to acute rheumatic fever (which can damage the heart valves), post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (kidney inflammation), ear and sinus infections, peritonsillar abscess, scarlet fever, and, rarely, invasive infections. Rheumatic fever is now uncommon in the United States — and rare in children under 5 — but preventing it remains the central reason antibiotics are recommended.

Finish the entire course, even if you or your child feels completely well after a couple of days. Stopping early can allow the bacteria to persist and increases the risk of the very complications treatment is meant to prevent. For comfort while the antibiotic works, clinicians typically suggest rest, plenty of fluids, warm salt-water gargles, and over-the-counter pain or fever reducers used as a doctor or pharmacist advises. Do not give aspirin to children or teens, because it is linked to Reye syndrome, a rare but life-threatening condition.

If your symptoms point instead to a viral illness, both the timeline and the care differ: a viral sore throat tends to behave more like a cold, the flu, a sinus infection, or bronchitis than bacterial strep, and recovery from non-infectious injuries follows entirely different healing curves.

This article is health information, not medical advice. Duration, contagious periods, and warning signs vary from person to person. If you think you or your child may have strep throat — especially with any of the red-flag symptoms above — contact a doctor or seek emergency care rather than self-diagnosing or self-treating.

guides.title: How Long Does a Sinus Infection Last? Timeline & Stages
guides.excerpt: Acute viral sinus infections last 7–10 days; bacterial cases tend to last beyond 10 days, and chronic cases persist 12+ weeks. Here is the timeline, symptoms, and when to see a doctor.
guides.content:
How Long Does a Sinus Infection Last?

An acute sinus infection (sinusitis) caused by a virus typically lasts 7 to 10 days and most often develops on the heels of a common cold, clearing on its own without antibiotics. When symptoms drag on past 10 days without improvement — or get worse after they had started getting better — a bacterial infection may be to blame, and those cases can linger for weeks if left untreated. Sinusitis that persists for 12 weeks or longer despite medical treatment is classified as chronic sinusitis.

The CDC is blunt about the viral majority: "Most sinus infections usually get better on their own without antibiotics." Johns Hopkins adds that inflammation caused by a virus "may resolve in about 10 days and won't need antibiotics." In other words, the calendar — not a prescription — resolves most cases.

Sinus Infection Timeline: Stages and Durations

Doctors sort sinusitis into categories based on how long it lasts and how often it returns. The breakdown below draws on classifications from the Cleveland Clinic and MedlinePlus (NIH); exact cutoffs vary somewhat among medical references, and a few older sources use an 8-week threshold for chronic sinusitis rather than 12.

TypeDurationTypical causeWhat distinguishes it
Viral (acute)7–10 daysCold and flu virusesFollows a cold; clears without antibiotics
Bacterial (acute)More than 10 days, or worsens after initial improvementBacteriaOften called "double sickening"; antibiotics may help
Acute (overall)Up to 4 weeksVirus or bacteriaAll symptoms resolve within four weeks
Subacute4–12 weeksPersistent inflammationBridges the gap between acute and chronic
Chronic12 weeks or longerOften bacteria plus ongoing inflammationPersists despite treatment
Recurrent acute4 or more separate episodes per year, each under 2 weeksRepeated infectionsKeeps coming back as discrete bouts

A typical day-by-day arc of a viral case looks like this: days 1–3 bring escalating congestion, facial pressure, and postnasal drip (often layered on top of a fading cold); days 4–7 are the peak, with thick discharge and pressure that worsens when you bend forward; and days 8–10 mark a gradual easing as the immune system clears the virus. If day 10 arrives with no improvement — or you felt better on day 5 and worse again on day 7 — that pattern points toward a bacterial infection rather than a lingering virus.

Common Symptoms

The CDC, Cleveland Clinic, and Johns Hopkins describe a consistent symptom set. Most people experience several of the following:

  • Thick yellow or green mucus from the nose, or dripping down the back of the throat (postnasal drip)
  • A stuffy, congested nose that makes breathing through it difficult
  • Facial pain, pressure, or tenderness around the eyes, cheeks, nose, or forehead that worsens when bending over
  • Headache and aching in the upper teeth
  • Ear pressure or pain
  • Reduced sense of smell and taste
  • Cough (often worse at night), bad breath, tiredness, and low-grade fever

These overlap heavily with cold, flu, and allergy symptoms, which is why duration — not the symptom list alone — is the key clue to telling them apart. Note, too, that green or yellow mucus alone does not mean you have a bacterial infection or need antibiotics; many people recover fully without them.

When a Sinus Infection Is Contagious

Here is the reassuring part: sinusitis itself is not contagious. The Cleveland Clinic states it directly — "Sinusitis itself isn't contagious. But the viruses and bacteria that can cause it are." That distinction matters because most acute sinus infections begin as a viral cold, and the CDC confirms that viruses cause most sinus infections.

So while you cannot "catch" someone's sinus infection, you can catch the cold virus that triggered it. Those viruses spread through coughs, sneezes, unwashed hands, and shared surfaces. Cold viruses can spread from about a day before symptoms appear until symptoms clear. Practical prevention lines up with the CDC's guidance: wash your hands, avoid close contact with people who have colds, don't smoke or expose yourself to secondhand smoke, use a clean humidifier, and stay current with recommended vaccines like the flu and pneumococcal shots.

When to See a Doctor — and When It Is an Emergency

Most viral sinus infections can be managed at home, but certain signs mean it is time to call a healthcare provider, and a smaller set means go to the emergency room immediately.

See a healthcare provider if you have:

  • Symptoms that last more than 10 days without getting better (CDC)
  • Symptoms that get worse after they seemed to be improving — the pattern often called "double sickening" (CDC)
  • A fever that lasts longer than 3–4 days (CDC)
  • Severe symptoms, such as a severe headache or intense facial pain (CDC)
  • Multiple sinus infections in the past year, or a history of chronic sinusitis (CDC)

Go to the emergency room immediately if you have any of these red flags:

  • Swelling, redness, or pain around the eyes, or vision changes (Cleveland Clinic, Johns Hopkins)
  • A high fever — the Cleveland Clinic specifically flags fever over 103°F (40°C)
  • Confusion or other mental changes, or trouble thinking clearly (Cleveland Clinic, Johns Hopkins)
  • A stiff neck (Cleveland Clinic, Johns Hopkins)
  • Seizures (Cleveland Clinic)
  • Severe, intense facial pain or pressure, or shortness of breath (Johns Hopkins)

These can signal that infection has spread toward the brain, the tissues around the eye, or the membranes around the spinal cord — rare but serious complications that MedlinePlus (NIH) and Johns Hopkins describe as potentially life-threatening. They are medical emergencies, not wait-and-see situations.

Treatment Context: Rest, Relief, and Antibiotics

Because viruses cause most sinus infections, antibiotics are usually not part of the picture. The CDC is explicit that antibiotics "won't help you" when they are not needed, and their side effects — ranging from rash and digestive upset to severe allergic reactions, antibiotic-resistant infections, and C. diff colitis — can cause real harm.

For symptom relief while your body clears the virus, the CDC, Cleveland Clinic, and MedlinePlus describe several supportive measures:

  • Apply a warm compress over the nose and forehead to ease sinus pressure.
  • Use a saline nasal spray or rinse to flush mucus, or a decongestant spray for short-term relief (the ACAAI cautions against using decongestant sprays for more than 3–4 days to avoid rebound congestion; MedlinePlus likewise warns against use beyond 3–5 days).
  • Breathe steam from a bowl of hot water or a hot shower.
  • Drink plenty of fluids and rest, and use over-the-counter pain relievers as directed.

When a bacterial infection is likely — symptoms beyond 10 days, the double-sickening pattern, or persistent facial pain and fever — a clinician may prescribe antibiotics. In borderline cases the CDC describes watchful waiting (waiting 2–3 days to see if you recover on your own) or delayed prescribing (leaving a prescription to fill only if symptoms do not improve). Chronic sinusitis often needs a longer view, sometimes including prescription steroid nasal sprays, evaluation by an allergist or ear-nose-throat specialist, and — when structural problems like polyps or a deviated septum are involved — surgery.

One important note for families: the CDC advises against giving over-the-counter cough and cold medicines to children under 4, and cautions never to give aspirin to children because of the risk of Reye's syndrome. Children younger than 6 months should receive only acetaminophen for pain or fever.

The Bottom Line

In short: a viral sinus infection usually clears in 7 to 10 days; a bacterial one tends to run past 10 days or worsen midway through; and anything still present at 12 weeks is considered chronic. The same viruses behind colds, bronchitis, and strep throat are common neighbors of sinusitis, so the habits that prevent those illnesses — handwashing, avoiding sick contacts, and staying current on vaccines — help prevent this one too.

This article is health information, not medical advice. Durations and symptoms vary from person to person. If you are concerned about a sinus infection — especially any red-flag symptom listed above — please see a doctor or seek emergency care.

guides.excerpt: Acute bronchitis usually lasts 1–3 weeks, with a cough that can linger up to 3–6 weeks. It is almost always viral. See a doctor for fever, blood, or breathlessness.
guides.content:
How long does bronchitis last?

Acute bronchitis — often called a “chest cold” — usually lasts 1 to 3 weeks, with most people feeling better in about 7 to 10 days. The viral infection and fever typically clear within a week to ten days, but the nagging cough can linger for three weeks or longer even after you otherwise feel well. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) defines acute bronchitis as symptoms that last less than 3 weeks, and the Cleveland Clinic notes the full recovery window can stretch to three to six weeks in some people.

This is the short-term (acute) form. Chronic bronchitis is a different condition: a productive cough that lasts at least three months per year for two consecutive years, and it is one of the conditions that makes up COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). The timelines below apply to acute viral bronchitis, which is by far the most common kind.

StageTypical timingWhat happens
First days (days 1–3)OnsetCold-like symptoms appear: sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, mild body aches, fatigue, low-grade fever and chills.
Days 3–7Cough developsThe cough moves into the chest. Mucus (clear, white, yellow, or green) may be produced, along with chest discomfort, wheezing, and shortness of breath.
Days 7–10Acute phase endsMost cold and flu-type symptoms (fever, aches, sore throat) improve. The American Lung Association notes acute bronchitis “usually comes on suddenly and lasts for a week to 10 days.”
Weeks 2–3Lingering coughThe CDC classifies the illness as lasting under 3 weeks; the dry, nagging cough is often the last symptom to clear.
Weeks 3–6Extended recoveryCleveland Clinic reports some people take as long as three to six weeks to fully get over bronchitis. A cough past 3 weeks warrants a doctor visit.

Why does the cough drag on? Even after the virus is gone, the inflamed lining of the bronchial tubes takes time to heal, and an irritated airway can stay twitchy for weeks. That lingering cough is normal — but it is also the symptom that most often sends people back to a clinic, so it is worth knowing the difference between “slow healing” and “something more serious.” Compare this with how long the flu lasts or how long a cold lasts, since acute bronchitis often follows one of them.

Is it viral or bacterial? (This changes the timeline)

Acute bronchitis is caused by a virus in roughly 90–95% of cases — usually the same viruses that cause colds and flu (influenza, RSV, rhinovirus, adenovirus, coronavirus). Bacteria are responsible for only a small fraction of cases (such as Bordetella pertussis, which causes whooping cough, or Mycoplasma pneumoniae). This matters because:

  • Antibiotics do not work against viruses. A Cochrane review of randomized trials found antibiotics shorten the cough by only about half a day on average, while exposing you to side effects.
  • The CDC is explicit: “Antibiotics will not help you feel better if you have a chest cold,” and they are not recommended even when bacteria are the cause of straightforward acute bronchitis.
  • Antibiotics are used if your clinician diagnoses whooping cough (pertussis) or pneumonia, which can share symptoms with bronchitis.

In short, for the typical viral chest cold, time and symptom relief — not a prescription — are what bring recovery.

When bronchitis is contagious

Because acute bronchitis is usually viral, you are contagious with the underlying virus — not with “bronchitis” as a standalone illness. The inflammation itself cannot be passed to someone else; the respiratory virus that caused it can. Practical takeaways:

  • Contagious window: you can spread the virus from the first day of symptoms. The Cleveland Clinic notes viral cases are typically contagious for a few days to about a week.
  • How it spreads: mainly through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks, and by touching contaminated surfaces and then your eyes, nose, or mouth.
  • Bacterial cases: if the cause is bacterial (e.g., pertussis), you are generally no longer contagious 24 hours after starting antibiotics — another reason an accurate diagnosis matters.
  • Reducing spread: the CDC recommends covering coughs and sneezes, washing or sanitizing hands often, cleaning frequently touched surfaces, staying up to date with vaccines (including the flu shot), improving indoor air, and staying home while sick.

If symptoms have fully resolved and you have been fever-free without fever-reducing medicine, the risk of passing the virus on is low — though a lingering cough alone does not necessarily mean you are still contagious.

When to see a doctor or seek emergency care

Most acute bronchitis clears on its own, but some signs mean you should contact a clinician promptly. The following red-flag symptoms are drawn from the CDC, Cleveland Clinic, and NHS guidance.

See a healthcare professional if you have any of the following:

  • A cough that lasts more than 3 weeks (CDC, Cleveland Clinic, NHS).
  • A fever greater than 102°F (38.9°C) (Cleveland Clinic), a fever that lasts longer than 5 days, or a fever of 104°F or higher (CDC).
  • Coughing up blood or bloody mucus (CDC, Cleveland Clinic).
  • Shortness of breath, trouble breathing, or wheezing that is new or worsening (CDC, Cleveland Clinic).
  • Serious signs such as a bluish, pale, or blotchy tint to the lips, tongue, or skin, sudden confusion, or — in a baby — being unable to wake or appearing floppy (NHS).
  • Repeated episodes of bronchitis — this can point to COPD or another underlying condition (CDC, Cleveland Clinic).

For infants and children: the CDC advises talking to a healthcare provider right away if a child under 3 months old has a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. Do not give cough or cold medicines to children under 6, and never give honey to a child under 1 year old (risk of infant botulism). The NHS adds: call emergency services if there are breathing difficulties, confusion, or — in a baby — an inability to wake.

Higher-risk groups who should check in with a clinician sooner include adults over 65, pregnant women, people with asthma, COPD, heart disease, diabetes, a weakened immune system, and infants. For these groups, what looks like ordinary bronchitis can progress to pneumonia, so early evaluation matters more.

Treatment context: how to feel better (without antibiotics)

Because acute bronchitis is viral and self-limiting, treatment is about relieving symptoms while the airway heals — not about “curing” the infection. The CDC and NHS recommend:

  • Rest and plenty of fluids to keep mucus thin.
  • A clean humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer, saline nasal spray, and steam (e.g., a warm shower) to loosen congestion.
  • Throat lozenges or cough drops for adults and older children (the CDC says do not give them to children younger than 4).
  • Pasteurized honey in warm drinks to soothe the cough — safe for adults and children 1 year and older only.
  • Over-the-counter pain relievers/fever reducers (acetaminophen or ibuprofen) as needed, following age guidance: no fever reducers for infants under 3 months without a clinician’s okay; acetaminophen only from 3–6 months; either option at 6 months and older. OTC cough and cold medicines are not recommended for children under 6.

A clinician may prescribe an inhaler or bronchodilator if wheezing is significant, and antibiotics only if a bacterial infection such as pertussis or pneumonia is diagnosed. Otherwise, holding off on antibiotics is itself the right medical decision — it avoids side effects and helps slow antibiotic resistance.

One practical note: avoid tobacco smoke and other lung irritants while you heal, since smoke prolongs airway inflammation and is the leading cause of the chronic form of the disease.

Acute vs chronic bronchitis: a quick contrast

People often confuse the two, but they are very different in duration and meaning. Acute bronchitis is a short-term viral infection measured in days to weeks. Chronic bronchitis is defined by a productive cough on most days for at least three months a year, for two consecutive years, and it is part of COPD — a long-term, often smoking-related lung disease that requires ongoing medical care. Repeated bouts of “regular” bronchitis can be an early clue to chronic bronchitis, so mention any pattern of recurrent chest colds to your clinician. For other recovery timelines on related respiratory and healing topics, see how long a sinus infection lasts or how long strep throat lasts.

This article is health information, not medical advice. It summarizes publicly available guidance from the CDC, Cleveland Clinic, the American Lung Association, the NHS, and peer-reviewed sources; it does not diagnose, treat, or prescribe. Duration, contagious periods, and warning signs vary from person to person. If you are ill — especially with fever, breathlessness, bloody mucus, or a cough lasting more than three weeks — see a doctor. For severe symptoms such as trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or bluish lips, seek emergency care or call your local emergency number immediately.

How Long Does a Stomach Bug Last?

Most stomach bugs last 1 to 3 days. The classic stomach bug is viral gastroenteritis, most often caused by norovirus, and the CDC reports that most people with norovirus illness get better within 1 to 3 days. Some causes run longer: the CDC notes that rotavirus vomiting and diarrhea can last 3 to 8 days, and Mayo Clinic adds that gastroenteritis symptoms occasionally persist for up to 14 days. You are most contagious while symptoms are present and for roughly the first 48 hours after they stop, though the virus can keep spreading for two weeks or more after you feel better. This article is general information, not medical advice — always check with a healthcare provider about your specific symptoms.

What a "Stomach Bug" Actually Is

Despite the nickname "stomach flu," a stomach bug is not the flu. Influenza is a respiratory illness; a stomach bug is viral gastroenteritis, an infection that inflames the lining of your stomach and intestines. According to the CDC, norovirus is the leading cause of vomiting and diarrhea — and of foodborne illness — in the United States. Cleveland Clinic notes that norovirus is the leading cause of stomach flu in adults, accounting for an estimated 50% of cases worldwide, while rotavirus is the leading cause in children worldwide, with most children catching it before age 3. Less common culprits include astrovirus and adenovirus. These viruses spread easily in closed environments like schools, nursing homes, and cruise ships. Typical symptoms include nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, stomach pain, and chills.

Stomach Bug Timeline: From Exposure to Recovery

Every stomach bug follows the same arc — exposure, incubation, acute infection, recovery — but the pace depends on the virus. Here is the typical progression.

StageTimingWhat happens
ExposureDay 0The virus enters your body via a sick person, contaminated food, or a contaminated surface. No symptoms yet.
Incubation12–48 hours after exposureThe virus replicates inside you. You feel normal, but you may already be contagious.
Symptom onsetUsually 1–2 days after infectionNausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, and stomach cramps begin, sometimes with chills.
Acute illnessDays 1–2Peak symptoms and peak contagiousness. Dehydration is the main risk.
RecoveryDays 2–3Symptoms taper and stop. Most norovirus cases are over within 1–3 days.
Extended courseDays 3–14Rotavirus runs 3–8 days; severe cases can last a week or two, occasionally up to 14 days.
Post-recovery shedding48 hours or more after symptoms stopYou are still contagious — the virus can spread for 2 weeks or more.

The first 12 to 48 hours: incubation

You feel completely fine while the virus quietly replicates. The CDC says norovirus symptoms usually develop 12 to 48 hours after exposure. Mayo Clinic gives a broader window for viral gastroenteritis — symptoms may appear within 1 to 3 days after infection, depending on the cause — and Johns Hopkins Medicine notes they often begin 1 to 2 days after the virus enters the body. Cleveland Clinic points out that norovirus is already present in your stool before symptoms begin, and that you are contagious from the moment of infection — so you may spread the virus before you know you are sick.

Days 1 and 2: the acute phase

This is when the illness hits hardest: sudden nausea, repeated vomiting, watery diarrhea, and stomach cramps, sometimes with chills. You are most contagious during this stage, and dehydration risk peaks, because vomiting and diarrhea drain fluid and electrolytes at once. In most otherwise healthy adults, no treatment is needed — Johns Hopkins Medicine notes the illness usually runs its course in a few days, with dehydration the biggest risk.

Days 2 and 3: symptoms fade

For most people, the worst passes as quickly as it arrived. Mayo Clinic notes that symptoms usually last just a day or two, and the CDC puts full recovery from norovirus at 1 to 3 days. Once vomiting stops, appetite and energy return gradually.

When it lingers: 7 to 14 days

A stomach bug that drags on usually comes down to a slower virus (rotavirus runs 3 to 8 days), a severe case, or a weakened immune system. Cleveland Clinic says the stomach flu may last up to a week or two in severe cases, and Mayo Clinic states that symptoms occasionally last up to 14 days. If you are still sick beyond that window, it may not be a stomach bug at all.

How Long Are You Contagious?

The contagious window is longer than most people assume. Cleveland Clinic's norovirus guidance is blunt: you are contagious from the time you are infected until 48 hours after your symptoms stop. The CDC adds that you can still spread norovirus for 2 weeks or more after you feel better. The practical rule from Cleveland Clinic: stay isolated until two days after symptoms stop, and keep washing your hands well beyond that — hand sanitizer alone is not reliable against these viruses.

Factors That Affect How Long a Stomach Bug Lasts

  • Which virus you caught. Norovirus clears in 1 to 3 days, while rotavirus — the leading cause in young children — lasts 3 to 8 days.
  • Your immune system. People with weaker immune systems may have a harder time defeating the virus, and it may take longer. Mayo Clinic notes that if you are otherwise healthy you will likely recover without complications, but gastroenteritis can be dangerous for infants, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems.
  • Your age. Infants and older adults are the key exceptions to the "mild and quick" rule, which is why pediatric warning signs deserve a faster response.
  • Hydration. Dehydration is the biggest risk: losing fluids and electrolytes faster than you replace them turns a short illness into a medical problem.
  • Severity. Cleveland Clinic says severe cases can stretch recovery out to a week or two.

Practical Recovery Tips

  1. Sip fluids before you feel thirsty. Cleveland Clinic recommends small sips throughout the day or sucking on ice chips — steady intake stays down better than large gulps.
  2. Try an oral rehydration solution. The CDC says over-the-counter oral rehydration fluids are most helpful for mild dehydration, because vomiting and diarrhea cost you electrolytes as well as fluid.
  3. Rest and eat a little if you can. Staying home and giving your body energy to fight the infection is the best support for your immune system, per Cleveland Clinic.
  4. Stay home an extra two days. Isolating until two days after symptoms stop protects others during your most contagious window.
  5. Watch your urine. Deep yellow urine or little or no urine is an early dehydration warning sign, per Mayo Clinic — step up fluids and seek care if it persists.

When Symptoms Mean Something Else

Not every bout of vomiting and diarrhea is a stomach virus. Food poisoning causes similar cramping, vomiting, and diarrhea, but as Cleveland Clinic explains, the two names describe different origins: viral gastroenteritis is a virus passed between people, while food poisoning comes from eating contaminated food — which may carry a virus (in which case it is effectively a stomach bug) or bacteria, and bacterial food poisoning behaves a little differently. When symptoms refuse to improve on the expected timeline, Cleveland Clinic cautions that you may have a different condition altogether. Blood in vomit or stool, severe abdominal pain, and a high, persistent fever all point away from a simple stomach bug — and are reasons to seek care.

When to See a Doctor

Most stomach bugs resolve on their own, but certain red flags call for medical attention. According to Mayo Clinic, adults should see a healthcare provider if they:

  • cannot keep liquids down for 24 hours;
  • have been vomiting or having diarrhea for more than two days;
  • have a fever above 104 F (40 C);
  • are vomiting blood, see blood in bowel movements, or have severe stomach pain;
  • show signs of dehydration — excessive thirst, dry mouth, deep yellow urine or little or no urine, severe weakness, dizziness or lightheadedness.

Cleveland Clinic adds these adult warning signs: no improvement after four days, a fever above 102 F (39 C) lasting four days, and being unable to urinate or have a bowel movement for two days.

For children and infants, the bar is lower. Mayo Clinic advises seeing a child's provider right away for a fever of 102 F (38.9 C) or higher, bloody diarrhea, marked tiredness or irritability, or dehydration signs such as a dry mouth, thirst, and crying without tears. For babies, call the doctor for frequent vomiting, no wet diaper in six hours, bloody stools, a sunken soft spot on the head, or unusual sleepiness and unresponsiveness.

The bottom line: a stomach bug usually lasts 1 to 3 days, sometimes 3 to 8 days with rotavirus, and only occasionally up to 14 days. Hydrate in small sips, rest, stay home two extra days after symptoms stop — and call a healthcare provider if red-flag symptoms appear.

How long does pink eye last?

Pink eye usually clears within 1 to 2 weeks. Viral pink eye typically lasts 7 to 14 days (most mild cases resolve within 5 to 7 days), bacterial pink eye often clears in 2 to 5 days — discharge usually gone about 3 days after starting antibiotic drops — and allergic pink eye lasts as long as exposure to the trigger continues. The cause also decides how long you are contagious and when kids can return to school or daycare. This guide is general information only, not medical advice, so use the warning signs below to decide when to contact a doctor.

Pink eye duration by cause: quick comparison

Pink eye, medically called conjunctivitis, is inflammation of the thin tissue lining the white of the eye and inner eyelid. The cause is the single biggest driver of duration. The American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) notes that conjunctivitis usually goes away on its own within 1 to 2 weeks, the CDC puts the usual viral course at 7 to 14 days without treatment, and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) reports that most viral cases resolve within 5 to 7 days.

CauseHow long it usually lastsWhat shortens itContagious?
Viral (most common type)7 to 14 days; cold-related cases often about 7 days; some cases take 2 to 3 weeks or moreNothing — it has to run its courseYes — very, while redness and discharge last
BacterialOften clears in 2 to 5 days without treatment, but can take 2 weeks to go away completely; on antibiotic drops the discharge usually clears in about 3 daysAntibiotic eye drops, which also help stop the spread to othersYes — very
AllergicAs long as allergen exposure continues; often seasonalAllergy eye drops and removing the triggerNo
Chemical or irritantUsually clears on its own within about a day after the eye is rinsedRinsing the eye thoroughlyNo

Day-by-day timeline: what to expect

Most pink eye follows a predictable arc, pieced together from CDC, AAO, AAP, and Mayo Clinic recovery guidance so you can tell whether your case is on schedule.

StageTimingWhat happens
OnsetDays 0 to 2The eye turns pink or red, waters, and feels gritty or itchy. Viral pink eye often begins in one eye and affects the other within a few days, and you can spread it before symptoms even appear.
PeakDays 2 to 4Redness and discharge are at their worst. Viral cases stay watery; bacterial cases produce thick yellow-green pus that can stick the eyelashes together overnight.
Turning pointDays 3 to 7On antibiotic drops, bacterial discharge typically clears within about 3 days. Untreated bacterial cases often clear in 2 to 5 days, and most viral cases resolve within 5 to 7 days.
RecoveryDays 7 to 14Redness fades and comfort returns. Most pink eye is fully gone within 1 to 2 weeks, though the CDC and Mayo Clinic note some viral cases take 2 to 3 weeks or more.
PersistentBeyond 14 daysNo longer typical. The AAO recommends seeing an eye doctor if symptoms last longer than 1 to 2 weeks to rule out a more serious eye problem.

Factors that affect how long pink eye lasts

  • The cause. This outweighs everything else. An irritant case can end within a day, bacterial cases within days to two weeks, and viral cases one to two weeks — occasionally three.
  • Treatment matched to the cause. Antibiotic drops help only bacterial pink eye. The CDC, AAO, and Mayo Clinic all stress that antibiotics do nothing for viral or allergic pink eye — most viral cases need no prescription at all.
  • Which virus is involved. Most viral pink eye is caused by adenovirus, Mayo Clinic notes, and it often arrives alongside a cold. Herpes simplex virus cases are less common but may need prescription antiviral medicine.
  • Ongoing exposure. Allergic pink eye continues as long as the pollen, dander, smoke, or chlorine is around, and contagious cases can pass around a household on shared hands and towels, restarting the clock.
  • Contact lens wear. The AAO and Mayo Clinic both say to stop wearing lenses until the conjunctivitis is gone; Mayo urges wearers to see an eye professional if symptoms do not begin improving within 12 to 24 hours.
  • Age and setting. Children are more likely than adults to get viral and bacterial pink eye because germs spread easily on unwashed hands and shared surfaces in schools and daycare centers, the AAO notes.

How long is pink eye contagious? School and daycare rules

Viral and bacterial pink eye are very contagious, while allergic and irritant pink eye are not contagious at all, the CDC states. The contagious kinds spread through close contact, droplets from coughs and sneezes, and germy hands or surfaces touched before rubbing your eyes — and just like a cold, a child is often contagious before symptoms are even noticed, the AAP explains. Treat viral pink eye as contagious while redness and discharge last: the AAO says not to return to school, work, or the gym until the eyes are no longer red with discharge.

When can a child go back to school or daycare?

  • Bacterial pink eye: many schools allow return 24 hours after antibiotic drops begin, a policy the AAP highlights. AAP symptom guidance adds that a child can return once discharge has dwindled to a small amount and drops have been used for 24 hours.
  • Viral pink eye: no drops shortcut exists. The AAO advises staying home until the eyes are no longer red with discharge, and the CDC says not to attend while symptoms persist if activities involve close contact with others. The AAP notes that mild watery pinkeye from a cold does not require missing any school — follow school policy and your pediatrician.
  • Fever or general illness: if the child feels ill overall or has a fever, keep them home regardless of the eye, the AAP recommends.
  • Allergic pink eye: not contagious, so school, work, and the gym are fine, per the AAO.

Tips to recover faster and keep it from spreading

  1. Apply a cool, wet compress — or a warm one, whichever feels better — several times a day, using a clean washcloth every time.
  2. Use artificial tears to ease grittiness, and discard the bottle once you recover so it cannot reinfect anyone.
  3. If antibiotic drops are prescribed, use them exactly as directed for as long as directed.
  4. Stop wearing contact lenses the moment symptoms start. Throw out soft lenses worn during the infection and disinfect hard lenses overnight before reuse.
  5. Wash hands with soap and water — the CDC says scrub for at least 20 seconds — after any contact with the eyes, and never share towels or washcloths.
  6. Skip eye makeup while infected, and replace any makeup or drop bottles used near the eyes during the infection.
  7. For allergic pink eye, allergy eye drops and limiting exposure to triggers like pollen, animal dander, cigarette smoke, and pool chlorine bring the fastest relief.

When to see a doctor

Most pink eye is harmless and self-limiting, but a red eye can occasionally signal something more serious. Contact a clinician in these situations:

  • Contact an eye doctor promptly for moderate to severe eye pain, blurred vision, increased light sensitivity, intense redness, symptoms that keep worsening, or a weakened immune system — the AAO says these can signal something beyond routine conjunctivitis.
  • Seek urgent care for eye pain, a feeling that something is stuck in the eye, blurred vision, or light sensitivity, which Mayo Clinic lists as possible signs of a serious eye condition.
  • A newborn with any pink eye symptoms should be seen by a doctor right away, the CDC advises.
  • See a provider if bacterial pink eye does not improve after 24 hours of antibiotic use, the CDC adds. After a chemical splash, rinse the eye and get care quickly if symptoms do not clear or the chemical was caustic, like lye.
  • Contact lens wearers should stop wearing lenses immediately and see an eye professional if symptoms do not begin improving within 12 to 24 hours.
  • See a doctor if symptoms last longer than 1 to 2 weeks, if a child's redness lasts more than a week, if pus appears in an eye that was previously watery, or if things worsen rather than improve.

The bottom line

Most pink eye is viral, clears on its own in one to two weeks, and needs nothing more than compresses, artificial tears, and good hygiene. Bacterial cases often clear fastest — 2 to 5 days without treatment, discharge usually gone about 3 days into drops — while allergic cases end only when exposure ends. Track the timeline, keep hands and towels separate, and let a doctor take over if pain, vision changes, or two weeks of symptoms break the pattern.

How long does shingles last?

Most shingles rashes heal within 2 to 4 weeks, and the full illness typically runs 3 to 5 weeks from the first twinge of nerve pain until the skin completely clears. According to the CDC, the blisters usually scab over in 7 to 10 days, and the rash clears up within 2 to 4 weeks. For some people, mostly older adults, nerve pain continues for months or even years after the rash heals — a complication called postherpetic neuralgia.

This guide is general information, not medical advice, and it cannot account for your individual situation. What it can do is walk you through the typical shingles timeline, the factors that speed up or slow down recovery, and the warning signs that mean you should call a doctor quickly — because starting treatment early genuinely changes how long shingles lasts.

Shingles timeline: the 5 stages from tingling to clear skin

Shingles (herpes zoster) is a reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus, the same virus that causes chickenpox. After you recover from chickenpox, the virus stays dormant in your nerves for the rest of your life, and it can reactivate years later as a painful, blistering rash, usually in a single stripe on one side of the torso or face that does not cross the body's midline. About 1 in 3 people in the United States will develop shingles at some point, and the CDC estimates roughly one million cases occur each year. The illness unfolds in recognizable stages.

StageWhat happensTypical timing
1. Early symptoms (prodrome)Pain, burning, itching, or tingling in one patch of skin; some people also feel feverish, headachy, chilled, or generally unwell1 to 5 days before the rash appears
2. Rash appearsA rash of small red spots develops where the pain was, most often as a single stripe on one side of the torso or faceUsually 1 to 5 days after symptoms start
3. Blisters formThe red spots turn into fluid-filled blisters that eventually break openAbout 3 to 4 days after the rash appears
4. Crusting and scabbingBlisters dry out, crust over, and form scabs; you stay contagious until they dry and scabBlisters scab over in about 7 to 10 days
5. HealingScabs gradually fall off and the skin clearsRash clears within 2 to 4 weeks; the full illness usually runs 3 to 5 weeks

Most people have shingles only once in their lifetime, although the CDC notes the virus can reactivate more than once.

Factors that affect how long shingles lasts

Two people can have very different shingles experiences. These are the main factors that shape your timeline:

  • Your age. The risk of shingles and its complications rises sharply after 50, and Mayo Clinic notes that people over 60 are more likely to have more severe complications.
  • Your immune system. Weakened immunity — from HIV, cancer, chemotherapy or radiation, transplant medications, or long-term steroids — makes a more severe, longer-lasting rash more likely.
  • How quickly you start antivirals. Treatment works best when it begins within 72 hours of your first symptoms, and it can shorten the course of the illness.
  • Where the rash sits. Shingles on the face, especially near an eye, needs urgent care because it can threaten vision.
  • How intense the initial pain is. Johns Hopkins Medicine identifies severe pain during the active rash as a risk factor for lingering nerve pain after the skin heals.

The 72-hour antiviral window

According to the CDC, shingles treatment is most effective within 72 hours of symptom onset. Three antiviral drugs are standard: acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir. Started early, they speed up how quickly the lesions resolve, reduce new blisters and viral shedding, and decrease the severity of acute pain. Johns Hopkins Medicine notes that antivirals may also lessen the chance of nerve damage and postherpetic neuralgia. That is why a suspicious band of one-sided pain or rash is worth a same-day phone call rather than a wait-and-see weekend.

Postherpetic neuralgia: when shingles pain outlasts the rash

The most common complication of shingles is postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) — nerve pain in the area where the rash was, continuing after the skin has cleared. The CDC reports that about 10% to 18% of people who have shingles also experience PHN, and Cleveland Clinic puts the figure at up to 1 in 5. PHN can last for months or years after the rash goes away, and it ranges from annoying to debilitating.

Your risk of PHN increases with age: people younger than 40 rarely develop it, and older adults who get it tend to have longer-lasting and more severe pain. Early treatment matters here, too — Johns Hopkins Medicine notes that early treatment of shingles may prevent PHN, one more reason the 72-hour window matters so much.

Practical tips while you recover

  1. Start antivirals immediately. If you are within 72 hours of your first symptoms — or new blisters are still forming — ask a provider about antiviral medication right away.
  2. Cover the rash and protect others. You are contagious through direct contact with fluid from open blisters until they have dried and scabbed over. Keep lesions covered, and avoid contact with people who have never had chickenpox or the vaccine, pregnant women, newborns, and anyone with a weakened immune system. An exposed person would develop chickenpox, not shingles.
  3. Manage the itch and pain. Cool compresses and soothing creams or lotions can ease itching. Pain relievers help many people, and providers can prescribe stronger options, including medicines developed specifically for nerve pain, when needed.
  4. Keep the area clean. Watch for spreading redness, pus, or increasing soreness — the rash can become infected with bacteria, which needs its own treatment.
  5. Pace yourself. Fever, headache, chills, and fatigue are common early on. Rest gives your body the best shot at the shorter two-to-four-week course.

Shingles duration: quick answers

How long are you contagious with shingles?

You can spread the virus from when the blisters appear until they have dried and scabbed over — the scabbing that, per the CDC, typically takes 7 to 10 days. The virus spreads through direct contact with blister fluid, and an exposed person develops chickenpox rather than shingles.

Can you get shingles more than once?

Yes. Most people have shingles only once, but the CDC notes that herpes zoster can recur — though Cleveland Clinic says repeat episodes are uncommon unless you have a weakened immune system. That possibility is one more reason adults eligible for vaccination should consider it even after an episode.

A note on the shingles vaccine

Shingrix, the recombinant zoster vaccine, is recommended for adults 50 and older — and for adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems — even if you have already had shingles or received the older Zostavax vaccine, which is no longer available in the United States. It is given as two doses spaced 2 to 6 months apart, and Mayo Clinic reports that studies suggest it offers protection for more than five years. The vaccine cannot treat an active shingles infection; it works by prevention, lowering the chance you get shingles at all and making any breakthrough case milder.

When to See a Doctor

Contact a healthcare provider as soon as you suspect shingles — early treatment shortens the illness and reduces complications. Mayo Clinic says to seek care promptly in these situations:

  • The pain or rash is near an eye. Shingles in or around the eye can lead to permanent eye damage if left untreated.
  • You are 50 or older. Age increases the risk of complications, including postherpetic neuralgia.
  • You or a family member has a weakened immune system due to cancer, medications, or chronic illness.
  • The rash is widespread and painful rather than confined to a single stripe.

Also call if pain persists in the rash area after the skin has healed, or if the rash shows signs of bacterial infection. And while they are very rare, the CDC warns that shingles can occasionally lead to pneumonia, hearing problems, or brain inflammation (encephalitis) — so new breathing trouble, hearing changes, or other neurological symptoms after shingles deserve a prompt call.

How long does a colonoscopy take?

The colonoscopy itself usually takes 30 to 45 minutes — Cleveland Clinic figures about 15 minutes to guide the scope in and 15 more to examine the colon on the way out — and the whole visit runs about two hours once you add check-in, preparation, and 30 to 60 minutes of monitored recovery. NIDDK notes the procedure itself "usually takes less than one hour." Counting the bowel prep, which starts several days earlier, the full process spans a few days — and most people are back to a normal diet and routine by the morning after the exam.

This article is general information, not medical advice. Exact timing depends on your health, your prep, and your facility, so follow the specific instructions your own healthcare team gives you.

Colonoscopy timeline at a glance

Three clocks hide inside this question: the prep clock, the facility clock, and the recovery clock. Here is how they fit together:

StageTypical timeWhat happens
Low-fiber dietSeveral days beforeYou avoid high-fiber foods — whole grains, raw vegetables, beans, nuts, and seeds — so the bowel is easier to clear.
Clear-liquid dietThe day beforeClear liquids only, with the first laxative dose at night.
The procedure30-45 minutesThe scope is advanced to the end of the colon (about 15 minutes) and withdrawn in a second, slower examination (another 15 minutes).
Polyp removalAbout 15 extra minutesPolyps turn up in about 30% of routine colonoscopies and are usually removed on sight.
Monitored recovery30-60 minutesYou wake up from sedation while your care team monitors you.
Total visitAbout two hoursWaiting, preparation, the exam, and recovery — about what your driver should expect.
Full recoveryAbout 24 hoursThe anesthesia takes about a day to clear completely; most people eat normally and resume activities the next day.

The day before: bowel prep is the real time commitment

The procedure is short; the preparation is the part people remember. Your colon has to be completely clean — NIDDK warns that stool inside your large intestine can prevent your doctor from clearly seeing the lining, and Cleveland Clinic notes that an inadequate prep can mean rescheduling and redoing the whole thing. The typical sequence:

  • Several days before: switch to a low-fiber diet, cutting out whole grains, raw vegetables, beans, nuts, and seeds.
  • The day before: clear liquids only — fat-free bouillon or broth, pulp-free apple or white grape juice, lemon-, lime-, or orange-flavored sports drinks, plain coffee or tea without milk, water, and gelatin. Your doctor may also recommend avoiding red- and purple-colored drinks or gelatin.
  • The night before: drink the first dose of the laxative prep and stay close to a bathroom for several hours as it works. NIDDK says the liquid laxative is most often taken the night before and again the morning of the procedure.

If vomiting or side effects make the prep hard to finish, call your healthcare provider instead of quitting: a complete prep is what makes the exam accurate.

Minute by minute: what happens during the exam

A doctor performs a colonoscopy in a hospital or an outpatient center. After check-in, a nurse places an IV line in your arm or hand to give you sedatives, anesthesia, or pain medicine. Lying on your side, you are monitored while the doctor — usually a gastroenterologist — guides the colonoscope through your anus and along the full length of your colon. The scope inflates the colon with air for a better view. Cleveland Clinic estimates about 15 minutes for the trip in.

The withdrawal is itself a second exam: the doctor slowly draws the scope back, inspecting the lining again on the way out — about another 15 minutes. Polyps turn up in about 30% of routine colonoscopies. Most are benign, but removing them on sight is standard, and doing so may add another 15 minutes. You will not feel the polyp removal, and if anything looks abnormal the doctor can also take a painless biopsy, sending tissue to a lab.

Factors that affect how long a colonoscopy takes

  • Polyp removal or biopsy. The biggest driver of extra procedure time — treating what is found can add about 15 minutes.
  • Prep quality. A poorly cleaned colon is harder to examine, and a failed prep can mean rescheduling and starting over.
  • Type of sedation. Sedatives and anesthesia wake up at different speeds, which shifts the recovery clock.
  • Facility schedule. Check-in paperwork and room turnover add waiting time — the reason the exam itself takes 30 to 45 minutes while the whole visit runs about two hours.

Recovery: when can you drive, work, and eat normally?

You will spend the first 30 to 60 minutes after the exam in recovery, waking up while your care team monitors you. ASGE says patients are required to have a family member or friend drive them home, and Cleveland Clinic says that person should expect to wait about two hours altogether. From there the timeline is predictable:

  • First hour or two: cramping and bloating are normal while air from the procedure passes, and you can return to your normal diet as soon as you feel ready.
  • Rest of the day: no driving, operating equipment, or important decisions. ASGE warns the medications used for colonoscopy can affect judgment and reflexes for the rest of the day, and Cleveland Clinic notes the anesthesia takes about 24 hours to wear off completely.
  • Next day: NIDDK says to expect a full recovery and a return to your normal diet by the next day. Light bleeding from the anus is normal if polyps were removed or a biopsy was performed.

How often do you need a colonoscopy?

Because colorectal cancer is the second most common cause of cancer death in the United States when men and women are combined, screening intervals are tightly standardized. The American Cancer Society recommends people at average risk start screening at 45 and continue through age 75 while in good health with a life expectancy of more than 10 years. If your colonoscopy is normal, you typically will not need another for 10 years — the longest interval of any recommended colorectal screening test. If polyps were removed, the ACS says most people need another colonoscopy after about 3 years; a strong family history of colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, or an inherited syndrome such as Lynch syndrome also means earlier, more frequent screening. From ages 76 to 85 the decision depends on your preferences, health, and prior screening; after 85, screening is no longer recommended.

Tips to make the day go smoothly

  1. Block out the prep day. Treat the day before as a stay-home day near a bathroom, not a work day.
  2. Shop before you start. Stock broth, pulp-free juice, sports drinks, and gelatin, and check the allowed colors on your instructions.
  3. Finish the entire prep. An incomplete prep is a common reason for a poor view — or a repeat procedure.
  4. Line up your driver early. You will be required to have a family member or friend take you home.
  5. Plan a quiet evening. Anesthesia needs about 24 hours to fully clear, so keep your schedule light after the exam.
  6. Ask about results. Most results you will know right away, but Cleveland Clinic notes biopsy results take another few days to weeks.

When to see a doctor

Colonoscopy is safe, and serious complications are rare: in a study of screening colonoscopies cited by NIDDK, perforation occurred in about 3 of every 10,000 procedures and bleeding in about 15 of every 10,000, mostly in people who are older or who had polyps removed. But problems can appear after you are home. NIDDK says to seek medical care right away if you have:

  • severe pain in your abdomen;
  • fever;
  • bleeding from your anus that does not stop, or bloody bowel movements that do not get better;
  • black stools;
  • dizziness or weakness.

Delayed bleeding is possible up to 2 weeks after the procedure, so keep that window in mind even once you feel fine. If you cannot finish the bowel prep because of vomiting or other side effects, call your healthcare team before the appointment rather than arriving under-prepped. For heavy bleeding, severe pain, or feeling faint, seek emergency care.
guides.excerpt: The exam itself takes 30 to 45 minutes, but plan on about two hours at the facility — plus a clear-liquid prep day beforehand.

How long does an MRI take?

A typical MRI scan takes between 30 and 60 minutes, although short scans can finish in as little as 15 minutes and a cardiac MRI can run up to 90 minutes. The UK's National Health Service (NHS) describes the usual window as "between 15 minutes and 1 hour, but can take longer," while Cleveland Clinic says a standard MRI "usually takes 30 to 60 minutes." RadiologyInfo.org, produced by the Radiological Society of North America and the American College of Radiology, puts the typical total at 30 to 50 minutes. Your exact time inside the machine depends on which body part is being imaged, how many image sequences your radiologist orders, and whether you receive contrast dye. This article is general information only, not medical advice. Always ask your own care team about your specific scan.

MRI scan times by body part

The area being scanned is the single biggest driver of how long you will be inside the machine. Here are typical durations from major hospitals and radiology organizations:

Scan typeTypical scan timeGood to know
Brain MRI30-60 minutesTakes longer when contrast dye is used
Cervical spine (neck) MRI30-60 minutesMay take longer depending on the images needed
Knee or single-joint MRI30-60 minutesThe machine is loud; earplugs are offered
Cardiac (heart) MRI30-90 minutesContrast, when used, is given through an IV line, often gadolinium
Any MRI with contrastAdds time to the aboveYou may wait up to 30 minutes afterward so staff can check for a reaction

These ranges line up across sources. UCSF Health says the test "most often lasts 30 to 60 minutes, but may take longer" for both knee and cervical spine scans. Cleveland Clinic says a brain MRI "can take about 30 minutes to an hour to complete," and notes that cardiac MRI scans "should take a half hour to an hour and a half."

Where the time goes: an MRI timeline, stage by stage

Understanding the stages of the appointment explains why a scan described as "30 to 60 minutes" can occupy a bigger slice of your day:

StageWhat happensTime it takes
Check-in and safety screeningYou complete a metal-implant questionnaire and change into a gownVaries by facility
PositioningYou lie on the scanning table while the technologist sets up equipment and hands you earplugsA few minutes
Imaging sequencesThe scanner runs multiple image sequences, each several minutes long, with loud thumping and hummingThe bulk of the scan
Contrast injection (if used)Gadolinium dye flows through an IV line and further sequences followAdds time to the scan
Post-scan observation (if contrast)You wait so the team can make sure you do not have a reaction to the dyeUp to 30 minutes

RadiologyInfo.org explains the rhythm of the noises you will hear: "MRI exams generally include multiple runs (sequences), some of which may last several minutes," and "each run will create a different set of noises." That is why the sound changes pattern several times during the exam. Each change simply means a new set of images is being captured.

Factors that affect how long an MRI takes

  • Body part and number of sequences. More anatomy or more detail means more sequences. A single knee, the brain, and the neck all commonly land in the 30 to 60 minute band, while the heart needs extra timed imaging that can push the scan toward 90 minutes.
  • Contrast dye. A brain MRI with contrast may take longer than one without, and after any contrast scan the NHS says you "may be asked to wait in hospital for up to 30 minutes" so staff can make sure you do not have a reaction.
  • The scanner itself. RadiologyInfo.org notes that total time depends on "the type of exam and the equipment used," so the same body part can scan faster on one machine than another.
  • How still you can lie. UCSF Health warns that "too much movement can blur MRI images and cause errors." Blurred sequences generally have to be redone, which stretches your appointment.
  • Relaxation medicine. If claustrophobia means you take medicine to relax, arranging and recovering from it can extend the total visit.

Claustrophobia, noise, and open MRI machines

Standard MRI scanners surround your body, and Cleveland Clinic notes that while most exams are painless, "some people find it uncomfortable to remain still for 30 minutes or longer." The machine is also loud. UCSF Health describes "loud thumping and humming noises," which is why earplugs or headphones are standard. If you have claustrophobia, Cleveland Clinic says "your provider may recommend giving you medicine that helps you relax during the exam," and the NHS similarly notes that people anxious about small spaces may be able to have medicine to help them relax. You can also ask whether the facility has an open MRI. "Open MRI machines have a more spacious design than traditional MRI machines," Cleveland Clinic explains, and that design "can help people who feel anxious in enclosed spaces." Raise this when you book, because not every location offers every machine type.

Metal implants and MRI safety screening

Before your scan you will complete a safety form asking whether you have metal in your body. The NHS lists surgical clips, a pacemaker, and dental fillings or bridges among the items it asks about. This is not a formality. In most cases an MRI is safe for people with metal implants, but RadiologyInfo.org identifies exceptions, including some cochlear (ear) implants, some clips used for brain aneurysms, some metal coils placed within blood vessels, some older cardiac defibrillators and pacemakers, and vagal nerve stimulators. Cleveland Clinic likewise asks you to tell your provider and the technologist if you have a heart pacemaker or defibrillator. Screening can affect timing, too. As RadiologyInfo.org puts it, "the technologist cannot perform the MRI exam without confirming and documenting the type of implant and MRI compatibility," so an undocumented implant can delay your slot while records are tracked down.

Practical tips to keep your MRI on schedule

  1. Use the bathroom just before the scan. You will need to hold still for the whole exam, and Cleveland Clinic notes that remaining still for 30 minutes or longer is exactly what some people find uncomfortable.
  2. Dress metal-free. Cleveland Clinic says to "leave all jewelry and other accessories at home" and lists metal zippers and underwire bras among items that must come off, because metal can interfere with the machine or cause burns.
  3. Ask for a time estimate when you book. Cleveland Clinic notes that your provider "will be able to give you an exact time range based on the specific reason for your scan."
  4. Practice lying still. UCSF Health warns that "too much movement can blur MRI images and cause errors," and errors are what stretch an appointment.
  5. Take the earplugs. They make 30 to 60 minutes of thumping much easier to rest through.
  6. Flag implants, kidney problems, and claustrophobia in advance. UCSF Health asks patients with kidney problems to tell their provider before the test, noting that people with kidney disease or on dialysis may not be able to receive contrast, and both relaxation medicine and open machines are easier to arrange ahead of the day.

When to see a doctor

Start with the provider who ordered your MRI if you have questions about why you need it, what it will show, or how long your specific scan should take. Contact the imaging facility or your doctor promptly if anything unusual happens after you receive contrast dye. The NHS keeps contrast patients for up to 30 minutes precisely to watch for reactions, so symptoms that start after you leave deserve a phone call. If anxiety or claustrophobia has made you delay or avoid booking, tell your doctor rather than skipping the scan, because relaxation medicine and open MRI options exist. And if new or severe symptoms appear while you are waiting for your appointment, such as sudden pain, weakness, or changes in consciousness, seek urgent care instead of waiting for the scan date.

For planning purposes, treat the scan itself as a 30 to 60 minute block, up to 90 minutes for cardiac MRI, then add check-in, screening, and if contrast is used, up to 30 minutes of observation afterward. Build in that buffer and follow the preparation instructions, and the imaging itself is usually the most predictable part of your visit.
