guides.content:
How Long Is a Soccer Game?

A soccer game is 90 minutes of playing time — two 45-minute halves — but a real match runs about 1 hour 55 minutes to 2 hours from kick-off to the final whistle once you count stoppage time and the 15-minute halftime interval. In the Premier League this season, the average match has run 100 minutes and 36 seconds of match time, with the ball actually in play for only about 55 minutes. Budget roughly two hours for a normal league game, and closer to two and a half — sometimes beyond — if a knockout tie needs extra time and a penalty shootout.

What the Rulebook Says About the 90 Minutes

Regulation time: two 45-minute halves

Law 7 of the IFAB Laws of the Game — the rulebook used by FIFA, the Premier League, MLS and essentially every organized league in the world — is blunt: a match lasts for two equal halves of 45 minutes. The same rule governs a World Cup final and a Sunday-league fixture, and the halves can only be reduced by agreement between the referee and both teams before kick-off, where competition rules allow it — which is how youth leagues play shorter matches.

The halftime interval

Players are entitled to a halftime interval of no more than 15 minutes. Competition rules must state the exact duration, and it may be altered only with the referee's permission. That single block is the biggest chunk of non-playing time in a normal match.

Stoppage time (added time)

Soccer's clock never stops. Instead, the referee adds time to the end of each half to recover playing time lost to substitutions, assessment or removal of injured players, time-wasting, disciplinary sanctions, drinks and cooling breaks, VAR checks and reviews, goal celebrations, and any other significant delay. The fourth official posts the minimum added time in the final minute of each half — and the referee may increase it, but never reduce it. If a penalty kick still has to be taken or retaken, the half is extended until the kick is completed.

Extra time and penalty shootouts

The 90 minutes can stretch dramatically when a winner must be decided. Under Law 10, the permitted tie-breaking procedures are two equal periods of extra time — each capped at 15 minutes — followed, if the teams are still level, by a penalty shootout: five kicks per team, taken alternately, with sudden-death rounds until one side wins.

Regulation Time vs. Real Time: Doing the Clock Math

Here is how a "90-minute" professional match actually adds up on your watch:

  • 45 minutes of first-half play, plus first-half stoppage time
  • Up to 15 minutes of halftime interval
  • 45 minutes of second-half play, plus stoppage time — where most of the padding lives

Counting stoppage time but not the halftime break, the average Premier League match through mid-October of the 2025-26 season ran 100 minutes and 36 seconds — about ten and a half minutes beyond the nominal 90 — and the ball was in play for only 54.7% of that, roughly 55 minutes. Add the halftime interval and a routine league fixture lands just under two hours of real time. The long-game era is recent: Opta's tracking shows average ball-in-play time jumping from 54 minutes 49 seconds in 2022-23 to 58 minutes 11 seconds in 2023-24 as referees added more stoppage time, before sliding to 56 minutes 59 seconds in 2024-25 and back to about 55 minutes early in 2025-26.

Soccer Game Length by Level and Competition

Playing time shrinks as the players get younger. US Youth Soccer's rules set the standard age-group durations used across American youth leagues, while high school and college play their own formats:

Level or competitionFormatPlaying timeNotes
Professional (Premier League, MLS, World Cup)Two 45-minute halves90 minutesHalftime up to 15 minutes; PL matches average 100:36 of match time this season
Knockout ties (World Cup and Champions League knockout rounds)Two 45-minute halves, then extra time and penalties if level90 minutes plus up to 30 minutes of extra timeCan stretch past two and a half hours end to end
NCAA college (men's and women's)Two 45-minute periods90 minutes15-minute halftime; postseason adds up to two 10-minute sudden-victory overtimes
US high school (NFHS rules)Two 40-minute halves80 minutesOvertime formats vary by state association
Youth 19U–17UTwo 45-minute halves90 minutesSame length as the pro game; overtime two 15-minute halves
Youth 16U–15UTwo 40-minute halves80 minutesMatches high school length; overtime two 15-minute halves
Youth 14U–13UTwo 35-minute halves70 minutesOvertime: two 10-minute halves
Youth 12U–11UTwo 30-minute halves60 minutesOvertime: two 10-minute halves
Youth 10UTwo 25-minute halves50 minutesNo overtime
Youth 8UFour 12-minute quarters48 minutesNo overtime
Youth 6UFour 6-minute quarters24 minutesNo overtime

Those totals are pure playing time. Add a halftime break — up to 15 minutes under the Laws of the Game — plus stoppage time, and the real-world commitment grows to about two hours for a professional match, roughly an hour and a half for high school, and an hour or less for most youth games.

Factors That Affect How Long a Soccer Game Takes

  • Goals and celebrations. Every celebration is a listed cause of added time, so high-scoring games finish later.
  • Substitutions. Each change of personnel is time lost that the referee claws back at the end of the half.
  • Injuries. Assessing and removing an injured player can eat several minutes on its own.
  • VAR checks and reviews. Video review time is explicitly added back to the clock.
  • Weather breaks. Drinks breaks should not exceed one minute; cooling breaks run ninety seconds to three minutes.
  • Time-wasting and discipline. Cautions, arguments, and deliberate delaying are all recoverable time.
  • A late penalty. The half is extended until the kick is completed, so a game can end seconds after a converted spot kick.
  • A tie that must be broken. Up to 30 minutes of extra time plus a five-kick-each shootout tacks on the better part of an hour.
  • The level of play. Younger age groups play 24 to 50 minutes of actual clock, so a 6U match and a World Cup final differ by more than an hour of scheduled playing time.

Planning Your Viewing: Time the Match Like a Referee

Because the clock never stops, soccer is one of the easiest sports to schedule around — if you anchor your timers to the right moments:

  1. Anchor to kick-off, not the broadcast slot. The listed start time is the kick-off. Switch the TV on a minute or two early and skip the pre-match show unless you want it.
  2. Expect the first half to run long. Forty-five minutes plus first-half stoppage means the halftime whistle usually arrives around the 47-to-50-minute mark.
  3. Start a 15-minute countdown at halftime. That is the maximum legal interval, so the second half restarts roughly an hour after kick-off — usually a few minutes later once teams are back on the pitch.
  4. Set your final-whistle timer for about 1 hour 55 minutes after kick-off. That covers the 100-plus minutes of match time a modern professional game averages plus the 15-minute halftime interval; a routine evening lands just under two hours.
  5. Never treat the assistant's board as a finish line. The announced added time is a minimum that the referee can extend but not reduce — plenty of "90+4" games become 90+7.
  6. For knockout games, pre-book an extra 45 minutes. Thirty minutes of extra time, a short break before it, and a possible shootout push the finish toward — and sometimes past — the two-and-a-half-hour mark.
  7. Youth parents, check the age chart. A 10U game wraps in about an hour; a 6U game packs just 24 scheduled minutes of play.

The Bottom Line

Ninety minutes on paper, about two hours in practice. Two 45-minute halves plus stoppage time and a 15-minute halftime make the average professional match just under two hours end to end — 100 minutes and 36 seconds of match time in the current Premier League, with only about 55 minutes of ball actually in play. College matches the 90-minute format, high school trims it to 80, youth steps down from 90 to as little as 24 minutes by age group, and only knockout football threatens your evening with extra time and penalties. Set a timer at kick-off, restart it at the halftime whistle, and the game will tell you exactly when to be back on the couch.

How long is a baseball game?

Quick answer: the average MLB game now runs about 2 hours 38 minutes from first pitch to final out, and the pitch-timer era has settled baseball into a narrow 2:36-to-2:40 window. A regulation game is nine innings, and because baseball has no game clock, the only thing that ends it is the final out. In 2025, the most recent full season, the average nine-inning major league game lasted 2:38 — down from 3:04 in 2022, the last season before the pitch timer. Extra innings are open-ended, so a tie game can stretch well past three hours, but the typical experience is a game you can comfortably fit into an evening.

Why baseball has no game clock

Nearly every major team sport is ruled by time: the buzzer sounds, the game ends. Baseball is the exception. The clock on the scoreboard is informational, never operational. A game ends when the team that is behind records its 27th out — nine innings, three outs per half-inning, home team batting last — or earlier, if the home team wins on a walk-off. That is why the honest answer to "how long is a baseball game" is an average rather than a rule, and why duration has swung so much across eras.

What baseball does have is a web of pace timers governing the dead air between action, and since 2023 they have teeth. Pitchers get 15 seconds to deliver the ball with the bases empty and 18 seconds with runners on (it was 20 seconds in 2023, trimmed for 2024). Batters must be in the box and alert to the pitcher by the 8-second mark of the timer. A 30-second timer runs between batters. Step over the line and the penalty is an automatic ball or strike — which is why these timers actually bite.

And when the score is tied after nine? The game simply continues, inning after inning, until someone breaks the deadlock. Every half-inning beyond the ninth begins with an automatic runner placed on second base — the so-called ghost runner. Introduced as a pandemic-era measure in 2020, the rule was made a permanent part of the rulebook ahead of the 2023 season specifically to accelerate extras. It applies to regular-season games only; postseason extra innings start with the bases empty.

Regulation time vs. real time: what fills the 2:38

The rulebook's contribution to duration is just "nine innings." Everything else is choreography you can plan around, because almost every idle moment in a modern MLB game is on a countdown:

  • Between pitches: 15 seconds with the bases empty, 18 seconds with runners on. This change helped cut 24 minutes from the average game in 2023, which fell from 3:04 to 2:40 in a single season.
  • Between batters: a 30-second timer from one hitter's at-bat to the next.
  • Between innings: a 2:00 break in the regular season (2:55 in the postseason), started when the final out is recorded and run by the field timing coordinator — a real person, hired by the league, whose entire job is operating the game's clocks.

Run the timer math yourself, because this is where a no-clock sport becomes strangely clock-like. A nine-inning game schedules 16 or 17 between-inning breaks — 17 when the home team bats in the ninth — and at 2:00 apiece that is roughly 32 to 34 minutes of pure countdown baked into every broadcast. The next half-inning's first pitch is due the moment that break expires. Add timed mound visits, pitching changes and replay reviews on top, and you can see how a game with no game clock still lands inside a predictable window almost every night.

The minor leagues ran the experiment first. According to MLB, the pitch timer reduced average game time in the Minor Leagues by about 26 minutes — proof of concept MLB imported to the big leagues in 2023.

Game length by league and era

Competition / seasonLength (average nine-inning game)
MLB 2021 — all-time record3:10
MLB 2022 — final pre-timer season3:04
MLB 2023 — pitch timer debuts2:40
MLB 2024 — timer trimmed with runners on2:36 (lowest since 1984)
MLB 2025 — most recent full season2:38
Modern-era low — 1984 season average2:35
Minor League Baseball — where the timer was adoptedAbout 26 minutes shorter than pre-timer games
MLB postseasonNo fixed average; breaks stretch to 2:55 and extras start empty

The trend is the story. Average game time first crossed the three-hour mark in 2016 and peaked at a record 3:10 in 2021, a season in which 391 nine-inning games ran 3:30 or longer. In 2025, exactly three nine-inning games reached 3:30. The sport that once seemed to be drifting toward four-hour broadcasts now posts its fastest seasons since the mid-1980s: 2024's 2:36 was the lowest average since 1984's 2:35.

Factors that affect how long a baseball game takes

  • The timers themselves. Every pace setting — 15 seconds empty, 18 with runners, 30 between batters, 2:00 between innings — is a ceiling on dead time. Loosen them and games lengthen; 2023's 20-second setting with runners became 18 seconds in 2024 precisely to claw back a few more minutes.
  • Runners on base. A busy bases-loaded game runs slower than a pitcher's duel: the 18-second clock replaces the 15-second one, and pitchers are limited to two disengagements — pickoff tries or step-offs — per plate appearance before a balk is called, with every step-off resetting the clock.
  • Runs and pitching changes. Scoring is slower than retiring. High-scoring games mean more batters, more baserunners, more mid-inning pitching changes — each with its own warmup window.
  • Extra innings. The only truly unbounded factor. The automatic runner on second usually ends games quickly, but extras add innings with no ceiling, and postseason extras (no ghost runner) can marathon.
  • October baseball. Postseason games run longer than the regular-season average: between-inning breaks stretch to 2:55 for broadcast, and higher stakes mean more pitching changes and more replay reviews.
  • Weather and replays. Rain delays stop everything — a delayed game can double your evening — while umpire reviews add minutes the timers cannot compress.

Planning your viewing: timing a game with no clock

Baseball is the one sport where you cannot read remaining time off the scoreboard, so bring your own. A few timer-first habits:

  1. Budget 2:40, not 2:38. The league average rounds to about two hours and forty minutes; pad by 30-45 minutes if the game matters, since extras and a rainy forecast are the two things that break the model.
  2. Switch on at first pitch. Early innings are the fastest baseball ever played — every pitch is inside 15 or 18 seconds and every break is two minutes sharp. Tune in late and you have already missed the most efficiently timed chunk of the broadcast.
  3. Forget halftime — think half-innings. Baseball has no midpoint break; its natural pauses arrive with every half-inning and last 2:00. The seventh-inning stretch is the biggest of them, arriving a little under two hours into an average-length game.
  4. Work backward from your bedtime. A 7:05 p.m. local start at the league-average pace puts the final out around 9:45 p.m. — late extras push you past 10:15.
  5. Set a countdown. Start a 2:40 timer at the first pitch and you will know at a glance whether tonight's game is beating the league average — the purest way to watch a sport that refuses to keep time on itself.

That is the quiet irony of modern baseball: a game with no game clock is now, minute for minute, one of the best-planned broadcasts in sport. Nine innings, 27 outs, and a hundred small countdowns in between.

How long is halftime in the NFL?

NFL halftime is 13 minutes long. That is the number written into the NFL rulebook (Rule 4, Section 1, Article 3) for the regular season and the playoffs: “Between the second and third periods, there shall be an intermission of 13 minutes.” The same article names the official in charge — “The Back Judge will time halftime.” The one giant exception is the Super Bowl, where the break stretches to roughly 25 to 30 minutes so the stage can be assembled and the halftime show performed. In practical terms: a game that contains 60 minutes of playing time pauses for about a quarter of an hour in the middle, and the second half reliably starts less than 15 minutes after the first half ends.

What actually happens during the 13 minutes

The rulebook keeps halftime simple. Between the second and third periods there is an intermission of 13 minutes; play is suspended, and teams may leave the field. The Back Judge times the break — a notable assignment, because the rest of the game runs on the stadium electric clock, which the Side Judge supervises. Halftime is the one piece of game timing the rulebook hands to a single official.

For players, those minutes go fast. Then-Saints coach Sean Payton explained in 2013 that the short window leaves little time for elaborate strategy sessions: Guys are getting something to drink, going to the bathroom and we talk amongst the coaches on a few things we want to hit on. By the time a team has walked down the tunnel and come back out, most of the intermission is already spent.

Regulation time vs. real time

An NFL game is 60 minutes of playing time, divided into four periods of 15 minutes each. Add what the rulebook schedules around that: intervals of at least two minutes between the first and second quarters and between the third and fourth quarters, plus the 13-minute intermission. That is a minimum of 77 minutes of scheduled clock time before a single timeout is called.

Real time is another story. The game clock stops on incomplete passes, runners going out of bounds, score changes and possession changes; restarts run on a 40-second play clock; each team gets timeouts; and replay reviews, injuries and the two-minute warnings all stack additional real minutes that appear nowhere in the rulebook. Broadcast commercial breaks ride on top of all of it. That is why the clock says 60 minutes, the schedule says 77-plus, and your afternoon says considerably more — while halftime itself stays pinned to 13 minutes no matter how the first half went.

Halftime length compared: NFL, playoffs, Super Bowl, college

CompetitionHalftime lengthWhat sets it
NFL regular season13 minutesRulebook, Rule 4 Section 1 Article 3; timed by the Back Judge
NFL playoffs (non-Super Bowl)13 minutesSame rulebook intermission; no playoff extension
Super Bowl25 to 30 minutesStage build and teardown plus the halftime show
Super Bowl show aloneAbout 12 to 14 minutesThe musical performance inside the longer break
Thanksgiving holiday gamesRoughly 20 to 30 minutesProduced holiday shows; six to seven minutes longer than a normal week
NCAA college football20 minutesCollege rule set; seven minutes longer than the NFL
NFL quarter breaksAt least 2 minutesBetween the 1st-2nd and 3rd-4th quarters

The comparison that surprises most fans is the college one: NCAA halftimes last 20 minutes, a full seven minutes longer than the NFL break, which is why a Saturday game can feel like it drifts at the midpoint while an NFL game snaps back into action.

Why the Super Bowl break is twice as long

Halftime at the Super Bowl typically lasts between 25 and 30 minutes, roughly twice as long as a normal NFL week, and the reason is engineering, not entertainment: while the teams are in the locker room, crews handle the setup and teardown of the stage, lighting, audio equipment and field protection required to stage a stadium-scale concert without damaging the playing surface.

The show that all of that work supports is comparatively compact. The musical act is traditionally allotted 12 to 13 minutes, and the recent run of performances sits right on that number: Kendrick Lamar’s Super Bowl 59 set ran about 13 minutes, and Usher’s and Rihanna’s were both about 13. Even performers who bargain for more rarely get it — Usher negotiated for a 15-minute show before Super Bowl 58 and still came in just under 13.

Television wrote this clock: a short history

The NFL’s halftime has always been shaped by the broadcast schedule more than by locker-room needs. Regular-season halftime breaks were 15 minutes long — the same length as a quarter — until 1990, when the league shortened the break to 12 minutes. That 12-minute standard carried the league through the next three decades, and some coverage still repeats it today; the current rulebook lists the intermission at 13 minutes. The direction of travel has been consistent for more than three decades: the break stays short, and every scheduled exception exists to hold an audience in front of featured entertainment.

Special broadcast slots still bend the rule. Thanksgiving halftimes have historically run about six to seven minutes longer than a regular game — roughly 20 to 30 minutes in full — to fit staged holiday performances. And when Beyoncé headlined the halftime of the Ravens-Texans Christmas game streamed on Netflix in 2024, her set ran about 13 minutes: the show effectively became the intermission.

Factors that affect how long halftime actually runs

  • The broadcast window. Ordinary Sundays get the standard 13-minute break; featured holiday slots such as Thanksgiving stretch to roughly 20 to 30 minutes for produced entertainment.
  • Live entertainment. Any game with a produced halftime show needs setup and teardown time; only the Super Bowl scales this to 25 to 30 minutes.
  • First-half flow. The length of halftime is fixed, but its start time is not — replay reviews, scoring plays and injuries in the second quarter push the whistle that opens the break later into the broadcast.
  • Timing slippage. Officials aim for the exact figure, but precisely hitting 13 minutes is difficult in a stadium; the reliable real-world benchmark is that the second half starts less than 15 minutes after the first half ends.
  • Stage logistics at the Super Bowl. The size of the production — not the game — decides the length of the break.

Plan your viewing: time halftime like the Back Judge

The NFL trusts one official and one clock to run halftime. You can run the same system from your couch, and a countdown timer does the job better than the broadcast’s friendly reminders.

  1. Start a 13-minute countdown the moment the second quarter ends. That is the rulebook number the Back Judge is timing on the field.
  2. Use 15 minutes as your safety margin. Since the second half reliably starts less than 15 minutes after the first half ends, a 15-minute timer guarantees you are back in your seat before the third-quarter kickoff, snacks in hand.
  3. Super Bowl? Switch to a 30-minute timer. Plan for the full 25-to-30-minute break, and expect roughly 12 to 14 minutes of it to be the show itself.
  4. Know when halftime starts before it starts. The Super Bowl kicks off at 6:30 p.m. ET and halftime typically begins between 8:00 and 8:15 p.m. ET depending on game flow, scoring, reviews and commercials in the first half — so a 90-minute timer started at kickoff will have you looking up right as the break arrives.
  5. Tuning in for the second half only? Turn the television on when your halftime timer crosses the halfway mark; you will catch the back end of the studio show and the opening kickoff of the third quarter without sitting through the intermission.

Thirteen minutes is short by design — just long enough for adjustments and a breather, short enough to keep a national audience in its seat. Time it right, and you will never miss a second-half kickoff again.

guides.content:
How long is a basketball game?

Quick answer: an NBA game is 48 minutes of playing time, and in real time it runs about 2 hours 15 minutes from tip-off to the final buzzer. Men's college basketball plays 40 minutes (two 20-minute halves), women's college and FIBA games play 40 minutes in quarters, and American high school games are 32 minutes of clock. The playing clock is only half the story: halftime, timeouts, fouls and possible overtime stretch every one of these formats well past its face value.

Regulation time vs real time: why two clocks matter

Basketball runs on two very different clocks. The playing clock only runs while the ball is live. The real-time clock on your wall runs through every whistle, substitution and commercial break. The gap between them is enormous, and it is built directly into the rulebooks.

In the NBA, regulation play is four periods of exactly 12 minutes each — 48 minutes total — with overtime periods of 5 minutes each, according to the league's official rulebook. Around that playing time the rules schedule a 15-minute halftime, 2:30 between the first-second and third-fourth quarters (3:30 for national TV games), and 2:30 before any overtime. Each team is entitled to seven charged timeouts during regulation play. Mandatory TV timeouts run 2:45 in local games and 3:15 in national games, and any other team timeout still consumes 1:15 of real time.

Run the arithmetic on what the rulebook alone schedules: 48 minutes of playing time, plus a 15-minute halftime, plus 2:30 between the first and second quarters, plus 2:30 between the third and fourth. That is 68 minutes of guaranteed broadcast time on a local telecast — 70 on national TV — before a single timeout, foul or review is counted, which is why nobody has ever finished watching a basketball game in 48 minutes.

Before the 2017-18 season the league trimmed this padding: the maximum number of timeouts in a regulation game dropped from 18 to 14, each team was limited to two timeouts inside the final three minutes, and every team timeout was standardized at 75 seconds. Announcing the changes, Commissioner Adam Silver noted that the average NBA regular-season game had already declined from about 2 hours 23 minutes to approximately 2:15 — and that remains the single best planning number for how long an NBA game takes on your evening.

College basketball follows the same pattern with a shorter engine. Men's teams play two 20-minute halves (40 minutes total), women's teams play four 10-minute quarters, and both formats use a 15-minute halftime intermission and 5-minute overtimes. (The men have played 20-minute halves since the 1954-55 season, while the women's game switched from halves to quarters beginning in 2015-16.) In the women's quarter format the break between the first-second and third-fourth quarters is just 75 seconds — or the length of the electronic-media timeout. So while the college playing clock is 8 minutes shorter than the NBA's, the broadcast breaks built into each half keep real-world game nights in familiar territory.

How long is a basketball game by league and level?

LevelFormatPlaying timeHalftimeOvertime
NBA4 quarters of 12 minutes48 minutes15 minutes5 minutes
NCAA men2 halves of 20 minutes40 minutes15 minutes5 minutes
NCAA women4 quarters of 10 minutes40 minutes15 minutes5 minutes
FIBA (international)4 quarters of 10 minutes40 minutes15 minutes5 minutes
US high school (NFHS)4 quarters of 8 minutes32 minutes10 minutes (up to 15)4 minutes

A few details the table hides: FIBA schedules 2-minute intervals between the first-second and third-fourth quarters and before each overtime; high school games get 1-minute breaks after the first and third quarters, and the 10-minute halftime can be extended to a maximum of 15 minutes for special activities; and college overtime comes with a one-minute intermission before each extra period. Playing time is the floor, never the total.

Factors that affect the length of a basketball game

Television timeouts

The single biggest inflator. NBA rules require two mandatory timeouts in each period — 2:45 apiece on a local broadcast, 3:15 on a national one — and even after the 2017-18 cuts a regulation game can still absorb up to 14 team timeouts, eight of them those longer mandatory breaks. College broadcasts layer electronic-media timeouts into every half. A nationally televised game simply breathes more slowly than one streamed without commercials.

Fouls and free throws

Every foul sequence stops the clock while players walk to the line. In the men's college game the bonus begins with a one-and-one after the seventh team foul of a half, with two shots awarded from the tenth onward; the women's quarter format puts a team in penalty for two shots on the fifth foul of a quarter. In the NBA, the rulebook permits four team fouls per quarter without penalty — from the fifth onward, fouls are penalized with two shots. A hack-heavy fourth quarter can add a fat slice of dead time to any game.

Replays and official reviews

Official reviews of close calls — who touched the ball last, whether a shot beat the buzzer — freeze the game clock while the referees consult video. Reviews are usually brief but unpredictable, and they cluster in the final minutes, exactly when casual viewers are watching the clock most closely.

Overtime

Overtime periods are 5 minutes at the NBA, college and FIBA levels (4 minutes in high school), and they continue until someone wins. The longest Division I men's game on record — Cincinnati's 75-73 win over Bradley on December 21, 1981 — needed seven overtimes and 75 minutes of playing time, 35 of them after regulation. If you have a hard stop, an extra period is the wild card in your schedule.

The score itself

A 25-point blowout cruises: the clock keeps running, timeouts go unused, benches empty early. A one-possession game in the final two minutes produces fouls, reviews and timeouts on nearly every dead ball. Same 48 minutes of playing time; very different finishing times.

Planning your viewing: time it like a broadcast producer

Now that you know the numbers, put them to work. If tip-off is scheduled for 7:30 p.m., an average-length NBA game finishes around 9:45 p.m., so set expectations with the household accordingly. If you are joining late rather than leaving early, the same averages tell you when to switch the television on: for a 7:30 tip, tuning in around 8:45 to 9:00 lands you at the start of the fourth quarter with the outcome still live. A few timing tricks worth stealing:

  • Start a 15-minute countdown at the halftime horn. NBA and college halftimes are both exactly 15 minutes by rule, so one timer doubles as your snack alarm and your back-on-the-couch alarm.
  • Only care about the fourth quarter? Working from the 2:15 league average, the final period typically tips about an hour and a half after the opening jump — set a 1 hour 30 minute timer from tip-off and walk in for the pressure only.
  • Bedtime math for weeknights. A 2 hour 30 minute timer started at tip covers an average NBA game plus most single-overtime finishes; budget roughly an extra quarter-hour of real time for each additional extra period.
  • Practice with the shot clock. NBA teams get 24 seconds to shoot (14 off an offensive rim touch); college teams get 30 (20 off the rim). Perfect settings for driveway scrimmages and timer apps.

One last rule of thumb: the schedule tells you exactly when a game starts, but nothing tells you when it ends. Plan around the averages above, add cushion for a close finish, and the clock will never surprise you again.

guides.content:
How long is a hockey game?

60 minutes of playing time, about two and a half hours end to end. An NHL game is three 20-minute periods separated by two 18-minute intermissions, and because the game clock stops for every whistle, the real running time from puck drop to final horn typically lands near 150 minutes. A 7:00 p.m. puck drop usually wraps by roughly 9:30 p.m., and a game that needs overtime and a shootout pushes closer to 9:45.

NHL regulation time vs. real time

The rulebook side of the equation is exact. NHL Rule 77.1 sets the time allowed for a game at three 20-minute periods of actual play, and Rules 77.2 and 34.2 set the intermission at 18:00, timed from the moment the last official exits the ice. Add it up and only 96 minutes of your evening are actually scheduled: 60 minutes of hockey and 36 minutes of ice resurfacing. Everything else is stoppage time.

  • Playing time: 3 x 20-minute periods, played on a stopped clock. Play halts on every whistle and resumes at the faceoff, so a "20-minute" period never lasts 20 minutes of wall-clock time.
  • Intermissions: two breaks of 18:00 each, sized for a full resurface of the ice.
  • Stoppages: icings, offsides, goals and penalties freeze the clock, and league-run television commercial time-outs pad the broadcast, stretching each period to roughly 35 to 40 minutes of real time.
  • Tiebreakers: sudden-death overtime typically adds seven or eight minutes to the night, and a game that reaches a shootout finishes around two hours 45 minutes after the puck drops.

Before any of that, the evening has a runway: warm-ups, introductions and the anthems all happen before the clock ever starts, which is why the arena doors open well before the puck does. If you are timing the night from home, the moment that matters is the puck drop, not the listed start time.

So the honest answer to how long an NHL game lasts is: 60 minutes of sport wrapped in roughly 150 minutes of scheduling. The clock, not the scoreboard, is what decides your evening plans.

When 60 minutes is not enough: overtime, shootouts and playoffs

In the NHL regular season, a tie after regulation goes to a five-minute sudden-death overtime played three skaters a side. There is no full intermission first. The rulebook expects overtime to start roughly two minutes after the third period ends, once the ice has been shoveled. If overtime solves nothing, the game moves to a shootout: three rounds per team, then sudden-death rounds until one team wins the duel.

Three skaters a side is a wide-open format with just six skaters on the ice instead of ten, which is why overtimes rarely burn their full five minutes. In practice the average overtime adds only about seven or eight minutes to the night, and a game that reaches a shootout finishes about two hours 45 minutes after puck drop.

The Stanley Cup Playoffs do it differently. There is no shootout and no five-minute cap. Teams take a 15-minute intermission and then play full 20-minute sudden-death periods, over and over, until somebody scores. One overtime is common; the classics roll into a second, a third or beyond, and a June playoff night can stretch well past three hours.

How long is a hockey game by league and level?

CompetitionPlaying timeBetween periodsIf tied
NHL regular season3 x 20 min (60)Two 18-min intermissions5-min 3-on-3 overtime, then shootout
Stanley Cup Playoffs3 x 20 min (60)Two 18-min intermissions; 15 min before each OTUnlimited 20-min sudden-death periods, no shootout
NCAA men's college3 x 20 min (60)Two intermissions of 12 or 15 min5-min 3-on-3 sudden-victory OT, then a mandatory three-player shootout; postseason uses repeated 20-min sudden-victory periods
IIHF and Olympic3 x 20 min (60)Two 15-min intermissions5-min 3-on-3 OT plus shootout in round robin; 10-min sudden-death OT in playoff and bronze games; repeated sudden-death periods in gold-medal games

The pattern holds everywhere: 60 minutes of stop-time hockey is the global standard. What changes the length of your evening is the length of the breaks and the format of the tiebreaker. Olympic and world-championship games, with 15-minute intermissions, still take about two and a half hours on average to complete. College hockey trims the scheduled portion by up to 12 minutes by using 12- or 15-minute intermissions instead of the NHL's 18.

Factors that affect the length of a hockey game

  • Whistle count. Every icing, offside, frozen puck and goalie stoppage halts the clock, and every restart needs a faceoff. A chippy, turnover-heavy game simply has more clock pauses than a clean one.
  • Penalties. Power plays concentrate play and produce more whistles, and penalties that overlap or get reviewed add extra ceremony at the box.
  • Television commercial time-outs. The league schedules broadcast breaks during stoppages, and the rulebook expressly bars them after goals and icings, but they still add minutes to every period.
  • Coach's challenges and video reviews. A disputed goal can bring the game to a standstill while officials watch replays.
  • Injuries and equipment repairs. A downed player or a shattered pane of glass is unscripted dead time nobody can budget for.
  • Scrums and fights. Post-whistle pushing matches need sorting out, penalties need reporting, and players need re-alignment at the faceoff before the clock can run again.
  • The tiebreaker format. A regular-season overtime is a five-minute coin flip; a playoff overtime can add a full extra period, or three, to your night.

Planning your viewing: run the night like a game clock

Hockey is the most timer-friendly sport to plan around, because its structure is a stack of fixed countdowns: three 20-minute clocks and two 18-minute breaks. Here is how a typical NHL evening with the classic 7:00 p.m. start runs:

  1. 7:00 p.m. — puck drop. The pre-game runway of warm-ups, introductions and anthems is already over by now.
  2. About 7:40 p.m. — first period ends. An 18:00 intermission clock starts; the zambonis take the ice. Enough time for dinner, not enough for errands.
  3. About 7:55 p.m. — second period.
  4. About 8:35 p.m. — second intermission. Your last fixed 18-minute window of the night.
  5. About 8:53 p.m. — third period. If you only care about the outcome, this is the moment to switch the TV on: roughly 1 hour 55 minutes after puck drop.
  6. About 9:30 p.m. — final horn. If tied, overtime begins about two minutes later, and a game decided in overtime or a shootout typically finishes closer to 9:45.

Two practical timer tricks: set an 18-minute countdown the moment each intermission begins so you never miss a restart, and if the third period ends level, budget an extra 15 to 20 minutes before you assume the night is over.

One caveat: the playoff clock has no finish line. Because sudden-death periods repeat until a goal, a Stanley Cup game can overflow any countdown you set. From April through June, treat your two-and-a-half-hour estimate as a floor, not a ceiling.

The bottom line

A hockey game is 60 minutes of playing time, always. Everything wrapped around those 60 minutes — 36 minutes of intermissions, a rolling series of whistles, and possibly a five-minute overtime plus shootout — is what stretches puck drop to final horn to about two and a half hours. Block out the evening, set your intermission countdowns, and the clock will never surprise you.

guides.content:
How long is the Super Bowl halftime show?

The performance itself runs about 12 to 14 minutes, and the full halftime break at the Super Bowl lasts 25 to 30 minutes — roughly double the 13-minute halftime of a regular-season NFL game. Kendrick Lamar's 2025 set clocked in at 13 minutes 20 seconds, and Rihanna squeezed 13 songs into about 13 minutes in 2023. The rest of the extended break disappears into stage assembly, commercials, and studio analysis, which is a big reason the Super Bowl broadcast stretches to roughly three and a half to four hours even though the game itself contains only 60 minutes of playing time.

The rulebook number vs. what you actually watch

The NFL rulebook is refreshingly blunt about time. The 2026 Official Playing Rules define the length of the game as 60 minutes, divided into four periods of 15 minutes each, with intervals of at least two minutes between the first and second periods and between the third and fourth. On halftime, Rule 4, Section 1, Article 3 keeps it simple: between the second and third periods there shall be an intermission of 13 minutes, play is suspended while teams may leave the field, and the Back Judge times it. In a normal Sunday game, that is the whole story — whistle, 13 minutes, second half.

The Super Bowl breaks that template on purpose. With a stadium-sized stage, a television audience in nine figures, and the most expensive commercial slots of the year, the league stretches the intermission to 25 to 30 minutes, about double a regular-season break. The musical performance fills only 12 to 14 of those minutes; the remainder goes to the stage crew, advertising, and the network's studio team.

Run the math from a typical 6:30 p.m. ET kickoff. A first half that lasts about 75 minutes in real time, a 25 to 30 minute intermission, then roughly another 75 minutes of second half, plus timeouts, replays, reviews, and commercial breaks. The final whistle tends to land near 10 p.m. ET, which is how 60 minutes of football becomes a broadcast window of about three and a half to four hours. The 2024 edition ran even longer: it needed overtime — only the second in Super Bowl history — and became the longest Super Bowl ever played at 74 minutes and 57 seconds of playing time.

Super Bowl clock, segment by segment

What you are timingHow long it lastsGood to know
One NFL quarter15 minutes (official)The game clock stops constantly, so real time always runs longer
Full game, playing time60 minutesFour 15-minute quarters, per the rulebook
Break between quartersAt least 2 minutesBetween the 1st and 2nd, and 3rd and 4th quarters
Regular-season halftime13 minutesTimed by the Back Judge
Super Bowl halftime break25 to 30 minutesRoughly double a normal halftime
Halftime show performance12 to 14 minutes13:20 in 2025; 13 songs in about 13 minutes in 2023
Gap from halftime whistle to first noteAbout 12 minutesIn 2024 the half ended around 8:13 p.m. ET and the show began at 8:25 p.m. ET
First half, in real timeAbout 75 minutesThis is what sets the show's start time
Whole Super Bowl broadcastAbout 3.5 to 4 hoursThe longest edition (2024, with overtime) ran 74:57 of playing time

Factors that affect how long halftime runs

  • Stage build and teardown. The stage does not wait in the middle of the field all game. A crew with roughly 40 carts assembles it and can be performance-ready in about six minutes of on-field setup, and Sporting News documented a 12-minute gap in 2024 between the end of the first half at around 8:13 p.m. ET and Usher's first note at 8:25 p.m. ET. Building it, playing the show, and clearing it is why the break is doubled in the first place.
  • The medley the artist designs. There is no fixed performance length in any rulebook; the show's runtime is a production decision. Rihanna's set rushed through snippets of 13 songs in 13 minutes, Kendrick Lamar's ran 13:20, and Usher's and Bad Bunny's sets each carried 12 songs.
  • The pace of the first half. Incomplete passes, penalties, scoring plays, and timeouts all stop the game clock, so a first half floats around 75 minutes of real time against 30 minutes of playing time. A sloppy, penalty-filled half pushes the show later; a crisp one brings it earlier.
  • Commercials and studio analysis. Roughly half of the Super Bowl intermission is not the show at all. It is the most valuable advertising inventory of the television year plus network commentary, and the halftime performance is scheduled around it, not the other way around.
  • Overtime and the unexpected. Halftime itself is fixed, but the broadcast is not. The 2024 Super Bowl needed an extra period to be decided, stretching the whole night and producing the longest Super Bowl in history by playing time; the 2026 game, by contrast, ended in regulation.

Recent halftime shows, 2023 to 2026

Super Bowl LVII, February 12, 2023 — Rihanna. The shortest-feeling set of the modern era: 13 songs packed into roughly 13 minutes on Fox, a medley one critic described as rushing through snippets of hits, watched by more than 121 million viewers.

Super Bowl LVIII, February 11, 2024 — Usher. A 12-song career retrospective broadcast by CBS that drew 129.3 million viewers in the United States — the most-watched halftime show ever at the time, and now third on the all-time list.

Super Bowl LIX, February 9, 2025 — Kendrick Lamar. A precisely timed 13 minutes 20 seconds on Fox, watched by 133.5 million viewers — it edged Michael Jackson's 133.4 million from 1993 to become the most-watched halftime show on record.

Super Bowl LX, February 8, 2026 — Bad Bunny. At Levi's Stadium on NBC, the first Latino solo headliner ran a 12-song set with guests including Lady Gaga and Ricky Martin, drawing 128.2 million viewers — the fourth-most-watched halftime show in history.

Planning your viewing: run Super Bowl Sunday like a clock

If you only care about the halftime show — or you need to schedule dinner, a nap, or a commute around it — treat the evening as a series of timers instead of trusting the schedule on screen.

  1. Anchor on kickoff, not on the broadcast start. The pregame show runs for hours; the game itself has kicked off around 6:30 p.m. ET in recent years. Start your evening plan from that mark.
  2. Start a 75-minute countdown at kickoff. First halves run about 75 minutes in real time, and the two-minute warning of the first half — an automatic timeout in the rulebook — is your cue that the intermission machinery is about to move.
  3. Expect the first note between 8:00 and 8:30 p.m. ET. Sporting News projected around 8:00 p.m. for the 2025 show; the 2024 show did not begin until 8:25 p.m. If you are switching the television on just for the music, be watching by about 7:45 p.m. ET so a slow first half cannot beat you to it.
  4. Set a 15-minute timer when the stage crew appears. The medley runs 12 to 14 minutes, so a 15-minute timer fired at the first sign of the crew rolling staging onto the field will outlast the performance and catch the beginning of the post-show analysis.
  5. Budget 25 to 30 minutes from whistle to second-half kickoff. That is the true length of Super Bowl halftime. If you are stepping away, you have the show plus the commercial return before football resumes — set the countdown, not your intuition.

The bottom line

Twelve to fourteen minutes of music, inside a 25 to 30 minute break, inside a broadcast that runs about four hours from a 6:30 p.m. ET kickoff to the trophy. A regular-season halftime, by rule, is 13 minutes. The Super Bowl doubles it for one night a year so the biggest stage in television can be built, played on, and cleared before the third quarter kicks off.

guides.content:
How long is a football game (NFL)?

An NFL game contains 60 minutes of actual playing time — four 15-minute quarters — but an average game takes about 3 hours and 12 minutes from opening kickoff to the final whistle. The rulebook clock and the clock on your wall tell two very different stories, and the gap between them is packed with huddles, penalty explanations, replay reviews and roughly 45 minutes of commercials. Once you understand where the time really goes, planning your Sunday around a game — or timing your halftime errands to the minute — becomes surprisingly easy.

The rulebook answer: 60 minutes, four quarters

The NFL's official playing rules are refreshingly simple on this point. Rule 4 states that the length of the game is 60 minutes, divided into four periods of 15 minutes each. Between the first and second quarters, and again between the third and fourth quarters, the rules require intervals of at least two minutes while teams change ends of the field. Halftime is longer: the rulebook sets that intermission at 13 minutes, timed by the back judge.

Overtime adds a wrinkle. If the score is tied after four quarters, a regular-season game continues with a single 10-minute extra period — and if it is still tied when that period ends, the game ends in a tie. Postseason overtime periods run 15 minutes and repeat for as many periods as necessary until a winner is decided. That is why some broadcasts blow far past the average — an overtime game is longer by definition, and the extra football brings extra stoppages with it.

Regulation time vs. real time: where the extra two hours go

If only 60 minutes of football are played, why does the average broadcast run more than three hours? Because the game clock stops constantly — on incomplete passes, when a ball carrier steps out of bounds, after scores, during measurements — while real time keeps marching forward. Pro Football Network's breakdown of the modern NFL broadcast finds:

  • Live action is a sliver of the telecast. Roughly 18 minutes of actual gameplay fills an average NFL broadcast today — and a Wall Street Journal analysis in 2010 counted just 11 minutes of live action. The rest is build-up between snaps.
  • Commercials are the single biggest add-on. Advertising accounts for approximately 45 minutes of an average NFL broadcast — around 25 percent of the telecast, with 15 to 25 commercials per quarter and as many as 100 or more over a full game.
  • Dead time fills the gaps. The 40-second play clock resets between snaps, penalties require explanations, injuries stop play, and booth reviews stretch single decisions into multi-minute waits — all with the game clock frozen.
  • Halftime is a fixed 13-minute intermission by rule, though the studio coverage wrapped around it stretches the break you actually experience at home.

Add it all up and the pattern is clear: 60 minutes of clock time swells to roughly 3 hours and 12 minutes of real time. Whenever you are planning, think of an NFL game as a three-hour commitment with a quarter-hour of slack.

Game length by league and level

Playing time is nearly identical across most levels of football, so the differences in real-time length come from clock rules, halftime length and commercial load:

CompetitionPlaying time (rules)HalftimeTypical real-time length
NFL regular season60 min (4 × 15-min quarters)13 min~3 hr 12 min
NFL overtime, regular seasonOne 10-min period (may end tied)—Extends the broadcast further
College football (NCAA)60 min (4 × 15-min quarters)20 min max~3 hr 24 min
High school football48 min (4 × 12-min quarters)Varies by stateVaries by state
Super Bowl60 min (4 × 15-min quarters)~25–30 minRoughly 3.5 hours

The comparison that surprises most fans is the last one: because of the extended halftime show and the heaviest commercial load of the year, the Super Bowl is typically a three-and-a-half-hour evening even though its playing time is identical to any week in October.

Factors that affect how long a football game takes

  • Commercial breaks. The clearest driver of broadcast length: about 45 minutes of a typical NFL telecast is advertising, and marquee standalone games carry the fullest loads.
  • Style of play. Passing-heavy games stop the clock constantly — incompletions, sideline catches, scoring plays — while run-heavy games keep it rolling.
  • College football's extra football. NCAA games feature roughly 40 more plays than NFL games — a gap that has been shrinking toward 20 to 25 — plus halftimes that can run up to 20 minutes, which is why they average about 3 hours 24 minutes even after recent timing reforms.
  • Replay reviews and penalties. Every booth review and lengthy penalty discussion stops the game clock entirely while the broadcast clock keeps running.
  • Overtime. A tied game adds a single 10-minute period in the NFL regular season — and there is no upper bound in the postseason.

The leagues keep re-engineering the clock

Game length is not left to chance — both the NFL and college football have rewritten their timing rules in recent years:

  • College football's 2023 timing rules. After college games drifted to averages of around three and a half hours — roughly 20 minutes longer than the NFL — rule changes that keep the clock moving after first downs and out-of-bounds plays cut about 10 minutes from the average game.
  • The NFL's 2024 dynamic kickoff. Only 22.1 percent of kickoffs were returned in 2023, the lowest rate in NFL history, turning most kickoffs into a touchback followed by a commercial. The league's redesigned dynamic kickoff flipped that instantly: 70.5 percent of kickoffs were returned during the 2024 preseason. It is the clearest recent example of the league deliberately converting dead time into live plays.

Plan your viewing like a clock, not a guess

Because the averages are so stable, you can time a football Sunday with real precision:

  1. Anchor on the kickoff, not the schedule block. The average broadcast runs about 3 hours 12 minutes, so a 1:00 p.m. kickoff ends near 4:12 p.m. If you only care about the football itself, switch the TV on at the opening kickoff and start a three-and-a-quarter-hour countdown right then — skip the pregame show entirely.
  2. Time halftime to the rulebook. Regular-season halftime is a 13-minute intermission by rule, so set a 13-minute countdown when the second quarter ends — then add a little padding for the studio segment before the third quarter. For the Super Bowl, stage setup and teardown stretch the break closer to 25 to 30 minutes, so budget for that instead.
  3. Budget each quarter at 45–50 real minutes. Divide the 3-hour-12-minute average by four quarters of clock time and you get a reliable planning unit. If a quarter is running past 50 real minutes, expect a flag, a review or a scoring flurry to have eaten the difference.
  4. Keep your phone timer honest late in the game. The final two minutes of a close game are the least predictable stretch in sports — timeouts, incompletions and reviews can stretch them well beyond two minutes of real time. Never plan a hard stop for the moment the clock hits zero.
  5. Use the commercial time deliberately. With roughly 45 minutes of advertising in every broadcast, a game hands you dozens of two-minute windows — enough to run the dishwasher, flip the laundry or start dinner, if you trigger a short countdown at each break rather than drifting back whenever.

The short version: an NFL football game is 60 minutes of football that behaves like a three-and-a-quarter-hour appointment. Block the afternoon, set your timers around the 13-minute halftime, and let the league's own averages do the scheduling for you.

guides.content:
How Long Is Halftime in the NBA?

NBA halftime is 15 minutes long, on the arena clock, in every single game — the same scheduled break on a Tuesday night in November as in Game 7 of the NBA Finals. Around that fixed quarter-hour sits 48 minutes of playing time wrapped in a broadcast that averaged about 2 hours 13 minutes end to end in 2021-22, the most recent season in The Hoops Geek's game-length data. So when the second-quarter buzzer sounds, you get a quarter-hour of locker-room talks, highlight reels and snack runs before live basketball comes back.

The Official Rule: Fifteen Minutes Between Halves

The number comes straight from the NBA rulebook. Rule No. 5, Section II — Timing is blunt: "Fifteen minutes will be permitted between halves of all games." Not most games — all games. There is no playoff bonus minute and no Finals exception written into the playing rules; the league runs one identical 15-minute interval from opening night through the championship round.

The rulebook also fixes the smaller pauses around it. Between the first and second quarters, and again between the third and fourth, teams get 2:30 in locally televised games and 3:30 when the game airs on national TV, with 2:30 permitted before any overtime period. And halftime is not a loose suggestion: the rules state that at halftime the coach and players are to leave the court and go directly to their dressing room, without pause or delay. Fifteen minutes, enforced — then the third quarter.

Does halftime get longer in the playoffs or Finals?

Not on paper. The 15-minute interval applies to all games, and the league does not publish a different playoff figure. What changes in the postseason is everything around the rule — bigger stage productions, longer television windows and more ceremony — which is why a playoff or Finals break can feel longer than a regular-season one even though the rulebook number never moves. Playoff broadcasts as a whole do run longer, roughly 12 to 13 minutes more per game in The Hoops Geek's data, but that extra time comes from more timeouts, reviews and tighter finishes, not from a longer halftime.

Regulation Time vs. Real Time: Where the Other 85 Minutes Go

An NBA game is officially 48 minutes of play: four quarters of 12 minutes each, with five-minute overtime periods if the score is level. But nobody watches a 48-minute game. Even the fixed, scheduled skeleton runs past an hour:

  • 48:00 — regulation playing time, four 12-minute quarters
  • 15:00 — halftime
  • 5:00 to 7:00 — the two quarter breaks (2:30 each in local games, 3:30 each on national TV)
  • 5:00 more — every overtime period, plus 2:30 before it

Everything on top of that skeleton is live-basketball overhead: 1:15 team timeouts and the longer mandatory TV timeouts (2:45 in local games, 3:15 on national broadcasts), fouls and free-throw rallies, replay reviews, out-of-bounds restarts. The result, per The Hoops Geek's analysis of more than 6,000 regular-season games, is that a game that never reaches overtime ran 2 hours 13 minutes on average in 2021-22 — and average length has varied only between 2:12 and 2:14 in every season from 2016-17 through 2021-22. A game that goes to overtime simply keeps running from there: with one extra period, the average climbed to about 2 hours 35 minutes. Halftime, sitting near the midpoint, is roughly one-ninth of a typical broadcast and the single longest scheduled pause in an NBA night.

Halftime Length by League: NBA vs. NFL, NHL and Soccer

Put beside the other big leagues, the NBA's break sits in the middle of the pack — identical to soccer's cap, a touch longer than the NFL's, and shorter than the intermissions hockey takes twice a game.

LeagueMid-game breakPlaying clock
NBA15 minutes (one halftime)48 minutes
NFL13 minutes (one halftime)60 minutes
NHL18 minutes (two intermissions)60 minutes
Soccer (IFAB Laws of the Game)Up to 15 minutes (one halftime)90 minutes

A few details behind the table. Soccer's Laws of the Game grant players an interval at half-time "not exceeding 15 minutes," the same ceiling the NBA treats as its standard. The NFL rulebook is the stingiest: a 13-minute intermission between the second and third periods, timed by the Back Judge. Hockey goes the other way — NHL rules order play to resume promptly after eighteen minutes, and it happens after every period, largely so the ice can be resurfaced. Basketball fans get one break; hockey fans get two, and each of theirs is longer.

What Actually Happens During Those 15 Minutes

The moment the second quarter ends, both benches clear. Teams head to the locker room, where coaches rip up the game plan, adjust matchups, and — depending on the scoreboard — either calm nerves or light a fire. Trainers treat bumps; players refuel and reset.

Away from the benches, halftime is a show slot. In the arena, the break is filled with music and dance performances, slam-dunk exhibitions and fan contests; on television, networks cut to studio analysis from former players and coaches, with a wall of commercials built around it. In the final stretch of the break, both teams return to the floor for a short shooting warmup — the rulebook even refers to "halftime warm-ups" in passing — before the third quarter tips.

Factors That Stretch NBA Halftime Past 15 Minutes

Fifteen minutes is the rulebook figure, but the real-world break breathes. As Dunk or Three notes, special halftime performances, advertisements, specials, or shows can all push the actual halftime length up to 20 or 30 minutes during the postseason. What stretches the clock:

  • Produced entertainment. A concert-style act or choreographed arena show needs stage build and teardown time the standard turnaround does not budget for.
  • Showcase nights. Marquee, All-Star-style events lean on exactly these special productions — a produced concert slot rather than a quick turnaround — so the real break there runs long.
  • Broadcast padding. National TV windows wrap the break in extended studio segments and advertising before handing back to the arena.
  • Ceremonies. Tributes, award presentations and jersey retirements scheduled into the slot add minutes the 15:00 countdown never counted.
  • Game-flow spillover. A second quarter ending in a pile of replays, fouls or free throws pushes the buzzer — and everything that follows it — back a few minutes.

Plan Your Viewing: Timing Halftime Like a Clock-Watcher

Because the interval is fixed by rule, NBA halftime is one of the most schedulable pauses in sports. A few timing habits make game night easier:

  1. Start a 15-minute countdown at the second-quarter buzzer. That is the league's own number, and the arena scoreboard counts it down in front of you. When your timer beeps, the second half is imminent.
  2. Pad the timer when entertainment is on the card. If the night features a produced halftime show or ceremony, budget 20 to 30 minutes instead of 15 — the game will still be there when you get back.
  3. Switching the TV on mid-game? Aim near the hour mark. With an average broadcast of about 2:13, halftime usually lands close to the midpoint — tuning in roughly 60 to 70 minutes after tip-off typically catches the end of the first half, the break, or the opening minutes of the third quarter.
  4. Watch the arena clock, not the broadcast. Television pads the break with studio talk; the third quarter starts on the building's countdown. When the in-arena timer hits zero, live basketball is next.
  5. Use the break as a hard checkpoint. Fifteen minutes is enough to cook nothing, order everything and clean up nothing — but it is a perfect window for a snack run, a dog walk or a bedtime story if the game runs past the kids' hour.

Whether it is a kitchen timer on the pizza or a countdown on your phone, halftime is the one pause in an NBA evening you can genuinely set your watch by: 15:00 on the arena clock, every night of the season, with a little extra whenever the show runs long.
guides.excerpt: NBA halftime lasts 15 minutes by rule in every game — regular season to Finals — though special shows can stretch it longer. Here's how to time it.

guides.content:
How long is a quarter in a football game?

A quarter of football is 15 minutes of game-clock time in the NFL, college football, and the CFL, and 12 minutes under high school rules. But because the clock stops on every incomplete pass, penalty, and television timeout, almost no quarter lasts 15 minutes in real life. A typical NFL or college quarter occupies roughly 40 to 50 minutes of wall-clock time, which is why a game with just 60 minutes on the clock usually finishes in about three hours — and why the average college game in 2024 ran 3 hours and 27 minutes.

Regulation time vs. real time

Every rulebook defines the quarter as 15 minutes of playing time, not 15 minutes of your evening. The NFL rulebook states that "the length of the game is 60 minutes, divided into four periods of 15 minutes each," with intervals of at least two minutes between the first-second and third-fourth periods, and a 13-minute halftime between the second and third. The NCAA rulebook sets the same 60/15 structure for college games, with one-minute breaks between quarters — extendable for radio and television timeouts — and a 20-minute halftime in regular-season games, unless both schools agree before kickoff to shorten it. The CFL also plays four 15-minute quarters, and its rule book goes one step further: the kickoff to start the second half must take place exactly 16 minutes after the conclusion of the first half.

Real time is another story. The average NFL game runs just over three hours from kickoff to the final whistle, so once you subtract a 13-minute halftime and split what remains across four quarters, each NFL quarter takes roughly 40 to 45 minutes of real time. College games run longer: CBS Sports, citing the 2024 season, reported that the average college game lasted 3 hours, 27 minutes — tied for the second-longest season since the NCAA began tracking game length in 2008. With a 20-minute halftime, that works out to about 45 to 50 minutes of real time per college quarter. High school games, with only 48 minutes of total clock, are the shortest of all.

Quarter length by league and level

The table below shows how the same basic game shrinks and stretches across levels of play.

LevelQuarter lengthTotal game clockHalftime
NFL15 minutes60 minutes13 minutes
College (NCAA)15 minutes60 minutes20 minutes (regular season)
CFL15 minutes60 minutessecond half kicks off 16 minutes after the first half ends
High school (NFHS rules)12 minutes48 minutesset by each state's rules

One pattern stands out: the NFL, NCAA, and CFL share an identical 15-minute quarter, and the high school game is the only one that shortens it, to 12 minutes. The real differences in how long a game feels come from everything packed around those quarters — longer halftimes, heavier commercial loads, and different overtime systems — rather than the quarter itself.

Factors that affect the length of a quarter

  • Clock stoppages. The game clock stops for incomplete passes, ball carriers going out of bounds, penalties, scoring plays, and charged timeouts. Every stoppage is dead time: huddles, substitutions, and official conferences all happen while your watch keeps running.
  • Television timeouts. College broadcasts run on what CBS Sports calls a 4-5-4-5 model: four network breaks lasting two to three minutes per quarter, which become 5-5-5-5 once end-of-quarter breaks are added — potentially 36 minutes tacked onto a single broadcast.
  • Halftime length. An NFL halftime is 13 minutes; a college halftime is 20. That seven-minute difference explains a chunk of the gap between a three-hour Sunday broadcast and a longer Saturday one.
  • Replay reviews, injuries, and weather. These have no fixed cost. A long replay review can freeze the final two minutes of a half, and a weather delay can stop a quarter indefinitely.
  • Overtime. A tie at the end of the fourth quarter means extra football — and the pro and college codes handle that extra football very differently.

Overtime: extra football that is not on the schedule

In the NFL, a tied game goes to a modified sudden-death overtime. In the regular season it is a single 10-minute period in which both teams must have an opportunity to possess the ball — unless the kicking team scores a safety on the opening possession — and if the score is still tied when the period ends, the game ends in a tie. In the postseason, overtime periods are 15 minutes each, separated by two-minute intermissions, and play continues in 15-minute installments until a winner is decided.

College overtime is a tiebreaker, not a timed period. Each extra period consists of two possession series, with each team putting the ball in play at the opponent's 25-yard line. Beginning with the second extra period, a touchdown must be followed by a two-point try; from the third extra period on, every possession collapses into a single two-point attempt from the three-yard line. That is how marathon multi-overtime games happen: possessions simply alternate until the tie breaks, with no fixed ceiling on how long it can take.

Planning your viewing: timing a football broadcast like a stopwatch

Once you know the real-time math, scheduling your day around a game becomes simple arithmetic. Here is how to work the clock:

  1. Switch the TV on at kickoff, not at the start of the broadcast window. The average NFL game runs just over three hours, and USA TODAY pegged the minimum for watching a Super Bowl in full at 3 hours, 14 minutes. The average of the last 20 Super Bowls is about 3 hours, 37 minutes, and two of them have run past four hours — the longest reaching 4 hours, 14 minutes.
  2. Set a 13-minute halftime timer for NFL games. That is the rulebook number — enough time to cook a meal, place an order, or take a walk. For a college game, set the timer to 20 minutes, and for the Super Bowl, plan for much longer, since its halftime stretches to accommodate the show.
  3. Use the quarter breaks, not halftime, for quick tasks. The NFL gives you at least two minutes between quarters; college gives one minute, stretched longer when television needs it. These are your refill-and-check-your-phone windows.
  4. Estimate every quarter at about 45 real minutes. Joining at the start of the third quarter of an NFL game? Budget roughly 90 minutes plus halftime to reach a decision — more if the game goes to overtime.
  5. Do not leave at the two-minute warning. The NFL stops the clock for the two-minute warning inside the final two minutes of each half, and those final ticks are the slowest of the entire game, packed with timeouts and clock-stopping plays. Nothing is decided until 0:00 — or, in a tie, until overtime has run its course.

The bottom line

Fifteen minutes is the answer in the rulebook — 12 if you are watching a high school game — but 40 to 50 minutes is the answer on your watch. Treat every quarter as roughly three times its official length, add the halftime, and you can predict almost any game's finish time within ten minutes, whether you are planning dinner around the second half or setting a countdown to switch the coverage on.
guides.excerpt: A football quarter is 15 minutes of game clock in the NFL, NCAA and CFL — 12 in high school — but takes 40–50 minutes of real time.

guides.content:
How long is a tennis match?

A typical professional tennis match lasts about 90 minutes: around 1 hour 20 minutes for a straight-sets win in best-of-three, about 2 hours if it goes the distance, and about 2 hours 45 minutes for the best-of-five format played at the Grand Slams. Add warm-ups, changeovers, set breaks and possible weather delays when planning your evening, because tennis is the rare major sport with no game clock at all. A match ends when a player wins the required number of sets — whether that takes 30 minutes or, in the most extreme case on record, 11 hours and 5 minutes spread across three days.

Regulation time vs. real time: the sport with no clock

Soccer plays 90 regulated minutes and basketball runs four timed quarters. Tennis does the opposite: the rules set a target length, not a fixed one. Matches are built from points (four to win a game, with a two-point cushion needed), games (first to six, with a two-game margin, wins the set), and sets (first to two sets in best-of-three, first to three in best-of-five). If a set reaches 6-6, a first-to-seven tiebreak usually decides it — the tiebreak being tennis' one and only sprint to a finish line.

That structure is why "regulation time" in tennis is really just the format. Most tour events — the WTA Tour, the ATP Tour outside the majors, and doubles — play best-of-three. Grand Slam men's singles play best-of-five, the great lengthener of matches. On top of the tennis itself, real elapsed time includes the pre-match warm-up, short changeovers between games, a longer break at the end of every set, medical timeouts, and suspensions for rain or darkness. In 2010, darkness twice stopped the Isner-Mahut match before it finally ended on a third day — so the gap between scheduled start and handshake is always longer than the tennis.

Tennis match lengths by format and competition

The table splits typical durations — what you plan around — from the verified all-time records, the marathons that happen when two players refuse to lose.

Match typeDurationWhat to expect
Best-of-three, two quick setsAbout 30 minutesA one-sided blowout, done almost before you sit down
Best-of-three, tour averageAbout 90 minutesThe standard length for ATP and WTA tour events
Best-of-three, three close sets2 hours to 3 hours plusEvery set decided by the finest margins
Best-of-five, Grand Slam averageAbout 2 hours 45 minutesMen's singles format at all four majors
Best-of-five, typical range2 hours to 3 hours 20 minutesStraight-sets wins sit low; four or five sets push it high
Average length of one setJust over 40 minutesFaster on grass at Wimbledon, longer on clay in Paris
College (NCAA) dual match2 to 3 hoursDoubles plus singles, done inside 3 hours
Wimbledon 2010, Isner d. Mahut11 hours 5 minutes over 3 daysThe longest match in professional history
Wimbledon 2018, Anderson d. Isner6 hours 36 minutesA Wimbledon semifinal that stretched past six and a half hours
French Open 2004, Santoro d. Clement6 hours 33 minutes over 2 daysLongest French Open match
Australian Open 2012, Djokovic d. Nadal5 hours 53 minutesLongest Australian Open match
Longest women's match, 19846 hours 31 minutesVicki Nelson d. Jean Hepner, ending 6-4, 7-6 (13-11)

Factors that affect how long a tennis match runs

Best-of-three vs. best-of-five

Format is the single biggest lever. A best-of-five match cannot end before three sets are won, which drags the average up by about 75 minutes, and it allows matches to keep escalating — the fifth set at a Slam is where the famous marathons live.

Court surface

Surface changes rally length, and rally length changes everything. On average a set runs a little under 40 minutes on Wimbledon's grass, where points are short, and significantly over 40 minutes on the French Open's clay, where the ball sits up and rallies stretch out. The same two players can produce a 90-minute match at Wimbledon and a 3-hour war in Paris.

Tiebreaks and the deciding-set rules

Tiebreaks cap normal sets at 6-6, but the final set was historically the wild card. The US Open used a final-set tiebreak from 1970 all the way to 2018 — the only major to do so. The Australian Open introduced a first-to-ten "super tiebreak" at 6-6 in 2019; Wimbledon the same year used a first-to-seven tiebreak at 12-12; the French Open played advantage sets (win by two games, forever) until 2021. That patchwork ended in March 2022, when the ATP, WTA and ITF announced a standardized 10-point tiebreak at 6-6 in the deciding set of Grand Slam matches. This is the single most important timing change of the modern era: it put a ceiling on deciding sets and made another 70-68 fifth set impossible at the majors.

Pace of play

Between points, professional tennis plays under the ITF's 25-second serve-clock standard, which keeps servers and receivers moving and stops slow play from bloating a match. It cannot speed up the rallies themselves.

Serving dominance and weather

A match between two players who hold serve easily generates games without end — that is exactly how Isner-Mahut reached 70-68 in the fifth set, a deciding set that alone ran 8 hours and 11 minutes. Rain delays and the sunset at outdoor tournaments then stretch elapsed time further: the longest match needed three calendar days to finish.

The extremes: 11 hours, 5 minutes, 183 games

John Isner's 2010 Wimbledon first-round win over Nicolas Mahut, 6-4, 3-6, 6-7 (7-9), 7-6 (7-3), 70-68, is the longest match in professional history: 11 hours and 5 minutes of play across June 22-24, and a record 183 games. Around it cluster the other outliers — Anderson over Isner in 6 hours 36 minutes at Wimbledon 2018, Santoro over Clement in 6 hours 33 minutes at Roland Garros 2004, Djokovic over Nadal in 5 hours 53 minutes at the 2012 Australian Open, and the longest women's match, Nelson over Hepner in 6 hours 31 minutes in 1984, which included a 29-minute, 643-shot rally inside its 13-11 second-set tiebreak, plus Federer's 19-17 third set over del Potro at the 2012 Olympics. By rule, the pre-2022 records are unrepeatable at the Grand Slams.

Planning your viewing: how to time a match with no clock

No scoreboard tells you how much time is left, so you work from formats and averages.

  1. Size your timer to the format. Start a 90-minute countdown for a best-of-three tour match and a 2 hour 45 minute countdown for a men's Grand Slam match. If the timer expires, the match is almost certainly in a deciding set — reset for 45 minutes.
  2. Switch the TV on for the first match of a session, not a "not before" slot. Later matches start when earlier ones end — a listed time is only a promise not to start earlier. The opening match on a show court is the only one that reliably starts on time.
  3. Count sets, not minutes. At just over 40 minutes per set on average, a best-of-three match that has just started its second set has roughly 80 minutes of tennis left, and a men's match entering a fourth set is roughly two average sets from the finish.
  4. Use the set break as your halftime. Tennis has no mid-match interval, so the pause between sets is the natural moment for food, a stretch, or a quick check of the other courts.
  5. Record with generous padding. If you are DVRing, extend the recording window well past the scheduled slot — best-of-five matches routinely blow through evening schedules, and a deciding set since 2022 ends at 6-6 with a 10-point tiebreak, not after another hour of advantage games.

The short version: plan for about 90 minutes of tennis in a standard match, about 2 hours 45 minutes at the Slams, and keep your stopwatch handy — tennis is the one sport where the only honest answer to "how long?" is "until somebody wins."
