guides.content:
How long does a marathon take?

Quick answer: the average marathon finisher takes about 4 hours 30 minutes to cover the 26.2 miles. Recreational men average close to 4:21 and recreational women close to 4:51. At the sharp end, elite men now finish in about two hours — the world record is 1:59:30 — and elite women in roughly 2:10 to 2:16. Most big-city courses stay open for six and a half hours or more, so from the first gun to the final cutoff, a marathon is an entirely clock-driven event.

The distance is fixed. The clock is not.

A marathon is 42.195 kilometers — 26 miles 385 yards, the 26.2 miles every runner quotes. The distance was standardized in 1921 and traces to the 1908 London Olympic course, which ran from Windsor Castle to the White City Stadium. What a marathon does not have is a regulation playing time. There is no game clock, no halftime, no innings. The stopwatch starts when your start wave is released and stops when you cross the finish line, which means the answer to "how long" is simply your own pace multiplied by 26.2.

That makes the math refreshingly honest. A two-hour marathon averages 4:35 per mile. The average global finisher, at 4:32:49, is running about 10:25 per mile. Boston's fastest qualifying standard for young men, 2:55:00, works out to 6:41 per mile. Every marathon time prediction you will ever need is just division.

Regulation time vs. real time

Marathoners live with two clocks. Your net (chip) time starts when you personally cross the start line; your gun time starts when the race goes off. At mega-marathons that release tens of thousands of runners in waves, those two numbers can differ by many minutes. And your day is longer than your result either way: an early start in the runner village, a wait in your corral, 26.2 miles, the medal, the long walk out. The clock time is between 1:59:30 and about 6:30; the experience is most of a morning.

How long does a marathon take? Every benchmark compared

Runner or benchmarkTimeContext
Men's world record — Sabastian Sawe, London 20261:59:30First sub-2:00 in race conditions
Top three men, London 20261:59:30 to 2:00:28All under the previous record of 2:00:35
Women's world record (mixed race) — Ruth Chepngetich, Chicago 20242:09:56Fastest women's marathon ever run
Women's world record (women-only race) — Tigst Assefa, London 20262:15:41For races without men on the course
Average finisher worldwide (2018)4:32:49RunRepeat study of 107.9 million results
Average man / average womanabout 4:21 / about 4:51Same dataset
Fastest age band (30–50) vs. over-70s4:24 vs. 5:40Same dataset
Chicago Marathon course limit6:30:00Roughly 15:00 per mile
Boston qualifying, ages 18–34, men / women (2027 race)2:55:00 / 3:25:00Cutoff just to apply for entry
Boston qualifying, ages 80+, men / women4:50:00 / 5:20:00The oldest age band

Average marathon time by age and sex

RunRepeat's global study of 107.9 million race results put the average 2018 marathon finisher at 4:32:49 — but that single number hides a wide spread. Runners aged 30 to 50 are the fastest band, averaging about 4:24. Under-30s average about 4:32, runners aged 50 to 60 about 4:34, and finishers over 70 about 5:40. By sex, the average man lands near 4:21 and the average woman near 4:51. The gap shrinks dramatically at the elite level: the women's mixed-race record of 2:09:56 sits far closer to the men's elite times than the recreational averages would suggest.

Factors that affect how long a marathon takes

  • Fitness and target pace. 6:41 per mile earns a young man a Boston application; 10:25 per mile is the global average; 15:00 per mile is the survival pace at the back of a big race.
  • Age and sex. Averages climb gradually with age, which is exactly why Boston's qualifying standards step from 2:55 at ages 18–34 to 4:50 at 80-plus for men.
  • Course profile. Flat, fast city courses are where records fall; hills and bridges quietly tax your pace.
  • Weather. Cool, calm conditions produce the fast times; heat slows entire fields by minutes.
  • Start waves and congestion. In huge races the first mile can be a shuffle, and your gun time suffers even when your chip time does not.
  • Walk breaks and aid stops. Water-station queues and walk breaks cost seconds at a time, and those leaks add up across 26.2 miles.
  • The cutoff clock. Course limits like Chicago's 6:30 create a hard mathematical edge: slower than about 15:00 per mile and the race literally leaves without you.

Cutoff times: the clock that ends the race

The Chicago Marathon keeps its course open for 6 hours 30 minutes — about a 15-minute mile — and official race guidance warns that runners finishing after 4 p.m. may not be recorded as official finishers. Boston's famous cutoff works the other way: it is a performance bar you must clear before you even apply. For the 2027 race, men aged 18–34 need a prior marathon of 2:55:00 or faster and women 3:25:00, with the standards stepping up by age group all the way to 4:50:00 and 5:20:00 for runners aged 80 and over. Between entry standards at the front and course caps at the back, nearly every major marathon is bracketed by clocks at both ends.

Planning your marathon viewing: a timer fan's playbook

Marathons are wonderful television for clock-watchers, because everything reduces to predictable arithmetic. Here is how to time a race day like a professional:

  1. Compute the finish window before you switch the TV on. Find the published elite men's start time and add two hours — that is your likely winning moment. Tune in 15 to 20 minutes early and you will catch the race-winning break as it happens.
  2. Set milestone alerts, not just a finish alarm. On 1:59:30 record pace, the leaders pass halfway (13.1 miles) at about 59:45, 30 kilometers at about 1:25, and 35 kilometers at about 1:39. Those three checkpoints are where a record attempt lives or dies.
  3. Track a friend with pace math. A 4:30 runner is moving about 10:18 per mile: halfway near 2:15 elapsed, 20 miles near 3:26. Set alarms for those splits, then walk to the barricades with time to spare.
  4. Watch the sweep clock, not just the lead clock. At Chicago, the 15:00-per-mile pace vehicle marks the true back of the race, and the most emotional finishes of the day happen in the minutes just ahead of it.
  5. Count down to the gun, not to the broadcast. Television coverage pads heavily around the start; a countdown timer set to the official start time keeps your split math honest.

The months before the clock starts

The race lasts hours, but the making of it lasts months. Classic plans such as Hal Higdon's Novice 2 marathon program run 18 weeks and build to a longest training run of 20 miles in week 15 before tapering toward race day. When people ask how long a marathon takes, that is the honest full answer: roughly half a year of weekends, one long morning, and about four and a half hours on the clock for the average finisher.

So, how long does a marathon take? For the fastest man in history, 1:59:30. For the average runner, about 4:30. For the oldest Boston hopeful, a 4:50 qualifying mark, and for Chicago's final official finisher, 6:30. Pick your clock, set your timer, and settle in for one of sport's great four-hour spectacles.

How long is a boxing match?

A 12-round professional boxing match contains 36 minutes of actual fighting and lasts about 47 minutes from the first bell to the final bell — twelve rounds of 3 minutes plus eleven 1-minute rest periods between them. Wrap ring walks, fighter introductions, the decision and a post-fight interview around that, and a championship main event fills roughly an hour of broadcast. Most bouts are shorter: a 4-round fight is about 15 minutes bell to bell, women's world-title fights are fought over 10 rounds of 2 minutes (about 29 minutes bell to bell), and an Olympic bout is just three 3-minute rounds — 9 minutes of boxing, roughly 11 minutes bell to bell.

Scheduled time vs. real time

The length of a boxing match depends on which clock you are watching. The regulation clock is written into the rules: rounds of a fixed length, rest periods of a fixed length, and a scheduled number of rounds. The real-time clock is what you actually experience as a viewer, and it runs much longer, because ring walks, television production and undercard fights are not part of the bout but are part of the night.

The 12-round championship math

The Unified Rules of Boxing adopted by most American athletic commissions are blunt about the format: each round shall consist of a three-minute duration, with a one-minute rest period between rounds. Nevada, the sport's historical home, goes further and writes the ceiling into state law: no boxing contest may be more than 12 rounds, rounds must be no more than 3 minutes, and there must be a 60-second rest between successive rounds. That makes the arithmetic of a full championship distance fight fixed and predictable:

  • 12 rounds x 3 minutes = 36 minutes of boxing
  • 11 rest periods x 1 minute = 11 minutes of corner work
  • Total from first bell to final bell = about 47 minutes

Add ring walks, the announcer's introductions, the reading of the decision and the immediate aftermath, and a fight that reaches the final bell occupies roughly an hour of your evening from the moment the fighters enter the arena.

Why the event runs longer than the fight

Nobody tunes in for a single fight anymore. A typical televised card stacks several bouts before the main event, and each one carries its own ring walks, introductions and decision. Do the arithmetic with the table below and you can see why broadcast windows balloon: a five-bout card built from a 4-, a 6-, an 8- and a 10-round fight ahead of a 12-round main event contains 155 minutes of scheduled ring time — two full hours of actual boxing plus another 35 minutes of rest periods — if every contest goes the distance, before a single second of television padding. Early knockouts are the only thing that reliably shrinks the night.

Boxing match durations by bout type

Bout typeFormatFighting timeBell to bell
Men's world-title fight (championship distance)12 rounds x 3 min36 min~47 min
Men's 10-round main event10 x 3 min30 min~39 min
Men's 8-round bout8 x 3 min24 min~31 min
Men's 6-round bout6 x 3 min18 min~23 min
Men's 4-round bout4 x 3 min12 min~15 min
Women's world-title fight10 x 2 min20 min~29 min
Olympic / elite amateur (men and women)3 x 3 min9 min~11 min
Youth (U17) amateur3 x 2 min6 min~8 min

A few rows deserve explanation. The 12-round cap is a legal ceiling, not a default: professional bouts are approved at shorter scheduled distances — commonly 4, 6, 8 or 10 rounds — so undercard fights are much quicker than the headline act. Women's boxing at the top level is contested over 10 rounds of 2 minutes each, a full minute shorter per round and two rounds fewer than the men's championship format, as ESPN has documented in its coverage of the debate over three-minute rounds for women. In the amateur and Olympic code the format is identical for men and women — three rounds of three minutes with one-minute breaks between them, a schedule the women's senior code adopted in 2016 — per the World Boxing competition rules that govern the international amateur game, with World Boxing's U17 youth categories running the same three rounds shortened to 2 minutes each.

Factors that affect how long a boxing match lasts

  • Stoppage endings. Any round can be the last. Deontay Wilder's October 2022 comeback against Robert Helenius, a 12-round heavyweight main event, ended in the first round — the knockout punch landed at 2:57, three seconds before the bell, per ESPN. A bout built for 47 minutes of ring time was over in under three.
  • Cuts and injury stoppages. A ringside physician can halt a fight between rounds or during the action if a cut becomes too dangerous to continue. In the amateur code, World Boxing's rules allow the ringside doctor a maximum of one minute to treat an injury, once per bout per boxer.
  • Fouls and recovery windows. Low blows and accidental fouls stop the clock and open timed recovery periods. Under World Boxing rules, a boxer hurt by a low blow can be given up to one minute and 30 seconds to recover before the referee must decide whether the bout can continue.
  • The scheduled distance. The single biggest factor is set before anyone throws a punch: the commission-approved number of rounds. A 4-round fight cannot last longer than 15 minutes bell to bell no matter how dramatic it gets.
  • Round length itself. The women's 2-minute round compresses everything: a full 10-round women's title fight contains less fighting time (20 minutes) than an 8-round men's bout (24 minutes).
  • Broadcast production. Extended ring walks, waiting on a television window, replay reviews and in-ring interviews stretch the real-time length of a bout far past its athletic length.

One curiosity from the rulebook shows how literally boxing treats the clock: if a boxer is in the ring, fully attired and ready, and the opponent fails to appear within one minute of the bell being sounded, the referee awards the bout to the present fighter by walkover. Even a no-show is a timed event.

Planning your fight night around the clock

Run the fight on your own timer

Because professional boxing is nothing but fixed intervals — 3:00 of action, 1:00 of rest — you can run the entire evening from a countdown timer and always know exactly where you are. Start a 3-minute countdown when the bell rings and a 60-second countdown the instant the round ends; that second timer is precisely the race the corner teams are running. If you arrive mid-fight, multiply the completed rounds by four minutes and you know how much of the scheduled distance is left: a 12-round fight entering round 8 has used 28 minutes and has 19 minutes of ring time remaining if it goes the distance.

When to switch the TV on

  1. Start from the main event's advertised slot and work backwards. The main event goes on last, and boxing almost never runs meaningfully ahead of schedule, because every fight has a fixed minimum length.
  2. Estimate the undercard from the table. If the two featured supporting bouts are a 10-rounder and an 8-rounder and both go the distance, that is 70 minutes of bell-to-bell ring time, plus ring walks, decisions and gaps between fights — call it about an hour and a half for the pair.
  3. Adjust for probable early endings. A card full of mismatches usually runs fast; a competitive card where everything reaches the scorecards runs long.
  4. Set a countdown to the main event's expected ring walk and treat the 47-minute championship distance as your worst case: a 12-round fight that starts at 11:00 p.m. and goes the distance delivers its decision at roughly 11:50 p.m.

That is the quiet appeal of boxing for anyone who thinks in timers: it is one of the few sports where the maximum length of the contest is known to the minute before it begins. Twelve rounds, three minutes apiece, sixty seconds between them — the only unknown is whether the final bell gets the chance to ring.

How Long Is a NASCAR Race?

A typical NASCAR Cup Series race lasts about three hours from green flag to checkered flag. Official time-of-race figures from recent seasons land in a consistent band: 2:48:03 for the 300-mile Enjoy Illinois 300 at Gateway in 2024, 3:05:29 for Nashville's 400-miler in 2025, 3:10:52 for the 2024 Daytona 500, 3:23:56 for the 2026 Daytona 500, 3:53:26 for the caution-filled 2025 Daytona 500, and 4:25:08 for the Coca-Cola 600, the longest race on the calendar. One caveat: official race times stop the clock during red flags, so a rain-hit race can occupy far more of your day than the number suggests. The key thing to understand is that a NASCAR race is never a timed event — the distance is fixed, and the clock simply follows the cars.

Regulation vs. Real Time: NASCAR's Distance-Based Clock

In football or basketball, the rulebook sets a playing clock. In NASCAR, the regulation length of a race is a fixed distance — a set number of laps on a specific track — and the first driver to complete that distance wins. The Cup Series runs 36 points races per season, a number that still held in 2026, and scheduled distances range from 210.4 miles (400 laps around Martinsville Speedway's 0.526-mile short track) all the way to 600 miles (400 laps on Charlotte Motor Speedway's 1.5-mile oval).

Real elapsed time is just that distance divided by pace, plus everything that interrupts the pace:

  • Daytona 500: 200 laps on a 2.500-mile trioval equals 500.000 scheduled miles. William Byron completed it in 3:10:52 in 2024 at an average speed of 157.178 mph.
  • Coca-Cola 600: 400 laps on a 1.500-mile oval equals 600.000 miles — the longest single race of the year, run on Memorial Day weekend. Ross Chastain's 2025 victory took 4:25:08.
  • Standard 400-miler: Nashville Superspeedway's Cracker Barrel 400 is 300 laps on a 1.333-mile track, or 399.9 miles, and it ran 3:05:29 in 2025 — almost exactly the three-hour benchmark.

One structural rule shapes every modern race: since 2017, NASCAR has split each points race into three stages, with the top 10 finishers in the first two stages earning championship points under the format NASCAR announced in January 2017. Those stage endings force two scheduled caution periods per race — the closest thing stock car racing has to a halftime — and they are the most predictable time checkpoints in the sport.

How Long Marquee NASCAR Races Actually Took

Here are official time-of-race figures for recent editions of the Cup Series' marquee events, with the caution data that explains most of the spread:

Race (season)Track (length)Scheduled distanceTime of raceCautions
Daytona 500 (2026)Daytona International Speedway (2.5 mi)500 mi / 200 laps3:23:565 for 32 laps
Daytona 500 (2025)Daytona International Speedway (2.5 mi)500 mi / 200 laps + overtime3:53:268 for 47 laps
Daytona 500 (2024)Daytona International Speedway (2.5 mi)500 mi / 200 laps3:10:525 for 20 laps
Coca-Cola 600 (2025)Charlotte Motor Speedway (1.5 mi)600 mi / 400 laps4:25:088 for 52 laps
Cracker Barrel 400 (2025)Nashville Superspeedway (1.333 mi)399.9 mi / 300 laps3:05:297 for 35 laps
Cook Out 400 (2024)Martinsville Speedway (0.526 mi)210.4 mi / 400 laps + overtime2:52:075 for 51 laps
Enjoy Illinois 300 (2024)World Wide Technology Raceway (1.25 mi)300 mi / 240 laps2:48:035 for 32 laps

Two patterns stand out. Distance sets the floor: the 600-miler needs nearly four and a half hours, the 500-milers run three to three and a half, and the 300-miler comes in under three. Cautions set the ceiling: the Daytona 500 swung 42 minutes in two years — 3:10:52 with five cautions in 2024 versus 3:53:26 with eight cautions and 47 yellow-flag laps in 2025 — then swung back to 3:23:56 in 2026 when the caution count dropped to five again.

Notice the Martinsville row, the great counterexample. It has the shortest scheduled distance on this list at 210.4 miles, yet it still consumed 2:52:07 — and even that required an overtime finish that stretched the 2024 Cook Out 400 from 400 to 415 laps, about 218 miles. On a tight 0.526-mile paperclip the average speed was just 76.096 mph — less than half of Daytona's pace — and 51 of the 415 laps run were completed under caution. In NASCAR, short track does not mean short race.

Factors That Affect How Long a NASCAR Race Takes

Cautions and crashes

Every yellow flag bunches the field and burns laps at reduced speed. In the 2025 Daytona 500, eight cautions consumed 47 laps — the race data logs 23.4 percent of the event under caution with an average green-flag run of just 17.1 laps. That alone is the difference between a 3:10 race and a 3:53 race.

Stage breaks

Two planned cautions are baked into every points race. In the 2025 Daytona 500, the end of Stage 2 brought out a caution that ran from lap 132 to lap 137 — right on schedule at roughly two-thirds distance.

Weather and red flags

Rain can pause a race for minutes, hours, or a full day — the 2024 Daytona 500 was run on Monday, February 19 rather than its scheduled Sunday, and the 2025 edition's official caution breakdown includes a 14-lap rain caution from laps 10 to 23. When NASCAR throws a red flag, the official clock stops entirely until the track is ready; the 2025 Daytona 500 sat under three red flags totaling three hours, 36 minutes, and 33 seconds on top of its official 3:53:26.

Overtime finishes

If a caution comes out near the finish, NASCAR's overtime procedure adds laps so the race can end under green. The 2025 Daytona 500 was officially extended to 201 laps due to overtime — one lap beyond the scheduled 200 — and the 2024 Martinsville race stretched from 400 to 415. A few extra laps mean a few more minutes on your afternoon.

Track type and pace

Fast tracks cover distance quickly: Daytona averaged 157.178 mph in 2024, and Gateway's 1.25-mile oval got its 300 miles done in 2:48:03. Short tracks trade speed for contact — slower laps, more cautions, and races that run long for their mileage.

Planning Your Race Day: Timing a NASCAR Broadcast

Because every race distance is published before the green flag drops, NASCAR is one of the easiest sports to schedule around — if you think in laps instead of quarters. Here is how to time a race day:

  1. Block three hours for a standard race. A 400-mile race typically finishes near the three-hour mark (Nashville's 2025 race ran 3:05:29). Give a 500-miler about three and a half hours, and reserve a four-and-a-half-hour window for the Coca-Cola 600.
  2. Use the stages as your clock. Stage endings fall at roughly one-third and two-thirds of the scheduled distance — in the 2025 Daytona 500, the Stage 2 caution came out on lap 132 of 200. If you are joining late, skip straight to the final stage; that is where the race is decided.
  3. Start your timer at the green flag, not the broadcast. Pregame coverage can run long before the cars actually roll. When the green flag drops on a standard 400-miler, start a three-hour countdown — that is your realistic checkered-flag window.
  4. Count the cautions. Every yellow adds minutes of slow laps and pit stops. A race that has already logged six or more cautions will finish well past its typical slot — Daytona ran 3:10 with five cautions in 2024 and 3:53 with eight in 2025.
  5. Treat stage breaks as halftimes. Each stage-end caution lasts a handful of laps — a natural pause to refill snacks or check other scores. You get two guaranteed ones per race, and both end with a restart that resets the action.

The bottom line for your calendar: plan on about three hours for a typical Cup Series race, pad it toward four for superspeedway dates, and clear a full evening for the Coca-Cola 600. And if rain is in the forecast, leave the whole afternoon open — that is the one clock NASCAR cannot control.

How long does it take for eyebrows to grow back?

Most overplucked or shaved eyebrows do grow back, but they are slow about it. Expect the first visible new hairs in about 2 to 3 months, a complete eyebrow growth cycle of 3 to 4 months, and up to 6 months for a brow to fully fill in. Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Shilpi Khetarpal, MD, puts it plainly: give it at least two to three months to see hair growth, because the hair growth cycle for eyebrows runs between three and four months. The one real exception is brows that get plucked every single day. Repeated trauma can scar the follicles, and scarred follicles may stop producing hair for good.

The eyebrow regrowth timeline at a glance

All body hair cycles through growing, transition, and resting phases, so regrowth arrives in stages rather than all at once. From the day you put the tweezers down, here is what the timeline typically looks like:

MilestoneTypical timingWhat you will notice
First new hairs appearAbout 2 to 3 monthsFine, short hairs sprout in the sparsest patches. This is the soonest it is fair to judge results.
One complete growth cycle3 to 4 monthsThe full length of the eyebrow hair cycle, which is the minimum window for a brow to meaningfully rebuild itself.
Complete fill-inUp to 6 monthsIn a small 1999 study, all five people who fully shaved off one eyebrow had complete regrowth by six months.
Time to call a dermatologist4 months with no changeCleveland Clinic says if you still do not see the results you want after four months, it is time for prescription options and in-office treatments.

Results vary with hair density and color. In that 1999 study, the one female participant with naturally sparser, lighter-colored brows waited longer than everyone else for full regrowth, so a fine brow may need the full six months.

Why eyebrows grow back so slowly: the hair growth cycle

All body hair moves through three phases: anagen (active growth), catagen (transition), and telogen (rest and shedding). The hair on your head stays in anagen for two to eight years, which is why it can grow past your shoulders. Eyebrow hairs run the same cycle on far shorter shifts, and that is the core reason brows stay short and regrowth feels so slow.

PhaseWhat happensDuration for eyebrow hair
Anagen (growth)The follicle actively produces hair fiber2 to 3 months, versus 2 to 8 years on the scalp
Catagen (transition)Growth slows and then stopsAbout 2 to 3 weeks
Telogen (rest)The follicle lies dormant before the cycle restarts2 to 3 months

The resting phase is the hidden time sink. A follicle can sit dormant through an entire two-to-three-month telogen phase before the cycle restarts and a replacement hair grows in. A brow that looks completely lifeless at month one can therefore still fill in by month four with no treatment at all.

Why overplucked brows sometimes never grow back

The skin around your brows is thin and delicate, which makes its follicles easy to traumatize. Pluck a few strays every couple of weeks and the follicles recover. Pluck every day with a magnifying mirror and the story changes. "If you pluck your eyebrow hair every day, you're doing damage, maybe even causing scarring. Then, the hairs won't grow back," Dr. Khetarpal warns.

Medical News Today makes the same point in gentler terms: frequently plucking or waxing the eyebrows can damage the hair follicles, so the hair takes longer to regrow. With enough repeated damage, longer becomes never. Cleveland Clinic draws the same line in its guidance on madarosis, the medical term for eyebrow and eyelash hair loss: non-scarring loss usually regrows once the underlying cause is treated, but if whatever caused it significantly damaged your hair follicles, the hair loss might be permanent.

Factors that affect how fast your eyebrows grow back

  • Plucking frequency and technique. How traumatized the hair gets is the biggest controllable factor. Occasional precision plucking is recoverable; daily plucking is what leads to scarring.
  • Age. "As we get older, we lose some amount of hair — including eyebrow hairs," Cleveland Clinic notes, and Healthline adds that both men and women typically start noticing thinner hair in their 40s.
  • Thyroid function and nutrient levels. Both an overactive and an underactive thyroid can disrupt hair growth, and deficiencies in iron, vitamin D, or zinc are linked to hair loss.
  • Autoimmune and skin conditions. Alopecia areata attacks follicles directly and causes random spots of hair loss, trichotillomania (compulsive hair pulling) wears them out, and frontal fibrosing alopecia scars the frontal scalp and takes the brows with it. Each needs medical treatment, not patience.
  • Hormones and stress. Pregnancy and childbirth can send hormones into a tailspin and disorganize the normal growth cycle, and research links significant stress to temporary hair loss.

What actually helps eyebrows grow back

  1. Stop plucking, and throw out the magnifying mirror. Nothing else works while you keep re-traumatizing the follicles. Give the brows space and time to recover.
  2. Upgrade your tweezers and timing. Choose tweezers with an angled tip so you can pull in the direction of hair growth, skip rubber grips because they add friction and trauma, and pluck right after a shower when skin is soft and hairs slide out with minimal force.
  3. Feed the follicles. A balanced diet supports regrowth. Cleveland Clinic specifically suggests 3 to 5 milligrams of biotin daily, iron if you eat red meat fewer than two or three times a week, and omega-3s if you do not regularly eat fish or shellfish. Talk to your doctor before starting supplements.
  4. Consider minoxidil, with two cautions. Over-the-counter 2% or 5% minoxidil (Rogaine), though designed for the scalp, can also be used on thin eyebrows. It may cause a burning sensation if it gets into your eyes, and it has a field effect, meaning hair may grow elsewhere on your face wherever the solution drifts.
  5. Ask about prescription bimatoprost (Latisse). The topical used to lengthen and thicken eyelashes has been shown to help brows too, and it works by extending the growth cycle so hairs have more time to grow.
  6. Give any routine a full four months. That is one complete growth cycle. If there is still no improvement at four months, a dermatologist has stronger options.

Regrowth myths versus what the evidence says

  • Myth: castor oil regrows brows. Castor, coconut, and olive oil are popular home remedies, but the reports supporting them are anecdotal and none is a proven regrowth treatment.
  • Myth: shaving ruins regrowth. Shaving cuts hair at the skin surface without touching the follicle. In the 1999 study, every shaved eyebrow grew back fully within six months.
  • Myth: filling in brows slows regrowth. There is no evidence that eyebrow pencils or other makeup slow regrowth or affect thickness, though harsh products worn for long periods can irritate the area, so remove makeup gently.
  • Myth: a serum can resurrect brows plucked away decades ago. Growth serums can nudge intact but sluggish follicles. If repeated plucking has already scarred your follicles, the hairs will not grow back no matter what you apply.

When to see a dermatologist

The four-month checkpoint is the practical rule: if you have left your brows completely alone for four months and see no new growth, it is time for professional help. Go sooner if the loss comes with other warning signs. Fatigue, weight changes, or brain fog can point to thyroid disease, and loss that shows up in random spots suggests an autoimmune condition such as alopecia areata rather than overplucking. Dermatologists can prescribe topical corticosteroids, minoxidil, or off-label bimatoprost, and Cleveland Clinic also lists platelet-rich plasma injections and eyebrow hair transplants for stubborn cases. They can also tell you whether your follicles are dormant or permanently scarred.

The bottom line

Plan on 2 to 3 months to see the first new hairs, 3 to 4 months for a full growth cycle, and up to 6 months for complete fill-in. Stop plucking, ditch the magnifying mirror, eat for hair health, and consider minoxidil or a prescription option if you want to nudge things along. As Dr. Khetarpal puts it, "Most of the time, they grow back."

guides.author: Suraj Giri

guides.content:
How long do eyelashes take to grow back?

If the follicle is undamaged, most eyelashes grow back in about 6 weeks — and one complete growth cycle, from a new lash emerging to it shedding, takes 4 to 11 months. As long as the follicle is alive and undamaged, regrowth happens on its own schedule; the hard part is waiting out the cycle without making things worse.

The timeline feels slow because lashes are never synchronized. Your upper lid carries roughly 90 to 160 lashes arranged in five to six rows, and your lower lid about 75 to 80 lashes in three to four rows. Each follicle sits in a different phase of the growth cycle — an arrangement that lets lashes shed without leaving the eye unprotected — and that same staggering is why a bare spot refills gradually instead of all at once.

The eyelash growth cycle, stage by stage

Every eyelash moves through three phases: active growth (anagen), transition (catagen), and resting (telogen), after which it falls out and the follicle starts over. A 2023 clinical review in the American Journal of Clinical Dermatology maps the timings:

PhaseHow long it lastsWhat happens
Anagen (active growth)about 4 to 10 weeksThe lash grows from the follicle at roughly 0.12 to 0.14 mm per day.
Catagen (transition)about 15 daysThe follicle shrinks and the lash stops growing but stays anchored.
Telogen (rest and shed)about 4 to 9 monthsThe lash rests, eventually falls out, and a new one begins forming.
One complete cycleabout 4 to 11 monthsThe full lifespan of a single eyelash from regrowth to shedding.

Notice how long the resting phase is compared with the growing phase: a lash spends only 4 to 10 weeks actively growing but up to 9 months resting in place before it sheds. Stress can also push follicles into the resting phase early — a shedding pattern called telogen effluvium — and because that phase lasts months, stress-related thinning can take months to reverse as each follicle takes its turn re-entering growth.

Two other details from that research explain most of what people notice in the mirror. First, lashes grow slowly — about 0.12 to 0.14 millimeters per day — so weekly progress is subtle. Second, lash length is capped by the short anagen phase: scalp hairs keep growing for 2 to 8 years, but an eyelash gets only 4 to 10 weeks before its follicle moves on. That is why lashes stay short no matter how healthy you are, and why a regrowing lash needs its full growth phase to reach normal length.

How long until a specific gap fills in?

What happened to the lash — and whether the follicle survived it — matters more than anything else:

SituationTypical regrowthWhat to expect
Lash shed naturally or pulled out onceabout 6 weeksRegrows on its own if the follicle and eyelid are undamaged.
Lash cut, singed, or broken offabout 6 weeksThe follicle was never touched, so the same timeline applies.
Lashes lost to extensions or false lashesabout 6 weeks per shed lashExtensions and their glue can injure follicles — sometimes permanently — so stop the stress first and never rip them off.
Loss from chemotherapy or medicationvariesRegrowth often begins within several weeks of finishing chemo; ask your care team, as prescription options have helped post-chemotherapy lashes in trials.
Scarring injury or skin conditionmay not regrow on its ownDamage to the follicle itself needs a dermatologist or ophthalmologist.

Extension wear deserves a special mention because damage arrives from two directions at once: the extensions and the glue used to attach them can injure the follicle itself, causing temporary or even permanent damage, and removal can dislodge lashes that were still anchored. Lashes shed at removal generally regrow in about 6 weeks like any other lost lash — but only if the follicle underneath survived, which is why repeated heavy wear and rough removal are the habits most worth breaking.

Factors that affect how fast eyelashes grow back

  • Follicle damage. This is the single biggest variable. An intact follicle regrows a lash automatically; a scarred or destroyed one will not, no matter how long you wait.
  • Repetitive pulling. Tugging from extensions, aggressive makeup removal, or trichotillomania (compulsive hair pulling) slows replacement. Trichotillomania typically affects the longer lashes of the upper lid and leaves broken hairs of uneven lengths, and psychotherapy — not lash products — is the mainstay of treatment.
  • Skin and medical conditions. Blepharitis (eyelid inflammation that leads to rubbing and dislodged lashes), alopecia areata, thyroid disorders, and lupus are all documented causes of eyelash loss, and each needs its own treatment before lashes fully recover.
  • Medications and chemotherapy. Chemotherapy drugs and some thyroid medications, such as carbimazole and propylthiouracil, are known to thin lashes; timing of regrowth is tied to the treatment itself.
  • Age. Eyelash thinning and whitening are recognized signs of physiologic aging, so regrowth in older adults can be slower and finer.
  • Nutrition and hormones. Zinc deficiency has been reported to cause eyebrow and eyelash loss, and thyroid disease — over- or under-active — can interfere with hair growth across the lids.

Practical tips while you wait

  1. Stop the tug. Give extensions and strip lashes a break, and never yank them off. The eye area recovers quickly once you do: in a 2024 study of 31 regular extension wearers, dry-eye discomfort and tear quality both improved within four weeks of removal.
  2. Be gentle at cleanup. Soak eye makeup off with a gentle remover instead of scrubbing, and skip waterproof formulas that demand hard rubbing on nights you do not need them.
  3. Know which serum actually has evidence. Bimatoprost 0.03% (brand name Latisse) is a lash-growth treatment the US FDA approved for sparse lashes in 2008. In a randomized trial of 278 adults, 78.1% of the bimatoprost group showed at least a one-grade improvement in lash prominence by week 16, versus 18.4% on vehicle, with significantly greater length, thickness, and darkness too — and benefits were maintained through a year of use in later research. It is prescription-only, and eye redness (conjunctival hyperemia) was the side effect that stood out versus vehicle in trials, so it is a conversation for your doctor, not a checkout-aisle purchase.
  4. Do not overpay for castor oil promises. Castor oil is popular, but the evidence behind it is limited; at best it conditions lashes so they break less, which protects the length you already have.
  5. Feed the follicle. Zinc deficiency is a documented cause of lash loss, so an overall adequate diet matters more than any single supplement. Biotin is heavily marketed for hair, but unless a doctor has found a deficiency, save your money.
  6. See a professional if a gap will not fill. If a patchy spot shows no new short stubble after a couple of months, if lashes keep falling with redness, scaling, or itching, or if you cannot stop pulling them — see a dermatologist or ophthalmologist. Conditions like blepharitis and alopecia areata are treatable, and earlier treatment protects the follicles.

The bottom line

Losing lashes is almost always temporary: an individual lash regrows in about 6 weeks when its follicle is healthy, and one complete cycle tops out at 4 to 11 months. The fastest thing you can do for regrowth is also the cheapest — stop pulling, tugging, and gluing, protect the follicles, and let the cycle run. If the follicles are healthy, the lashes will come back; if they are not, a dermatologist or ophthalmologist has real tools, including the one FDA-approved growth serum, to help.

guides.content:
How long does a perm last?

A perm usually lasts between 3 and 6 months, and most people find the curl has relaxed enough to re-perm around month 3 or 4. The chemical process permanently reshapes the strands it touches — the catch is that your scalp keeps growing new, straight hair at roughly 1 cm (a little under half an inch) per month, so the style gradually grows out from the roots instead of wearing off in the shower.

How long each type of perm lasts

Not every perm is built to survive the same stretch of time. The technique your stylist chooses sets the clock before you even leave the salon.

Perm typeTypical lifespanWhy it lasts that long
Traditional cold perm (full head)3–6 monthsThe whole length is reshaped; it loosens gradually as new growth appears at the roots
Root permA few weeksOnly the root area is treated, so regrowth shows almost immediately
Straight (relaxing) permAbout 3 monthsTreated hair is reshaped straight rather than curled, and the result softens within months
Re-perm or touch-upBooked from month 3WebMD notes that a touch-up at month 3 may be safe

Healthline puts the classic full-head perm at three to six months depending on hair type and aftercare, while root perms fade in a few weeks and straight perms hold for around three months. WebMD and the cosmetology educators at Hair Professionals Career College agree on the three-to-six-month window for perms overall.

The perm life cycle, month by month

Here is what the average perm goes through between the salon visit and the day it retires:

  • Days 0–2 (setting): the curl is at its most fragile. Hair should stay dry and relatively untouched for the first 48 hours while the new bonds finish setting — advice shared by Healthline, WebMD, and Hair Professionals Career College.
  • Weeks 1–4 (tightest curl): the curl is usually at its tightest just after it sets and loosens from there. Resist restyling impulses: no dye for two weeks on either side of the appointment, per Hair Professionals Career College.
  • Months 1–2 (settling): the curl relaxes into its final shape. By the end of month 2, about 2 cm of straight regrowth is already pressing into the style at the roots, based on the roughly 1 cm per month growth rate documented in StatPearls' hair follicle anatomy reference.
  • Month 3 (touch-up zone): with around 3 cm of regrowth, roots visibly drop and the shape softens. WebMD says a touch-up at month 3 may be safe.
  • Months 4–6 (grown out): the line between permed and new hair becomes obvious, ends relax into looser waves, and most perms are retired by month 6.

The curl cannot simply be reactivated later, because hair replacement never stops. According to the Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care, the active growth phase of a scalp hair lasts years, followed by a short two-to-four-week transition phase and a resting phase of several months — there is always new hair pushing in behind the perm.

Factors that affect how long a perm lasts

Hair type and condition

Perms grip different hair differently. Healthline notes that thicker, slightly wavy hair tends to hold the process more easily, while thin, stick-straight hair often requires expert help. Hair Professionals Career College lists the type of perm solution used and the condition of your hair among the biggest factors in how long the result survives.

Length and amount of hair

Longer hair often keeps a perm longer — WebMD says perms on long hair are likely to last longer than perms on short hair — but sheer volume works against you at the salon, where Healthline cautions that the more hair you have, the more difficult a perm can be. Spiral perms work best on hair at least eight inches long, Healthline adds.

Rod size

Rod diameter decides the curl pattern from day one. Thicker rods produce looser waves and thinner rods produce tighter curls, according to Healthline — and a tight curl has more relaxing to do before it reads as straight, which can make it feel longer-lasting.

How fast your hair grows

Regrowth is the real countdown clock. Scalp hair grows about 1 cm per month, StatPearls reports, and Hair Professionals Career College names faster hair growth as a factor that shortens a perm's useful life. Fast growers see that straight band at the roots sooner.

Aftercare — especially the first 48 hours

The first two days decide a lot. Healthline recommends keeping hair dry and relatively untouched for 48 hours after a perm; WebMD calls letting the curl set during the first 48 hours the most important rule of perm care; Hair Professionals Career College says to wait at least 48 hours before shampooing and to skip combing entirely for the first 24 hours.

Sun, chlorine and humidity

The environment attacks a perm from the outside. Chlorinated water can have disastrous effects on perms, Healthline warns, and WebMD advises steering clear of chlorine, heat styling, and alcohol-based products once the first two days are over — it also cautions that humidity can cause frizz that ruins a fresh perm. The American Academy of Dermatology notes that sun can leave hair weak, dry, rough, faded and brittle — especially hair that has been permed or colored — and recommends a wide-brimmed hat outdoors.

How to make a perm last longer

  1. Keep hair dry and untouched for the first 48 hours. No washing, no swimming, no ponytails — the bonds are still stabilizing, and WebMD suggests skipping heavy workouts and cap-less showers while the curl sets.
  2. Do not comb for 24 hours, then detangle with a wide-tooth comb or your fingers instead of a brush, working from the ends upward, per WebMD.
  3. Delay the dye. Avoid coloring for two weeks before and after a perm, per Hair Professionals Career College, and wait at least a month after perming before dyeing, per Healthline.
  4. Skip heat styling. Blow-dryers and flat irons do not just risk damage — they physically loosen the curl.
  5. Moisturize regularly. WebMD recommends leave-in conditioner and protein treatments to prevent the dryness and frizz that make a perm look finished before its time.
  6. Protect the curl overnight. Sleeping on your stomach or side, or under a silk cap, reduces the friction that flattens curls — both are WebMD recommendations.
  7. Shade your hair outdoors. A wide-brimmed hat is the American Academy of Dermatology's own recommendation for permed hair in the sun.
  8. Trim every 6–8 weeks. Hair Professionals Career College recommends a trim every six to eight weeks to remove dry ends and keep the shape while you wait for re-perm day.

When should you get a perm redone?

Most people re-perm every 3 to 4 months. That cadence matches Healthline's suggested haircut schedule of every three to four months for permed hair and WebMD's guidance that a touch-up at month 3 may be safe. The tell-tale signs it is time: roughly 3 cm of straight regrowth pressing the roots flat, ends that have relaxed from curl into wave, and styles that no longer hold through the day. One caution — WebMD warns that perms are riskiest on hair that is already overly processed, weak, or damaged, so previously treated lengths deserve a lighter hand (or a break) at the next appointment.

How long does the perm appointment itself take?

Plan for a long sit. WebMD notes that getting a perm can take several hours end to end, with only about 15 to 20 minutes of that being the solution processing on the rods — the rest is sectioning, wrapping, rinsing, and neutralizing. Healthline puts the full appointment at one to five hours. Cost scales with length, per WebMD: roughly $30–$150 for short hair, $60–$200 for medium hair, and $80–$400 for long hair, so the touch-up every few months is worth budgeting in advance.
guides.excerpt: Most perms last 3-6 months before new growth softens the curl. Timeline, factors that shorten it, and aftercare to stretch it to month 6.

guides.content:
How long does hair grow in a month?

Scalp hair grows about 1 centimeter (a little under half an inch) per month, which works out to roughly 12 centimeters, or about 4.7 inches, in a year. That is the average rate cited by dermatology sources such as the Cleveland Clinic, and it is remarkably steady. Your personal number can sit above or below it: a worldwide study of 2,249 young adults from 24 ethnic groups measured clearly different growth rates between hair types, with African-textured hair growing more slowly and Asian hair faster on average. A single month of growth is small — often too little to see in the mirror — but it compounds, and the sections below show exactly what to expect and what moves the number.

The one-month timeline: what average growth adds up to

Because hair extends at a near-constant rate, you can project future length the way you would project interest on a deposit. The table below applies Cleveland Clinic's average of about 1 centimeter per month to the milestones people actually care about.

Time periodGrowth at the average rateIn inchesWhat you notice
1 weekAbout 0.25 cmAbout 0.1 inToo little to see without measuring
1 monthAbout 1 cmAbout 0.4 inFaint new length at the roots
3 monthsAbout 3 cmAbout 1.2 inThe first clearly visible change for most people
6 monthsAbout 6 cmAbout 2.4 inA haircut-length difference
12 monthsAbout 12 cmAbout 4.7 inA full year of visible progress

One caveat: the table tracks growth from the scalp, not the length you keep. Split ends, breakage, and trims subtract from what you actually see, which is why two people with identical growth rates can appear to grow at different speeds.

The hair growth cycle: why not every hair grows at once

Each follicle runs on its own clock through a repeating cycle of growth, transition, and rest. The phase durations below come from the Cleveland Clinic and a 2020 review of telogen effluvium published in Cureus.

PhaseWhat happensHow long it lastsShare of your hairs
Anagen (growth)The follicle actively builds the hair shaft2 to 7 yearsAbout 90%
Catagen (transition)The follicle shrinks and detachesAbout 2 to 6 weeksA small fraction
Telogen (rest)The finished hair rests, then sheds3 to 5 monthsAbout 10%

Two consequences follow. First, your maximum hair length is set by how long anagen lasts: at about 1 centimeter a month, a 2-year anagen phase caps hair near 24 centimeters (about 9 inches), while a 7-year phase could reach roughly 84 centimeters (about 33 inches). Second, everyday shedding is the cycle working normally — the American Academy of Dermatology calls losing 50 to 100 hairs a day normal.

Factors that affect how fast hair grows

Genetics and ethnicity

One major worldwide study — 2,249 adults aged 18 to 35 from 24 ethnic groups on five continents, published in the European Journal of Dermatology — found that growth rate differs by geographic origin, scalp area, and gender. African hair showed a slower average growth rate and lower density, Asian hair grew faster with a thicker diameter, and Caucasian hair showed high density. These are averages with wide individual variation, so ancestry points to a tendency, not your personal number.

Age and hormones

With age, hormone-driven pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) becomes nearly universal: it affects at least 80% of men and 50% of women by age 70, according to a 2023 therapy review in the journal Drugs. In pattern loss, follicles spend less time in anagen and become miniaturized, so hair both thins and falls short of its old maximum length. Childbirth shifts the cycle in a different way: new mothers typically see excessive shedding about two months after delivery, peaking around four months, with normal fullness returning within six to nine months.

Health shocks and stress

A cluster of stressors can push hairs into the resting phase early. The AAD lists losing 20 pounds or more, giving birth, high fever, an operation, recovering from an illness, stopping birth-control pills, and intense stress. The confusing part is the delay: because affected hairs rest for months before falling, shedding usually starts two to three months after the trigger, by which time most people have forgotten the cause. The growth rate itself generally recovers once the stressor has passed. When heavy shedding lasts longer than six months, dermatologists call it chronic telogen effluvium, a condition that most often affects middle-aged women.

Breakage: the fake slowdown

Constant tension from braids, cornrows, ponytails, and extensions causes breakage — and permanent loss if it continues, the AAD warns. Brushing 100 strokes a day causes split ends, and wet hair breaks more easily than dry hair. None of this slows the follicle, but it erases the length your follicles produced, which reads as slow growth in the mirror.

What actually speeds hair growth, and what does not

The trimming myth

Trims cannot make hair grow faster, because growth begins at the root — the dermal papilla inside the follicle, which draws blood supply and nutrients — not at the ends. Cutting the shaft never touches the machinery that builds it. Regular trims do keep ends intact and stop splits from traveling up the shaft, so they protect the length you already have; they simply do not add millimeters per month.

Minoxidil: the best-evidenced option

For people with pattern hair loss, topical minoxidil has the strongest evidence for changing growth dynamics. A 2019 review in Drug Design, Development and Therapy explains that minoxidil shortens the resting phase, shifts resting follicles back into active growth, and prolongs the anagen phase. A meta-analysis cited in the review reported a mean gain of 8.11 hairs per square centimeter for 2% minoxidil versus placebo and 14.90 for the 5% formulation; a five-year follow-up found peak regrowth at one year. The commitment is real, because stopping treatment leads to progressive hair loss within 12 to 24 weeks.

Practical tips: protect every millimeter you grow

  1. Measure before judging. Photograph a small section near your front hairline against a ruler on day one, then again exactly 30 days later. At the average pace you should record close to a centimeter.
  2. Handle wet hair gently. Wet hair breaks more easily when combed or brushed, so let it partially air dry before you style or comb it. The exception: if your hair is tightly curled or textured, brushing it when wet lowers the chance of breakage.
  3. Loosen daily styles. Alternate looser styles so no section is under constant tension; continuous pulling can lead to permanent hair loss, not just breakage.
  4. Cap the heat. Use flat irons on dry hair only, on a low or medium setting, and no more often than every other day.
  5. Skip the 100 strokes. Daily 100-stroke brushing is a split-end generator, not a growth ritual.
  6. Put shedding on a timeline. If you are clearly losing more than 100 hairs a day after a stressful event, mark the calendar: the shed usually appears two to three months after the trigger, and regrowth follows. If heavy shedding passes the six-month mark, see a dermatologist.

Set your expectations with the base rate — about a centimeter a month, roughly 12 centimeters a year — and judge progress in three-month blocks rather than week to week. Growth is slow, constant, and largely inherited; the part you control is how much of it you keep.

guides.content:
How long do nails take to grow?

Fingernails grow an average of 3.47 millimeters per month — about 3.5 mm, or roughly a centimeter every three months — while toenails grow just 1.62 millimeters per month. That is the finding of a University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill study published in the Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology, which tracked the nails of 22 healthy young adults over one to three months. At that pace, the American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) notes that an entirely removed fingernail can take six months or longer to regrow, while a toenail can take 12 to 18 months. In other words, a fingernail replaces itself in roughly half a year, but a toenail can need close to a year and a half of quiet, steady growing.

Nail growth timeline at a glance

Nail growth is steady rather than dramatic — not quite a millimeter a week on your fingers. Here is what the measured averages add up to over time.

MilestoneTime it takesWhat you will notice
About 3.5 mm of new fingernail1 monthA visible sliver of fresh nail below the cuticle after a trim
Roughly 1 cm of fingernailAbout 3 monthsAn old chip or stain has traveled about a centimeter toward the tip
Fully regrown fingernail6 months or longerA lost or removed nail is completely back
Fully regrown toenail12 to 18 monthsThe slowest reset on the body, so be patient

The regrowth figures come from the AAD's guidance on nails that are removed; the NHS gives the same picture, saying a fingernail that falls off after an injury should grow back within 6 months and a toenail can take up to 18. The monthly milestones are simple arithmetic based on the UNC study's measured rates.

Growth rate by nail: fingers, toes, and the digits in between

The UNC team measured nails on both hands and feet, and the differences between them were among the study's clearest findings.

NailGrowth rateFull regrowth time
Fingernails (average)3.47 mm per month6 months or longer if the nail is removed
Toenails (average)1.62 mm per month12 to 18 months
Little (pinky) fingernailGrew slower than the other fingernailsA little behind the finger average
Great (big) toenailGrew faster than the other toenailsStill many months, within the toenail range

One popular claim the study did not support: there was no significant difference between right-hand and left-hand nail growth, so the oft-repeated tip that the nails on your dominant hand grow faster is not backed by these measurements.

How a nail grows: three stages

Stage 1: The matrix creates the nail

Nails start growing in the nail matrix, an area of living tissue tucked under the skin behind your cuticle — Cleveland Clinic describes it simply as the place where nails start to grow. The cells it produces harden into the nail plate. Because the matrix is hidden, most people never think about it — until an injury or illness interferes with it and the effects appear on the visible nail as it grows out.

Stage 2: The nail plate rides forward

The hardened plate is pushed slowly forward across the nail bed toward your fingertip. A nail cannot repair itself in place; damage, stains, and grooves are locked into the plate until they travel past the free edge and are trimmed off. This is why a stain from dark polish or a bruise under the nail takes months to disappear — the mark itself is not healing, it is moving.

Stage 3: Interruptions are recorded as Beau's lines

When illness, severe stress, or injury briefly stalls the matrix, the pause gets recorded as a groove across the nail — a Beau's line. Cleveland Clinic notes that these lines grow out gradually after you recover or treat the underlying cause, a process that takes about six months, and the NHS likewise says the deep lines that appear when you have been ill should grow out. The nail you can see today is, in effect, a multi-month record of your recent growth history.

Factors that affect how fast nails grow

  • Which nail it is. Fingernails outgrow toenails by more than two to one: 3.47 versus 1.62 millimeters per month in the UNC measurements.
  • Which digit. The little fingernail grew measurably slower than the other fingernails, and the great toenail grew measurably faster than the other toenails — both statistically significant differences.
  • Age and sex. Younger participants and men tended to grow nails faster, though with 22 people in the sample those differences were not statistically significant.
  • Nail biting. Onychophagia, the medical term for habitual nail biting, was also associated with faster growth — again without reaching statistical significance.
  • Illness and stress. According to the AAD, a fever, injury, chemotherapy, or major stress can cause nails to grow slowly or stop growing.
  • Chronic conditions and circulation. Cleveland Clinic lists diabetes, hypothyroidism, peripheral artery disease, and Raynaud's phenomenon as long-term conditions that can interfere with blood flow to the nail matrix.
  • The modern era itself. The UNC researchers concluded that nail growth rates have increased compared with estimates conducted decades ago.

When slow nail growth signals something

Slow growth on its own is rarely an emergency, but your nails quietly record information about the weeks before you could see it. Dermatologists suggest watching for these signs:

  • Deep grooves across the nail (Beau's lines). The AAD explains these mean something slowed or stopped your nail growth for a while.
  • A gap in the nail. When something causes a nail to stop growing completely for a time, you may see an actual gap, the AAD cautions.
  • Yellow, thickened nails that seem to have stopped. This can be a sign of something going on inside the body, per the AAD — lung disease and rheumatoid arthritis are two possible causes of yellow nails.
  • Nutrition clues. Cleveland Clinic lists zinc deficiency and not eating enough protein among the causes of Beau's lines. The NHS adds that spoon-shaped nails curving inward can signal iron-deficiency anaemia.

The AAD's bottom-line advice: if you cannot think of anything that could explain slowed or stopped nail growth, see a dermatologist.

Tips for growing (and keeping) healthy nails

  1. Trim after a bath or shower. Nails are softer then, the AAD notes, so trimming is easier.
  2. Use a nail clipper or nail scissors, and cut fingernails almost straight across, rounding only a little at the corners to keep them strong.
  3. Cut toenails straight across. This reduces the chance of a painful ingrown nail.
  4. File in one direction. The AAD recommends pulling the file across the nail in the same direction each time, because filing back and forth can weaken nails.
  5. Leave your cuticles alone. Cuticles protect the nail root, so the AAD advises against cutting or pushing them back.
  6. Measure like a researcher. The UNC team had participants mark the nail close to the cuticle with a file, then record the date and the distance from the cuticle to the mark; one to three months later they measured again. Mark yours, set a monthly reminder, and you will learn your personal rate — the study's averages were 3.47 mm a month on fingers and 1.62 mm on toes, but individuals vary.

The bottom line

How long do nails take to grow? Fingers add about 3.5 millimeters a month — roughly a centimeter every three months, and six months or more to fully replace a lost nail — while toenails grow 1.62 millimeters a month and need 12 to 18 months for a full regrow. Nothing measured in the study sped nail growth up meaningfully — even the apparent boost from nail biting fell short of statistical significance — but you can protect the matrix: guard against trauma, keep cuticles intact, eat adequately, and treat the illnesses and deficiencies that pause growth. Then mark the nail, set a timer, and let biology do the rest.
guides.excerpt: Fingernails grow about 3.5 mm a month — roughly 1 cm every 3 months — and take 6+ months to fully regrow; toenails take 12–18 months.

guides.content:
How long does paint take to dry?

Latex wall paint is dry to the touch in about 1 to 2 hours and ready for a second coat in 4 hours, while oil-based paint needs 6 to 8 hours to dry to the touch and 24 hours before recoating. Those are the baseline numbers from Glidden's and Sherwin-Williams' published guidance. Full cure — when paint reaches its optimum performance — takes far longer: two to three weeks for latex and acrylic, and roughly 5 to 15 days for oil-based paint, according to Sherwin-Williams and Benjamin Moore. Cold air, high humidity, or thick coats can stretch every one of those timers.

Dry, recoat, cure: the three clocks people confuse

Paint does not simply "dry" once. Sherwin-Williams splits the process into two measures, and recoat timing sits between them: "dry time is how long paint takes to be dry to the touch," while "cure time refers to how long paint needs to exhibit optimum performance results." Treating those as the same thing is how fresh walls get dents, lap marks, and peeling corners.

1. Dry to touch

The surface no longer feels tacky and light touch leaves no mark. For interior latex that is roughly one hour — Benjamin Moore says acrylic paint "can dry in one hour," and Sherwin-Williams lists 1 to 2 hours for latex and acrylic. Oil-based paints are far slower: 6 to 8 hours to the touch by Glidden's guidance, and Benjamin Moore puts oil-based drying as high as 8 to 16 hours.

2. Recoat-ready

Dry to the touch does not mean ready for coat two. The paint film still contains moisture and solvent working its way out. Glidden's rule: latex can be safely recoated in 4 hours, oil-based in 24 hours. The label on your specific can overrides every generic number — as Glidden puts it, labels on all paint cans specify the dry and recoat times for that particular paint.

3. Full cure

This is the finish line most DIYers never wait for. Sherwin-Williams says acrylic and latex paints typically take two to three weeks to cure, while oil-based paints take as little as five days — its reference table shows 5 to 15 days for oil-based coatings, and Benjamin Moore agrees oil-based paint "can cure in just five days." Benjamin Moore adds the sequencing rule: paint cannot cure if it is not dry. Nothing makes paint cure faster; you can only get it drying sooner.

Paint drying time chart by paint type

Paint typeDry to touchReady to recoatFull cure
Latex / acrylic (water-based)1-2 hours4 hours2-3 weeks
Oil-based (alkyd)6-8 hours24 hours5-15 days
Spray paint (aerosol)Up to 8 hoursFollow labelUp to 48 hours

Primers run on their own, faster schedule. Sherwin-Williams notes that latex-based primers are typically dry to the touch 30 minutes to an hour after application, while oil-based primers take one to three hours. Aerosol products can take up to 8 hours to dry and up to 48 hours to cure, which matters if you are spraying furniture or trim rather than rolling walls.

Factors that affect how long paint takes to dry

Benjamin Moore names the three main drivers plainly: "temperature, humidity and airflow are the three main components that affect the dry time of paint." Paint type and coat thickness do the rest. Here is what each condition does to your timeline, with the numbers manufacturers actually publish.

ConditionEffect on drying time
Around 77F / 25CBenjamin Moore's optimal painting temperature; it calls 35-100F (about 2-38C) the acceptable range.
Below 50F / 10CTraditional latex should not be applied this cold — Sherwin-Williams' standard guidance is a 50F minimum (specialty exterior products such as Duration, Resilience, and SuperPaint allow down to 35F / 2C).
Below 60F / 16CTraditional latex needs temperatures above 60F to cure properly, because warmer temperatures are needed for the latex particles to coalesce, or melt together (Sherwin-Williams).
Above 100F / 38CThe film can dry before it has a chance to properly adhere to the surface (Sherwin-Williams); heat can also cause wrinkling, blistering, and peeling (Benjamin Moore).
High humidity"Moisture is the enemy" of fast dry times (Sherwin-Williams); drying takes "considerably longer" (Glidden); keep the surface more than 5F / 3C above the dew point (Benjamin Moore).
Still airCirculating air is a great way to make paint dry faster — fans and ventilation are the fastest legitimate accelerators (Sherwin-Williams, Benjamin Moore).

Humidity deserves special attention indoors. Sherwin-Williams advises against opening the windows on a humid day and suggests installing dehumidifiers around the room you just painted; Glidden recommends closing the windows and turning on the air conditioning or running a fan — and Benjamin Moore notes that air conditioners also act as dehumidifiers. Coat thickness is the other silent time-thief: Glidden warns that paint applied too thickly takes considerably longer to dry, and Benjamin Moore says to keep each coat light and even and avoid overloading your brush. Horizontal surfaces are where DIYers most often apply too much.

Second-coat timing mistakes that ruin finishes

Almost every streaky, blotchy paint job traces back to the wait between coats. These are the four errors manufacturers warn about most:

  • Recoating before the first coat is fully dry. Glidden is blunt: paint recoated too early takes considerably longer to dry, may dry gloppy and uneven, and can end with a discolored or streaky finish. Sherwin-Williams adds that additional coats applied too soon "will result in uneven dry times and uneven coverage."
  • Trusting your eyes instead of the label. Benjamin Moore recommends two coats for the best hide and color development, and tells painters to check the recoat recommendation on the back of the can, confirming the paint is dry to the touch first. Glidden says the same: labels list the tested dry and recoat times for that exact formula.
  • One thick coat instead of two thin ones. All three manufacturers recommend thin, light, even coats — Benjamin Moore's phrasing is to keep each coat light and even and avoid overloading the brush. Two light coats dry faster in total than one heavy one and hide better.
  • Rushing with heat. Benjamin Moore does not recommend heaters, infrared heat lamps, or heat guns, noting that an 11-degree (Celsius) swing in temperature can potentially impact the paint's color. Sherwin-Williams gives the same warning: heat changes can affect the overall color.

How to make paint dry faster (without wrecking it)

  1. Ventilate the space — open windows when the air outside is dry and warm, so moisture-laden air leaves the room; Benjamin Moore cautions that the outside air must not be more humid than the air inside.
  2. Run a fan. Sherwin-Williams and Benjamin Moore both recommend keeping it a few feet away and aimed at an indirect angle rather than straight at the surface — and Sherwin-Williams says to make sure the blades are clear of dust and debris that could stick to the wet paint.
  3. Run the air conditioning or a dehumidifier on muggy days; the AC doubles as a dehumidifier, and Sherwin-Williams suggests installing a couple of dehumidifiers around the painted room.
  4. Apply thin, even coats and resist overloading the brush — especially on horizontal surfaces.
  5. For exterior work, paint early enough in the day's temperature window: Sherwin-Williams notes most exterior products require at least 4 hours of dry time before moisture can settle on the surface, and oil-based products need a minimum of 8 hours at temperatures above 70F / 21C.
  6. Read the can before you start and schedule the second coat around the printed recoat time, not around dinner.

When can you actually use the room?

Once latex is dry to the touch, the room is usable again — but treat the walls gently. Cure time is defined by both Sherwin-Williams and Benjamin Moore as the point where paint exhibits optimum performance, so hold off on scrubbing, washing, or leaning furniture against the film for the full two to three weeks latex needs to harden. Oil-based coatings reach full performance in 5 to 15 days, and aerosol finishes in up to 48 hours. If rain hits before exterior paint has thoroughly dried, Benjamin Moore warns the film may form bubbles — wait a day or two before doing anything, because the bubbles may subside on their own; any that persist mean the surface has to be scraped, sanded, cleaned, and repainted.

The short version: plan a painting day around the 4-hour latex recoat window, keep the air warm, dry, and moving, and give the finish its full cure before you demand anything from it. The wall rewards patience; the label already did the testing for you.

guides.content:
How long does it take for caulk to dry?

Quick answer: caulk dries in stages, and the first stage is fast. DAP Alex Plus acrylic latex skins over in about 2 to 5 minutes and is paintable in 30 minutes, silicone sealants are tack-free in 10 to 30 minutes, fast-cure 100% silicone is water-ready in 30 minutes, conventional silicone waits 12 hours before water exposure, and silicone fully cures in 24 to 48 hours. The timing depends on which of the two caulk chemistries is in your gun, water-based acrylic latex or moisture-curing silicone, and on the temperature, humidity, and thickness of the bead you lay down.

The trap behind the question is that a caulk label can mean four different things by "dry": skin-dry, paintable, water-ready, and fully cured. A bead can pass the touch test in minutes and still wash out if you aim the shower at it that same night. Here is what each stage means, using published times from DAP, GE Sealants, and Gorilla.

The four stages: skin-dry, paintable, water-ready, fully cured

Stage 1: Skin-dry, or tack-free

This is when the surface of the bead stops being sticky. DAP says its Alex Plus acrylic latex caulk skins over in about 2 to 5 minutes, which is your entire window to tool the bead smooth, while DAP's 100% silicone kitchen-and-bath formula is tack-free in 10 to 20 minutes and GE lists its Silicone 2 as tack-free in 30 minutes. Skin-dry only means a thin outer film has formed; the core of the bead is still soft and stays that way for hours.

Stage 2: Paintable

DAP Alex Plus can be painted within just 30 minutes using either latex or oil-based paints. That speed is where latex holds a decisive advantage, because standard 100% silicone is not paintable at all: Gorilla lists its 100% silicone sealant as paintable "no," GE's Advanced Silicone 2 Kitchen & Bath sealant is labeled non-paintable, and DAP's guidance for silicone is to paint the surface first and apply the sealant afterward.

Stage 3: Shower-ready, or water-ready

Modern fast-cure silicones are startlingly quick at this stage. GE's Advanced Silicone 2 Kitchen & Bath Sealant is water-ready in 30 minutes, and Gorilla describes its 100% silicone sealant as 30-minute water-ready. Conventional formulas sit at the other end of the scale: DAP's kitchen-and-bath silicone is ready for water exposure in just 12 hours, and DAP's siliconized Kwik Seal Ultra is designed to tolerate water in as little as 4 hours. If your tube's label does not say, treat 24 hours as the safe default.

Stage 4: Full cure

Full cure means the whole bead, surface to core, has reached its final rubbery strength. GE's FAQ says its silicone is water-resistant in as little as 30 minutes and cures within 24 hours, and GE's Silicone 2 specification lists full cure at 24 to 48 hours. Only after full cure should you scrub the joint, put the bead under stress, or count on the published waterproof performance.

Caulk dry and cure times by type

Caulk type (example product)Skin-dry / tack-freePaintableWater-readyFull cure
Acrylic latex (DAP Alex Plus)Skins over in 2–5 min30 min, latex or oil paintUse a wet-area formula for tubs and showersNot published
Siliconized sealant, wet areas (DAP Kwik Seal Ultra)Dries in about 4 hours—4 hours—
Fast-cure 100% silicone (GE Advanced Silicone 2 Kitchen & Bath; Gorilla 100% Silicone)—No30 min24 h typical
Conventional 100% silicone (DAP 100% Silicone Kitchen & Bath)10–20 minNo12 hours24 h typical
General-purpose 100% silicone (GE Silicone 2)30 minNo30 min24–48 hours

Manufacturers publish these figures for moderate conditions. GE says plainly that cold weather means slower cure times, and because silicone needs moisture in the air to cure, very dry air can leave a bead lagging too, which is one reason GE Silicone 2 hedges with a 24-to-48-hour cure window instead of a single number.

While you are planning the job, it helps to know how long the bead will last once cured. GE's FAQ says a high-quality silicone sealant should last 3 to 5 years in a shower, depending on use, ventilation, and cleaning habits, and that with proper prep GE silicone sealants can last 5 to 20 years depending on use and exposure. Its Advanced Silicone 2 Kitchen & Bath product carries a 10-year mold-free product protection claim. In a busy bathroom, plan on inspecting the tub and shower joints every few years rather than waiting for a leak.

Factors that affect caulk drying time

  • Chemistry: drying versus curing. GE's FAQ draws the line clearly: acrylics dry fast while silicones cure more slowly. Latex caulk gives up its water and hardens; silicone has to chemically react with moisture in the surrounding air.
  • Humidity. Silicone needs moisture in the air to cure, as GE's FAQ explains. That cuts both ways: humid air feeds the reaction, while heated winter air or a desert-dry climate can stretch cure time toward the 48-hour end of GE Silicone 2's published range.
  • Temperature. GE is blunt about it: cold weather means slower cure times. Gorilla specifies its silicone sealant is best used above 40°F. A bead laid down in a cold garage or a drafty January window frame simply will not keep pace with the label.
  • Bead depth. Thicker layers take longer to cure, GE notes. A deep filler bead closing a wide gap can lag well behind a thin finish bead laid beside it, because the cure works inward from the exposed surface.
  • Formula differences within the same category. "Silicone" alone tells you almost nothing about the schedule: DAP's kitchen-and-bath silicone waits 12 hours for water while GE's fast-cure formula is rated at 30 minutes. Always read the specific tube in your hand.

Practical tips while your caulk dries

  1. Tool the bead immediately. Alex Plus skins over in 2 to 5 minutes, and Gorilla says to smooth its silicone right after application, before a skin forms. Smooth it with a finishing tool or gloved finger in one pass; dragging across a skinned surface tears it.
  2. Paint latex caulk at the 30-minute mark, gently. DAP allows latex or oil-based paint within 30 minutes. Lay the paint on lightly rather than scrubbing it into the fresh bead.
  3. Give silicone a full day before heavy use. A 30-minute water-ready rating means the bead resists water contact, but GE still gives silicone 24 hours to cure fully, so schedule the first long, steamy shower for the next day and do not scrub or pick at the joint until then.
  4. Paint first when using silicone. Because 100% silicone rejects paint, DAP recommends painting the surface before the silicone is applied. The alternative is a paintable latex or siliconized sealant if the color has to match.
  5. Keep the room warm while curing. Since cold slows the cure, avoid leaving a fresh bead in an unheated bathroom overnight in winter; give it a stretch of moderate temperatures instead.

What if caulk is still tacky after 48 hours?

A silicone bead that has not cured after two full days usually points to the conditions, not the clock. Revisit the three factors GE flags: cold weather slows the cure dramatically, very dry air starves the moisture-cure reaction, and a bead laid too thick cures from the outside in and can lag deep inside. Warm the room, wait another day, and test a corner of the bead before assuming the tube itself was bad. Latex caulk that stays soft is a different story, since it dries by losing water, so persistent softness in a thick latex bead usually means it needs more time, warmth, or airflow.

How long should you actually wait?

For painting over fresh latex caulk: 30 minutes. For the first shower after re-caulking a tub: as fast as 30 minutes with a fast-cure silicone, about 4 hours with a siliconized sealant such as Kwik Seal Ultra, or 12 hours with a conventional silicone, though letting any caulk sit overnight is the comfortable margin. For full, no-reservations cure: 24 hours, stretching toward 48 in cold, dry, or thick-bead conditions. The extra half-day costs nothing compared with digging out a bead that washed out of the joint.
guides.excerpt: Acrylic latex caulk skins over in 2-5 minutes and is paintable in 30 minutes; silicone is tack-free in 10-30 minutes, water-ready in 30 minutes to 12 hours, and fully cured in 24-48 hours.
