guides.content:
How long does it take for concrete to cure?

Concrete needs 24 to 48 hours before it is safe to walk on, about 7 days before it can carry light vehicle traffic, and a full 28 days to reach its specified design strength. That 28-day figure is not arbitrary: measuring compressive strength at 28 days is standard industry practice, which is why engineers, specifiers and ready-mix suppliers treat it as the finish line. Confusingly, a slab can feel rock-hard within a day while the real curing process has barely begun, because curing is a chemical reaction rather than simple drying.

Curing vs. drying: what actually hardens concrete

When cement mixes with water, a reaction called hydration begins: compounds in the cement dissolve and grow into interlocking crystals that bind the sand and stone together. That reaction, not the loss of water, is what turns a wet mix into concrete. Drying refers only to moisture evaporating from the surface — a slab that is dry to the touch may have completed just a fraction of its potential strength gain.

This distinction matters because hydration needs water to continue. QUIKRETE's own product data warns that in hot, dry or windy weather water is lost to evaporation, which hinders the hydration reaction and can cause finishing difficulties and shrinkage cracking. The cement and concrete FAQ published by the American Cement Association (formerly the Portland Cement Association) likewise notes that concrete continues to harden and gain strength over time, with most of that strength developing in the first few weeks after placement. In other words, the worst thing you can do to fresh concrete is let it dry out.

Concrete curing timeline: how long to wait for each use

The wait depends on what you plan to do with the slab. The timeline below reflects standard concrete in moderate weather; mix types designed for rapid strength gain move much faster, as the second table shows.

Use or milestoneWait timeWhat has happened by then
Put strain on a set fence post24 hoursQUIKRETE's data sheet says to wait 24 hours before a post is subjected to any strain
Walk on the slab24 to 48 hoursHard enough to walk on without leaving footprints, but keep cars, bicycles and skateboards off
Park a car on a driveway7 to 10 daysSlab has cured to at least 70% of full strength and can support a car and heavy furniture
Full design strength28 daysMaximum strength reached; ready for normal foot and vehicle traffic
Heavy trucksAfter 28 daysOnly now for very heavy vehicles such as garbage trucks and moving vans

Stage 1: The first 24 to 48 hours

The mix stiffens, bleed water evaporates and finishing is completed. The surface becomes solid enough to walk on, but the slab is at its most fragile — one freezing night or a drying wind in this window can do permanent damage, which is why cold-weather protection matters most now.

Stage 2: Days 3 to 7 — rapid strength gain

Hydration accelerates, and a standard QUIKRETE Concrete Mix reaches a tested 1,500 psi at 3 days and 2,500 psi at 7 days. By seven to ten days the slab has cured to at least 70% of its full strength and can support a car and heavy furniture. Manufacturers recommend keeping the curing going the entire time: 5 days of moist curing in warm weather of 70°F or higher, extended to 7 days in cooler weather between 50°F and 70°F.

Stage 3: Days 7 to 28 — approaching full strength

Strength gain slows but continues steadily toward the specified design strength. The same standard mix tests at 4,000 psi at 28 days. This is the period people cut short, and it shows: a 3-day-old slab is rated at 1,500 psi, while the same concrete at 28 days is rated at 4,000 psi, so every extra day of patience adds real load capacity.

Stage 4: Beyond 28 days

Curing never truly stops. As the American Cement Association explains, concrete continues to harden and gain strength over time — 28 days is simply the agreed testing age, not the point where the chemistry ends.

How mix type changes the cure time

Not all bagged concrete cures at the same pace. High-early and rapid-hardening mixes trade a short working time for strength that arrives days sooner, which is why they cost more.

MixEarly strength28-day strengthWalk-on time
Standard concrete mix (No. 1101)1,500 psi at 3 days; 2,500 psi at 7 days4,000 psi24 to 48 hours
High-early mix (QUIKRETE 5000, No. 1007-80)1,500 psi at 1 day5,000 psi10 to 12 hours
Rapid-hardening mix (Q•Max Pro, No. 1004-81)3,000 psi at 24 hours6,500 psi3 hours
Fast-setting mix (No. 1004)Sets in 20 to 40 minutes4,000 psiFor setting posts without mixing

Factors that affect how long concrete takes to cure

Temperature

Hydration is temperature-dependent. QUIKRETE's data sheet states that in near-freezing temperatures the hydration process slows considerably, and it stretches the recommended moist-curing period from 5 days to 7 days when weather is between 50°F and 70°F. At the other extreme, heat accelerates setting but robs the mix of the moisture hydration needs.

Freezing

Fresh concrete must be protected from freezing during the first 48 hours; ice forming in young concrete permanently damages strength. If temperatures below 32°F are expected, cover the pour with plastic sheeting or insulation blankets.

Moisture retention

Moisture is the single biggest lever a homeowner controls. According to the Concrete Network, concrete moist-cured for 7 days is about 50% stronger than concrete left uncured — a large gain from nothing more than keeping the surface wet for a week.

Wind, sun and low humidity

Hot, dry or windy conditions pull water out of the surface faster than hydration can use it, which QUIKRETE warns can hinder the reaction and lead to shrinkage cracking. On such days, plan to mist, cover or shade the slab from the moment finishing ends.

Mix design

As the table above shows, high-early and rapid-hardening products reach in 24 hours what a standard mix takes 3 days to achieve, at a premium price. For a fence post that is a fair trade; for a large patio, a standard mix with proper curing is usually the better value.

Practical tips for curing concrete correctly

  1. Start curing as soon as finishing is done. QUIKRETE instructs that curing should begin as soon as possible after the surface can take treatment — every hour of delay lets moisture escape.
  2. Wet-cure for 5 to 7 days. Keep the surface continuously wet with a lawn sprinkler, soaking hose or soaked burlap; the Concrete Network also lists ponding, or flooding the slab, as an option. Interruptions set the curing process back.
  3. Or apply a curing compound. A spray-on acrylic cure-and-seal is the most convenient method. Apply it soon after final finishing, when the surface is hard and damp but not wet, and make sure coverage is complete.
  4. Use plastic sheeting when water is impractical. Lay it flat, seal the joints and anchor the edges so wind cannot lift it. QUIKRETE lists plastic sheeting alongside wet burlap and waterproof paper as a proper curing method because it prevents moisture loss.
  5. Do not apply curing compound in the wrong conditions. Skip it if rain or temperatures below 50°F are expected within 24 hours.
  6. Protect the pour from freezing for 48 hours. Use plastic sheeting or insulation blankets whenever the forecast dips toward 32°F.
  7. Schedule your loads around the timeline. Rope off the slab for the first two days, keep vehicles away for a week to ten days, and reserve the surface for full use at 28 days.

The bottom line

Walk on it in 24 to 48 hours, park on it after 7 to 10 days, and treat it as fully cured at 28 days — then keep it moist for that crucial first week, because a slab that never dries out early is dramatically stronger than one that did.
guides.excerpt: Concrete is walkable in 24-48 hours, drivable in 7-10 days, and fully cured at 28 days — because curing is hydration, not just drying.

How long does acrylic paint take to dry?

A thin film of acrylic paint is dry to the touch in roughly 10 to 30 minutes under normal room conditions — Liquitex cites 10–12 minutes for thin applications, while Winsor & Newton lists 10–20 minutes for thin films of its student-grade Galeria acrylic and 20–30 minutes for its Professional line. Extremely thin washes can feel dry within seconds. Touch-dry is only the first stage, though: a thin film typically needs a few days to dry through completely, and thick impasto builds of a quarter inch or more can keep drying for months to years. Where your painting lands on that timeline comes down to film thickness, humidity, temperature, and the specific formulation on your brush.

The drying stages: from first skin to full cure

Acrylic drying is not one event but a sequence. Golden Artist Colors' technical notes describe two distinct stages: a skin first forms over the surface of the paint, which is the point at which acrylics are "dry to the touch," and the entire thickness of the film then takes longer to become thoroughly dry. Those stages set every practical milestone in the table below, which assumes moderate studio conditions of roughly 70–85°F with humidity under 75%, which Golden calls ideal for drying.

StageWhat is happeningTypical time for a thin film
Surface skin formsA skin forms over the surface; the paint stops spreading and blendingSeconds for very thin washes; minutes for normal brush-outs
Dry to the touchThe surface is firm enough to touch without lifting color10–12 minutes (Liquitex, thin applications) to 10–30 minutes (Winsor & Newton thin films)
Dry enough to paint overThicker passages have set; new layers will not disturb the one belowWithin the hour for thin films; one to two hours for thicker films
Through-dry (fully cured film)The entire thickness of the film is thoroughly dryA few days for very thin films; Golden allows 1–3 days before oils over a thin acrylic underpainting on canvas
Impasto cured throughVery thick builds keep drying long after the surface has skinned overFilms of 1/4 inch or more take months and even years to be completely dry

One reassuring finding from Golden's notes: in most cases you can apply multiple layers at any time, because fresh acrylic readily attaches to other acrylic paint films. You can keep working wet-into-wet, over a layer that has just skinned over, or onto a film that dried long ago.

Why acrylic dries so fast

Acrylic paint is a dispersion of pigment and acrylic polymer particles in water. As the water evaporates or is absorbed, the polymer particles draw together and lock into a stable, flexible film — a purely physical process, not the slow oxidation that hardens oil paint. That is why a thin acrylic passage can be touch-dry before your rinse water is dirty. But the same mechanics have a limit: the particles can only fuse within a workable temperature window. Golden's notes give an ideal drying range of 70–90°F and warn that below 49°F (9°C) the polymer solids will not properly coalesce to form a continuous film, so the paint can fail outright. A cold garage does not just slow drying — it can weaken the paint itself.

Drying times by product type

Formulation moves the clock more than brand loyalty does. The same industry sells fast-setting fluids and slow-drying lines designed to behave like oils, so check which product is actually on your palette:

Paint or mediumTouch-dry timeNotes
Student acrylic, thin film (Winsor & Newton Galeria)10–20 minutesThicker films can take an hour or more
Professional acrylic, thin film (Winsor & Newton Professional)20–30 minutesThicker films can take an hour or two
General acrylics, thin application (Liquitex)10–12 minutesThick applications take longer
Slow-drying acrylics (Golden OPEN)Up to a full dayBuilt for blending and wet-on-wet techniques
Glazing medium (Golden Gloss Glazing Liquid)Up to an hourExtended open time is part of the design
Any acrylic plus a slow-dry medium (Liquitex Slow-Dri)Open time extended about 40%Liquitex rates the extension at 40%

Factors that affect how long acrylic takes to dry

  • Humidity. Acrylic dries by evaporating water, and damp air stalls that process: Golden's notes flag relative humidity in excess of 75% as the point where evaporation slows. The reference times in this guide assume you stay below that.
  • Temperature. Ideal drying falls between 70 and 90°F. Cold is the bigger danger: below 49°F (9°C) the polymer solids will not properly coalesce into a sound film at all.
  • Film thickness. This is the single biggest factor. A skin can form in minutes while paint underneath stays wet for days, and films of a quarter inch or more take months and even years to be completely dry.
  • Surface absorbency. Porous canvas and paper pull water out of the film faster. On less porous supports like metal, masonite, or plywood, Golden notes that thicker films may take several weeks to dry sufficiently.
  • Airflow. Moving air carries evaporating water away and speeds the first stage of drying; still, humid air does the opposite.
  • Additives and paint line. Slow-drying paints, glazing liquids, and retarder-style mediums deliberately extend open time — Liquitex Slow-Dri, for example, extends working time by 40%.

Practical tips for controlling drying time

Because drying is simply water leaving the film, every lever you have is a lever on water: how much is there, and how quickly it can escape.

To slow acrylic down

  1. Mist your palette and painting surface with water as you work, or use a stay-wet palette.
  2. Mix in a slow-dry medium or retarder — Liquitex Slow-Dri extends open time by about 40%.
  3. Switch to a slow-drying line when a project demands long blends; Golden OPEN can take a full day just to become touch-dry.
  4. Paint in the comfort zone: roughly 70–85°F with humidity under 75%. Avoid damp basements and cold rooms, which either stall drying or weaken the film.

To speed acrylic up

  1. Work in thin layers rather than one heavy pass; thin films touch-dry in minutes, not hours.
  2. Keep the room warm and the air moving — a fan across the surface accelerates evaporation.
  3. Choose faster-setting products when speed matters: fluid and student acrylics generally set quicker than heavy-body or slow-drying lines.
  4. Judge color only after the film dries — acrylics usually darken in tone as they dry, because the binder changes from white to transparent.

When is acrylic safe to varnish, frame, or pack away?

Finishing is where patience pays, because varnish and isolation coats trap any water still leaving the film. Golden's suggested schedule, assuming moderate conditions, works like this: let gesso dry at least one hour between coats, and a minimum of three days if you plan to oil paint over it. Before applying an isolation coat, wait a day or two on thin paintings and a week or two where paint is thick or impasto; let the isolation coat itself dry a minimum of one day before varnishing. Between varnish coats, four to six hours is the bare minimum, and waiting overnight is better. And for oils over an acrylic underpainting rather than gesso, Golden's technical notes allow 1–3 days for thin films on canvas.

The bottom line

Thin acrylic paint is touch-dry in about 10–30 minutes and safe to paint over within an hour or two, but the film keeps drying for days — and very thick paint for far longer. Give a normal painting a few days before finishing it, keep the room warm, dry, and airy, and reach for a slow-dry medium or a slow-drying paint whenever the clock works against you.
guides.excerpt: Thin acrylic paint dries to the touch in 10–30 minutes and dries through in a few days; thick impasto can take months. Full drying timeline inside.

guides.content:
How long does it take for oil paint to dry?

A thin film of conventional oil paint becomes touch-dry in two to 12 days: fast pigments such as raw umber feel dry in around two days, mid-speed colors in about five, and slow pigments like titanium white take more than five. Mix in an alkyd medium such as Liquin and the same paint can dry in less than 24 hours, while alkyd-based paints like Winsor & Newton's Griffin are touch-dry in 18 to 24 hours. But touch-dry is only stage one. Because oil paint cures by oxidation rather than evaporation, Winsor & Newton recommends waiting at least six months before varnishing, and the film keeps changing for months after that — cracking and film-strength problems usually take years, more likely decades, to show up.

The oil paint drying timeline, stage by stage

Oil paints dry through oxidization — the oil reacts with oxygen in the air — as Golden Artist Colors' technical testing puts it. Nothing evaporates the way water does in acrylics. That single fact explains almost everything about oil paint timelines: "dry" is a series of stages, not a moment, and a painting that passes the fingertip test on day two is still chemically active underneath.

StageTypical timeWhat is happening
Touch-dry, thin conventional film2–12 days (fast pigments ~2 days, medium ~5, slow 5+)The surface no longer transfers paint, but the film underneath is still soft and curing
Touch-dry with an alkyd mediumUnder 24 hours; alkyd paints 18–24 hoursSynthetic alkyd mediums are fast drying and speed the whole film
Firm through thick passages1–2 months for impasto or heavy textureOxygen works inward from the surface, so thick areas lag behind thin ones
Ready for a traditional final varnishAt least 6 monthsThe paint film is cured enough that strong solvents will not disturb it
Ready for a modern mild-solvent varnish2–3 weeks (thin paintings) to 1–2 months (thicker work)Firm-in-the-thickest-area is the standard, not the calendar
Long-term hardeningMonths to yearsCracking and film-strength problems usually take years, more likely decades, to develop

Why thick glazes and impasto take so long

Oxygen enters the film from the air, so the surface of a thick passage sets first and the paint below cures more slowly. Gamblin's varnishing guidance is built around exactly this lag: its Gamvar varnish may be applied only when the painting is dry to the touch and firm in its thickest areas — tested by gently pressing a fingernail into the thickest part — and heavily textured work may need one to two months to get there, while a thin painting may be ready in as little as two to three weeks. A fat glaze can feel perfectly dry on top while the layer beneath is still moving, which is one reason rushed varnishing and rushed layering both end in cracking.

Factors that affect how fast oil paint dries

1. Pigment chemistry — the metal inside the color

Pigment is the single biggest variable. In Winsor & Newton's Artists' Oil Colour range, umbers, Prussian blue, raw sienna and cobalt blues dry in around two days; ultramarines, ochres, Mars colors and cadmiums take around five; titanium white, zinc white, arylide yellows and quinacridones need more than five. The reason is chemistry. Golden's testing notes that the pigments in three colors — cobalt blue, raw umber and phthalo green — contain elements that act as driers, such as cobalt, manganese and copper, which help catalyze the oxidization of the oils. Those were exactly the colors that dried at the same speed even in a dark room in Golden's light tests.

2. The oil itself — linseed vs safflower and poppy

Not all binders oxidize at the same speed. Linseed is a true drying oil; poppy and safflower are semi-drying oils that are paler in color but dry more slowly. Paints ground in safflower or poppy will therefore lag behind linseed-based equivalents — one reason a pale titanium white passage can still be soft when the umber shadow next to it has long since set.

3. Film thickness and medium choice

Thinner layers dry faster — Winsor & Newton lists "thick over thin" as one of the three classic oil painting rules, because a thin layer applied over a still-curing thick one can crack as the paint below it continues to move. Your medium matters too: natural oil mediums are slower drying, while synthetic alkyd mediums are fast drying, so the same tube of paint moves at very different speeds depending on what you mix into it.

4. Light, temperature and humidity

Drying is dramatically slower in the dark. In Golden's tests, titanium white dried in 7 days in an open shadow but needed 22 days in a dark room; titanium-zinc white went from 28 to 90 days; and cadmium red medium jumped from 16 days to 135 days — about four and a half months. Winsor & Newton adds that paint thickness and room temperature both affect drying times, plus a second reason to avoid poor drying conditions: paintings dried in continuous darkness or high humidity may yellow.

5. Driers and alkyd mediums

Manufacturers can speed oxidation chemically. "Drying" linseed and poppy oil products contain added metal driers — Winsor & Newton's Drying Poppy Oil has driers added to give it a drying rate comparable to linseed — and alkyd mediums are the fastest lever of all: using Liquin Original increases the drying rate by approximately 50 percent, and paintings mixed with it dry in less than 24 hours. Alkyd paints like Griffin stay workable for four to eight hours, are touch-dry in 18 to 24 hours, and remain mixable with conventional oils.

Practical tips: drying faster without cracking later

  1. Go lean, then fat. Build lower layers with minimal medium and increase the medium content with each layer. Winsor & Newton frames the fat-over-lean rule as "flexible over less flexible" — each upper layer must stay more flexible than the one below so it can move as the stack cures.
  2. Go thick over thin, and slow over fast. Reserve fast-drying pigments (umbers, siennas, Prussian blue) for underlayers and put slow-drying colors on top; a fast layer sealed over a still-curing slow one is the classic recipe for cracked paint.
  3. Use an alkyd medium when time is short. Liquin-mixed paint dries in under 24 hours, letting you build fat-over-lean layers in days rather than weeks.
  4. Dry paintings in daylight, not a cupboard. Light cut some colors' drying times by a factor of three or more in Golden's tests, and light, ventilated rooms avoid the yellowing that continuous darkness and high humidity can cause.
  5. Test the thickest area, not the edge. Gamblin's standard is that the painting be dry to the touch and firm in its thickest areas — press a fingernail into the thickest part to check. Golden describes the same milestone as hard dry, the point at which a fingernail can no longer leave a mark in the surface. The thin edges you are tempted to check dry first and mean the least.
  6. Respect the six-month rule for traditional varnish. Even the thinnest oil painting should dry for six months before a traditional final varnish such as dammar; Winsor & Newton's readiness check is to rub a cotton bud dampened with Sansodor solvent on an inconspicuous area — if no color transfers, varnishing can begin. Modern mild-solvent varnishes like Gamvar can go on far sooner — two to three weeks on thin work — because their mild solvent is not strong enough to dissolve the paint film underneath.

The bottom line on oil paint drying times

Plan on two to 12 days to the touch for conventional oils, about a day if you paint with alkyd mediums or alkyd paints, one to two months for thick texture to firm through, and six months before a traditional varnish. The slow part is not a flaw — it is the same oxidation that slowly builds the paint film, and it keeps going long after the surface first felt dry.
guides.excerpt: Oil paint is touch-dry in 2–12 days but keeps curing for months — wait 6 months before a traditional varnish (2–3 weeks for modern ones). Full timeline, pigment speeds, and ways to dry paint faster.

guides.content:
How Long Do Tires Last?

Most tires last three to four years of typical driving — roughly 36,000 to 60,000 miles for a commuter — and every tire also carries an age limit of six to 10 years recommended by some vehicle and tire manufacturers, no matter how much tread is left. The time figure comes from Edmunds, which notes that a commuter driving 12,000 to 15,000 miles a year will usually wear out a tire's tread in three to four years; at that pace the math works out to roughly 36,000 to 60,000 total miles. The age figure comes from NHTSA, which reports that some vehicle and tire manufacturers recommend replacing tires once they are six to 10 years old, even when the tread still looks healthy. And when the tread itself runs out, the standard replacement threshold is 2/32 of an inch of remaining rubber.

Tires run down on two separate clocks. The first is mechanical wear: every mile grinds compound off the tread until the grooves are too shallow to channel water away. The second is chemical aging: heat, sunlight, and time slowly harden and crack the rubber even if the tire never leaves the garage. Michelin's owner's manual states plainly that accurately predicting the serviceable life of any specific tire is impossible, because weather, storage conditions, load, speed, inflation pressure, and maintenance all change the outcome. That is why manufacturers give you both a tread limit and a birthday rule — and why you need to track both.

Tire Life Timeline: What Happens at Each Stage

Because you cannot know in advance which clock will run out first, it helps to see a tire's whole service life laid out. The table below follows a tire from the day it is mounted to final replacement, using age checkpoints published by NHTSA, Michelin, and major automakers.

StageWhat happensSource
Day oneRecord the DOT date code so you always know the tire's true age, and check pressure monthly from the start.NHTSA
Years 1-3Peak performance. Rotate every 6,000-8,000 miles to keep wear even and the treadwear warranty valid.Michelin
Years 3-4Typical tread wear-out for commuters driving 12,000-15,000 miles a year — roughly 36,000-60,000 total miles.Edmunds
Year 5Tires that have been in use five years or more should be inspected by a tire specialist at least annually.Michelin
Year 6Several major automakers, including Ford, Nissan, and Mercedes-Benz, advise replacing tires six years after production regardless of tread life.Edmunds
Years 6-10The manufacturer age-replacement window applies no matter how deep the tread measures.NHTSA
Year 10Absolute ceiling: tires in service 10 years or more from manufacture, including spares, should be replaced even if they appear serviceable.Michelin

Notice how wide the practical window is. A rideshare driver covering 25,000 miles a year can burn through a 50,000-mile treadwear warranty in about two years, while a garage-kept convertible may hit the six-year birthday rule with plenty of tread showing — and still need new tires.

Expected Treadwear by Tire Type

Manufacturers publish their confidence in each model as a mileage warranty, and the spread between tire types is enormous. Michelin's own warranty guide runs from 20,000 miles on soft performance summer tires up to 80,000 miles on long-wear all-season models.

Tire type (Michelin example)Mileage treadwear warranty
Long-wear all-season (Defender2, Defender T+H)80,000 miles
Mainstream all-season (CrossClimate2)60,000 miles
Touring all-season (Primacy A/S)55,000 miles
Winter studless (X-Ice Snow)40,000 miles
Performance summer (Pilot Sport 4 S)30,000 miles
Performance summer (Pilot Sport 4)20,000 miles

A warranty is not an expiration date; it is the manufacturer's bet on how long the tread survives under proper care. Performance tires trade longevity for grip by using soft compounds that wear quickly, while touring all-season tires are engineered in the opposite direction — the warranty chart shows the gap directly. Exact coverage varies by speed rating and fitment: the Primacy A/S, for instance, carries 55,000 miles in T-, H-, and V-speed ratings but 45,000 in W and Y. Michelin also conditions its treadwear warranty on rotating the tires every 6,000 to 8,000 miles, and skipping rotations voids that treadwear coverage.

Factors That Affect How Long Tires Last

  • Inflation pressure. NHTSA calls pressure maintenance the most important part of tire care: properly inflated tires can extend average tire life by 4,700 miles and save as much as 11 cents per gallon at the pump. Even so, only 19 percent of consumers properly inflate their tires.
  • Rotation and alignment. Front and rear tires wear at different rates and need periodic rotation to even out. NHTSA lists rotation, balance, and alignment among the services that help tires last longer, and Michelin voids its treadwear warranty when rotations are skipped.
  • Climate and sun exposure. Tire aging is a greater concern in the southern Sun Belt states, NHTSA warns, because sunlight and warmer climates accelerate rubber degradation. Edmunds, citing NHTSA research, adds that coastal climates speed the aging process as well.
  • Driving style and load. Michelin lists load, speed, and conditions of use among the variables that determine how a tire ages, and its care rules tell owners to avoid potholes, curb strikes, overloading, and excessive speed — all of which shorten tread life in practice.
  • Storage and the spare. A tire ages even when it is not rolling. NHTSA recommends that a full-size spare be treated as an emergency-only tire rather than rotated into service, and Michelin's 10-year replacement rule explicitly includes spares.

How to Check Your Tires: Penny Test, Wear Bars, and DOT Code

Three quick checks tell you exactly where your tires stand on both clocks, and none requires special tools.

  1. The penny test. Place a penny upside down in a tread groove with Lincoln's head facing you. Edmunds describes a pass as Lincoln's head being fully or partially covered by the tread blocks; NHTSA's version is simpler — if you can see the top of Lincoln's head, replace the tires.
  2. Tread wear bars. Michelin builds wear bars into the tread grooves at exactly 2/32 of an inch (1.6 mm). When the surrounding tread wears down level with those bars, the tire must be replaced — Michelin calls tires worn beyond this stage extremely dangerous.
  3. The DOT date code. Find the DOT Tire Identification Number on the sidewall. Its last four digits give the week and year of manufacture: NHTSA's example is 0308, meaning the third week of 2008, and Michelin's is 2214, the 22nd week of 2014. Check both sidewalls, because the full code may appear on only one side.

Practical Tips to Reach the Full Service Life

  1. Check pressure monthly when the tires are cold, using the figure on the driver's door jamb placard — not the maximum pressure printed on the tire's sidewall.
  2. Treat the TPMS warning light as a late alarm, not a maintenance reminder. On cars from model year 2008 and newer, the light means at least one tire is already significantly underinflated and needs attention as soon as possible.
  3. Rotate on schedule — every 6,000 to 8,000 miles, or sooner if your owner's manual calls for it — and keep the receipts, since they protect the mileage warranty.
  4. Book a professional inspection every year once the tires pass five years of age, even if they look fine. Aging damage cannot be detected just by looking.
  5. Check the DOT code before buying new tires and record it at installation. Even unused tires age on the shelf, so a new-looking tire is only as new as its birth date.
  6. Include the spare in every age and pressure check, and never press an aged spare into daily service.
  7. When either clock expires — tread level with the wear bars, or the age limit set by your automaker or Michelin's 10-year ceiling — replace the tires. In 2024, 511 people died on U.S. roads in tire-related crashes, and NHTSA warns that poor maintenance such as underinflation and skipped rotations can lead to flats, blowouts, and tread separation.

The short version: keep the air right, keep the rotations on schedule, and let the earlier of the two clocks — miles or birthdays — decide when the set comes off the car.
guides.excerpt: Most tires last 3-4 years or roughly 36,000-60,000 miles of typical driving; NHTSA says replace by age at 6-10 years even if the tread looks fine, and Michelin's ceiling is 10 years, spares included.

How Long Does It Take to Charge a Tesla?

Charging a Tesla takes as little as 15 to 30 minutes at a Supercharger for a typical road-trip session to about 80%, about 7 to 14 hours on a 240-volt home charger, or several days on a standard 120-volt household outlet. The U.S. Department of Energy notes that electric-car charging times run from "less than 20 minutes using DC fast chargers to 20 hours or more using Level 1 chargers," and a Tesla lands anywhere on that spectrum depending on which plug you use. Tesla's headline Supercharger figure is up to 200 miles (about 320 km) of range added in 15 minutes — 162 to 175 miles on the smaller-battery Models 3, Y and X — so "how long" is really a question about your charger, not your car.

Tesla charging times by charger level

Tesla drivers realistically use three charging speeds. Here is how each one behaves, using Tesla's published charge rates and Department of Energy benchmarks.

ChargerPower sourceRange addedTime to a full batteryBest for
Level 1 — Mobile ConnectorStandard 120 V household outlet2–3 miles (3–5 km) per hourRoughly 4–8 days from emptyEmergencies and overnight top-ups
Level 2 — 240 V outletDryer-style 240 V outlet with adapterUp to 30 miles (48 km) per hourRoughly 10–14 hoursHomes with an existing 240 V outlet
Level 2 — Wall ConnectorHardwired 240 V home chargerUp to 44 miles (71 km) per hourRoughly 7–10 hours (overnight)Daily home charging
Supercharger V3250 kW DC fast chargerUp to 200 miles (320 km) in 15 minutes (Model S); 162–175 miles for Models 3, Y and X~15–30 minutes to about 80%Road trips
Supercharger V4Posts rated up to 325 kW; 500 kW cabinets for 800 V vehiclesSimilar to V3 for today's 400 V Teslas~15–30 minutes to about 80%Newest stations, non-Tesla EVs

Two notes on that table. First, the "full battery" figures for Level 1 assume you start empty, which almost nobody does; Tesla says the 120 V Mobile Connector should meet your needs if you charge overnight and drive less than 30 to 40 miles (48–64 km) per day. Second, Supercharger times are for a 10–80% session: the Department of Energy's benchmark for DC fast charging is roughly 100 to 200+ miles of range per 30 minutes, and Tesla's 15-minute rates sit at the top of that band.

Charging time by Tesla model

Battery size is the other half of the equation: the same charger fills a bigger battery more slowly. These figures come from the EPA's published records for the 2025 model year, which list each car's driving range and its 240-volt charging time from empty to full; the last column is simply that range divided by Tesla's maximum 44-miles-per-hour home charging rate.

2025 modelEPA rangeLevel 2 time, 0–100% (EPA)Approx. 0–100% at the 44-mph home rate
Model 3 Long Range AWD346 miles (557 km)11.7 hours~8 hours
Model Y Long Range AWD311 miles (500 km)12.0 hours~7 hours
Model S410 miles (660 km)9.7 hours~9.5 hours
Model X329 miles (529 km)14.0 hours~7.5 hours

For context, the Department of Energy pegs typical residential Level 2 power at about 7.2 kW, with Level 2 equipment spanning 2.9 to 19.2 kW. Tesla's Wall Connector adds up to 44 miles of range per hour, which is how even the big-battery Model S fills overnight.

What actually happens during a Supercharger stop

Fast charging is not one steady flow. Tesla notes that rates at a Supercharger site "vary based on several factors such as size and age of battery pack, state of charge, ambient temperature conditions and vehicle configuration," and that charging speeds slow as the battery fills — reaching 100% "will typically take significantly longer than reaching 80%." A session breaks into four rough stages:

  1. Ramp-up (the first few minutes). The car and stall negotiate power and a cold pack warms toward its ideal window, so the rate climbs rather than starting at peak.
  2. Peak charging (roughly the lower half of the battery). This is where V3's 250 kW capability gets used, and it is what makes Tesla's 15-minute figures possible.
  3. Taper (roughly 50–80%). Power falls steadily as the battery fills. Each additional 10% takes longer than the one before.
  4. Crawl (80–100%). Rates drop toward Level 2 territory. This is why long-distance drivers unplug at 80% — and why Tesla applies congestion fees at busy sites once your battery is already at or above 80%, waived only for the first five minutes.

Factors that affect Tesla charging time

  • Charger power output. The biggest lever. Going from a 120 V outlet (2–3 miles per hour) to a Wall Connector (up to 44 miles per hour) is a roughly 15–20x jump, per Tesla's published rates. Residential Level 2 typically supplies about 7.2 kW and Level 2 equipment tops out at 19.2 kW, per the Department of Energy.
  • Battery size and state of charge. A bigger pack takes longer to fill, and charging slows sharply past about 80% — Tesla says reaching 100% will typically take significantly longer than reaching 80%.
  • Battery temperature. Tesla lists ambient temperature among the factors that change Supercharger rates, so a cold pack charges more slowly until it warms and winter stops run longer.
  • Supercharger hardware. V3 stalls introduced in 2019 deliver up to 250 kW each; V4 posts can deliver up to 325 kW, though so far only the 800 V Cybertruck charges that fast, and the new V4 cabinets supply up to 500 kW to 800 V vehicles. On older shared-stall sites, pairing with a neighboring car can split the power.
  • Your starting level. Charging from 40% to 80% takes a fraction of the time of 10% to 100%, which is why daily top-ups feel effortless while rare full charges feel slow.

Practical tips for faster, smarter charging

  1. Charge overnight at home whenever possible. The Department of Energy notes Level 2 equipment can charge a typical EV battery overnight, and Tesla's Wall Connector adds up to 44 miles of range per hour.
  2. Let the car plan road-trip stops. Tesla's Trip Planner picks Superchargers along your route and recommends how much to charge at each stop; at busy, high-use stations the car may automatically set its charge limit to 80% to keep stalls turning over.
  3. Stop at 80% on the highway. Beyond 80%, rates drop hard, and congestion fees can apply at busy sites once you are at or above 80% (waived for the first five minutes). Unless the next charger is far away, unplug and drive.
  4. Top up a little every night instead of rarely charging to full. At 30 to 44 miles of range per hour, a typical day's driving is replaced in an hour or two of home charging, so the slow final stretch to 100% is reserved for the night before a long trip.
  5. Arrive at Superchargers low, not empty. Peak charging happens in the lower part of the battery, so a 10% arrival charges much faster than a 50% one. Plan arrivals around 10–20% for the shortest stops.
  6. Treat 120 V charging as a fallback, not a plan. At 2–3 miles of range per hour, a fully drained Model 3 Long Range needs five to seven days on a household outlet — fine for a week of barely driving, not fine as your routine.

The bottom line

For daily life, a Tesla effectively charges while you sleep: 7–10 hours on a Wall Connector, or overnight at any 240-volt rate, and you start every day full. For road trips, the answer is a coffee stop — 15 minutes can add up to 200 miles on a Model S, or 162–175 miles on a Model 3, Y or X — and a typical 10-to-80% session runs about 15–30 minutes. The only scenario in which a Tesla genuinely takes days to charge is a plain 120-volt wall outlet, and even that covers a normal 30–40-mile daily commute if you plug in every night.

How Long Does It Take to Charge an EV?

Charging an electric vehicle takes anywhere from less than 20 minutes on a DC fast charger to 20 hours or more on a household outlet. That spread comes straight from the U.S. Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC), and it makes the most important point on this page: the variable that matters most is not your car; it is what you plug it into. A highway fast charger can bring a compatible EV to 80% in about 30 minutes, according to the DOE's fueleconomy.gov. A home Level 2 wall unit recharges a typical battery pack fully in 3 to 12 hours — an overnight job. And a standard 120-volt outlet adds only about 5 miles (8 km) of range per hour, so filling a fully drained long-range pack that way can stretch past two full days.

Charging Times by Level: The Quick-Reference Table

U.S. Department of Energy guidance sorts EV charging into three levels, and each answers the "how long?" question differently. Here is how they compare, using figures from the AFDC and fueleconomy.gov.

Charger levelVoltagePowerRange addedRealistic charging time
Level 1 (AC)120 VAbout 1.9 kWAbout 5 miles (8 km) per hour8 hours adds about 40 miles (64 km); a full charge from empty takes 20 hours or more
Level 2 (AC)240 V (home) / 208 V (commercial)2.9 to 19.2 kW; typical home unit 7.2 kWAbout 25 miles (40 km) per hour on average, ranging from a few miles per hour up to about 403 to 12 hours for a full pack — an overnight session
DC fast (often labeled Level 3)480 V or moreUp to 500 kWAbout 100 to 200+ miles (160 to 320+ km) per 30 minutesAs fast as less than 20 minutes; even a fast charge to 80% takes about 30 minutes

A note on that full-charge column: fueleconomy.gov's 3-to-12-hour estimate covers fully recharging a typical pack on AC charging. On Level 1 the same job runs to 20 hours or more, per the AFDC — and the math shows why. At about 5 miles of range per hour, a pack rated for 200-plus miles needs 40 hours, and the biggest packs, which fueleconomy.gov notes can exceed 400 miles of range, would need 80. That is why most drivers treat the included 120-volt cord as a backup rather than a plan.

Where You Plug In Matters: Home, Public, Highway

Home: the included Level 1 cord vs. a Level 2 wall unit

Most plug-in vehicles come equipped with a cord for Level 1 charging, per fueleconomy.gov — one end is a standard household plug, the other an SAE J1772 connector that both Level 1 and Level 2 equipment share, so you can charge from any 120 V outlet with no extra equipment. It works, but slowly. The AFDC's answer is Level 2 equipment, which can charge a typical EV battery overnight. Most residential Level 2 chargers run at up to 30 amps and deliver 7.2 kW on a dedicated 40-amp circuit. Compatibility at home is never a question: all commercially available EVs in the United States can charge on both Level 1 and Level 2 equipment — only speed differs.

Public and workplace charging: mostly Level 2

As of 2023, nearly 80% of public charging ports in the United States were Level 2, and fewer than 1% were Level 1, according to the AFDC. Public Level 2 fits the dwell time a parking session already has: a work shift, a grocery run, a night at a hotel. Plug in for three hours at the typical 25-to-40 miles per hour and you realistically add somewhere between 75 and 120 miles.

Highway corridors: DC fast charging

DC fast chargers deliver direct current straight to the battery at power outputs up to 500 kW. Fueleconomy.gov describes them as the fastest charging type, usually located along heavy-traffic corridors and not practical for home installation. More than 20% of U.S. public ports were DC fast chargers as of 2023, per the AFDC. Connector families matter at this level: most EV models on the market can use CCS, some use CHAdeMO, and Tesla vehicles use the J3400 connector — and every Tesla comes with a J1772 adapter so it can also use non-Tesla Level 2 equipment.

Why Charging Slows Down Sharply After 80%

Every fast-charging statistic you have seen — "30 minutes to 80%," "100 to 200+ miles per 30 minutes" — stops at 80% for a reason. Fueleconomy.gov notes that charge rate depends on the battery's state of charge, among other factors, and that even a fast charge to 80% capacity can take 30 minutes. Most of today's EVs run on lithium-ion batteries, per the AFDC, and a lithium-ion pack accepts current freely when it is partly empty but resists it as it fills. To keep heat and cell stress in check, the car's battery management system deliberately dials the current down through that upper zone — protective behavior built into the chemistry, not a charger malfunction. The practical takeaway on a road trip: the stretch from 80% to 100% drags on far longer than the sprint up to 80%, so most long-distance drivers unplug around 80% and drive on.

Estimate Your Own Charging Time: The kWh Math

You can predict almost any charging session with one division:

Charging time (hours) = energy to replace (kWh) divided by charger power (kW)

Fueleconomy.gov's own cost example uses an EV that consumes 35 kWh per 100 miles — a fair mid-size figure. Suppose you come home needing to replace 100 miles of driving: that is roughly 35 kWh. On a typical 7.2 kW home Level 2 unit, 35 divided by 7.2 is just under five hours. On a 1.9 kW Level 1 outlet, the same 100 miles needs about 18 hours. Double the battery or halve the power and the time scales in a straight line. Real sessions run a little longer than the raw division, because the rate tapers as the pack fills and shifts with conditions.

Factors That Affect EV Charging Time

  • Charger level and power output. The single biggest factor. Level 2 units alone span 2.9 to 19.2 kW — a more than sixfold spread before you even leave home.
  • Your vehicle's acceptance rate. Charge rate varies by vehicle model across all charging types, fueleconomy.gov cautions; check your owner's manual for estimated charge times. Not every EV can accept DC fast charging at all.
  • Battery size. More kWh of capacity means more kWh to replace at the same power.
  • State of charge. The taper described above: sessions slow noticeably as the battery fills.
  • Ambient temperature. Charge rate also depends on outside temperature, so cold mornings stretch charging sessions.
  • Connector compatibility. J1772 covers Levels 1 and 2; DC fast charging uses CCS, CHAdeMO, or J3400 depending on the vehicle.

Practical Tips to Charge Faster and Smarter

  1. Start with the manual. Fueleconomy.gov's direct advice is to check the owner's manual, since estimated charge times are model-specific.
  2. Install Level 2 at home if you drive the car daily. A 7.2 kW unit finishes most overnight windows comfortably; a 120 V outlet alone will not keep up with a long commute.
  3. Unplug near 80% on road trips. The last fifth of the battery charges the slowest; the first 80% is where DC fast chargers earn their name.
  4. Match the charger to the car. Paying for more kW than your vehicle can accept buys nothing — charging power varies by vehicle — so size the wall unit to the car's capability.
  5. Plan corridors in advance. The DOE's Alternative Fueling Station Locator, referenced by fueleconomy.gov, maps public Level 2 and DC fast stations along your route.
  6. Pad your estimates in winter. Because charge rate depends on ambient temperature, allow extra time on cold days rather than planning to the minute.

The gap is narrowing at the top end: the Department of Energy's Transportation Technologies Office funds battery research with an explicit target of decreasing charge time to less than 15 minutes. For now, the honest answer to "how long does it take to charge an EV?" is the one experienced drivers internalize — about as long as whatever else you were doing anyway: half a coffee stop on the highway, or a night's sleep in your garage.

guides.content:
How long is Hamilton (the musical)?

Hamilton runs 2 hours and 45 minutes, including one 15-minute intermission — on Broadway, on the North American tour, and in London's West End alike. The figure comes straight from the show's producers: the official Hamilton site lists the Broadway production at "2 hours 45 minutes including intermission," the Broadway Across America touring FAQ gives "2 hours and 45 minutes with a 15-minute intermission," and London Theatre matches it at "2hr 45min. Incl. 15min interval." If you're watching the filmed version on Disney+, expect a fixed 160 minutes — 2 hours 40 — because that capture is a pre-edited recording of the stage show rather than a live performance whose timing flexes nightly.

In practice, that means you are planning for a roughly three-hour evening. An 8:00 PM curtain has you walking out around 10:45 PM, a 2:00 PM matinee ends near 4:45 PM, and anything you schedule afterward — a dinner reservation, a train, a babysitter's pickup time — should be built on that back-end estimate, with a small cushion for a night the crowd runs hot.

Hamilton runtime at a glance, by production

Hamilton's staging travels intact — right down to the two concentric turntables the touring productions roll on, which are built into the show's choreography — so the running time stays remarkably consistent from production to production. The producers publish one number everywhere, which is why the official New York listing, the touring FAQ, and the West End listing all agree. Here is how every major way to see Hamilton compares:

ProductionTotal runtimeBreakNotes
Broadway (Richard Rodgers Theatre, New York)2 hours 45 minutesOne intermissionOfficial runtime listed on the show's website
North American tour2 hours 45 minutesOne 15-minute intermissionIdentical to Broadway per the touring FAQ
West End (Victoria Palace Theatre, London)2 hours 45 minutesOne 15-minute intervalLondon production matches the U.S. timings
Disney+ film (2020)160 minutes (2 hours 40)A one-minute intermission card onlyFilmed June 2016 with the original principal cast; a 2025 theatrical re-release stretched the card to ten minutes

Strip out the intermission and you're left with roughly two and a half hours of actual performance. The Disney+ edit fills 160 minutes because it wraps that stage time in a one-minute intermission card and closing credits — and because it was filmed over three live performances at the Richard Rodgers Theatre in June 2016, not on a silent soundstage. It is the same show either way; the clock just behaves differently at home.

Act 1 and Act 2: where the time goes

Hamilton is built as two acts with a single break between them, and the split lands at a clean story seam.

Act One: arrival to "Non-Stop"

Act One races from Hamilton's arrival in New York as an immigrant teenager, through his rivalry and friendship with Aaron Burr, the Revolutionary War, and his marriage to Eliza Schuyler, and it ends with his appointment as the nation's first Treasury Secretary under President Washington — closing on the song "Non-Stop." Then comes the 15-minute intermission.

Act Two: 1789 to the duel

Act Two jumps to 1789 and opens with "What'd I Miss" as Thomas Jefferson returns from France to serve as Secretary of State. From there it carries through the cabinet battles, the personal scandals, the losses in Hamilton's family, and the 1804 duel with Burr that ends the show.

One honest caveat: the producers publish a single total running time, not per-act timings, so any "Act One is exactly X minutes" figure floating around online is someone's stopwatch, not an official spec. What is official is the total — about two and a half hours of stage time split across the two acts, with the intermission arriving right after "Non-Stop."

Factors that affect how long Hamilton runs

The 2h 45m figure is the published baseline, but live theater breathes. A handful of things nudge any given performance a few minutes in either direction:

  • Audience reaction. Entrance applause, laughter, and mid-song cheers are baked into every Hamilton performance, and in the room they stretch the clock. A hyped Friday-night crowd will run longer than a quiet Tuesday.
  • Musical tempo. The rap-driven score sits at a relentless pace, but conductors and cast members phrase and pace slightly differently from night to night, and an alternate or understudy step-in can shift cue timings.
  • Venue mechanics. Touring houses replicate the Broadway staging, including the double turntable, but each theatre has its own scene-change equipment, crew, and house rules — small differences that add or trim minutes across a two-act evening.
  • Start-of-show delays. A curtain hold for a late-arriving house or a technical check pushes everything downstream — a delayed 8:00 PM curtain means a delayed 10:45 PM finish.
  • The film never drifts. The Disney+ version is locked at 160 minutes every single time; it was edited once from performances recorded in June 2016, before the original principals — including Lin-Manuel Miranda, Leslie Odom Jr., and Phillipa Soo — left the cast.

Planning your night: practical tips

  1. Do the curtain math before you book dinner. Using the official 2h 45m runtime, an 8:00 PM curtain ends around 10:45 PM and a 2:00 PM matinee wraps near 4:45 PM. Build your plans off the back end of the show, not the front.
  2. Be in your seat at curtain. On the tour, latecomers are held in the lobby for the first scene of the show — approximately 9 minutes — before ushers seat them. In a show this dense, that opening stretch is not one to skip.
  3. Treat the 15-minute intermission as the only break. It is the one chance for restrooms and concessions without missing anything, and lines peak the moment it starts. Move fast.
  4. Watching on Disney+? Block one uninterrupted 2-hour-40 stretch. The film's only break is a one-minute intermission card, so there is no natural pause point. It arrived on the service on July 3, 2020.
  5. Check the age guidance before bringing kids. The touring FAQ rates the show suitable for ages 10 and up due to some strong language, and children under 4 are not permitted into the theatre — factor that into whether a near-11 PM finish suits your family on a school night.
  6. Confirm your performance's start time. Matinee and evening curtains differ by venue and day, and the runtime is counted from curtain, not from the time on your calendar reminder. A quick check of your ticket removes the guesswork.
  7. Compare versions, not stopwatch reports. If a friend's Hamilton "felt longer" than yours, it may genuinely have been: same 2h 45m script, but live-audience variance and venue mechanics can separate one night from another by a few minutes.

Bottom line: whether you catch Hamilton at the Richard Rodgers Theatre, on tour, at London's Victoria Palace Theatre, or on Disney+, you are committing to just under three hours — 2 hours 45 minutes with a 15-minute break in the theater, or a locked 2 hours 40 at home. Arrive early, settle in, and don't throw away your shot at a good seat.
guides.excerpt: Hamilton runs 2 hours 45 minutes with one 15-minute intermission on Broadway, tour, and London. The Disney+ film version runs 2h 40m.

guides.content:
How long is a concert?

Quick answer: a headline set usually runs between 75 minutes and about two and a half hours, with marathon acts pushing past three hours — and the full night out, from doors and opening acts to the final encore, typically lasts around three hours. Festival headliners get the tightest slots (75–90 minutes at Coachella 2024), stadium and arena headliners generally play two hours or more, and Las Vegas residency shows settle at around the two-hour mark. At a festival, "how long is the concert" really means "how long is the day": roughly ten hours can separate the first main-stage set from the last note in the tents.

Part of the confusion is that "a concert" can mean three different clocks. The headline set is the artist you bought tickets for. The show is everything that happens on stage, including one or two support acts and the changeovers between them. The event is doors to curfew. When you are booking trains home or a babysitter, it is the event length that matters — and that is where curfews, openers and stage changeovers quietly add an hour or more to the night.

Concert length by act type

The surest way to estimate a set is to look at what kind of slot the artist is playing. The documented examples below come from published festival schedules, tour opening nights and residency records.

Act typeTypical set lengthDocumented example
Festival newcomer (small stage)30–45 minutesCoachella 2024 published 30–40-minute slots on the Sonora stage and 40–45-minute slots on the Gobi stage
Festival support act (main stage)45–60 minutesSabrina Carpenter played 6:00–7:00 p.m. on the Coachella Stage; Blur played 7:40–8:40 p.m.
Festival headliner75–90 minutesLana Del Rey 11:20 p.m.–12:50 a.m., Tyler, The Creator 11:40 p.m.–12:55 a.m., Doja Cat 10:25–11:50 p.m. (Coachella 2024)
Arena or stadium headlinerAbout two hoursOasis opened their Live '25 reunion tour in Cardiff with a two-hour-plus, 23-song set in front of 74,500 fans
Marathon tour showThree hours or moreTaylor Swift's Eras Tour typically ran 3 hours 15 minutes across 44–46 songs
Las Vegas residency showTwo hours or slightly overAdele's "Weekends with Adele" at the Colosseum at Caesars Palace spans more than two hours across 20 songs

Two patterns stand out. Festivals compress everybody: the biggest names on the poster still get less stage time than they would on their own tour. Residencies, meanwhile, settle at the two-hour mark — long enough to feel major, short enough to be repeated several nights a week.

What a full concert night actually looks like

Openers and changeovers

Support acts and changeovers are what turn a two-hour headline set into a three-hour evening. Big tours typically carry one or two openers — Cast and Richard Ashcroft both played before Oasis in Cardiff — and every act change means a stage reset. Festival running orders make those gaps visible: on Coachella's main stage in 2024, the published schedule left 35 minutes between Sabrina Carpenter and Lil Uzi Vert, about 45 minutes between the early-evening acts, and a full 70 minutes to build the headliner's production before Lana Del Rey went on. Add a two-hour-plus headliner to an hour of support slots and 35–70 minutes of changeovers, and door to encore you are easily at three hours or more.

Festivals are a full day

A festival replaces the evening show with a running order that starts in the afternoon. At Coachella 2024, the Sunday schedule on the main Coachella Stage began at 2:50 p.m., while the Yuma tent was scheduled until 1:00 a.m. on the Saturday night — roughly ten hours of possible live music in one day. That is exactly why festival sets are short: the schedule, not the artist, sets the length, and the headliner's 75–90 minutes is one slot among dozens.

Factors that affect how long a concert lasts

  • Venue curfews. Many large venues have hard cut-offs written into their licence or operating rules, and overrunning them is expensive. When Madonna's Celebration Tour opened at London's O2 arena, the shows overran the 10:30 p.m. curfew by about 30 minutes and finished around 11 p.m. — reportedly risking a £300,000 penalty under a fine structure reported at £10,000 per minute of overrun. Greenwich Council said the venue's wider midnight curfew was not broken and that it did not intend to investigate. This is why a late start at a curfew venue usually means a shortened set or a trimmed encore, not a later finish.
  • Number of support acts. One opener adds roughly 45–60 minutes plus a changeover; two openers can add two hours or more to your night before the headliner even appears.
  • Festival slot versus own show. The same artist might play 75–90 minutes at a festival and two hours or more on their own tour, because a festival stage runs on a shared, fixed clock.
  • Back catalogue and show concept. Artists touring a whole career play longer. Taylor Swift built the Eras Tour around her entire recording history — it ultimately spanned all 11 of her studio albums — and typically played 44–46 songs in 3 hours 15 minutes. Bruce Springsteen opened his first E Street Band tour in six years with a 28-song set in Tampa. An act touring one new album usually lands closer to the two-hour mark.
  • Residency design. Las Vegas residencies are built to be repeatable several nights a week, so they sit near two hours — Adele's "Weekends with Adele" show at the Colosseum at Caesars Palace spans more than two hours.
  • Production size. Spectacular stage builds eat time between acts — much of the 70-minute gap before Coachella's Friday headliner was production changeover — and heavier shows sometimes push the headliner's start later to protect the curfew.

Practical tips for planning your night

  1. Check the venue's event page for stage times. Arenas typically publish door times, and often stage times, in the days before a show. At the O2 in London, assume a finish around 11 p.m. — Madonna's shows there ended at 11 p.m. even after overrunning the 10:30 p.m. curfew.
  2. Look up the tour's recent setlists before you go. Sites like setlist.fm publish what an artist played at last night's show. Song counts translate well to duration: Oasis played 23 songs in a two-hour-plus Cardiff set, while Taylor Swift's Eras Tour typically packed 44–46 songs into 3 hours 15 minutes.
  3. Expect a gap between acts — a long one. A 35–70 minute wait after the opener is normal changeover, not a delay, and at festivals the gap before the headliner can stretch to a full 70 minutes while the stage is rebuilt.
  4. Do not leave early to beat the encore. Encores at modern concerts are planned parts of the show, usually holding back some of the biggest songs. But at curfew venues, do not be surprised if the encore is trimmed to a song or two when the night has run late.
  5. Treat a festival as a full day, not an evening. With main stages starting mid-afternoon and some tents running as late as 1 a.m., plan food, rest and sun protection — then use the set-times grid and its 35–70 minute changeover gaps to move between stages.
  6. Book flexible transport around the curfew. When thousands leave at the same 11 p.m. cut-off, stations and car parks jam quickly; a later train or a short walk to a further stop saves the longest queues.

The short version: budget about two hours for the headliner alone, around three hours for a normal arena night door to encore, 75–90 minutes for a festival headliner, and a full day for a festival — and always check the venue's curfew before you book that last train home.
guides.excerpt: Most headline sets run 75 minutes to about 2.5 hours; with openers and changeovers, a typical concert night lasts around three hours.

guides.content:
How long is a movie?

The average movie released wide in U.S. theaters now runs about 114 minutes — just under two hours — and the average across all films released worldwide in 2024 was 103.6 minutes, so a typical movie lands between roughly 100 and 115 minutes. Blockbusters run longer: films budgeted over $100 million now average around 130 minutes, the top ten box office hits of 2022 averaged 141 minutes, and marquee releases such as The Batman (176 minutes), No Time to Die (163 minutes) and Oppenheimer (180 minutes) routinely land between 150 and 180 minutes, with epics like Killers of the Flower Moon (206 minutes) pushing well past three hours.

Those figures come from a 2026 Stephen Follows analysis of 36,431 feature films built on OpusData/The Numbers box-office data, a 2023 What to Watch study of top-ten box office runtimes, and a long-running IMDb-based dataset from data scientist Randal Olson. The short version: most movies still fit inside two hours, but the share crossing that line keeps growing. In the 1980s, about 14% of wide theatrical releases ran over two hours; in the 2020s, that figure is 32%. At the other end, only about 7% of wide releases now come in under 90 minutes, down from 13% in the 1980s.

Average movie length by type

A single "average" hides big differences between a family cartoon and a superhero epic. Here is how runtimes break down by category, based on wide U.S. theatrical releases in the 2020s unless otherwise noted:

Type of movieTypical length
Modern Disney/Pixar animation100–118 minutes
HorrorAbout 103 minutes
ComedyAbout 107 minutes
Typical wide release, all genres (2020s)About 114 minutes
Franchise filmsAbout 121 minutes (vs. 112 for standalones)
ActionAbout 128 minutes
Blockbusters budgeted over $100 millionAbout 130 minutes
Top 10 box office films of 2022141 minutes (average)
14 highest-grossing live-action films of all time (as of 2009)About 159 minutes (average)

Two patterns stand out. Animation is consistently the shortest genre — Disney's 1990s "Renaissance" features typically ran just 83 to 95 minutes (The Lion King is 88; Aladdin, 90), and even modern Disney and Pixar films top out around two hours. Action has stretched the most, growing from a 103-minute average in the 1980s to about 128 minutes today.

How long recent hits actually ran

MovieRuntime
Killers of the Flower Moon (2023)206 minutes (3 hr 26 min)
Avatar: The Way of Water (2022)192 minutes
The Batman (2022)176 minutes
No Time to Die (2021)163 minutes
Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021)148 minutes
Top Gun: Maverick (2022)131 minutes
Minions: The Rise of Gru (2022)87 minutes

How average movie length changed over time

Movies have not simply gotten longer forever. Olson's analysis of the 25 most popular films of every year from 1931 to 2013 found that features gained about 30 minutes between 1931 and 1960, lost about 10 minutes between 1970 and 1985, recovered to their 1960s length by 2000, and have stayed roughly flat since. What has held steady is the ceiling: since the 1960s, the longest mainstream features have hovered around three hours, a mark set by old-school epics like Gone with the Wind (238 minutes on IMDb), The Ten Commandments (220 minutes), and Lawrence of Arabia (216 minutes in its restored director's cut).

The box-office leaders tell the sharper recent story. The average runtime of each year's top-ten U.S. box office films has climbed steadily:

  • 1981: 110 minutes
  • 1991: 117 minutes
  • 2001: 126 minutes
  • 2011: 122 minutes
  • 2021: 131 minutes
  • 2022: 141 minutes

For context, the 50 biggest films of 2008 averaged 110 minutes — almost exactly today's all-genre theatrical average — and the 14 highest-grossing live-action films of all time averaged about 159 minutes as of a 2009 analysis. Overall, movies now run nearly 15% longer than films of the 1980s, when the blockbuster "sweet spot" was 100 to 120 minutes, and releases over 150 minutes are becoming a regular occurrence.

Does a movie's runtime include the credits?

Yes — every advertised runtime includes the end credits, and credits are a bigger slice of the total than most people realize. A 2026 study of 6,515 films released between 1920 and 2025 put the median credit roll at 4 minutes 26 seconds, with half of all films landing between three and six minutes. In the 2020s, the median credit roll is 5 minutes 43 seconds — almost thirteen times longer than in the 1950s — largely because visual-effects artists now account for around 12% of crew credits, versus under 0.5% in the 1970s. Animation carries the longest credit rolls of any genre, and superhero films run a median of 7 minutes 9 seconds, against 5:08 for other films; Avengers: Infinity War holds the record with 5,109 credited people, 2,659 of them in visual effects. So on a modern blockbuster, expect roughly 5 to 8 minutes of the listed runtime to be credits — time you are sitting through if you stay to the end.

What factors affect how long a movie is?

  • Budget. Money buys runtime. Films budgeted over $100 million now average about 130 minutes, up from roughly 122 minutes in the 2000s, while films made for under $10 million have barely changed in length across four decades.
  • Franchise status. In the 2020s, franchise films average 121 minutes versus 112 for standalones. In the 1980s and 1990s, franchise films were actually about three minutes shorter than standalones — the reversal is a modern phenomenon.
  • Genre. Action has swollen by about 25 minutes since the 1980s (103 to 128), while comedy gained about 8 minutes (99 to 107) and horror just 6 (97 to 103).
  • Crew size and VFX. Longer credit rolls are baked into the listed runtime. Animation has the longest credits of any genre, and visual-effects-heavy productions add thousands of names.
  • Release strategy. A film positioned as a must-see theatrical "event" is now more likely to be long, because scale is part of the pitch.

Why streaming changed movie lengths

Streaming is the biggest reason the blockbuster has ballooned. With audiences able to watch ordinary movies at home, theaters compete by offering experiences a living room cannot match, and long epics justify premium IMAX and large-format ticket prices that offset having fewer showtimes per screen per day. Years of binge-watching have conditioned audiences for long-form storytelling, and as mid-budget dramas migrated to streamers, star directors like Christopher Nolan and Denis Villeneuve gained the leverage to demand longer runtimes for their theatrical spectacles. Audience appetite has not quite kept up: in one poll of 2,000 Americans, the "ideal" movie length was 92 minutes, and only 2% said they were comfortable with anything over two and a half hours. The result is a split market: average movies hover near 114 minutes while the biggest releases push ever further past three hours.

Practical tips for planning around a movie's runtime

  1. Anchor on 114 minutes, then adjust. For a standard theatrical release, assume just under two hours; add 10–15 minutes if it is a franchise or action title, and expect 130 minutes or more for anything with a $100 million-plus budget.
  2. Do the credits math. The listed runtime includes a median of about four and a half minutes of credits — over seven minutes on superhero films. If you leave when the credits start, that is your exit head start; if you stay for a post-credit scene, add the full roll to your schedule.
  3. Plan blockbusters as a two-and-a-half-hour commitment. The 2022 top ten averaged 141 minutes of runtime alone — before previews, concessions, or a packed parking lot — so block out closer to three hours end to end.
  4. Expect kids' movies to stay short. Modern Disney and Pixar animation runs roughly 100 to 118 minutes, and Illumination's Minions: The Rise of Gru is just 87 minutes, so a matinee with young children is usually done inside two hours.
  5. Double-check the true epics before booking. Killers of the Flower Moon runs 206 minutes (3 hours 26 minutes) and Avatar: The Way of Water 192 minutes — the kind of runtime where you want to know in advance, choose seats accordingly, and plan the day around it.
  6. Use the pause button at home. The runtime is the same on streaming, but splitting a long film across two sittings is a legitimate strategy the theater cannot offer you.

The rule of thumb: a movie is about two hours, a blockbuster is about two and a half, and an epic is three or more — credits included.

How Long Is a Broadway Show?

Most Broadway shows run between 90 minutes and 3 hours, most musicals run about two and a half hours, and the biggest hits land almost exactly at 2 hours 30 minutes to 2 hours 45 minutes including one 15 to 20 minute intermission. That is the range laid out in Broadway.com's running-time guide, which states that most Broadway shows run between 90 minutes and three hours with a 15 to 20 minute intermission, and that most musicals run about two and a half hours. Straight plays trend shorter, stretching from 90-minute one-acts with no intermission up to epic dramas running three hours or more, while the biggest stage spectacles push close to that three-hour mark. For planning purposes, assume roughly three hours from curtain to curtain call for a musical, and confirm your specific show before you book dinner reservations around it. Note that Broadway running times are quoted with the intermission already counted in: Hamilton's official listing of "2 hours 45 minutes including intermission" means 2 hours 45 minutes from curtain to final bow, break included.

Broadway Running Times at a Glance

Every major show publishes its running time in its official FAQ or ticket listing, because that single number is what audiences plan the whole evening around. The table below gathers official running times for a mix of long-running hits and newer favorites playing Broadway.

ShowRunning timeIntermission
Hamilton2 hours 45 minutesOne intermission
Wicked2 hours 45 minutesOne 15-minute intermission
Moulin Rouge! The MusicalApprox. 2 hours 35 minutesOne intermission
The Lion King2 hours 30 minutesOne intermission
Aladdin2 hours 30 minutesOne intermission
Chicago2 hours 30 minutesOne intermission
The Book of Mormon2 hours 30 minutesOne intermission
SIX80 minutesNone
Oh, Mary! (play)80 minutesNone

Notice how tightly the blockbuster musicals cluster. Hamilton and Wicked sit at 2 hours 45 minutes, a whole band of long-running classics including The Lion King, Aladdin, Chicago, and The Book of Mormon land almost exactly at 2 hours 30 minutes, and Moulin Rouge! plays about 2 hours 35 minutes per its official FAQ. At the opposite end, the pop concert musical SIX and the comedy Oh, Mary! both wrap in just 80 minutes with no intermission. One caveat: when a production is still in previews, treat its published running time as an estimate, because the show is still being tightened before opening night.

Musicals vs. Plays: Why the Range Is So Wide

Musicals carry the length. A two-act structure, ensemble numbers, costume and scenery changes, and a built-in intermission add up to that familiar two-and-a-half-hour Broadway rhythm. Intermissions on Broadway are typically 15 to 20 minutes long, and the break usually arrives about an hour into the show, which is why a full-length musical plays like two roughly equal halves.

Plays have split in two directions. Immersive stage epics now rival musicals for length, with Broadway.com listing Harry Potter and the Cursed Child at 2 hours 55 minutes and Stranger Things: The First Shadow at 2 hours 45 minutes. Meanwhile, comedies have raced toward the opposite extreme. Broadway producer Ken Davenport, charting three decades of Broadway data, found a 20 percentage point increase in the share of one-act shows and predicted that "90 minutes no intermission" would simply become the norm as audiences grow used to shorter entertainment. Oh, Mary!, at 80 minutes straight through, is exactly that model in action.

Factors That Affect How Long a Broadway Show Lasts

  • Musical versus straight play. Musicals run about two and a half hours, while current plays range from 80-minute one-acts with no intermission to epics approaching three hours, depending on the title and the writer's choices.
  • Intermission count and length. The standard Broadway intermission runs 15 to 20 minutes and usually falls about an hour into the show. One intermission is the norm for full-length musicals; no intermission at all is increasingly common for plays and shorter pieces.
  • Spectacle and scale. Effect-heavy productions with big physical scenery, such as Harry Potter and the Cursed Child at 2 hours 55 minutes, simply need more stage time than a one-set, four-actor play.
  • Preview status. Shows in previews are still being tightened and trimmed, so a published running time for a preview performance can shift before opening night.
  • Live performance rhythm. Applause, laughter, and pacing vary slightly from night to night, so the same show can finish a few minutes earlier or later depending on the audience.

Curtain Times and the Total Night-Out Math

Evening curtains on Broadway are typically 7:00, 7:30, or 8:00 PM, and matinees start at 2:00 PM or 3:00 PM. Wicked, for example, plays 7:00 PM evenings most nights and 8:00 PM on Saturdays, with 2:00 PM matinees, while Oh, Mary! starts its evenings at 7:30 PM and adds a 3:00 PM Thursday matinee. Give yourself about 30 minutes before curtain to reach the theatre and settle in. From there, the arithmetic of your night is simple addition.

An 8:00 PM musical, hour by hour

  • 7:30 PM — arrive and settle into your seat; skim the Playbill, silence the phone
  • 8:00 PM — curtain rises
  • 9:00 PM — intermission begins, roughly an hour in, and lasts 15 to 20 minutes
  • 10:45 PM — curtain call for a 2 hour 45 minute show such as Wicked or Hamilton
  • 10:50 to 11:00 PM — exit with the crowd onto the street

A 2:00 PM matinee, hour by hour

  • 1:30 PM — arrive as the house fills
  • 2:00 PM — curtain rises
  • 3:00 PM — the 15 to 20 minute intermission, again about an hour in
  • 4:30 PM — curtain call for a 2 hour 30 minute show such as The Lion King, Chicago, or Aladdin
  • 4:45 PM — you are back on the street with the entire evening ahead

So an 8:00 PM curtain for a full-length musical means you are realistically free by 10:45 to 11:00 PM, which tells you exactly when to book a late table. A 2:00 PM matinee of a 2 hour 30 minute show like The Lion King or Chicago ends around 4:30 PM, leaving a relaxed evening afterward. And the short-show option changes the math entirely: Oh, Mary! runs just 80 minutes and even schedules 5:00 PM Saturday performances, which put you out the door by about 6:20 PM with the whole night ahead of you. Performance times vary by day, so check the current schedule when you buy.

Tips for Planning Around a Broadway Show's Length

  1. Look up the official running time first. Shows publish their running times on their official websites and FAQs, and those listings are the most current source there is. Check it the week you attend in case anything has changed.
  2. Arrive about 30 minutes before curtain. Settling a full Broadway house takes time, so arriving early beats rushing in at the stroke of curtain.
  3. Plan meals backward from curtain time, not from the running time. For an 8:00 PM musical, either eat a proper early dinner around 5:30 PM or book a late table for 10:45 PM and make the meal part of the night.
  4. Choose a short show when time is tight. SIX runs 80 minutes with no intermission, which makes it an easy Broadway outing to schedule around a sitter, a train, or an early morning.
  5. Use a matinee when you have a hard stop. A 2:00 PM matinee plus a 2 hour 30 minute running time puts you on the sidewalk by about 4:30 PM, with the full evening still open.
  6. Recheck runtimes for previews. If your ticket is for a preview performance, treat the published running time as an estimate that may shift before opening night.

The short version: budget three hours for most musicals, and anywhere from 80 minutes to nearly three hours for a play, depending on the title. The running time is published, official, and stable, so a well-planned Broadway night is one of the easiest evenings in New York to schedule to the minute. Write down the curtain time, add the published running time, and you know your exit time to within about ten minutes before you ever leave your hotel.
